By the KING,

A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS Our Parliament stands prorogued to Tuesday, the Eleventh Day of November next: We, with the Advice of our Privy Council, publish and declare our Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Eleventh Day of November next, be held, and sit, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs; and the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the.

Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, nfid Commissioners ffor Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are hereby required, and commanded, to give their Attendance accordingly, at Westminster, the said Eleventh Day* of November next.

Given at Our Court at Hampton-Court, the Twenty-ninth Day of September 1718, in the Filth Year of Our Reign.

GOD save The Kino.

MESSAGE from his Majesty, by Sir William Sanderson, Gentleman-Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Several Members, returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for that Purpose.

'then a Bill for the more effectual preventing and punishing the Stealing, or unlawful Killing, of Cattle, was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers; where his Majesty was pleased to say;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have given Order to mv Lord Chancellor to declare to you, in my Name and Words, the Causes of my meeting you in Parliament at this time.

And thereupon, his Majesty delivered into the Lord Chancellor s Hands, from the Throne, a Speech; which his Lordship read to both Houses: And of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent any Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Since your last Recess, I have, by the Blessing of Almighty God, concluded such Terms and Conditions of Peace and Alliance between the greatest Princes of Europe, as will, in all human Appearance, induce others to follow their Example, and make any Attempts to disturb the publick Tranquillity, not only dangerous, but impracticable:

These Engagements, I am persuaded, will be so much the more agreeable to all my good Subjects, as they bind the contracting Powers to support the Succession to these Kingdoms in my Family; to which some were not at all, and others not so fully, bound by any former Treaties.

During the w hole Course of these Negotiations, a most strict Regard has been had to the Interests of Spain; and better Conditions have been stipulated for that King, than were insisted upon in his behalf, even at the Treaty of Utrecht: But the War in Hungary, which* by our Mediation, is since happily ended, having tempted the Court of Spain, unjustly, to attack the Emperor; and the Hopes they have since conceived of raising Disturbances in Great Britain, France, and elsewhere, having encouraged them to believe* that we shoflld not be able to act irt pursuance

Vo l. 19.

of out Treaties, for the defence of the Dominions invaded by them, nor even to support those other essential and necessary Conditions of the treaty of Utrecht, which provide against the great Monarchies of Europe being at any time hereafter united under One Sovereign; they have not only persisted in such a notorious Violation of the publick Peace and Tranquillity; but have rejected all out amicable Proposals; and have broke through their most solemn Engagements for the Security of our Commerce:

To vindicate, therefore, the Faith of our former Treaties, as well as to maintain those which we have lately made, and to protect and defend the Trade of my Subjects, which has, in every Branch, been violently and unjustly oppressed, it became necessary for our Naval Forces to check their Progress: It was reasonable to hope, that the Success of our Arms; the repeated offers of Friendship, which I have never ceased to make, in the most pressing manner; and the Measures taken, irt Concert with the Emperor, and the most Christian King, to restore the publick Tranquillity; would have produced a better Disposition in the Court of Spain; But I have received Informations, That, instead of listening to our reasonable Terms of Accommodation, that Court has lately given Orders, at all the Ports of Spain, and of the West Indies^ to fit out Privateers, and to take our Ships.

I am persuaded, that a British Parliament will enable me to resent such Treatment, as becomes us; and it is with Pleasure that I can assure you of the ready and friendly Resolutions of our good Brother the Regent of France, to concur and join with me in the most Vigorous Measures.

The firm Confidence I repose in the Affections of my People, together with my earnest Desire to ease them of every Charge not absolutely necessary, determined me* immediately after the Exchange of the Ratifications of our great Alliance, to make a very considerable Reduction of our Land Forces; nor could I better express, than by so doing, how little we apprehend the Attempts of our Enemies to disturb the Peace of my Kingdoms; even though Spain should think fit to continue some time in War: Our Naval Force, employed in Concert with our Allies, will, I trust in God, soon put a happy End to the Troubles which the ambitious Views of that Court have begun, and secure to my Subjects the Execution of the many Treaties in force relating to our Commerce.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I must desire you to grant me such Supplies as wilt enable me to carry on the Service of the Year: 1 have given Orders to have the proper Estimates laid beforeyou; whereby you will perceive I have reduced the Expence, as much as our Circumstances can well admit: I have the Pleasure to observe to you, that the Funds appropriated for sinking the publick Debts have answered above Expectation; I must, however, recommend to you, to consider of proper Methods for improving them, by preventing the Frauds and Abuses daily committed in the publick Revenues; not doubting but, in all your Pro* ceedings, you will have that Regard to the inviolable IS a Pre>

t’.ual Orders! Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That in case it shall appear any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned as a Member of this House* or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or directly, or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any Case before the House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

May it please Your Majesty,

We your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, do return our most sincere and unfeigned Tliaaks to your Sacred Majesty, for your most gracious Speech from the Throne; and for the many and great Instances which you have been graciously pleased therein to give ‘ C your

ii’ — 13®-r — i4"

your People, of your constant Endeavours for their Security and Welfare.

It is with the greatest Pleasure, that we have this Op- portunity to assure your Majesty, That we have an entire Satisfaction in those Measures which you have already taken, for strengthening the Protestant Succession to the Crown of these Realms, in your 6wn Family; and for establishing lasting Tranquillity in Europe; and particularly in relation to the Crown of Spain: And we are resolved, on our Parts, to the utmost of our Power, to enable your Majesty, in Concurrence with your Allies, not only to resent the Injuries which that Crown has already ' 'done to the Commerce of these Kingdoms, in Breach of the Treaties subsisting between the Two Nations; but will likewise support your Majesty, in the most vigorous and effectual manner, in such farther Measures as in your great ^Wisdom you shall judge necessary to complete the publick Tranquillity, and to check the Growth of that Naval Power, which must otherwise prove dangerous to the vTrade of these Kingdoms, and the Repose of Europe.

We should be wanting in our Duty to your Majesty, if we did not express, in the most affectionate manner, the great Sense we have of that Instance of your tender , Concern for the Ease of your People, in the farther Reduction which you have made of your Land Forces; which must be accepted by all your good Subjects, as the strongest Proof of your Wisdom and Goodness.

We crave Leave to concur with your Sacred Majesty, ^That regard must always be had to the inviolable Preservation of the Publick Credit, for the Quiet and just Security of all those who have trusted to Parliamentary Engagements:

And do further assure your Majesty, That we will, by our Conduct in this important Juncture, give your Majesty, and the whole world, all imaginable Proofs of our

Zeal, and inviolable Duty and Affection, to your Person , and Government, and of our Love to our Country.

The said Address being read a Second time;

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Com* tnittee in the said Address, to be presented to his Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House did Yesterday Answer to attend his Majesty with their Address: To which his Ma- Address* jesty w as pleased to give this most gracious Answer;

Gentlemen,

I am extremely sensible of the Duty and Affection you express to my Person: Your Vigour and Resolution to support me, will encourage our Friends, and, by the Blessing of God, enable me to defeat the ill-grounded Hopes of our Enemies: As I am persuaded the Necessity and Usefulness of your Proceedings will be approved by the Event; I do return you my v:ery hearty Thanks for this loyal Address.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Assistants, and Common-Council, of the Borough of Cokhtstery in the County of Essex, on behalf of themselves, and the other free Burgesses, Traders, and Inhabitants, of the said Town, was presented to the House and read; setting forth, That the Borough of Colchester is, by reason of the Woollen Jda»ufactory,'a Place of great Trade and Commerce: That in the Ninth and Tenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, a Statute was made for the cleansing and making navigable the Chanel from the New Ilythe in Colchester to Wivenhoe, in the said County; and, for performing the same, a Duty was laid on all Sorts of Goods and Merchandizes brought into, or landed from, the said several Places therein mentioned; which Duty vras to commence 011 the Firsts Day of May 1698, and to continue Twenty-one Years; and which will expire the First of May 1719: That the Petitioners caused the said Chanel to be cut; and expended a very large Sum of Money, and contracted a heavy Debt, for which the whole Profits of the said Term were engaged by the Petitioners, who were not otherwise able to perform the same: That, by reason of the small Duty raised, the said Debt is not discharged, but there remains due Twelve hundred Pounds, notwithstanding the said Term is so near expiring: That there is an absolute Necessity to lay out a further Sum of Money to repair and amend the said Chanel, and to render it serviceable; \vhich additional Charge the Petitioners are not able to provide for: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for continuing such Chanel-Duty; and for discharging the Debt remaining due; as also for making the said _.River completely navigable.

The said Act of the Tenth Year of the Reign of King William was read.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the feaid Petition be referred to a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same to the House:

Sir Thomas Wheat reported, from the Committee, to whom the Petition of thq High Sheriff, Deputy Lieutenants, Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Freeholders, and other Inhabitants, of the County of Oxon, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of this House, of the 20th Instant, have examined several Witnesses; viz. Mr. Carter, Mr. Beeson, and Mr. Wheate: Who testified, That the Inhabitants of the several Parishes in which the Road mentioned in the said Petition doth lie, have not only constantly done more than their Statute-work, but also raised large Sums of Money, and duly applied the same towards repairing their Roads; and that proper Materials for amending the Highways lie at a great Distance from some Parts of the said Road; and that the Parishioners have often been obliged to pay 12 d. per Load, at least, for Stones: s

That, upon Examination of the whole Matter, it fully appeared to the Committee, That the Road from the Top of St oaken-Church-Hill to Enslow- Bridge, in the County of Oxon, is so very bad and ruinous in many Places thereof, in the Winter Season, that it is dangerous to Travellers; and that the same cannot be amended, and put into good Repair, and so kept, without the Assistance of an Act of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Roads from the Top of Stoken-Church-Hill to Enslow- Bridge, in the County of Oxon: And that Sir

Thomas JVhcat, Sir John Rushout, and Mr. Wylde, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

That, the Committee haying examined the Allegations contained in the said Petition, it appeared "to them, by the Testimony of the Reverend Dr. Thomas Green, Vicar of the said Parish; as also of Surveyors, and experienced Workmen, and several other Inhabitants; That the said Church was built of Rubble and Brick, so many Years past, that it is now become very ruinous; and is adjudged incapable of any Repair, by reason that both the Timber and Brick are so much decayed, and rotten; and that the Walls of the said Church are split in many Places, and cramped with Iron:

That there is not Two Piers in the Church but what are split; and the Walls bulged, so that it is impossible that the same can be repaired.

It also appeared to the Committee, That the Ground all about is higher than the Church near Five Foot; by means whereof the said Church is very damp, and unwholesome, which can no*ways be remedied but by a new Building:

That the said Parish, being the largest of the Out-Parishes, is burthened so greatly with Poor, that the Expence amounts to upwards of £.4,000.per Annum:

That the said (Church is so ruinous, and decayed, that it is not safe for the Inhabitants to resort thither for Divine Worship:

That, Two of his Majesty's Royal Palaces being situate in the ssid Parish, several of the Nobility, and other Persons of Quality and Distinction, residing in the said Parish, are hindered from resorting thither, for want of a convenient Reception.

All which Allegations were proved, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; and are humbly submitted to the Consideration of this House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to impower the Commissioners appointed to put in Execution the Acts of the Ninth and Tenth Years of herlate Majesty's Reign, for building Fifty new Churches in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs thereof, to direct the Parish-Church of Saint Martins in the Fields to be rebuilt, instead of one of the Churches which was designed for the said Parish: And that Mr. Comptroller, the Earl of Hertford, Sir Robert Dai its, and Sir Thomas Crosse, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the insolvent Debtors in Hereford County-Gaol, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands more in this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That by reason of many heavy Taxes, and otherMisfortunes, the Petitioners are reduced, and brought into Confinement; whereby they suffer under unspeakable Calamities and Miseries, through which they are subject to daily Wants and Necessities, and not in a Capacity to make Satisfaction to their Creditors; and they are ready to satisfy their just Debts, to the utiiK)st of their Ability; and, were they at Liberty, might be useful to the Commonwealth, themselves, and Families:

And praying to be relieved.

Sir Thomas Wheate reported from the Committee, to Wheatley-whom the Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, Bridge Roads. arid others, living on the North Side of the City of Oxon, in the County of Oxon, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerks Table:

Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee to whom the said Petition was referred, having taken the Matter of the said Petition into their Consideration, it appeared to the Committee, That the Road from Wheatley- Bridge, leading through the City of Oxon, to New Woodstock, in the said County, is a Branch of the Road leading from the City of Loiidon to the City of Worcester, and is frequently used as such:

That the greatest Part of the said Road is, by reason of the many heavy Carriages which daily pass that Way, become so ruinous and founderous, that Travellers cannot pass with Safety:

That notwithstanding much more than the Statute-work hath been performed, and more than Six pence in the Pound constantly contributed, and duly applied; yet that Part of the said Road cannot be amended, aqid kept in good Repair, but by Assistance of Parliament.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill for repairing the Roads from the top of Stoken-Church-Hill to Emlcrw- Bridge, in the County of Oxton, is committed, That they do provide, by the said Bill, for repairing the Road from Wheatley Bridge, leading through the City of Oxon, to New Woodstock, in the said County.

A Petition of Joshua Churchill Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That at the last Election of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Corse Castle, in the County of Dorset, in the room of William Okeden, Esquire, deceased, the Petitioner, and John Bankes Esquire, stood Candidates; That John Bcnfeild Mayor of the said Borough, espousing the Interest of the said Mr. Bankes, admitted of unqualified Votes to Poll for him; and several other indirect Practices were made use of in favour of the said Mr. Bankes; notwithstanding which illegal Proceedings, the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes: That the said Mayor has nevertheless, in farther Injury and Wrong to the Petitioner, and his Electors, made an illegal special Return of the said John Bankes and the Petitioner, although the Petitioner had a great Majority of Votcjs, even by the Mayor's Poll, after the Scrutiny: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: Vol. 19.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Common-Council, Arrears of Burgesses, and others the Freemen of the ancient City Seamen's of Rochester, in the County of Kent, together with several Wages‘ other Persons who are the Inhabitants of the Towns of Chatham and Stroud, in the aforesaid County, in behalf of themselves, and some Hundreds more, w'as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners having given Credit to His Majesty's Seamen, and their poor Families, upon account of Wages, due to them on List-Tickets, and Recalls, for their Service performed in the Royal Navy, by supplying them with Goods, and Money to buy them bread for themselves, and their poor Children; which otherwise must have famished, if they had not, by the Petitioners, been so relieved and supported: That the Petitioners, having been great Sufferers by the Non-payment of the said List-Tickets and Recalls; a great Part of which hath been Six, Seven, and Eight, and some Part thereof Nine, Ten, Eleven, and Twelve,

That the Committee proceeded to examine the Merits of this Election.

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Bailiffs, Magistrates, and Freeholders, of Forty Shillings per Annum; and all that hold by Burgage-Tenure; and in such Freemen only as are inrolled, paying Scotland Lot: With this Difference; the Petitioner’s Counsel insisted, It was necessary the Freemen should pay Scotland Lot at Litchfeild; which was denied by the Sitting Member’s Counsel: Who insisted, That the paying Scotland Lot where the Freemen lived, though not at Litchfeild,

w»as sufficient.

That the Committee came to this Resolution;

Lowther reported from the Committee, who w’ere iniheAvc* appointed to consider of proper Alethods for removing Uwsfc1115 ^le Difficu!ty Members have, to come to and go from this House, by reason of the frequent Stops in the narrow Passages leading to this House; the Alatter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

> That the Committee having taken into Consideration

the Matters to them referred; and having examined Mr. Campbell, and some other Officers of his Majesty’s Works; who, pursuant to their Direction, have taken a Survey of the Two Gates between Whitehall and Westminster; it ! appeared to the Committee, That the Gate next to the

Banqueting-House may be made near Two Feet and a Half wider than now it is; which will be sufficient for Coaches to pass with ease; the Expence whereof w ill be very inconsiderable.

That as to the other Gate-way, next to King-street, the Passage under it may be enlarged very considerably, without any manner of Obstruction, or without prejudicing the Lodgings over the Gate-w^ay; the Expence whereof will not amount to above £. 150.

It appeared to the Committee, That the whole Charge of widening the Two Gate-ways will not exceed Two hundred Pounds; and no Prejudice to the present Proprietors.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to give such Directions, That the Gates in the Passage between Whitehall and King-street Westminster, may either be taken down, or made wider, as his Majesty, in his great 1 v Wisdom, shall thhik proper.

A PETITION of the Grasiers, Butchers, §c, in and near the Towns of Droitwich and Broms-grove, in the County of Worcester, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of Families within the Kingdom of England, wfas presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Leather-Trade of this Kingdom, and which is one of the principal Manufactures thereof, is now* in a very declining condition, by reason of the Export of English Bark for Ireland; where they tan vast Quantities of Hides and Skins, and where no Duty is paid for Leather; so that the Irish Merchants, and Dealers in Leather there, serve all the foreign Markets with that Commodity at so cheap a Rate, that the English, who did serve the same, are forced to return with their Goods unsold, or else to sell them for much less than prime Cost; and if the Export of Bark for Ireland be not stopped, the English Hides and Skins must be taken over, and tanned in Ireland: And praying to "be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Company of Butchers, in the City of Worcester, in the behalf of themselves, and: many Thousands of Families within the Kingdom of Englandis referred.

A Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Dunstan, Stepney, within the Bills of Mortality, and County of Middlesex, in behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Parish-Church of St, Dunstan, Stepney, is become old and very ruinous; and the Body of the said Church is Six Foot lower than the Ground whereoait stands; whereby the said Church is -damp and unwholsome; and upon any great Rains, the Water sinks through the Walls of the said Church, and comes into the Body of the same; which Inconveniencies cannot be remedied by repairing the said Church, although the Expence of such Repairs would very near build a new Church in lieu thereof: That the said Parish is very much inhabited by Seafaring Persons, which by Losses in the late Wars, many of their Families are become a Charge to the Parish, and much increased the Poors Rate; and by the erecting Four new Churches within the said Parish, which are to have Parishes to belong to them, taken out of the said Parish of Stepney, by which means great Numbers of the better Sort of Inhabitants will be separated from the remaining Part of the Parish, where the old Church will belong to; which renders it impossible for them to maintain their Poor, and to repair, and keep up, their old Church: And praying, That Leave may given to bring in a Bill to empower the Commissioners appointed to put in Execution the Acts of the Ninth and Tenth Years of her late Majesty's Reign, for building Fifty new Churches, to direct the said Parish-Church of Saint Dunstan, Stepney, to be re-built; or to allot such Sum or Sums of Money as shall be necessary for that Purpose.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, and the ancient Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Botolph without Bishopsgate, London, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter, thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Mr. Comptroller, by his Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That all his Majesty's Endeavours, ‘and those of the most Christian King, to procure Redress of the many Injuries done to the Subjects of Great Britain by the King of Spain, to the unspeakable Detriment of the Trade of these Kingdoms; or even to obtain a Discontinuance of the unjust Hostilities carrying on by that Crown; having proved ineffectual; his Majesty has found it necessary to declare War against Spain.

A Motion being made, and the Question being put, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return his Majesty our most unfeigned Thanks for his having communicated to this House the necessary Resolution of declaring AVar against Spain; and to assure his Majesty, That this House will, with the greatest Chear-fulness, and with the utmost vigour, assist and support his Majesty in the AVar with the King of Spain, till Spain is reduced to accept of reasonable Terms of Peace, and to agree to such Conditions of Trade and Commerce as this Nation is justly intitled to by their several Treaties;

Oath, amounts to the Sum of £. 5,069. and the Collections on the said Brief amounts but to £. 1,141. 3s. 11 d. exclusive of the Charges; so that the Collection fell short £.3,927. iGj. \(l.; and the Petitioners are utterly unable to add more than they have done to the said Collection: And praying, That the said Church may be included in the Number of the Fifty Churches; or that the Commissioners appointed for building the said Fifty Churches may be impowered to receive, from the Trustees of the aforesaid Brief, the Money collected on the same; and to be enabled with a farther Sum to build a Church convenient for the said Parish; and that Power may be granted to remove the Situation of the said Church into a small Piece of plowed Land that joins to the present Church-yard, paying a valuable Consideration to the Proprietors for the same.

Line 24. After "shall," insert " be:"

At the end of the Bill, add Clause A; " And whereas " by the said recited Act, made in the Thirteenth Year " of King Charles the Second, it is Enacted, That no " Person or Persons shall be placed, elected, or chosen, " in or to any the Offices or Places relating to or concerning the Government of any City, Corporation, " Borough, Cinque-Port and their Members, and other " Port-Towns, or any other Offices in the said recited " Act mentioned or expressed* that shall not have, within " One Year next before such Election or Choice, taken " the Sacrament of the Lord’s Supper, according to the " Rites of the Church of England; and that, in Default " thereof, every such Placing, Election, and Choice, " shall be void; Be it further Enacted, by the Authority " aforesaid, That all and every Member and Members <c of any Corporation within this Kingdom, and all and " every Person and Persons that were required by the €i said above-recited Act to take the Sacrament of the t( Lord’s Supper, according to the Rites of the Church " of England, within One Year next before his Election a or Choice into such Office, shall be, and are hereby, " continued in their several and respective Offices and ct Places, notwithstanding their Omission to take the " Sacrament of the Lords Supper, as aforesaid; and " shall be indemnified, freed, and discharged, and of " and from all Incapacities, Disabilities, Forfeitures, and " Penalties arising from such Omission; and that none <c of their Acts shall be questioned or avoided for or by " reason of the same; but that all such Acts shall be, " and are hereby declared and enacted to be, as good " and effectual, as if all and every such Person and " Persons had taken the Sacrament of the Lord’s Supper, <£ in manner as aforesaid: And that no Prosecution shall, " at any time hereafter, be brought or commenced " against any Person or Persons placed, elected, or " chosen, in or to any the Offices aforesaid, for or by " reason of such Omission, nor any Incapacity Disability, Forfeiture, or Penalty, incurred by reason of the " same, unless such Prosecution be commenced within " Six Months after such Person’s being placed or elected " into his respective Office, as aforesaid."

The First of the said Amendments, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The Second and last of the said Amendments being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by inserting, between the Word " Person’s" and the Word " placed," these Words, " who shall be hereafter:"

Which was agreed unto.

The said Amendment, so amended, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The House being moved, That John Rankes Esquire, Corf-Castle might be at Liberty to withdraw his Petition, presented Election, to the House on the 11 th Instant, complaining of an undue Election, and Double Return, for the Borough of Corf-Castle, in the County of Dorset;

The Certificate made by the Clerk of the Crown of the; Double Return was read; and is as follow eth; viz.

THESE are to Certify, That the Sheriff of the County of Dorset hath returned the Writ which commanded him to cause a Burgess to be elected to serve in the present Parliament for the Borough of Corse-Castle, in that County; and certified, by Indorsement thereupon, that the Execution of the said Writ appears in an Indenture annexed to it: And these are also to certify, That in the said Indenture, the only Words relating to any Election are these following; This Indenture (after mentioning the Date of it, and the Names and Additions of the Parties to it) witnessed), That the said Mayor, Barons, Freeholders, Leaseholders, and other Electors, by virtue of a Precept under the Hand and Seal of the said Sheriff, on the*Twenty-seventh Day of November last, proceeded to an Election of a Member to serve in the present Parliament, in the room of William Okeden Esquire, deceased; and, on casting up the said Poll, and a Scrutiny had thereupon, it appeared, That John Rankes Esquire had One hundred Twenty-three Votes; and Joshua Churchill Esquire One hundred Twenty-one Votes: And the said Mayor doth, by these Presents, farther certify and return, That, over and besides the several and respective Votes hereinbefore specified, there were, at the said Election, Thirty-five Votes offered to poll, and did poll, as claiming a Title under the said William Okeden, deceased; Twenty-nine of which Votes were for the said Joshua Churchill, and Six of the said Votes were for the said John Rankes: And these Presents farther witness, That on taking the said Poll, a Debate and Contest arose on a Point ot Law, Whether the said William Okeden had a Power of granting such Leases and Conveyances to the Persons who claimed the said Votes: And, for the Reasons aforesaid, and the Difficulty being too weighty for the said Mayor to take upon him to determine, he the said Mayor, by virtue of the said Precept to him directed, hath returned, and by these Presents doth return, the said John Rankes and Joshua Churchill; humbly submitting it to the honourable House of Commons, which of them, the said John Rankes and Joshua Churchill, hath a legal Majority of Votes.

Given under my Hand this 8th Day of December, Anno Domini 1718. G. Wrighte, C. C.

Whereupon the Matter was debated, Whether the said Mr. Rankes should be at Liberty to withdraw the said Petition; but no Order was made thereupon.

An ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act For strengthening the Protestant Interest in these Kingdoms, was, according to Order, read a Second time.

And so much of the Act, of the Tenth Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for preserving the Protestant Religion, by better securing the Church of England as by Law established; and for confirming the Toleration granted to Protestant Dissenters, by an Act, intituled, An Act for exempting her Majesty’s Protestant Subjects, dissenting from the Church of England, from the Penalties of certain Laws, and for supplying the Defects thereof; and for the further securing the Protestant Succession, by requiring the Practitioners of the Law in North Britain to take the Oaths, and subscribe the Declaration, therein mentioned; as is intended to be repealed by the said Bill; was read;

That the said Church may be included in the Number of the Fifty new Churches; and that the Commissioners may be impowered to receive of the Trustees of the aforesaid Brief the Money collected thereon; and be enabled, with a farther Sum, to build a Church convenient for the said Parish.

That by this the Petitioner was deprived of his Ship, his Cargo, and his Right of trading for the 1,000l. in India, many Years before the Company got this last Bill for the sole Trade of India; and kept the Petitioner tiii this Day, before he could determine if he had any Right at all; so could not offer any Petition for a saving Clause in that Bill; but now the Law, the Chancery, and the House of Lords, have given the Petitioner Payment for what of the Ship and Cargo came to the Company’s Hands in India, with Interest; but could not give him his Right of trading for 1,000l. for One Voyage: And praying to be relieved.

After which Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had received a Letter from the said Jos. Blisse; by which he owned the printing the Pamphlet complained of; and acknowledged his Offence in so doing, and begged the Pardon of the House for the same; faithfully promising never more to print any of their Resolutions, any Part of their Votes, or other thing whatsoever that may be in Breach of their Order: And, as upon his Knees at the Bar of this House, humbly prayed, That the House would not proceed any further against him; which if they did, it wfould end in the Ruin of himself and his Children; he being wholly void of Friends and Money, and in no Condition to make Satisfaction for any Part of his Fees.

And the said Petition was read; setting forth, That the late Act of Parliament to prevent Frauds frequently committed by Bankrupts, expired in June 1716; since which time several Persons, against whom Commissions of Bankruptcy have issued, have refused to surrender themselves, and their Effects, to their Creditors, or make any Discovery of their Estate; but have privately conveyed the same, and their Persons, into secret Places; whereby their Creditors are deprived of having any other Satisfaction for their Debts than such Persons think fit to offer:

That Persons daily become Bankrupts, not so much by Losses, as with Intent to defraud their Creditors; which is a great Damage to Trade in general, and this City in particular: And praying, That a Bill may be brought in to prevent such Frauds committed by Bankrupts.

soners in the Castle of Norwich) for the County of Norfolk) in the Name of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That their chiefest Hopes have been, in persuading themselves of being set at Liberty, since his Majesty has been pleased, out of his princely "Clemency, and pious Inclination, to grant a free Pardon to all his rebellious and felonious Subjects: That their Numbers are great, and their Wants many, having lain confined many years, and are thereby rendered utterly uncapable of ever extracting themselves out of that Labyrinth of Hardships that surround them: And praying, That the Bill for Discharge of poor Insolvents may pass.

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors in his Majesty’s Gaol of Newgate, within the City of Bristol, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, after a long and severe Imprisonment in the said Gaol, are at length reduced to a most mean and miserable Condition and Extremity, and are not in the least capacitated to pay, oiuany otherways discharge, their Debts; and consequently uncapable, of themselves, of ever being redeemed from this Paradox *of Grief and Misery: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the poor Debtors of his Majesty’s Prison of South-gate, in the City of Exon, was referred, shall be made.

A Petition of the poor distressed Prisoners for Debt in his Majesty’s Gaol for the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, on behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by reason of unavoidable Losses, Mischances, and other heavy Pressures of Misfortune, becoming indebted, and unable to satisfy their Creditors, have, notwithstanding, been a long time confined in close Prison; where they suffer extreme Want and Misery: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom tho Petition of the poor Debtors in his Majesty’s Prison of Southgate, in the City of Exon, was referred, shall be made.

Mischiefs Mr. Godfrey reported, from the Committee, to whom

from keeping the Petition of the Inhabitants of IVapphig, Stepney, Saint

nca^London -lH V’cWn8>'> and Aldgate^ in behalf of themselves, and many Thousand Inhabitants, in and about the said -Parishes, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, ^vith the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he rfead the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report and Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

’> That the Committee have, according to Order of the House, taken into Consideration the said Petition; to whom it appeared, by a Scheme delivered to them, and by the Testimony of the following Persons, Inhabitants in the said Parishes; viz. Samuel Clartcy, Joseph Maksey, Robert Newell, John Keeler, James Britain, Dan. Savcry} Herbert EdgerLy’ James Curtis, Matthew Gregory, JoS. LozvfWilliam Saunders; That, near 60 Years ago, there was not a Fourth Part so many Warehouses for Gunpowder as at this time; and then. One only bfowing up did some Damage: That there has been built One Ware-,. house for Gunpowder about 40, and another about 27, Years past; and that there is now Seven Magazines divided into Twenty-two Warehouses; Six of them are within* 12 Yards of Dwelling-houses and but 400 Yards from his Majesty’s Victualling-Office; which, having been measured, are computed to hold 1,302 Barrels of Gunpowder, allowing room for Men to work: There’s Three contiguous to a Rope-yard, and House, where there is great Quantities of Hemp; and Tar is melted, which lately boiled over, and had like to have set the House on Fire; and it must of Necessity, if it had hot been happily prevented, have blown up the Powder; for nobody would have given their Assistance to extinguish it, knowing the Powder was so near; and those are estimated to hold 1,076 Barrels: There’s likewise Nine, but 80 Yards from Broad-street, in Wapping; and more, but Twenty Yards distant from other Houses; which together, will contain 4>7?6 Barrels; the whole Quantity that these Warehouses will hold being 7,154 Barrels of Gunpowder.

‘ Alai chew Gregory said, He could not see the Inside of several of the Warehouses; blit in One, which was estimated' to hold 404 Barrels, he believes there was stowed 440 Barrels of Gunpowder.

Captain Joseph Macksey said, He saw in One of them between Two and Three hundred Barrels of Gunpowder.

It also appeared to the Committee, That the Inhabitants are in continual Apprehensions, fearing the y will daily be destroyed by the Carelessness of Men at work in some of the Warehouses, where there hath been near 100 Barrels of Gunpowder, who have been heard to drive Nails with Iron Hammers, when the Gunpowder has been scattered upon the Floor like sand: That it has been strewed in the Rope-walk, by carrying to and from the Warehouses, that it has made a perfect Train; wtych, if it had took Fire, must consequently have blown up the Magazine, and Numbers of People would have been ruined and destroyed.

That it further appeared, That the Inhabitants were, and are, under as great Fears, as terrible Apprehensions, from any Nights of Lightning and Thunder; the Warehouses for the Gunpowder being only covered with Pan- tiles, which are almost always broke, and out of Repair; so that there is sufficient Reason to believe, that they may take Fire at such a time; or should a Fire happen though at a Distance, by the Sparks flying over, they are liable to be blown up.

It likewise appeared, That Barges lie at Wharfs, with Three or Four hundred Barrels of Gunpowder, without being covered; and that a Lighterman has been seen to smoke within Two Foot of them, and others walk over them with lighted Pipes in their Mouths; and that the Merchants have been complained to, to keep a Watch over them; but yet do not: *-

And also, That the late destructive Fire in Thames-street was occasioned with so small a Quantity as a Barrel.

The Committee game to the Resolutions following; viz. *- - "

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That- the Petitioners have proved. the Allegations contained in their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Gunpowder Warehouses above-mentioned are very dangerous to the Tower of London, his Majesty’s Victualing and other Offices, as well as to a Multitude of Inhabitants of the City and Suburbs of London.

« The Second Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out "above-mentioned," and, instead thereof, to insert " lately erected in the Suburbs of London

And the same was-, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That the Gunpowder Warehouses, lately erected in the Suburbs of London, are very dangerous to the Tmer of London, his Majesty’s Victualing and other Offices, as well as to a Multitude of Inhabitants of the City and Suburbs- of London.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent: Mischiefs which may happen by keeping or having too great Quantities of Gunpowder in Storehouses, or Warehouses, belonging to private Persons, in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof: And that Mr. Godfrey, Mr. London, and Sir William Pole, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

That Mr. Churchill's Counsel complained of great Partiality, and arbitrary Proceedings, of the Mayor* in favour of Mr. Banks: And, called,

Mr. Tho. Cooper junior: Who proved Service of an Order of the Committee, in December last, upon Mr.

Banks; and made unreasonable Objections to Mr. Churchill's Voters; viz. to qne, who had been in Possession, and had voted Forty Years, for not proving the Marriage of his Father, that had been dead Sixty Years; to a Dissenter, for not proving that he had received the Sacrament within a Year before the Election; to a Tenant by the Courtesy, for not producing his Title; and to others, who had voted Tw enty, Forty, and Sixty Years, for not producing their Titles; and where Titlej w'ere in the very same Circumstances as in Coparcenary, or the like, he refused themTor Mr. Churchill, and admitted them for Mr. Banks: That he put all possible Difficulties on Mr. Churchill's Side, and admitted all Mr,* Banks' Voters without any Scruple, though objected to; declaring, He knew those Votes to be good.

Abuses in A Petition of the Glovere and Dressers of Leather, ty ing skins, within the City of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there is a great Duty laid upon Sheep and Lamb Skins, and no regard had to the preventing the cutting, gashing, and scoring the same, by the Slaughterer, as there is to prevent the same in Ox or Cow Hides; whereby they receive great Waste and Damage in dressing and cutting their Leather, and the Duty to the King very much lessened, by turning such damaged Skins to Alum-Leather, which otherwise would have been dressed in Oil, which pay Three Pence per Pound, and Alum but Five Farthings: And praying, That a Penalty may be laid upon the Slaughterer for every Skin of Sheep, or Lamb, that shall hereafter be so gashed, cut, or scored.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Hampden, according to Order, reported, from the Shaftesbury Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as selection. it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Shafton, alias Shaftesbury, in the County of Dorset, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which Report and Resolutions he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow’; viz.

Upon the Petitions of Sir Edward Des Bouverie Baronet, and several of the Inhabitants, paying Scotland Lot, and Electors of the Borough ot Shafton, alias Shajtsbury, 'in the County of Dorset, complaining of an undue Election and Return of William Benson Esquire, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough:

The Committee have examined the Merits of this Election:

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Inhabitants of this Borough, paying Scotland Lot.

That the Poll was;

For Mr. Benson - - - 89.

For Sir Edward Des Bouverie 10.

That the Petitioner s Counsel complained of great Partiality in Mr. David loonier, the Mayor, for refusing 140 of the Petitioner’s Voters, because they would not acknowledge his Right to the Mayoralty: And they also complained of Bribery, and illegal Practices, in favour of the Sitting Member.

On the first Head they called the following Witnesses;

Richard Bingham Esquire, Henry Whitaker Esquire, and George Ryvts Esquire: WTho said, They were present during the whole Poll: That Mr. Toomer presided as Mayor, and had the Regalia before him: That, at the Beginning of the Poll, lie declared, That he hoped it would be a veiy fair Election; and desired, That there might be no Disputes there, but that the doubtful Votes should be queried, and determined after the Poll, by Persons to be chosen by the Candidates; and said, That there were in that Town Disputes about the Right to tho Mayoralty; that they had Two Mayors, or Two Half-Mayors, meaning himself and Mr. Gapper, who sat by him, which would make One whole one; and those that would acknowledge him to be Mayor, let them poll for who they would, he w ould take their V otes; and that he would not take the Votes of any who would not acknowledge his Right: That when the Voters came, he put this Question to them; Sir, Dojou acknowledge me to be Mayor? And ordered the Town-Clerk to poll those who did acknowledge him; and refused all who did not acknowlege him; T hut the Question of acknowlege-ing Mr. Toomers Right to the Mayoralty was put to every one of the Voters, either by Mr. Toomer huuselti or by Mr. Ring, the Town-Clerk, or by the Sitting Member;

' ' Jtfx\

1

Y* . 44°

Shaftesbury Mr. TVkitaker said, He observed Sixty refused for not Election. acknowledging Mr. Toomers Right: Mr. Ryvcs said, 146 were refused on that Account.

These Witnesses, being cross-examined, said, That Mr. Gapper sat upon the Behth, next to Mr. Toomer, both Days of the Poll; bqt did riot concern himself in the Election, nor take any Poll, or say any thing about it, as they observed; and that soirie of the Aldermen would not own Mr. Toomer to be. Mayor: That the Voters generally said, in Answer ko the Question put to them relating to Mr. Toomer, That they had a Right of voting at that Election, and came to vote for Sir Edwaril Des Bouverie; and expected their Votes should be taken.

James Glover said; That the 16 Voters taken for Sir Edward Des Bouverie, by M»\ Toomer, did acknowlege Mr. Tomer ft> be Mayor: That 146 others, who the Witness named by a List, voted for Sir Edward Des Bouverie; and were refused by Mr. Toomer, for no other Reason than because they would not acknowledge him to be Mayor; that there was no particular Objection to them at the Poll; that they have voted at former Elections; are Inhabitants; do pay Scotland Lot: And the Witness said, He knew all of them, except about Eight, have a Right of Voting: That the Question of acknow-leging Mr. Toomer to be Mayor was put to all the Voters tts soon as ever they appeared at the Rail, previous to their giving their Vote, and before they were asked who they voted for; the Answer they generally made, was, That they did not come there to dispute who was Mayor, hut to vote for Sir Edward Des Bouverie; and some said, They offered themselves to the Court; others said, to the honourable Bench: That none were admitted to vote who did not first of ail acknowlege Mr. Toomer to be Mayor:

The Witness also said, That Mr. Gapper was present both Days; but did not act as Mayor, as the Witness observed; nor did the refused Voters apply to him to take their Poll: That Mr. Toomer adjourned the Poll; and Mr. Gapper made no objection to it.

IVUliain Bowles Esquire, said, That the Question of fccknowlcging Mr. Toomer to be Mayor, was previously put to the Voters, before'ever they gave or offered their Poll; and the Answer given by those who were refused was, Wc come here to vote for a Parliament-man, and, not respecting who is Mayor, we give our Voice to the Court* for Sir Edward Des Bouverie; and that all those w ho did not own Mr. Toomer to be Mayor, were refused.

That, as to Bribery, and illegal Practices, the Petitioners Counsel called,

' Nicholas Wright: Who said, That Mr. Toomer and Mr. Pope, who voted for the Sitting Member, did, upon the Tuesday before the Election, desire him to go among the Petitioner’s Friends, and speak scandalous Words against the Sitting Member, of which they would take no Notice; and they promised him 50/. to set up his Trade, if he could make any Discovery of Bribery for the Petitioner.

Tho. Mitchell said, That Mr. Toomer asked him, about Two or Three Days before the Election, How he thought it would go? To which he answered, That he supposed Mr. Benson would not stand it, considering the re was Ten to One against him: Whereupon Toomer replied, That was nothing, for Mr. Benson had the Government on his Side; and if he had but Five Voices, he would return Him; and promised the Witness to see him rewarded, if he voted for the Sitting Member.

William Mayo said, That the Sitting Member promised him, for his Vote, double any Money the Petitioner should give, if he brought w hat the Petitioner gave him.

Tho. Young said, That he saw' Thomas Valentine give Two Guineas to Joseph Young, the Witness’s Father, to vote for the Sitting Member; and that Valentine asked* Votes for the Sitting Member.

Ambrose Sandle said, That Mr. William Hussey asked Votes for the Sitting Member, and gave the Witness Two Guineas to vote for him; but took a Note to him-12

'fanuarii. . 1718.

self for the Money; and that the Witness never asked to borrow any of him.

John Roach said. That he ^as to pay Five Shillings a Year Rent to the Sitting Member, for Wafer; and had Five Years Arrears remitted to him, when lie came to the Poll, for his Vote for the Sitting Member

In Answer to what had been offered, the Sitting Member s Counsel called the following Witnesses; viz.

Mr. William Ring, Who said, That, upon the^ight before the Election, Mr. Gapper came to Mr. Toomerr - and demanded the Precept of him, claiming it as Meyror: That at the beginning of the Poll, Mr. Gapper being upon the Bench before Mr. Toomer came, Mr. Toojijer , asked him, if he sat there as Mayor? To which he answered, That he did; and that he would take the Poll as Mayor; and he immediately ordered Mr. Goddard to take a Poll for him, as Mayor; which Goddard did accordingly: And Goddard applied, to Mr. Gapper, as Mayor, to determine his Doubts in the Poll:

That Mr. Toomer, at the Poll, publicly asserted his owii Right to the Mayoralty, and denied any other; and declared, That he would take the Poll of all such as would vote before him; and would do justice there: That several came, and voted for Sir Edward Des Bouverie, deny- ing Mr. Toomers Authority, and offering their Votes to Mr.\Gapper, as Mayor; and, that only 15 did directly-own Mr. Toomers Authority: That all that offered their Votes to Mr. Toomer were put down upon the Poll, whoever they voted for: Th h those who did not offer their Poll to him, were not put down; and that Mr. Toomer did not think himself obliged to take the Poll of such as did not offer their Poll to him: That several of the Voters for Sir Edward Des Bouverie declared, They offered their Votes for him ,to the honourable Bench; others to the Court, as they were directed by his Agents; several saying, They had nothing to do with. Mr. Toomer:

That Mr. Toomer has thje Insignia, has held all Courts, issued Process, and has doqe all Acts as Mayor, ever since his coming into the Office, which was the Friday after Michaelmas-day last; and that Mw Gapper never pretended to do any thing as Mayor, till the Election

This Witness being farther examined, said. He was present during the whole Poll: That the Question which Mr. Toomer put to the Voters, and which Question was put to every Voter, was this; Do you offer your Poll to me, or to me as Mayor ? If you do, I will take your Vote, vote for who you please: And this Witness said, He did not know that Mr. Toomer asked them to acknowledge his Right, as Mayor: That, in Answer to the aforesaid Question, the Voters for the Petitioner said to Mr. Toomer, No; they did not own him to be Mayor.

That Mr Toomer refused those who did not offer their Poll to him; and all that offered their Poll to him were received: That he has seen sometimes Mr. Toomer, and sometimes Mr. Gapper, sit in the Mayors Seat at Church; and that he who came first had the Spat.

Mr. Thomas Francis said, That, after reading the Precept, Mr. Toomer asked Mr. Gapper, who sat upon the Bench by him, Whether Jie came there, as Mayor ? Ansi Gapper declared lie did; and that he would take a Poll; and ordered Mr. Goddard to take a. Poll for him: Which Goddard did accordingly; and, upon disputable Votes, Goddard applied to Mr. Gapper, as Mayor, and followed his Directions therein. That Mr. Toomer declared himself to be the proper Officer, though Mr. Gapper pretended to the Mayoralty; and that Mr. Toomer declared* That whoever came to offer his Vote to him, as Mayor, he would take it, vote for who they would:

That the Question ofacknowleging Mr. Toomers Right was put to every Voter; but some who came for the Petitioner, cried out, before that Question could be put to them, That they offered their Votes for him to the Court, or to the honourable Bench: That several of the Petitioner's Voters were objected to as disqualified; and Queries were put upon them, to be examined after the Poll;

Being cross-examined, this Witness said, That Mr. Toomer never gave any Reason for refusing the Petitioner’s Voters; but they said, They refused to give their Votes to him, as Mayor: And the Witness said, He believed, they might vote at former Elections; and that he knew of no particular Objection to them at this time.

Mr. James Atchison produced a Copy of a Poll taken’ at tills Election, before Mr. Abraham Gapper, as Mayor of this Borough, by Mr. Goddard, who was appointed by Mr. Gapper to take the Poll for him.

Then the Sitting Member s Counsel objected to 79 Voters for the Petitioner, as not being Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot: But did not produce Evidence thereof:

That they alleged Bribery: and called,

Jane Johnson: Who said, That she saw the Petitioner give Six Guineas and Six Shillings to John King, a Bar* her, for his Vote; and tha^it was given to him at Mr. Whet comb's House, at Eight of the Clock in the Morning, upon the Friday when the Election begun:

That Mr. Goddard gave Robert Belvin Three Guineas, and promised him Two more, for his Vote for the Petitioner, who was then present; and that was in the Section-Week; but she could not Say whether it was before or after the Election. '

To invalidate this Person’s Evidence, the Petitioner’s Counsel called, -

Mr. Anthony Cooth: Who said, He saw the Petitioner in Bed at Ten of the Clock that Friday Morning, at Mr. Fyke's House. .: *

And that, upon the whole Matter the Committee c&md to these Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, ThotWilliam Benson Esquire, is not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Shafton, alias Shaftesbury, in the County of Dorset.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir Edward Des Bouverie Baronet, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Shqfton, alias Shaftesbury.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That William Benson Esquire, is not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Shqfton, alias Shaftesbujy, in the County of Dorset.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time.;

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That Sir Edward Des Bouverie Baronet, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Shafton, alias Shaftesbury;

The House divided.

Resolved, That Mr. David Toomer was guilty of arbitrary and illegal Practices, at the late Election of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Shafton, alias Shaftesbury, in the County of Dorset.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find, That an Act passed, in the first year of his present Majesty’s Reign, to revive and continue an Act, passed in the Eighth and Ninth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty Ring William, for repairing the Piers of Bridlington, in the said County; and that, since the Commencement of the said Act of the Fi^rst Year of his present Majesty, there has been expended in repairing the said Piers the Sum of£ 1,800. fend upwards.

It appeared to the Committed, That, for the better Security of Ships using the Harbour of Bridlington, it is absolutely necessary both of the said Piers should be lengthened; and that the whole South Pier should speedily be rebuilt, and the most Part thereof upon a new Founda* tion: The Charge of repairing and lengthening one of the said Piers, and rebuilding and lengthening the other, with other additional Works for Supporting and Preserving of the said Piers, will cost above the Sum of £. 7,50a

That for the speedy rebuilding and completing the said Piers, and other additional Works, it appeared to the Committee, That it is necessary the said Sum of £7,500. or the best Part thereof, should be forthwith raised; which cannot be done without some furtlver Assistance of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Time granted by an Act, passed in the First Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act to revive-and continue an Act, of the Eighth and Ninth Years of the Reign of, his late Majesty King William, for Repair of the Piers of Bridlington, alias Burlington, in the East Riding of the County of York; and for making the said Acts more effectual; and that Mr. Cholm ley, Sir William Strickland\ and Mr. Strickland, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Clandestine A Petition of the Clothiers, Serge-makers, and Makers Exportation of Shalloons, Dyers, Fullers, and others employed in the of Wool. Woollen Manufacture, in and near the Town of Andover,

in the County of Southampton, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by reason of the pernicious Practice of the clandestine Exportation of Wool into France from Ireland, and this Kingdom, the Petitioners cannot employ the Workers in the Woollen Manufactures, or be able to carry on their Trade; which will, if not timely prevented, soon prove destructive to all Traders therein; and at present puts a Stop to the Trade itself, many Hundred of Families being already reduced to Poverty, and take Relief from their Parishes; And praying, That the said Evil, for the future, may be effectually prevented.

Qfd.\; and for the Salaries of die Commissioners of Equivalent, the Fees and Salaries ot their Servants, and die incident Charges of die Office; viz. from 24th June 1717 to 24th June 1719: That, by the 15th Article of Union, it is agreed, That the Commissioners for Disposing of the Equivalent shall be impowered to call for, receive, and dispose of, all the Money which shall arise to Scotland upon the Agreements in the Treaty, and apply the same for the Payment of the publick Debts of Scotland', and afterwards, towards encouraging and Y promoting

promoting the Fisheries, and such other Manufactories, and improvements, in Scot la ml, as may most conduce to the general Good of the United Kingdom: That, by an Act, 6° An rue Regime, intituled, An Act for further directing the Payment of the Eqaivalent^money, the Commissioners, and other Officers, of the Revenue, wefe directed to make Two authentick Abbreviates of the Produce of such Revenues, with the Amount of the several Sums which should become due, by way of Equivalent, to be delivered half-yearly, one to the Commissioners of the Equivalent, the other to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury; who, upon Receipt of such Abbreviates, should and might grant their Warrant for immediate Payment of such Sums as should be so found due: That the Commissioners and Officers of the Revenue did not comply with this Direction; and the Commissioners of Equivalent, by reason of several Difficulties, and particularly for want of proper Vouchers and Accounts, whereby the Debts of England incurred before the Union, and for which Provision has been made since, might be distinguished from the Charges and Service of the several following Years, could neither make up Accounts, nor keep such Books as the 15th Article of Union directed; which gave Rise to the said Acts of the First and Third of Iris present Majesty’s Reign, appointingC oinmissioners to take and state the Debts due, and growing due, to Scotland, byway of Equivalent: That notwithstanding the Pains taken by the Commissioners appointed in pursuance of the Two Acts last mentioned, yet it seems plain from what they have already clone, that some Parts of that Account, through Length of Time, and Inadvertency to these Agreements, are become inextricable: That it will take a very long time yet to clear up, and bring to light, what by much Pains and Labour is practicable; and that an Account of that Kind must continue, and be carried on, so long as any of the present Debts of Britain remain unsatisfied: That the Condition of the Creditors of the Publick in Scotland can very ill bear with such long Delays as the Finishing of these Accounts seem to require; and one of the principal Benefits proposed to both Nations by the Treaty w ill be intirely disappointed; namely, the Applications towards encouraging and promoting the Fisheries, and such Manufactories, and Improvements, in Scotland, as may most conduce to the general Good of the United Kingdom: And praying, That Directions may be given for the Payment of the Sum of £. 31,823. 7 1 d. i which has grown

due since 23d June 1717, and settle a Fund of Interest lor this National Debt of Scotland; and that Provision may be made for encouraging the Fisheries and Manufactories.

The House, according to Order, took into Considera- Seducing Ar-tion the Report from the Committee, to whom the Peti- hlieers into tion of the Master, Wardens, Searchers, and Assistants, fom£nPans-of the Company of Cutlers, in Hallamshire, in the County of York, and within Six Miles Compass of the same, incorporate by an Act of Parliament, was referred:

And the said Report and Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee have, according to the Order of the House, taken the said Petition into Consideration:

And, upon the Examination of William Parkin and John Crawley, tind the Matter to be as follows; viz.

That divers ill-disposed Persons, Subjects of this Kingdom, confederating with Foreigners, are endeavouring tq, transplant several Branches of the Iron Manufactures into foreign Countries, out of his Majesty’s Dominions, by making Attempts, and using Endeavours, to entice, and draw away, into the said Places, Artificers, and Persons working in the said Steel and Iron Manufactures, ottering them greater Wages than they can have in this Kingdom: And also,

That great Numbers of Foreigners have been, and are endeavoured to be, put and placed Servants and Apprentices to the Manufacturers of Iron and Steel, and other Manufactures and Trades, by giving large Sums of Money, in order to learn the said Trades, and return to their own Country.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Allegations contained in the Petition are proved.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That divers attempts have been made to seduce the Manufacturers and Artificers in Iron and Steel to depart out of his Majesty’s Dominions to foreign Countries.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That divers Foreigners have, of late Years, been put Apprentices to the Iron and Steel Manufactures, and to several other Trades and Manufactures of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill to prevent the Inconveniences arising from the seducing of Artificers in the Iron and Steel Manufactures into foreign Parts; and from the taking of Foreigners Apprentices in the said Manufactures.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the Inconveniences arising from seducing Artificers in the Iron and Steel Manufactories into foreign Parts; and from taking Foreigners Apprentices in the said Manufactories: And that Mr. Jessop, Colonel Bladen, and Mr. Bankes, do prepare, and-bring in, the same.

[Insolvent Debtors.]

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors, Inhabitants of Suffolk Place, in the Borough of Southwark, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by Losses in Trade, and other Misfortunes, are so reduced, as to fly from their Habitations, or otherwise must have gone to foreign Countries, and have carried several useful Arts and Manufactories with them; to the great Detriment of this Nation: That many of them were ruined by the late Wars, and have several Debts due from the Government: That the Badness of Trade, and the Terrors of a Gaol, have drove so many into this Place, that they are in a starving Condition; which might be remedied, had they their Liberty; being willing to deliver up them Effects to their Creditors, so that they might have their Liberty, without being liable to be thrown into a Prison, to perish for past Misfortunes: And praying, That a Clause maybe inserted in the Bill for Relief of poor insolvent Debtors, for the Relief of the Petitioners.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Bill for the Relief of poor insolvent Debtors in the several Gaols of this Kingdom, is committed.

Inconveniencies and Alischiefs do frequently arise to the Persons and Goods of the said Inhabitants, and others, by the Stops, Letts, and Hindrances, of Hackney Coaches, Cars, Carts, Drays, and Waggons, occasioned through the irregular Standing, and unskilful Driving, thereof, amongst the great Concourse of People within the Cities of London and Westminster: That whenever such Stops happen when it is dark, especially where there are no Posts before the Houses, the Lives of Passengers on Foot are very much endangered; and Thefts and Robberies, in the long time that is spent in removing the same, are often committed; and Tumults, andy other Disorders, created thereby; to the great Disquiet of the said Inhabitants, and to their manifest Loss and Damage in their Trade and Commerce: That some of the said Petitioners, for several Years last past, at their own private Expences, hired and paid persons, by them employed, to prevent and remove the said Stops; but, for want of a sufficient Authority to effect the same, the Ends designed thereby were not answered: And praying the same may be redressed.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration ot a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same; with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill British for the recovering the Credit of the British Fishery in Lister?, foreign Parts; and for the better securing the Duties on Salt: And that Air. Charles Stanhope, Mr. Bayly, Mr. Lawson, Colonel Bladen, and Air. Lowther, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled:

The Governor, and Company of Merchants of Great South Sea Britain trading to the South Seas, and other Parts of Company’s America, and for encouraging the Fishery, being desirous l?rc, Pobal* to continue the Endeavours they have always shewn to render themselves serviceable, in the most effectual manner they can, to his Majesty, and his Government, and the Support of the publick Credit, do humbly propose,

That, if this honourable House be desirous to redeem the Fund of £. 135,000. per Annum, appropriated to the Payment of the Tickets of the Lottery for the Service of the Year 1710, by a voluntary Subscription of the Proprietors of those "Pickets, the said Company w ill consent, and do submit, that the said Tickets may be subscribed into the capital Stock of the said Company; and that their present capital Stock of Ten Millions be increased the Sum of Two Millions Five hundred thousand Pounds; whicEyvill make their Capital up to the Sum of Twelve millions Five hundred thousand Pounds; upon the Terpi^and Conditions herein after-mentioned; viz.

1. That the present Funds for the said Lottery 1710 be united to, and incorporated with, the Funds at present appropriated to the Payment of the Company’s Annuities; and all of them be made equally subject to the Payment as well of the Company’s present Annuities of £. 500,000. and £. 8,000. asof an increased oradditibnal Annuity of £. 125,000. per Annum, being after the Rate f of£* 5. per Cent, per Annum, for the said intended increased Stock of £. 2,500,000. together with an additional Annuity of £. 2,000. per Annum, tow ards the Charges of Management, being in proportion to the annual Sum at present allowed the said Company for that purpose; and that all the said Annuities be payable out of the said united Funds, preferable to all other Payments or Dispositions whatsoever; and that the Surplus, if any, of the said united Funds, be subject to the Disposition of Parliament.

3. That the said increased Annuity of £. 125,000. per Annum be redeemable by Parliament at the same time, and in the same manner, as the Company’s present Annuity of £. 500,000. per Annum is redeemable.

4. rImat the additional Annuity of £.2,000. per Annum, towards the Charges of Management, be secured to continue to be paid to the Company for the like time, and in the like manner, as their present £. 8,000.'per Annum is secured to be paid.

Mr. Hampden, according to Order, reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Complaint of a Preach of Privilege committed by Mr. John Murgatroyd, Mr. Edward Gee, Mr. Henry Jacomb, and Mr. Christopher Barnard, against Sir William Lorother Baronet, a Member of this House, and the Resolutions of the Committe thereupon; which Report he read in his Place; land afterwards delivered the same in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report and Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee have examined the Matter of the Complaint: That Mr. John Murgatroyd, Mr. Edward Gee, Mr. Henry Jacomb, and Mr. Christopher Barnard, have proceeded in the Court of Chancery against Sir William Lowther Baronet, a Member of this House, during the Time of Privilege, in Breach of the Privilege of this House:

It appeared to the Committee, That there were Cross Causes in Chancery: In the original Cause, Robert Law ther Esquire, is Plaintiff against Sir William Lowther; and, in the Cross Cause, Sir William Lowther Plaintiff against the said Mr. Lowther; which Cross Bill, upon the Hearing of that Cause, was dismissed, with Costs to be taxed.

That it was alleged by the Counsel for Sir William Lowther, That after the last Prorogation, and before the Meeting of this present Session of Parliament, a Commission of Sequestration against his Estate was issued and executed for Non-performance of a Decree in Chancery

for Payment of £. 382. 12s. 8d. to Mr. Lowther: That Mr Christopher Barnard was one of the Commissioners off Sequestration ;, and, though it could not be said, that any thing was done therein during Time of Privilege; yet the Counsel for Sir William Lowther mentioned this, to shew a rigorous Proceeding in Chancery against him.

That the Proceeding insisted on, to be in Breach of Privilege, was, the giving Two Notices of Motion, and the taking out a Summons to tax Costs:

And, on behalf of Sir William Lowther, the following Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr John Stillihgjleet (Sir William Lowther's Solicitor:) Who said, That, about the Tenth of December 1717, a Notice of Motion came to him from Sir William Lowther s Clerk in Court; purporting, That the Court would be moved in the Cause wherein Sir William Loxvther was Plaintiff against Mr. Lowther, to stay proceedings in that Cause, unless Sir Wm. Lowther, would wave his Privilege in the other Cause wherein Mr. Loxvther is Plaintiff against him; which Motion was made and granted the Twelfth of December; and the Order was drawn up, but not entered, nor ever served: That this Notice was not served upon him; nor could he say who gave it, or who drew up the Order.

William Raymond produced a Memorandum in his Book of the Eighth of March 1717, That a Notice in Lowther and Lowther was then given, to move to make an Order absolute: But he could not say in which of the Causes that Notice was given, or who gave it, or that any thing was done upon it.

Mr. Thomas Steele said, That he had the Honour to be concerned for Sir William Lowther, as his Solicitor, when this Notice of the Eighth of March 1717 was given; and that he having, for Sir William Loxvther, then given Notice in both Causes, to move, That Sir William Lowther might have a Commission in his Cause; and that Mr. Lowther might join and strike Commissioners Names ia a Week; or that Sir William might have it to his own Commissioners and might proceed thereon, ex parte; and that both sides might examine their Witnesses that Vacation, and Publication pass the First Day of the next Term; and that, in the mean time, Sir William Lowther might be at liberty to set down his Cause to be heard some time the same Term; and that both Causes might be thea heard together; and that the Depositions taken in one Cause might be read in the other: Upon Occasion of this Notice it was, that the Notice complained of, of the Eighth of March, was given; which Notice complained of was given in the Cause wherein Mr. Lowther is Plaintiff; and it was to move, at the same time that Sir William Lowther s Notice should be moved, That the Order, made bn the Hearing of the Cause wherein Mr. Lowther is Plaintiff ex parte, might be made absolute: That, Sir William Loxvther % Motion was made; but the other was not made; and that he could not say who gave that Notice.

That, as to taxing the Costs;

' Mr. Daniel Kingsman was called: Who said, There were Three Summonses taken out in November last, before the Meeting of the Parliament, to tax Mr. Lowther s Bill of Costs in the Cross Cause; one of which was, to attend the First; another, the Sixth; and the other, the Eighth of November: That, upon the last of these Summonses, the Taxation was put off, at the instance of Mr. Steele, Sir William Lowther s Agent; and the Costs were afterwards taxed, ex parte, Sir William Lowther s Agent not attending: That the Summons, upon which the Costs w'ere taxed, was taken out, by Mr. Steele, for Sir William Lowther: That he could not say when the Taxation was; nor why Mr. Steele put it off.

That the Counsel on the other Side complained of great Hardships, which, they said, Mr. Loxvther had suffered by Sir William Lowther s insisting on Privilege against a just Demand:

That Sequestrations are the common Executions of Decrees in Chancery; and may be executed, as»this was, in Time out of Privilege:
