A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and British Commonalty, of the Burgh of Great Yarmouth, in the l lbhei-v# County of Noifolk, in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That, by the printed Votes, they find, that Leave is given to bring in a Bill for the better Recovery of the Credit of the British Fishery in foreign Parts; and for the better securing the Duties on Salt; in both which cases those concerned, in this Town, either in the Importation of Salt, or the Exportation of their Fish, are entirely free from any Imputation of Fraud or Abuse therein; however, as it is suggested to them, that there may be some Intention to take off, or abate, the draw- \ back that is now payable on all salted Fish that is exported to Parts beyond the Seas; which would be so very discouraging and destructive to the Fishery in general, and ruinous to them in those Parts: And praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, before the Bill passes.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for recovering the Credit of the British Fishery in foreign Parts; and for the better securing the Duties on Salt; be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Merchants, Tradesmen, and Fisher- Ditto, men, in the Town of Lmcestoff, in the County of Suffolk, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That perceiving, by the printed Votes, that a Bill is brought in, for the better Recovery of the Credit of the British Fishery in foreign Parts; and for the better securing the Duties of Salt; and believing, that there may bean Intention thereby to take off, or abate, the Drawback on all salted Fish exported; which will be very prejudicial to all those concerned in the Fishery in this T‘own; the Petitioners being free from any Fraud relating to the Duty on Salt expended on the Fish exported, or of the Salt imported: And praying,

That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for recovering the Credit of the British Fishery in foreign Parts; and for the better securing the Duties on Salt; be read a Second time.

British A Petition of several of the Inhabitants of Mevagizey

fishery. and G or ran, in the County of Cornwall, concerned in the Pilchard Fishery, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That a Hogshead of Pilchards cannot be well saved or cured with less than Five Bushels of foreign Salt: The Price of Salt, since the Duty has been laid upon it, hath been advanced from One Peny per Gallon to Five Pence, and sometimes to Seven or Eight Pence, per Gallon: That they formerly bought their Salt for Eight Pence per Bushel; they now, since the Duty is laid on, pay from Ten to Fourteen Shillings per Bushel: That from the time the Salt comes into the Fishermen’s Cellars, to the time it is used in Curing of Fish, it wastes at least Ten per Cent. and is not used in One, Two, or Three Years: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for recovering the Credit of the British Fishery in foreign Parts; and for the better securing the Duties on Salt; be read a Second time.

Wtto. A Petition of several Inhabitants of the Parishes of

Saint Austell, Saint Blaze, and Saint Five, in the County of Cornwall, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Five Winchesters of foreign Salt is the least Quantity necessary for the well Curing of One Hogshead of Pilchards: That, since the Duty, laid upon Salt, the Price of foreign Salt hath been advanced from One Peny per Gallon to Five Pence, and often to Seven or Eight Pence: That they could formerly cure an Hogshead of Pilchards with foreign Salt for three Shillings and Four Pence; but cannot now for less than Fifty Shillings; so that the Pilchard Fishery is now upon a worse Foot, since the Duty on Salt hath been laid on, than it was before, notwithstanding the Drawback of Forty Shillings: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for recovering the Credit of the British Fishery in foreign Parts; and for the better securing the Duties on Salt; he read a Second time.

of the Nation; but the Manufacturing thereof must decay; the Smiths and Nailors lose much of their Employ; Gen-Yol. 19.

tlemen and Merchants be oppressed in the Charge of their '

I roil-work, for House and Ship-building; and our Colonies be supplied, as now in great measure they are, by a clandestine Importation of Iron-wares from Foreigners:

To prevent which Consequences, they conceive, that whereas our American Colonies abound with Wood, and Iron-ore, the Climate is healthful, and Provisions cheap, were Encouragement given to the making only Pig-Iron there, a sufficient Quantity might be made to supply our Demands athomfe; where the erecting more Forges would employ more Hands; make double the Quantity of Iron with the same Quantity of Wood now expended; the extravagant Price of Iron w ould become more moderate; and the Manufacturers thereof increase; Poor be employed;

Part of which has been sold for £. 32,400. for the Use of the Publick, and the Whole is forfeited from him, and his Family, for ever: That he wras likewise seised, as Tenant by the Courtesy, of the Estate of his late Wife, deceased, of the Value of about £. 800. per Annum in Land, with one Coal-mine, and three-eight Parts of another, and some uncertain Rents arising by Way-leaves; which is forfeited during the Petitioners Life only; and is decreed, by the Commissioners and Trustees for the Publick, to descend, alter his Death, to his Issue by his said late Wife; and is, in the mean time, to be preserved from Waste, which the Petitioner had no Power to commit: That £. 250. per Annum of the said Land is in Mortgage to Sir Robert Eden, and Mr. Swinburne, for £ 12,045. principal Money, for which their Claim is allowed by the said Commissioners and Trustees: That the River Tyne has lately broke in upon the richest Part of this Estate; which is every Day liable to more Damage, and will be chargeable in repair^ ing: That the old Searn of Coal being near wrought out, and not likely to yield any Profit, the Engines, which were set up at a great Expence, for draining the Water, have neither been kept at Work, nor in Repair, for some time past; whereby not only the little Remainder’of the said old Seam is overflowed, and the Pits ready to fall in: but the Prospect of gaining a new one will be irretrievably lost to the Reversioner: and the Rents of the Land (the Tenants, in a great measure, depending upon the Coal-works) will be much lessened: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Clause, to be added to the

Mr. Farrer, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, who were to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which they had directed to be reported to the House; anti he read the said Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the said Resolutions were read; and are as follow-; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Di li s of Three Shillings for every Chaldron of Coals and Culm, and Tun of Coals, to be imported and brought into the Port of the City of London, or River of Thames within the Liberty of the said City, upon the same River, before the Twenty-ninth Day of September 1724, payable by virtue of an Act of Parliament, made in the Ninth Year of her late Majesty’s lleign, intituled, An Act for granting to her Majesty several Duties upon Coals, for building Fifty new Churches in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof; and other Purposes therein mentioned; and the like Duties for Coals and Culm to be imported or brought into the same from and after the Twenty-seventh Day of September 1724, and before the Twenty-eighth Day of September 1725, being payable by an Act of Parliament, made in the First Year of his Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for making Provision for the Ministers of the Fifty new Churches which are to be built in and about the Cities of London and J Vest mins ter, and Suburbs thereof; and for rebuilding and finishing the Parish Church of Saint Ma/y Wool not ft, in the said City of London: be continued, and be charged, and made payable, to his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, for the Term of Thirty-two Years, to be reckoned from Lady-day 1719.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion, of this Committee,

1718.

That the said Duties, so to be continued, charged, and made payable, be apportioned, disposed, and settled, in such manner, that a certain Sum of Money shall be raised thereby, or upon Credit thereof, to be applied so far as the same will extend, in and for the Building and Finishing of Churches; purchasing Sites, Churchyards, Burying-places, and Houses for Ministers; repairing and finishing the Collegiate Church oi Saint Peter Westminster, and the Chapels of the same; finishingG?%eemcich Hospital, and the Chapel thereunto belonging; making Provision for Ministers, and other Charges relating to the said Churches; and that a certain Sum of Money may likewise be raised, by or upon Credit of the same Duties, to be applied to or for the making good of the Supply granted to his Majesty in this Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Twenty-one thousand Six hundred Pounds per Annum, during the said Term of Thirty-two Years, to be charged on the said Duties, be made a Fund or Security for raising a Sum, not exceeding Three hundred and sixty thousand Pounds, to be employed in and for the Building and Finishing of Churches; Purchasing of Sites, Church-yards, Burying-places, and Houses for Ministers; repairing and finishing the said Col-legiateChurch oi Saint PeterJfcstmiuster, and the Chapels of the same; finishing Greenwich Hospital, and the Chapel thereunto belonging; making Provision for Ministers, and other Charges relating to the said Churches; and for repaying and satisfying the Principal and Interest of the Money so to he raised; which Interest shall not exceed the Rate of Four Pounds per Cent, per A union.

Resolved', That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Thirty-one thousand Six hundred Ninety-nine Pounds Four Shillings One Peny Half-peny per Annum, during the said Term of Thirty-two Years, to be charged on the said Duties, be madea Fund or Security for raising a Sum, not exceeding Five hundred twenty-eight thousand Three hundred Twenty Pounds One Shilling and Nine Pence, by way of a Lottery, or otherw ise, to make good the Supply granted to his Majesty in this Session of Parliament; and for repaying and satisfying the Principal and Interest of the Money so to he raised; which Interest shall not exceed the Rate of Four Pounds per Cent, per Annum.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Surplus, if any he, which shall, quarterly, during the said Term, arise by the said Duties on Coals and Culm, over and above so much as shall be sufficient to discharge the Monies payable on the said yearly Funds; and the Surplus, if any be, of the said Dufies on Coals and Culm, which shall or may remain after all the Principal and Interest to be charged on the said Funds shall be paid off, and satisfied; shall be reserved for Disposition of Parliament, and not be disposed or applied to any Use or Purpose whatsoever, but by Authority of Parliament.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill, or Bills, be brought in, pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Farrer, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Chancellor of the Duchy, Mr Solicitor General, Mr. Clay tan, Mr. Lowndes, and Mr. Charles Stanhope, do prepare, and bring in, the said Bill or Bills.

The House, according to Order, took into Considera- state of tion the Report from the Committee, who were appointed Buildings to inspect the State and Condition of the Passage leading ^Thous!0 to the Painted Chamber, the Rooms adjoining to the House, and the Clerk s Rooms.

And the same was read; and is as follow’s; viz.

That the Committee have inspected the State and Condition of the Passage leading to the Painted Chamber, the Rooms adjoining to this House, the Clerk's Rooms, and Cotton Library; and it appears to the Committee, as well by their View, as by the Report of several experienced Men in Building, thereto annexed, That all the said Buildings may be repaired, except the Cotton Library.

The Report of the experienced Men in Building is as follows:

To the honourable Committee of the House of Commons appointed to inspect what State and Condition the Passage leading to the Painted Chamber, the Rooms adjoining to the House of Commons, and the Clerks Rooms, are in.

May it please this honourable Committee,

IN Obedience to your Order of the 6th Instant, the Particulars therein mentioned have been viewed and examined; and we, w hose Names are inserted in the said Order, together with other Persons who have assisted in the Inspection, humbly lay the following State thereof before you;

1. That, as to the Passage leading to the Painted Chamber, we do not apprehend any immediate Danger from the present State of the Parapet, which is of Brick, set,

E e as

io6 18° Februarii. ' 1718.

as an Addition, upon the Stone-uork; Part of which seems to be originally advanced on Corbels: We observe, however, that some of the upper Courses of the Brick Parapet are damaged by the Weather; but may be repaired at a small Expence.

There is a Prick Building at the North End of the said Gallery, that formerly belonged to Sir John Cotton, which is in a ruinous Condition; and, though we do not apprehend any present Danger from it to the Gallery, yet it may be requisite to take it down; and to rebuild it, if it be judged of any future Service.

We beg Leave to observe further on this Head, That, the Ceiling of the Gallery being at present of slit Deal, we conceive it may be put into a better State by making it a plaistered Ceiling.

2. As to the Rooms adjoining to the House, the Speaker s Chambers, the Clerk’s Rooms under the same, and the Housekeeper's Lodgings above; we do not find any visible Defects therein; the Floors and Ceilings seeming to be level, and to keep their Place, and the Roof to be in as good a Condition as can be expected in a Building of that Kind, the Front being only of Timber-work plaistered over.

3. As to the Rooms pertaining to the Clerk of the House of Commons, adjoining to the Court of Wards; we find the Timbers which support the Flats under the Lead-covering to be so sunk, as that there is not a sufficient Current to carry off the Water: And therefore we conceive it necessary, that, when the Season will admit, the Lead may be taken up, that the State of the Timbers may be examined^ which probably have been injured by the Drips of Wet, as we find some of the Wainscot to have been.

4. As to the Court of Request; we conceive, that the Side Walls are now in as good Condition as they have been for many Years past; and that they may long continue a sufficient Support to the Roof, being of good Substance, and, so far as appears, have been wrought with very durable Materials.

The Gable-end of this Room, to the South, being Ashler Stone on the Outside, the same is much decayed, and requires repairing.

As to the Roof of the said Room; several of the Rafters appear to be defective at the Foot, and not to reach the Wall-plate; but we judge them capable of being repaired with Safety. 1

5. As to the Cotton Library; we find it in so ruinous a Condition, that we can offer nothing less to your Consideration than rebuilding it.

All which is most humbly submitted to the Judgment of this honourable Committee by

Tho. Bateman,

11 th February 1718# John James,

James Gibbs,

Edward Tafoell,

Tho. Bath bone,

Benj. Jackson,

James Grove.

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the said Report be adjourned till Monday Morning next.

Mischiefs A PETITION of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Bin*-from keeping gesses, of the Borough and Corporation of Liver-ntarUndon. P00^' m County Palatine of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That as that Town is a Sea-port Town, and great Quantities of Gunpowder being frequently brought thither, which are often very inconsiderately lodged, and disposed of, in unsafe and inconvenient Places, by the Persons that bring the m,' and others, that have such Quantities in their Custody, that the Ships in their new Bason, and the Inhabitants of the Town, are in great Danger of being destroyed: And praying, That the Bill depending, for preventing the Mischiefs which may happen by keeping too great Quantities of Gunpowder in or near the Cities of London and Westminster, or the Suburbs thereof, may be extended to the said Borough; that the Mischiefs which may happen there may be prevented.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill for preventing the Mischiefs which may happen by keeping too great Quantities of Gunpowder in or near the Cities of London and Westminster, or the Suburbs thereof, is committed; That they have Power to receive a Clause, according to the Prayer of the said Petition.

Frauds by Bankrupts,

A Petition of John Chapman, of London, Mercer, one of the Assignees of the Commissioners in a Commission of Bankrupt awarded against Charles Hewett, John Lawson, and Comfort JVadley, of Cloth Fair, London, Mercers and Partners, on behalf of himself, and other Creditors of the said Bankrupts, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, about the One-and-thirtieth of December last, and before the Commission issued forth, the said Bankrupts went into the Mint, where they carried great Part of their Goods and Effects, with their Books of Accounts; and refuse to come before the Commissioners in such Commission named, or to surrender their Books and Effects, for the Use of their Creditors: And praying, That some Clause may be inserted in the Bill now depending, relating to Bankrupts, to compel the said Bankrupts to come in, and deliver up their Books, Goods, and Effects, for the Use of the Petitioner, and the rest of their Creditors.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the better preventing Frauds committed by Bankrupts, is committed.

whereby the Petitioner, and her Five poor innocent Children, are reduced to a miserable Condition, and utterly destitute of Maintenance, and without any Prospect of Relief: And praying, That Leave be given to add a Clause to the Bill for enlarging the time to determine Claims on the forfeited Estates, in order to enable his Majesty to grant such Provision or Maintenance, out of her Husband’s forfeited Estate (not exceeding what the Petitioner would be intilled to, had her Husband been naturally dead), as his Majesty, in his great Wisdom and Goodness shall think fit.

A Petition of the Tanners, Tawers, Shoemakers, and Dealers in Leather, in the Borough of Sunderland near the Sea, in the County of Durham, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act, of the Ninth of her late Majesty’s Reign, for laying a certain Duty on Hides and Skins tanned, 8$c. it was enacted, by a Clause in the said Act, That if the raw Hide of any Ox, Bull, Steer, or Cow, or the Skin of any Calf, shall wilfully or negligently be gashed, slaughtered, or cut, in Flaying thereof, and offered to Sale by any Butcher, <§r. who impaired the same, such Butcher, <§r. shall be liable to the Forfeitures in the said Clause mentioned: That, notwithstanding the said Clause, the Butchers in the said Borough do still continue, wilfully, or negligently, to gash and cut the Hides and Skins aforesaid, and to offer them to Sale, saying, they do it not wilfully: That the said Butchers do likewise, in Flaying of Sheep and Lambs, much abuse and impair the Skins, by cutting and gashing of them *, which is a great Disadvantage to the Petitioners, who are Traders or Dealers therein; and might, by a small Care of the said Butchers, in the Flaying, be prevented: And praying the same may be redressed.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir Oat id Dalrymple reported, from the Committee, to whom the Petition of James Fall, in the Name of the Magistrates, Common Council, and Inhabitants, of the Borough of Dunbar, in Scotland, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where it was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, in pursuance of the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find, by the Examination of Mr. White-man,

That the said Borough, lying on the Mouth of the River Forth, on the South Side of the German Ocean, is the most considerable Port on that Side, where Ships going in, or coming out of that River, or put in by Stress of Weather, may be sheltered or careened.

That the said Borough is likewise very considerable for the Number of Boats and Barks that attend the Herring Fishing, and lies very convenient for that Trade; and that the Magistrates and Common Council of the said Borough have exerted themselves to the utmost for cutting deep Rocks in the Mouth of the Harbour; whereby the Entry thereto is made much more safe and convenient for Ships, where they lie at Low-water on soft Clay or Ouze; but that the Pier Head and Harbour require present dfrd annual Repairs; \tfhich the said Magistrates can-fiot d6, without some other Assistance; the Revenue, or comnfon Good, of the said Borough, not being able to Support that Charge: And,

That, besides the necessary Repair of the Pier and Harbour, the Tewn-house and School are, by Age, decayed; and must go to Ruin, unless speedily repaired; and which Expence the common Good cannot ariswer.

And it appeared to the Committee, That the said Borough being a Mai ket and Sea-port Town, is of great Service to the County of East Lothian, where it is situated.

That, upon Examination of the whole Matter, it appeared to the Committee,

That1 the Inhabitants of the said Borough of Dunbar tire u6t able to repair the Works already made, of to build any new Work, for Improving arid Preserving of the Harbour of the said Town; and repair the Town-house, and the Towm-house, and building a School, and other publick Buildings, there; and for supplying the said Town with Water: And that Sir David Dalrymple and Sir George Warrender do prepare, and bring in, the same.

From the House of Commons.

Sir, 2d March 1718.

I AM commanded by the House of Commons to acquaint you, that you are, immediately on the Receipt of this, to summon the respective Representatives of your County, and Boroughs within the same, forthwith to attend their Service in Parliament, upon Pain of being proceeded against with the utmost Severity; notwithstanding any Orders of Leave to he absent; all such Orders being vacated by the House: And you are to give mean Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereupon, upon Pain of incurring the Displeasure of the House. Prayers.

Manufactur- A PETITION of the Iron-makers, Cutlers, Smiths,

ing iron iu j\ Artificers, and Freeholders* in and about the Town

Plantations. Birmingham, in behalf of themselves, and many others who are concerned in the Making and Manufacturing of Iron within this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, should there be Encouragement given to the Making or Manufacturing of Iron in any of the foreign Plantations belonging to his Majesty’s Dominions, it will inevitably tend to the Ruin and Destruction of the Iron Trade of this Kingdom; which is inferior to none but the Woollen, and maintains at least Two hundred thousand People; which if lost, must become an heavy Burthen to the Nation, besides the Prejudice it will be to the Merchants, and vast Number of Ships that are employed in the Exportations of the Iron Manufacture to the Plantations; as also the vast Loss a great Number of his Majesty’s Subjects will sustain in the Value of their Estates, who have Woods, and Ore for Making of Iron; and the Tenants employed in the Carriages to the Iron-works of this Nation must be totally ruined for want of Employment, and will be in no Condition to pay their Rents; but the Value of their Farms must be considerably reduced: And praying the re may be no Encouragement given to the Making of Pig or Bar Iron in America.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for giving further Encouragement for importing Naval Stores, be read the Third time.

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, Manufacturers, Artificers, Miners, Colliers, Founders, Forge-men, Workmen, and Labourers, concerned in the Manufactory of Iron, on the behalf of themselves, and many Thousands more within the several Counties of Gloucester, Hereford, and Monmouth, and his Majesty’s Forest of Dean, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, as well as many others within the Counties aforesaid, who are Freeholders, are Owners 1 of several large Quantities of Coppice-woods and other Woods, Iron, Cinders, and Ore; which are made use of for the Supply of the Iron-works within the same Counties, and the Value of their Estates much increased thereby; as also the Tenants are enabled to pay a greater Rent, and a vast Number of poor People employed, and kept at Work; all which Advantages they shall be deprived of, should there be [Encouragement given for making Pig or Bar Iron in the Plantations, ^ind importing the same into this Kingdom, as is designed by the said Bill; and will only tend to enlarge the Trade, and enrich the remote Parts; no forbidding Clause, or Restraint, if Iron be made in the Plantations, can prevent their Manufacturing of it in those Countries, where there is Coal in such Plenty, and Conveniences for it; and then this Nation will not only be deprived of that Advantage it reaps by the Making of Pig and Bar Iron; but also the Manufacturers, who are so very numerous, will be deprived of their Livelihood; and they, and their Families must be maintained by the Parishes: That the Petitioners could not apprehend a Bill, under the Title of encouraging the ' Importation of Naval Stores into this Kingdom,

could deprive a Nation of so valuable a Manufacture as the Making of Iron; which Attempt, were it made publick, would draw an Opposition from most Parts of this Kingdom: And praying to be heard by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for giving further Encouragement for importing Naval Stores, be read the Third time.

Ditto. A Petition of the Ironmongers, Cutlers, Smiths, Artificers, and Freeholders, in and about the Town of IVal-sal, in the County of Stafford, in behalf of themselves, and many others who are concerned in the Making and 10

Manufacturing of Iron within this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, if the foreign Plantations within his Majesty’s Dominions should be encouraged in the Making or Manufacturing of Iron, it must needs be very prejudicial to the Iron Trade of this Kingdom; which at present is very considerable, and maintains some Thousands of People; and also it will be very prejudicial to the Persons and Ships that are employed in exporting the Iron Manufacture; and particularly to such who have Wood on their Estates, and Iron-stone for Making of Iron; in carrying whereof, a great many of the Tenants and Freeholders of this Nation are employed, and thereby not only raise their Rents, but subsist themselves and Families: And praying, That there may be no Encouragement given to the Making of Pig or Bar Iron in America.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for giving further Encouragement for importing Naval Stores, be read the Third time.

Sir Nathanael Mead reported from the Committee, to obstruction whom the Report upon the Petition of the principal in Streets by Inhabitants and Traders residing and dwelling in, and *jackney near to the strait and narrow Parts of the high Streets Coaches'*r' leading from the Royal Exchange to Westminster, was recommitted, That the Committee had further considered the Matter; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the said Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the said Report and Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined several Witnesses, touching the Allegations of the said Petition; and find the Matter of Fact to be as follows; viz.

Frederick Stanton, William Davis, John Hoe, Thomas Port, and Robert Kendall, Inhabitants within the Street called the Poultry, London, all affirmed to the Committee, That by reason of the Narrowness of the said Street, and the great Thoroughfare thereof to and from the Bank, Excise Office, and elsewhere, many Mischiefs and Inconveniences frequently happen to the Inhabitants, and other Persons, by reason of the Plying the re by Hackney Coachmen, and the Stops occasioned by them, and Carts and Drays, for Two or Three Hours together;

notwithstanding

5 Geo. I.

notwithstanding the Inhabitants have paid their Beadle 12d. per Quarter per House, for several Years last past, to prevent the same; and within these Two Years last, Two Persons have been killed in that Street; viz. a Woman; and Christopher Denton, their then Beadle, in the Execution of his Office; and that they are informed, the Bank also pays something yearly to prevent these Stops thereabouts.

Clement Leworth, Beadle of the Poultjy, confirmed what is said before; and owns, He received 12d. a Quarter of the Inhabitants, to hinder Stops in the Street; which he is not able to do, by reason of the Unruliness of the Hackney Coachmen and Carmen, who either whip him, or run their Horses against him.

Mr. William Stone said, He has Three Houses at the Lower-end of Chancery-lane, near Fleet-street; one of which he cannot lett, by reason of the frequent Stops thereabouts by Coaches and Carts; and his other Two Houses, for the same Cause, are fallen £.15. per Annum in their Rent;

That, the said End of the Lane being narrow, and fenceless against Coaches and Carts, he applied to the Commissioners of Sewers; who viewed the same, and found it so dangerous to Foot Passengers, that, by their Order of the Ninth of November 1716, they gave the Inhabitants Leave to pave a Foot Passage Two Foot wide, and to set up Posts to preserve it; which Mr. Stone did, but others did not: And said, That a Man was there killed on New Years Day last.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the several Resolutions following; viz.

1. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have made good the Allegations of their Petition.

2. Resolved\ That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Waggons, Carts, and Drays, passing and repassing the Streets of the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs thereof, called Saint Mildreds Poultry, Cheapside, Saint Paul's, Churchyard, Lttd-gate-street and Hill, Fleet-street, the Strand, and King-street, Westminster, between the Hours of Eleven a Clock in the Forenoon, and Two of the Clock in the Afternoon, during the Sessions of Parliament, is a very great Annoyance, Inconvenience, and Obstruction, to the passing and repassing of the Members of Parliament to and from Westminster every Sessions of Parliament.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Waggons, Carts, Brewers Drays, and Hackney Coaches, irregularly standing and driving in the aforesaid Streets, causes great Stops therein; w hereby Passengers are often damnified, and their Access to Tradesmens Shops obstructed, and therefore ought to be regulated.

4. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Stage and Hackney Coaches ought, in the Streets of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs thereof, to give the Way to Noblemens or Gentlemens Coaches, provided such Hackney and Stage Coaches be not drawn by a greater Number of Horses than such Noblemen or Gentlemens Coaches.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That many of the Penalties given by former Laws, in relation to the'Offences of Hackney Coachmen, and Drivers of Carts, are so very small, that the same is a manifest Hindrance and Discouragement to Prosecutions against them for Offences in the Streets; and, some of such Penalties being not made forfeitable or payable to the Persons damnified, or to the Prosecutor, the Persons damnified, and the Prosecutors, are, by reason thereof, put to very great Trouble and Charge to obtain Redress, and also necessitated to bear their own Charges.

The Four last Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

B?k wire- The House proceeded to take into Consideration the luid. t Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of ‘the Company of Butchers, in the City of Worcester, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of Families within the Kingdom of England; as also several other Petitions, in relation to the Exportation of Bark to Ireland; were referred.

And the Report was read; and is as follows; viz*

That the Committee have, according to the Order of the House, the 9th of December, taken the said Petitions into Consideration; and it appears, upon examining Benjamin Hickman, That the Duty on Leather, and the Exportation of Bark to Ireland, has reduced the Price of Hides to a small Matter, and scarce saleable:

That, Three Years ago, they used to sell their best

Hides, rough and smooth, at 2d. and 2d. i,per Pound, And now not above Seven Farthings.

Robert Waller said to the same Effect.

Joseph Eaton: That there used to be Thousands of Hides imported to Bristol and I^ondon, to be tanned at those Places; and afterwards were exported abroad, and sold at good Prices: Now, Bark being exported into Ireland, they tan the Leather there; by which means grdat Numbers of Manufacturers of Leather here, being unemployed, have gone to foreign Parts, as Conitigsburgh, Prussia, Ireland, and elsewhere:

That 4,000 Ton of Bark will tan 100,000 Hides, which pay £. 15,000 Duty to the Crow n; and that Leather is sold One Peny per Pound cheaper than formerly.

John Woodroffe: That there is not near the Quantity of Leather bought now as formerly; for that the Irish Leather is preferable to the English, in Portugal, and the Markets up the Streights, though the Irish Leather is not quite so good as the English; and that his Correspondent has wrote him Word, that he cannot take his Leather as usual, because the Irish Leather is sold cheaper there.

Olley: That several Merchants he deals with, has told him the same that Mr. Woodroffe gave in Evidence: That Dublin is the chief Market for sending Leather from Ireland, and tans more Hides than they do at Bandon; because they kill so rqpny Beasts there, that they cannot tan them at Home:

That there are Abundance of rawr Hides exported from Cork; but, generally speaking, there are more tanned Hides, than raw, exported from Ireland.

Joseph May, an Exporter of Leather: That lie has formerly shipped more tanned Hides for the foreign Markets, at once, than he has done all this Year, those Markets being filled with Irish Hides: That his Goods have lain by for Two Years before they could be sold; for that there are Six Irish Hides to One English in those Markets.

Thomas Ileems, Merchant; That he was at Leghorn, in Trade, about Six Years ago, when the Markets were full of Complaints against the English Hides, of their being neither so well tanned, nor so dry, but heavier in Weight than the Irish Hides; and were not then esteemed so good by Fourteen or Fifteen Pounds per Centum; being better manufactured, and lighter, Hide by Hide, and are better and more carefully flayed than the E?iglish Hides, the latter being gashed; and that the English Leather has fallen, in the foreign Markets, Four or Five Years since past; and believes the Markets were not worse last Year, than Four or Five Years ago.

The Committee, for their better Information, have called for the following Accounts; viz.

An Account of raw Hides imported from Ireland in Three Years; and to what Ports; from Christmas 1715 to Christmas 1718:

An Account of Bark exported to Ireland in Three Years, distinguishing from what Ports, from Christmas 1715 to Christmas 1718:

An Account of Leather tanned, exported from England since the Duty laid thereon, and for three Years before:

An Account of Debentures paid for tanned Hides, &;c. exported from England and Wales, from the 24th June 1711 to 24th June 1718, to about the 9th of December following:

Which Accounts are as follow; viz*

A Petition of the Coopers, and others, of the Town of Plymouth, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the great Quantities of empty Casks, and Casks filled with W ater, imported from Holland, and other Places, is of great Prejudice to their Trade; and tends to the impoverishing of them, and their Families: And praying, That the Importation of empty Casks, or Casks tilled with Water, may be prohibited. Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table,

A Petition of the Traders of the City of Norwich was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are obliged to give great Credit in Trade: That, since the Expiration of the late Acts, made in her late Majesty’s Reign, to prevent Frauds committed by Bankrupts, Persons have broke for very great Sums of Money; and have either carried their Books and Effects into the Mint, or beyond the Seas, in Defiance of their Creditors, and to the great Discouragement of the Trade of this Kingdom, and of this City in particular: That, as the Laws now stand, in relation to Bankrupts, the Petitioners cannot, by a Commission, prevent such fraudulent Practices; there being no Penalty to oblige the Bankrupts to surrender, or deliver up, their Eftecte: And praying Relief.

A Petition of Henry Cornish and John Heylyn was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in November 1710, the Petitioners, in Consideration of the Sum of £.4,12,5. contracted with Lieutenant General Harvey for a full Cloathing, and Accoutrements, for the Use of a Regiment of Horse then under his Command in Spain; and, on the 15th of January following, the said Cloathing and Accoutrements, having been viewed, and approved of, by a Board of General Officers appointed by her late Majesty to view and inspect the Cloathing of the Army, were, according to contract, delivered to the said Lieutenant General Harvey, who thereupon gave the Petitioners an Assignment on the Off-reckonings of the said Regiment, therein acknowledging the Receipt of the said Cloathing and Accoutrements, and thereby impowering the Petitioners to receive the said Sum of £. 4,125. out of the said Off-reekonings; which said Sum was also certified, by a Board of General Officers, to be due and pay-; able to the Petitioners on the said Assignment; which was. regularly entered in the proper Offices: That the Off-; reckonings of the said Regirttent, when put upon the1 Irish Establishment, amounted, all former Assignments answered, to the Sum of £.1,544. 9s. 2d.i payable in England, and applicable towards Satisfaction of the said Sum of £.4,125. according to the Earl of Carnarvon's Certificate, sent to the Treasury in Ireland: That the Petitioners conceive themselves justly intitled to a Certificate from the Commissioners appointed to determine the Debts of the Army, for Payment of the said Sum of £.1,544. 9$. 2d,i; have very often applied to the said Commissioners, but without Effect: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Fill to continue the Commissioners appointed to take, examine, state, and determine, the Debts due to the Army; and to examine and state the Demands of several foreign Princes and States for Subsidies, during the late War; is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause for the Petitioners Relief.

A Petition of Major General Wightman was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, being Major General of her late Majesty’s Forces, was, by Commission bearing Date the 13th of June 1712, appointed Commander in Chief of her said Majesty’s Forces in North Britain, in the Absence of his Grace the Duke of Argyle, and Major General Wheiham: That, after the Receipt of the said Commission, he did repair to his Post; and, about the Beginning of January following, did take upon him the Command of the said Troops; and did continue in actual Service in North Britain from that time till the late unnatural Rebellion was entirely quelled: That the Petitioner hath been at very considerable Expence, beyond the Allowance made him for his Services in North Britain; having received no more than the Pay of Brigadier, although he was actually a Major General at the time he was first employed there: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill to coutinuc the Commissioners appointed to take, examine, state, and determine, the Debts due to the Army; and to examine and state the Demands of several foreign Princes and States for Subsidies, during the late War.

A Petition of several British Officers, wh6 served ai&fte Five, Yehrs in America, at the Reduction of

Port Royal, now Anapolis Royal, and on several other Commands, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, on the Arrival of General Nickol-son at Boston, the Thirteenth of October 1713, they were informed, by her late Majesty’s Orders, they were reduced to Half Pay, from the 2 2d Day of December

1.712; but they, not receiving the least Notice thereof before that time, did continue on Duty until the Arrival of the said General: That they, being very much aggrieved by those Orders, did apply to her late Majesty for Relief; on which the then Paymaster General was ordered, and thereupon did lay before the House, in the Year 1714, the Demand of the Petitioners; which, by the then select Committee of the Estimates, was reported as a just Debt; but, the Commissioners appointed to determine the Debts of the Army not thinking themselves sufficiently authorized, by any Acts, to certify, their Demands, they have not yet received the benefit of full Pay, as was then agreed unto by the House, on the Report from the said Committee: That the many Hardships the Petitioners suffered, in being broke before they had Knowledge thereof, and that in a foreign Country, where they had no Means to' get any Competency for their Support, or to defray the Expence they were at in performing above Nine Months Duty after December 1712, was the Matter which moved the late Queen and Parliament to approve and allow their Demand; in regard of which, and that his Majesty, as well as the late Queen, always allowed full Pay to Officers in actual Service, whether in their own Country, or in Places abroad: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill to continue ’ the Commissioners appointed to take, examine, state, and determine, the Debts due to the Army; and to exairtine and state the Demands of several foreign Princes and States for Subsidies, during the late War; is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause for the Petitioners Relief.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the Petition be brought up;

It passed in the Negative.

A Petition of divers Makers and Dealers in Cards and Cards and Dice, on behalf of themselves, and others, was presented ^sExport to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by the Act, passed in the Tenth Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, for laying Duties upon printed Calicoes, 8$c. it is provided,

That Cards and Dice may be exported free of the Stamp Duty, upon giving Bonds with sufficient Sureties for the due Export thereof; and that the same shall not be relanded in Great Britain; which Bonds are to be left in the Hands of the Commissioners for the Stamp Duties:

That the Exporters of such Cards and Dice have, pursuant to the said Act, entered into several Bonds in Penalties, and have duly made their Exports; notwithstanding( which, the Commissioners have lately caused divers of the said Bonds to be put in Suit; and Judgments have been obtained for the Penalties thereof, although no Proof hath been made of any Breach of the Conditions of the said Bonds; and the Petitioners are subject to pay the Penalties of the said Bonds, though innocent, unless they can produce living Witnesses from foreign Parts to prove such Exports actually made to the Places appointed, and that there has not been any re-landing within several Years before such Bonds put in Suit; which, in this Case, is impracticable, and impossible to be performed, in regard the Petitioners have not been guilty of any Crime:

And praying, That the said Act may be so explained and amended, that the Exportation of Cards and Dice may be made practicable; that the Duties may not be lost; and that the Securities given for such Exportation may be discharged, upon the Oaths of the Exporters, and proper Certificates, as in Cases of like Nature.

22.764 Quarters of Barley, and did receive Payment for 20,000 of that'Number; but, the Army of the Allies inarching into Arragon before Warrants were obtained from General Stanhope, to justify Mr. Mead in the Payment of the Remainder, there is still due to the Petitioners the Sum of £. 1,359- *5*. 9*/. being the Value of

2.764 Quarters, according to the Rate agreed: That, in the Year 1713, the Petitioners Demand was laid before a Committee of the House, and allowed to be a just

And the Amendments made by the Committee thereunto, were onte read throughout; and then a Second time, one/by one, as far as Clause A.; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, several of them were disagreed with, and the rest were agreed unto, by the House.. Clause A. being read a Second time, Thai P.o Person should be kept in Gaol by any, Perspri, whose Debt did not amount to above the Sum of Thirty Pounds, besides Interest, Costs, and Charges; and the same was amended; .,

And then the Question being pu^’ That the House do agree with the Committee, in the said Clause, so.amended;

It passed in the Negative. ‘ ,

The rest of the said Amendments, as far as Clause E. being read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed upto by the House.

Clause E. being read a Second time, That the Warden of the Fleet Prison, or Marshal of the King's Bench Prison, shall not be obliged to take such Oaths as are by the Act appointed, of or concerning such Prisoners who, on the Twenty-ninth of September 1718, resided within the Liberty of the Rules of either of the said Prisons; but shall respectively certify, for every such Prisoner, who shall desire the same, the Day of his or her Commitment, for what Debt, by what Judge, and at whose Suit; and that such Prisoner remains undischarged from the said Prison; and, if such Certificate be not true, such Warden, or Marshal, so certifying, shall forfeit and pay as any other Sheriff, Gaoler, or Keeper, for inserting a false Name in any of their Lists; and the Prisoner in such Rules shall take the Oath, and proceed in such manner, as any other Prisoner claiming the Benefit of the Act;

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the said Report be adjourned till Monday Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A Petition of Colonel James St. Clair, Colonel John Erskine, and William Morison of Preston Grange, Esquire, for themselves, and in the Name of many Thousands concerned in the Fishing and Salt-works in Scotland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That by the artful Insinuations and Suggestions of some Dealers in foreign Salt, Two several Acts were, with great Difficulty, obtained in the Parliament of Scotland, Amo 1705; by which it is provided, That all Herrings, and other Fishes and Flesh, to be exported, must be cured with foreign Salt only; though, before then, a much more national and beneficial Trade was carried on, by the Exportation of Herrings cured with Scots Salt, than that time, especially to the East Seas: That when a Motion was made, the then next Session of Parliament there, for redressing the Grievances occasioned by those Two Acts, the same was, without entering then upon the particular Consideration thereof, confirmed by the Eighth Article of the Union; but expressly subject to such Alterations as shall be made by the Parliament of Great Britain: That, as a farther Remedy to those and other Grievances then complained of, it is expressly stipulated and provided, by the Sixth Article of the Union, That all Parts of the united Kingdom shall, for ever after the Union, have the same Allowances, Encouragements, and Drawbacks, and be under the same Regulations of Trade, as to Import and Export, in all respects: That, nevertheless, the Petitioners are, to their great Loss, not only kept hitherto under the unequal and most injurious Prohibitions and Restrictions of the above-mentioned Two Acts, in relation to the Curing of Fish and Flesh for Exportation, while the English lie under no such Restraint; but even the Carrying of Salt, and Fish cured with Scots Salt, Coastways, from Scotland into England, is, contrary to the Articles of the Union, likewise manifestly discouraged: That the continuing tire Petitioners thus under the Prohibitions and Restrictions aforesaid, w hile the English are not so restrained, being directly contrary to the Sixth and other Articles of the Union, as aforesaid; and there being, moreover, such sufficient Evidence, as can be casually had at this . Distance, ready to be produced, for disproving the pretended Grounds and Suggestions upon which the above-mentioned Two Acts happened to be obtained: And praying to be heard, by their Counsel, against the Bill for the Encouragement of the Fishery.

And the Eighth Article of the Union was read.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for recovering the Credit of the British Fishery in foreign Parts; and for the better securing the Duties on Salt; is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do hear such Persons, to the Matters of the said Petition, as they shall think fit.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That the Lord Chancellor, Lord Keeper, or Commissioners, of the Great Seal, may order all Commissions taken out, and Depositions taken thereupon, and Certificates allowed and 'confirmed, and other Matters or Things relating to the Commissions, or the Proceedings thereupon, to be entered of Record, and safely kept

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill,

That the Creditors of any Bankrupt may meet together, upon publick Notice to be given, and either allow of, or remove, any Assignee chosen by the Commissioner* acting under any Commission of Bankrupt issued; and elect and appoint another Assignee in his Place, as the Creditors shall judge most fit; and, upon electing such new Assignee, the Commissioners shall be re-invested, and fully re-intitled to the Bankrupt s Estate, and be impowered to dispose of the same, as if no former Assignment had been made; and shall execute a new Assignment to such new Assignee elected; in which the former Assignee shall join, if thereunto required:

And the said Clause was once read.

Mr. Fairer, from the Commissioners appointed by his Fifty new Majesty for building Fifty new Churches in and about the Churches. Cities of London and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof,

§c. presented to the House, pursuant to Act of Parliament, a Duplicate of their humble Representation to his most gracious Majesty, touching the Manner of providing a Maintenance for the Ministers who are to officiate in the new Churches:

And the Title thereof was read.

The said Duplicate of the said Representation is as follows; viz.

May it please Your most Excellent Majesty,

WHEREAS in and by an Act of Parliament, passed in the First Year of your. Majesty's happy Reign, intituled,

An Act for making Provision for the Ministers of the^Fifty new Churches which are to be built in and about thei Cities of London and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof,

§c. it is required, That the Commissioners appointed by your Majesty to execute the Powers in that, and other Acts relating to the said Fifty new Churches, contained and specified, should inquire, and inform themselves, in wrhat manner, by and out of the Duties by the said Act granted, and otherwise, a due Maintenance may he provided and settled for the Ministers who are to attend the Service of God in the said Fifty new Churches; and should, in Writing under their Hands and Seals, report and certify to your Majesty such Matters and Things as should appear to them upon their Inquiries, as aforesaid, with their Opinions thereon; and present a Duplicate of such Report, or Certificate, to each of the Two Houses of Parliament; to the end such further Directions might be given thereupon, as might be pursuant to your Majesty’s pious Intentions in the Premises:

Now we, your Majesty’s most dutiful Subjects, Commissioners appointed, as aforesaid, having, in Obedience to the said Act, and the Direction of your Majesty’s Commission, inquired into, and informed ourselves of, this Matter, do, with all Humility, beg Leave to represent to your Majesty our Opinions thereupon, as follows:

In regard the Parish or District assigned to each of the Fifty new Churches will, most probably, contain Six thousand Souls, at fewest, the Duties incumbent on the Minister of every such Parish cannot be discharged as they ought, without the help of a Clergyman, who may read the publick Service; and al^o of, at least, One able and diligent Assistant Preacher, who may take his Part also in visiting the Sick, and other Ministerial Offices; the Expence of which Assistants being considered, we are humbly of Opinion, That no Provision can be reasonably esteemed a due Maintenance for the respective Rectors of such Parishes, with their Assistants, which doth not, in every one, amount to the clear yearly Income of Three hundred Pounds: And we conceive, that, in some among those Rectories, where the Parishes will be most populous and the

5 Geo. I. 21" Mar Hi.

'm

the Cures most painful, the Rectory with their Assistants, may very well deserve Four hundred Pounds per Annum.

In order to the providing and settling such a Main* tenance, we conceive the lollowing Expedients may be useful:

Jst, That a Clause of a Statute, in the Tenth of her late Majesty Queen Anne, of pious Memory, enacting, That no Burial shall be in or under any of the Fifty new Churches, be so explained by Parliament, as to give Leave for depositing dead Bodies in the Vaults under the said Churches, so as no Ground be broken; and that the Commissioners for the said Churches may have Power, at their Discretion, to ascertain such Fees for every Body so deposited, whether in the common Vaults, or in private and Family Vaults, as may not only satisfy the just Demands of the present Incumbents of the old Church, but may also contribute to the Maintenance of the Rector of the new Church:

2d, That your Majesty’s said Commissioners may have a Power granted to them by Parliament of assessing all Houses, whose Inhabitants are not, by reason of their Poverty, exempted from paying to Church and Poor, by n Pound Rate upon the yearly Rent, towards the Maintenance of the Ministers; which Power may be used in such new Parishes, and in such Proportions, only, as they the said Commissioners, in their Discretion, shall see fit; yet always so, that in no Place whatever the Rate made for this Use do exceed the Proportion of Six Pence in the Pound:

3d, That your Majesty’s said Commissioners may also have a Power of laying upon Pews, set up at the publick Charge in the new Churches, a moderate yearly Duty, towards the Maintenance of the respective Ministers, where they shall find, upon Inquiry, such Duty to be practicable and proper; and which, we presume, it will generally be thought, because already customary, and well received, in several Churches and Chapels of late Erection in and about these Cities:

4th, That such Methods for collecting and receiving quarterly the said Pound Rates and Duties upon Pews may be appointed by Parliament, as shall render such Payments most punctual, and effectual to the Ministers; and best prevent all reasonable Cause of Complaint, or vexatious Suits, between them and their respective Parishioners:

5th, That your Majesty’s said Commissioners may likewise have a Power granted to them by Parliament of drawing out, from time to time, as each of the new Churches shall be finished, and made fit for Use, such Part of the Monies reserved for this Purpose, by virtue of the Act passed in the First of your Majesty’s Reign, as shall be thought necessary for the different Circumstances of each Parish: That, for every Parish where such Application shall be found needful, the Money so applied belaid out in purchasing of Lands, Ground Rents, Fee-farm Rents, or other sure Perpetuities, of a greater or less Value, as the Condition and Necessities of that Parish shall require; but that to no one Parish whatsoever a greater Share of this Fund should be applied, than may assure to the Rector thereof, and his Successors, the clear yearly Income of One hundred and Twenty Pounds.

These Expedients are most humbly submitted to your Majesty’s Wisdom and Goodness, as, in our Opinion, the most likely, and least grievous, for providing and settling a due Maintenance for the Ministers w ho are to attend the Service of God in the new Churches already built, or to be built.

Iu the mean while we cannot intirely acquit ourselves of the Duty we owe to your Majesty, for the Trust reposed in us, without begging Leave, on this Occasion, humbly to represent, That your Commissioners are impowered, by the Acts in the Ninth and Tenth of Queerv Anne, to convert Chapels already erected, such as shall be judged fit and proper, into Parish Churches, which yet w ill not be intitled to any Share of the Maintenance provided in the Act passed in the First of your Majesty’s happy Reign: fer winch Reason it is, with all possible Submission, referred to your Majesty’s great G oodness, and V ou

to the Wisdom 6f yotii* f’arliament, w hat further Powers shall be deemed naedful to be given to your Commissioners* in order to remedy this Defect; and to appoint a like Maintenance for the Rectors and Curates of such Chapels as shall be turned into Parish Churches, as of Other the Churches newly erected.

From the Provision already made by Parliament towards the Maintenance of the said Ministers, pursuant to your Majesty’s Piety, and gracious Intentions to them signified, w^e assure ourselves, That due Encouragement will always be given to a Design of so excellent a Nature, and of so manifest a Tendency to promote the Honour and Practice of our most holy Religion; to supply the spiritual Wants of so many Thousands of your People; and to derive down, in most signal Mariner, the Blessings of Almighty God upon your Majesty's Person and Posterity.

In Witnessw'hereofyour Majesty’s Commissioners havb hereunto set their Hands and Seals this 12th Day of March 1714.

Mr. Heysharn reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of divers Makers and Dealers in Cards and Dice, on behalf of themselves, and others, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and have heard the Commissioners for the Stamp Duties, pursuant to the Instruction from the House:

And find, That, by the Act of the Tenth of Queen Anne, for laying Duties oh printed Callicoes, &;c. Cards or Dice may be exported free of the Stamp Duties, upon entering into Bonds^ with Sureties, in Penalties of double the Duties, with Condition, for exporting such Cards or Dice into shine Part, or Port, beyond the Seas, within a limited time; and that the same, or any of them, shall not be relanded in any Part of Great Britain; which Bonds are to be left in the Hands of the Commissioners for the Stamp Duties:

That it appeared by the Evidence of Archibald Vans, Samuel Decamper, John Yaldxvin, Robert Grosweller, and other Makers and Sellers of Cards and Dice, That, pursuant to the said Act, Bonds have been given upon the Exportation of Cards and Dice; and several of the said Bonds have been put in Suit, and prosecuted to Judgment and Execution, and the Penalties levied, notwithstanding a Certificate was produced at one of the Tryals, under the Hand of the Surety for the principal Obligor, attested by credible Witnesses, That the Cards \vere actually landed in Ireland, and expended there; and although no Fraud, or Ilelanding, was ever proved; It being required from the Obligors to prove, by living Witnesses, to be produced at Tryals here, where such Cards and Dice exported were landed in foreign Parts; which is impracticable; and there is no Provision in the said Act for discharging the said Bonds at any time.

It also appeared to the Committee, That the Sureties, bound with the Makers or Sellers of Cards and Dice for Exportation, are generally the Persons who actually exported the same; and who, by reason of such Sureti-ship, are objected to, as uot legal Evidence for the Principals in such Bonds:

That Prosecutions are depending upon several of the feaid Bonds, under the Circumstances aforesaid; and many others, as the Case now stands, are liable to the like Prosecutions in future times, when it may not be possible to make any legal Defence:

That the Difficulties before-mentioned have greatly VoL 19.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for recovering the Fund appropriated for Payment of the Lottery Tickets, which were made forth for the Service of the Year 1710, by a voluntary Subscription of the Proprietors in the capital Stock of the South Sea Company; and for raising a Sum of Money, to pay off such Debts and Incumbrances as are therein mentioned; is committed.

Ordered, That the said Committee have Power to receive a Clause, or Clauses, for Relief of the Makers and Dealers in Cards and Dice.

Mr. Charles Stanhope, according to Order, reported, Public Debts from the Committee of the w>hole House, w ho w ere to of Scotland, consider of the Equivalent due, and growing due, to Scotland, the Resolutions which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Tabic: Where they were read; and are as follotv; viz.

1st, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Debt due to the Creditors of the Publick in Scotland, as stated in the Act of the Twelfth Year of Queen Anne, and several oilier Acts of Parliament, amounting to the Sum of Tw o hundred forty-eight thousand Five hundred Fifty Pounds Nine Pence Half- peny, and no more, is a just and legal Debt, due from the Kingdom of Scotland, before the union, to the Creditors of Scotland; and ought to be provided for.

2d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Ten thousand Pounds per Annum, arising out of the Customs, Excise, and other Revenues in Scotland, be made a Fund for Payment of the Interest of the said Debt, at the Rate of Four Pounds per Coition per Annum.

3d, Resolved, '1 hat it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the further* Sum of Two thousand Pound - per Annum, arising out of the Revenues of Scotland, be applied to the Improvement of the Fishery and Manufactures of Scotland, in lieu and* full Discharge of ail Equivalents whatsoever claimed by Scotland.

4th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Sum of Two thousand Pounds per Annum be granted for the Term of Ninety-nine Years, redeemable by Parliament, upon Payment of the Sum of Forty thousand Pounds.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out the Words " and no more:’’

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

" Another Amendment w as proposed to be made to the said Resolution, by adding, at the End thereof, these Words, " besides the Sum due for Interest, at Five " Pounds per Centum, and Charges of the Commissions " for disposing of the Equivalent from the Twenty-fourth " of June 1717:"

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That the Debt due to the Creditors of the Publick in Scotland, as stated in the Act of the Twelfth Year of Queen Anne, and several other Acts of Parliament, amounting to the Sum of Two hundred forty-eight thousand Five hundred Fifty Pounds Nine Pence Halfpeny, is a just and legal Debt, due from the Kingdom of Scotland, before the Union, to the Creditors of Scotland; and ought to be provided for, besides the Sum due for Interest, at Five per Centum, and Charges of the Commissions for disposing the Equivalent, from the Twenty-fourth of June 1717.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time;

And likewise. That some others of the Petitioners had been Sufferers by the said returned Commission, and did* resettle on one of the said Islands within the Time limited by the said Act for Re-settlement; but, having not proved their Re-settlement before the 23th December 1712, as directed by the Act of the Tenth of the Queen, cannot, without the Favour of the House, have Debentures issued for their Losses; which Omission, they allege, was occasioned by the Death of some of their Agents, the Neglect of others, and the general Discouragement they laid under from the wording "the last Act of Parliament.

9th April 1719. Henry KelsalL

To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty’s Treasury.

May it please your Lordships*

IN humble Obedience to your Lordships Commands, signified to me by Mr. Stanhope, I have perused and considered of the inclosed Heads, proposed in order to a Grant of Cape Dore in Nova Scotia, for making a proposed Settlement there; and also of the Conditions proposed to be annexed thereto by the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations: And 1 do most humbly certify your Lordships, That the Heads proposed in the inclosed Draught of a Lease may be so far proper, being reduced into Form: And I submit to your Lordships, Whether it is not proper to add a Clause, obliging the Lessees to make a Settlement, upon some part of the granted Premises to lie ascertained, by building, peopling and cultivating the same, in such manner, and within such a time, as your Lordships shall think fit; and annually to render an Account to the Crown of their Proceedings therein; and, in Default of njaking such Settlement, fyc. the Lease to be Void, by a Proviso to be inserted therein for that Purpose:

And it is further humbly submitted, Whether, if the Place at present be well stocked with Wood, there may not be a Reservation to his Majesty of such Timber-trees as are proper to make Masts on; and a Clause to oblige the Planters to apply themselves to sudr Manufacture and Improvement as shall be agreeable to that Country, and may be useful to Great Britain; and a Power aUo reserved to his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, on such Part of the Waste-ground as shall be unbuilt, to erect Forts and Fortifications, and retain the same to his own Use; with the Liberty of making and using, by himself and Subjects, all Ports, arid Places of Entrance from the Sea, into the said Lands, and of proper Highways through the same: And, in regard the Fifth Part of the net Produce of all Mines of Gold and Silver, and the Fifth Part of all Gold, Silver, and Pearls, which shall be found on the Shore, or fished out of the Water, belonging to the Land ta be leased, are intended to be reserved to his Majesty, it may be proper to oblige the Lessees annually to redder ad Account of all the Gold, Silver, and Pearls, 50 to be gained.

All which is most humbly submitted to your Lordships great Wisdom.

Examined by the Edward Nor they.

Henry KekalL 3d January 171}-.

2Sth February 1719*

Sir,

In Obedience to the Commands of the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, signified to me by Mr. KelsalL the 22dof the last Month, I have

laid before my Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations the inclosed Draught of a Lease for a certain Portion of Land in Nova Scotia; who having considered the same, command me to signify to you, That, as it is his Majesty’s undoubted Right to make Leases of Lands belonging to the Crown, they are of Opinion, That Mr. Attorney General, or some of his Majesty’s Counsel, at Law', are the proper Judges whether the Draught of the Lease be in due Form: But, as the Lesses are not named in the Draught, their Lordships could not send for any Persons to discourse with them upon the Matter, as they did to Sir Alexander Cairns, upon a Petition of his, and others, frtr another Tract of Land in that Country; upon which they have writ a Letter to Mr, Secretary Addison, a Copy whereof is here inclosed; and submif it, Whether it may not be proper, that the Leases be under the same or the like Conditions as are proposed by Sir Alexander Cairnes, and others; which you will please to lay before my Lords Commissioners of the Treasury. I am, Sir, Your most humble Servant, Whitehall September the 26th, 1717. IFm. Popple.

Wm. Lowndes Esquire.

Sir,

In Obedience to his Majesty’s Commands, signified to us by your Reference of the Second Instant, we have considered the Petition of Sir Alexander Cannes Baronet, James Douglas, and Joshua Gee, Merchants, on behalf of themselves, and others concerned with them, praying his Majesty will be graciously pleased to grant them a Tract of Land upon the Coast of his Majesty’s Province of Nova Scotia in America, containing Five Leagues to the South-west, and Five Leagues to the North-east, of the River and Harbour of Chibcuton, and ten Leagues deep into the Country; with the Islands along the said District, within Three Leagues of the main Land: Whereupon we humbly take Leave to represent,

That having been attended by the Petitioners; and having inquired of them how far they would engage for the making such Settlement, and peopling the Place; " they have proposed to make a Settlement, on the River " Chibcuton, of Two hundred Persons, in the space of " Three Years, in case there be no War with France or " Spain: That the Number of Persons shall be increased, " from time to time, according as the Undertakers shall " find Encouragement from the Place, and Trade they " intend to carry on there.

" The First thing the y intend to do, is, the building " a small Town, stockaded round, for settling and.securing the People they shall send over, to be employed " in planting of Hemp, manufacturing Tar, in cutting " down Timber, and making Barrel and Pipe staves, or " whatever else the Place will be proper for:

" That if at any time his Majesty shall think it necessary, to erect a Fort on that Coast, for the better l)efence of the Country; the Undertakers agree, That €t such Place, as shall be pitched upon by those employed " by his Majesty for that Service, be assigned for that " End; provided it be a Place not already built upon.

" And, as this Country is at present of no Benefit, but " rather a Burthen, to the Kingdom, the Undertakers " hope, in a few Years, by their Industry, though at a. " great Charge, to introduce a considerable Trade from " thence; which may, in many respects, be of great " Advantage; that Country not being much above Half " so far from England as the Capes of Virginia are: It " is hoped a profitable Navigation may be carried on, to " the great Advantage of this Kingdom, from whence " their whole Dependence must be for Wearables; for ft " is to be observed, that, this Country being habitable " in Winter, the Inhabitants will settle and continue u there, as in other Plantations, and make Improvement " in all Naval Stores; in which respect it will be of more " Advantage to England than Newfoundland:

" And, as this Country is cold, and not fit for any " Manufacture, they must have their whole Supplies " from Great Britain.

" That

5 Geo. I.

9° Apri

153

" That they will not hinder any Persons from fishing u in the Seas of the Districts they petition for; but to " be under such Regulations, Orders, and Form of Government, as his Majesty shall hereafter be pleased to " appoint and establish there.

" As this Country is a mere Wilderness, ’tis hoped all u due Encouragement will be given to the Undertakers,

" who are the first Proposers, for the Settlement thereof;

" in doing of which they must lay out considerable Sums " of Money."

This Undertaking of the Petitioners appearing to us to be for his Majesty’s Service, in peopling the Place; and for the Benefit of this Kingdom, by laying the Foundation for a Trade from thence; we have no objection why his Majesty may not be graciously pleased to grant the Petitioners Request, upon the Conditions aforementioned. We are,

Sir,

Your most obedient and

most humble Servants Whitehall, Suffolk,
