GEORGE R.

Whereas our Trusty and Well-beloved John Dowsett and Peter Capon Esquires, have been humble Suitors to iis, to grant unto them, and their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, a Part or Portion of the Country commonly known by the Name of Nova Scotia, or Accadia, for them to inhabit, plant, and cultivate, at their own proper Cost and Charges, as well in regard to the Transportation of Inhabitants, as to the Provisions necessary for their Subsistence: Our Will and Pleasure therefore is, That you forthwith prepare a Bill for our Royal Signature, to pass our Great Seal of Great Britain, containing a Grant or Demise from us, our Heirs and Successors, unto the said John Dozvsett and Peter Capon, and their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, for and during the Term of Thirty-one Years, to commence from the Date thereof, of all that Tract or Parcel of Land, commonly known by the Name of Cape Dore, in the Bay of Fundy, being Part of A ova Scotia, or Arcadia, and situated on the Western Shore of the said Pay, about Eighteen Leagues N or th-west from Annapolis J Loyal, in the Way from thence to Minas; anti of all that Tract or Parcel of Land extending -along the Shore of the same, Two Leagues on each Side of the Point of the said Cape, and Four Leagues from the Shore to the Landward; so as the said Tracts or Parcels of Land, hereby intended to be granted, may, as near as possible, form a Square, including Cape Dore; each Side of which Square shall be Four Leagues, or Twelve English Miles, in Length: And the said Bill is also to contain our Grant to the said Lessees, their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, during the Term aforesaid, of all those Islands lying just before the Premises, within Two Leagues of the Shore, with all the Soil and Waters, and all "Woods and Trees, and all Mines of Gold, Silver, Tin, Lead, Copper, Surphur,

of all Gold, Silver, and Pearls, which shall be found on Grants to the Shore* or fished out of the Waters, belonging to the Members. Premises: And whereas we are willing and desirous to encourage the Inhabiting, Planting, and Cultivating, of our said County of A ova Scotia, or Accadia, for that End and Purpose; therefore it is to be declared, for us, our Heirs and Successors, in the Grant hereby intended, / That the same shall be a sufficient Licence and Warrant for any Person or Persons, being our natural-born Subjects, who shall be sent, or employed, to or on the Premises, by the said Grantees, their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, or who shall associate themselves by Agreement with them, to inhabit and cultivate the Premises hereby intended to be granted: And the said Grant is also to give full Power and Authority to the said Grantees, and their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, to build Houses on the Premises; and to separate the same into Farms and Tenements; and to grant Leases, to continue during the said Term, or less Time; and to keep Arms and Ammunition sufficient for Defence, against the Indians, or any Robbers or Pirates: And in our said Grant it is to be provided, That the said Grantees, and their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, and their Associates, Tenants, and Servants, shall be subject to such our Laws, both Ecclesiastical and Civil, as shall be established for the general Government of the said Province or County of Nova Scotia, or Accadia; saving always the Faith, Allegiance, and supreme Dominion, due to us, our Heirs and Successors: Also therein it is to be further provided, That whatever Gold, Silver, Copper, Sulphur, Brimstone, precious Stones, and Pearl, shall be dug out, or found on, or in the Premises: and all Timber which shall be cut down, and made fit for Masts and Shipping, and all Pitch and Tar which shall be mdde within the Premises fit for Sale; shall be transported and consigned to the Port of London, in our Kingdom of Great Britain, and not to any other Port or Place whatsoever; except such Timber, Pitch, and Tar, as may be necessary for the Grantees own Use in the Plantations, and for building Boats, Barks, and Vessels, for their owi*

Fishery and Traffick: And our said Letters Patents are further to declare and grant, That if the said Grantees, their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, shall hereafter conceive, or be advised, that there is any Defect, as to the V alidity or Meaning of our Grant hereby intended; and thereupon shall be desirous to renew the same from us, our Heirs and Successors, with Amendments of any such Defects; then, upon their humble Petition, and at their own proper Costs and Charges, such further and better Assurance of all and singular the Premises, or any Part thereof, shall, from time to time, by us, our Heirs and Successors, be made and granted unto the said Grantees, their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, as by the^ Attorney General us, our Heirs and Successors, shall, in that behalf, be advised: And you are to take care, that apt and proper Clauses be inserted in the said Bill, for the Purposes following; that is to say, For obliging the said Lessees, their Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, to make a Settlement upon Part of the Premises, so \o be demised, by building, peopling, and cultivating, the same,

And the same \Vere read; and are as follow; vie.

Press 3. Line 1. After " Enacted," insert " Dedared:"

Clause A: " Provided nevertheless, and it is hereby " further Enacted, by the Authority aforesaid, That it " shall and may be lawful to and for his Majesty’s Attorney General for the Time being, at the Relation of " the said Company, to exhibit Bill or Bills of Com-3

" plaint in his Majesty’s High Court of Chancery, or " Court of Exchequer, against any Person or Persons " trading, dealing, trafficking, or adventuring, or susspected to have traded, dealt, trafficked, or adventured, at any time from and after the said Fifth Day " of February 1718, in, to, or from, the East Indies, " or Places aforesaid, contrary to law, for Discovery of " such their Trading, Dealing, Trafficking, and Adventuring; and for Discovery of such Duties and Damages " as are herein after-mentioned; waying and disclaiming, " in every such Bill, all the Penalties incurred by such " Person or Persons for the Matters in such Bill contained; and that such Person or Persons shall answer " the said Bill or Bills, and not plead or demur to the " Discovery thereby sought; and paid, to his Majesty the " Customs and Duties of the Goods and Merchandizing " arising, produced, or purchased, by the said unlawful " Trade, Traffick, or Adventuring; and shall also answer and pay to the sand Company reasonable Damages, " to be ascertained by a jury, upon a Trial to be directed " far that Purpose: And if such Offender or Offenders " pay the said Duties and Customs to his Majesty, and " Damages to the said Company, by virtue of any Proceedings upon this. Act, he or they shall not be prosecuted, upon any other Law or Statute whatsoever, for " the same Offence: And if any such Bill or Bills bedismissed by the Court where the same shall be exhibited, " the said East India Company shall pay every such " Defendant or Defendants his and their full Costs of " Suit; and, in case there be a Decree obtained against the Defendant or Defendants, such Defendant or Defendants shall pay Costs to the Relator:"

Clause B: " Provided always, That this Act, or any " tiling herein contained, shall not extend, or be construed, deemed, or taken, to extend, to subject the " Governor or Company of Merchants of England tradering into the Levant Seas, or any Member thereof, to " answer any such Bill, for or in respect of his or their " trading into the Levant Seas, or within any such Limits " as the said Governor and Company of Merchants of " England trading into the Levant Seas, have been accustomed to trade; any thing herein contained to the " contrary in any-wise notwithstanding."

And the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Lords in the said Amendment;

And the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Lords in the said Amendment;

East India Mr. Comptroller reported from the Committee appoint-Trade. ed to draw up Reasons, to be offered to the Lords at a

Conference, for disagreeing to some of the Amendments, made by their Lordships, to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the better securing the lawful Trade of his Majesty’s Subjects to and from the East Indies; and for the more effectual preventing all his Majesty’s Subjects trading thither under foreign Commissions; That they had drawn up Reasons accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

To the First Amendment, made by your Lordships, Press 3. Line 1. the Commons agree:

They also agree to your Lordships Amendment, Line 5:

They also agree to your Lordships Amendments, Lines 38 and 39:

They also agree to your Lordships Amendment,

Press 4, Lines 20 and 21.

% The Commons cannot agree to the Amendment, made by your Lordships, Press ,5. Line 1. Before " Provided/* add Clauses A and B; because Clause A levies Money on the Subject by a new Subsidy, not granted by the Commons; and which it is the undoubted and sole Right of the Commons to grant; and from which they can never depart.

The Commons cannot agree to Clause B; because it is intirely dependent upon Clause A.

The said Reasons, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Felloxces and Mr. Me Her:

Mr. Speaker,

The, Lords do not insist on the Amendments made by their Lordships, to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the better securing the lawful Trade of his Majesty’s Subjects to and from the East Indies; and for the more effectual preventing all his Majesty's Subjects trading thither under foreign Commissions; to which this House disagreed. Also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, an Act for Naval Stores, giving further Encouragement for importing Naval Stores, with some Amendments: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House. Also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the further Punishment of such Persons as shall unlawfully kill or destroy Deer in Parks, Paddocks, and other inclosed Grounds, without any Amendment. And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act Lottery Fund for redeeming the Fund appropriated for Payment of the k South Sea Lottery Tickets, which were made forth for the Service Subscription. year 1710, by a voluntary Subscription of the Proprietors into the capital Stock of the South Sea Company; and for raiding a Sum of Money to pay off such Debts and Incumbrances as are therein mentioned; and for appropriating the Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament; and to limit Times for Prosecutions upon Bonds for exporting Cards and Dice; without any Amendment: And also,

To the Bill, intituled, An Act for enlarging the Time to determine Claims on the forfeited Estates, without any Amendment: And also,

To the Bill, intituled, An Act for appointing a Commissioner and Trustee to put in Execution the Powers and Authorities of the several Acts of Parliament relating to the forfeited Estates, and the Estate^ given to superstitious Uses, in the Room of George Treby Esquire, who has desired to be discharged from the said Trust, w ithout any Amendment: And also,

To the Bill, intituled, An Act for Relief of such Sufferers of the Islands of Nevis and ^Saint Christopher's as have settled in either of those Islands, and made due Proof of such Settlement, before the Twenty-fifth Day of December 1712, without any Amendment.

Piers reported from the Committee, to whom dulent Prac- 1VA the Petition of the Creditors of Joseph Long, a tices* Bankrupt; and the Petition of Nathanael Stallard, of London, Merchant, one of the Assignees of the Commission of Bankrupt awarded against the said Joseph Lo?ig; and likewise of Geot'ge Gari'ard, on behalf of himself,

and Joseph and George I/ing; were referred; the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to repfort.to the House; and he read the Report in his Place;

- and afterwards delivered the same in at the Clerk's Table: Where it was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee 'have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and have heard Council for all Parties:

The Council for the Petitioners, the Creditors, charged the said Joseph Long the Bankrupt with notorious Frauds, to the Value of £. 30,000. and upwards, contrived to cheat and defraud his Creditors, and committed by and with the Contrivance, Advice, Aid, and Assistance, of his Brothers, George and John Long, and Robert Scrle, Nathanael Stallard, John Burnett, and George Garrard, their Accomplices: And produced the following Evidence; VIZ:

Mr. William Poyntz Said, That, to his Knowledge, Joseph Long the Bankrupt did, upon no Foundation, gain Credit for Goods and Money, to the Amount oi£. 18,000. or thereabouts:

That, in July 1717,' he confessed a fraudulent Judgment for £. 1,400* to his Brother George, when there was but £. 200. due; and Conveyances and Assignments of the Bankrupt's Goods and Effects were prepared, to defraud his Creditors:

That, in January 1717, the said Bankrupt obtained Credit in London for Goods for Bi'istol Fair, to the V alue of £. 700. and upwafds; and made a Fraudulent Sale thereof to his Brother John, to alter the Property; and took Two Notes, therefore, from John, for £. 700. which Notes, as John hath since declared, w ere burnt and destroyed, without Payment: That, the said Goods being attached at Bristol, by some of the Bankrupt’s Creditors, John thereupon claimed them, by Pretence of the said fraudulent Sale; and brought several Actions against those Creditors, which are as yet depending:

That Mr. Robci't Serle was privy to the Bankrupt’s fraudulent Practices, and assisted him therein: That Serle laid Goods, to the Value of £. 500. in the Bankrupt s Shop at Bristol, Fair, in January 1717; which Goods passed for the Bankrupt’s, and were sold in his Name, but to the said Series Use; and; by Serle's Assistance, the Bankrupt gained great Credit at that Fair:

That John Long attended at the Fair, with promissory Notes in George Longs Name, in Blank, payable to the Bankrupt; and those Notes were filled up for Good§ bought by the Bankrupt; and, as soon as the Goods were , bought, Bills of Sale thereof were made to George, to

alter the Property; and the Witness was privy to one of these Instances, which was for above £. 1,000.

That the Goods, so bought, were sent to George, and he exported them to Holland:

That, in April 1718, a Commission of Bankrupt was taken Out against Joseph Long: and the Commissioners appointed Nathanael Stallard, and John Burnett Assignees, without the Knowledge of the Creditors:

That those Assignees refused to get in or secure the Bankrupt’s Effects, or to take any Measures for securing those in Holland; and thereby gave the Bankrupt an Opportunity of sending thither to his Brother George; and, by his Assistance, deprived the Creditors of Effects belonging to the Bankrupt, to above £. 7,000. Value, which was done with the Privity of both those Assignees:

That the said Assignees have, for £. 154. released and discharged George Long of all Demands in respect of the 7

A. 1719.

Bankrupts Estate: And Burnett has confessed, that he had sworn to John Long, upon the Bible, to do what lay in his Power in Favour of the Bankrupt:

That, by the Assignees w ilful Neglect and Refusal to prosecute several Persons indebted to the Bankrupts Estate, and who had Goods of his in their Hands, several Hundred Pounds have been lost to the Creditors:

That, when the Bankrupt was in the Kings Bench Prison, the Assignees would by no Means suffer him to be examined, for discovering his Effects; alleging, that their indulging him was more consistent with their private Interest and Advantage:

That, within few Days after the Commission issued, the Assignee Stallard received Letters from Holland, from George Long, directed to the Bankrupt; in one of which Two promissory Notes were inclosed, in George's Hand, payable to the Bankrupt, or Order, for £. 1,000. each, or thereabouts; and Two Bills of Exchange, for £. 500. or thereabouts, accepted by George, and intended to be signed by the Bankrupt, as drawn by him on George, payable to the Bankrupt’s own Order:

That Stallard [jroposed to the Witness to secrete the said £. 500. from the Bankrupt’s Estate:

That, in one of those Letters, George Long wrote, That the said Sums of £. 2,500. were for Goods received from the Bankrupt since the then last Bristol Fair:

That John Long told the Witness, in November and December last, That he had offered £. 600. to Stallard to assign over to him his Interest in the Bankrupt’s Estate as Assignee, though there was but £> 200. due to him:

That Stallard refused to do it for £. 600. but intimated he would do it for £. i,oooo. and that, by Mr. Series Interposition, they have since agreed in that Matter:

That John Long hath declared, that Mr. George Garrard did principally advise and assist the Bankrupt in his unfair Proceedings; and has above £. 500. in his Hands, of the Bankrupt's Monies, which he will not account for:

That, in February 1717, George Long commended his own Management as to his Brother Joseph's Affair; de: daring that he had only £. 800. to pay for Joseph, and had several £. 1,000. of his in his Hands:

That Joseph Long, upon his Marriage, cheated his Wife of her Fortune, by placing it into his Brother John Long's Hands; who pretended to settle an Estate of his upon her, which Instate was out of his Power, being before settled, and fraudulently incumbered over and over again, and the prior Incumbrances concealed from the subsequent Incumbrancers:

That the Assignee Burnet usually supplied the Bankrupt with Money, on Pledges of Goods, at £. 25. or £.30. per Cent. Premium; and that Joseph Long for several Years before he went off, made it his constant Practice to pawn Goods, and to sell what he took upon Credit for considerably less than they cost; and to discount Notes, and to borrow Notes, for that Purpose, and particularly of the Assignees, and Robert Scrle; and that such Notes were discounted at the Time of his being Bankrupt, to the Value of some Thousands of Pounds:

That Joseph Long, a little before he went oft', got Notes for above £. 200. from Edward Hale, then in the jlJint; and afterwards discounted those Notes with Mr. George Aiidersoii:

That he sold a Parcel of Wines to Thouas Pardoe for £. 200. or thereabouts, and took his Notes for it, though he knew Pardoe could not pay; giving this reason for it, That the Wines were w orth but little; and he could dispose of the Notes to Mr. Burnett, or Air. Anderson, as well as if Pardoe was a responsible Man:

That, when those Notes became payable, he got Par-doe to give fresh Notes for the same Sums, under Pretence of giving longer Time for Payment, and promising to deliver up the former Notes; but never did:

That Robert Serle was privy to Joseph Longs Intentions of going off after Bristol Fair, which began the 25th of January 1717; and therefore took an Assignment of the Lease of his House in Broad-street; which Assignment

By the Lords Justices*

A PROCLAMATION '^/>HEREx/VS this present Parliament stands prorogued y to the First Day of October next: We, with the Advice of his Majesty's Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare, That the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, on the said First Day of October’ next, to Monday the Three-and-twentieth Day of November next; and we have given Order, That a Commission be prepared for proroguing the same accordingly: And we do

hereby further declare his Majesty’s Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Three-and-twentieth Day of November next, he held, and sit, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners of Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are hereby required and commanded to give their Attendance, accordingly, at Westminster, on the said Three-and-twentieth Day of November next.

Given at Whitehall, the Twenty-ninth Day of September 1719, in the Sixth Year of his Majesty’s Reign.

GOD save the King.

A MESSAGE from his Majesty, by Sir William Saunderson, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod: Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Several Members, returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for that Purpose.

A Bill for the more effectual Preservation of the Game, was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to say;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have given Order to my Lord Chancellor, to declare to you, in my Name and Words, the Causes of my meeting you in Parliament at this time.

And the Lord Chancellor thereupon acquainted both Houses, That he had received a Speech from his Majesty, from the Throne; which the Lord Chancellor read; and of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent any Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz. 1

My Lords and Gentlemen,

THE Satisfaction with which I always meet you is very much increased at this time, when it has pleased Ahnightv God so to strengthen the Arms of Great Bri~

O v O

tain, and our Confederates, and so to prosper our several Negotiations, that, by his Blessing on our Endeavours, we may reasonably promise ourselves to reap very soon the Fruits of our Successes. I am persuaded it will be accounted, by all my good Subjects, a sufficient Reward for some extraordinary Expence, that all Europe, as well as these Kingdoms, is upon the Point of being delivered from the Calamities of War, by the Influence of British Arms and Counsels: One Protestant Kingdom has already been relieved by our seasonable Interposition; and such a Foundation is laid, by our late Treaties, for an Union amongst other great Protestant Powers, as will very much tend to the Security of our holy Religion.

Vol. 19.

I believe you cannot but be surprised at the Continuation of a War, where our Enemies have nothing to hope, and so much to fear: It is indeed difficult to frame any Judgment of those Counsels which have broke out of late in so many rash and ill-concerted measures: If they depend upon our Divisions at Home, I doubt not but, in a very short time; their Hopes, founded upon this Expectation, will prove as vain and ill-grounded as any of their former Projects.

In congratulating with you on this happy Posture of Affairs, I must tell you, That as I have been very just and faithful to my Engagements, so I have met such frank and powerful Returns of Assistance from my Allies, as will, I doubt not, establish a lasting Friendship among us.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,'

You wdll see, by the Accounts I have ordered to be delivered to you, how' moderate a Use I have made of the Powrer intrusted with me, to augment my Forces by Sea and Land/' I depend upon the eminent Duty and Affection you have always shewn to my Person and Government, that you will be vigorous in dispatching the necessary Supplies for the Year: To which Purpose I have ordered the Estimates to be laid before you; and, at the same time, I must desire you to turn your Thoughts to all proper Means for lessening the Debts of the Nation.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

You must all be sensible of the many undeserved and unnatural Troubles I have met with during the Course of my Reign: Our Divisions at Home have gone magnified abroad; and by inspiring into some foreign Powers a false Opinion of our Force, have encouraged them to treat us in a Manner which the Crown oi Great Britain shall never endure, while I wear it.

The Trouble and Expence which this hath brought upon us, have been most loudly complained of by those who were the Occasion of them: But, with your Assistance, I have hitherto got through all these Difficulties; and, by the Continuance of your Help, I hope very soon to overcome them, since the Hand of God has so visibly been with us in all our Undertakings.

If the necessities of my Government have sometimes engaged yo.ur Duty and Affections to trust me with Powers, of which you have always, with good Reason, been jealous; the whole world must acknowledge they have been so used, as to justify the Confidence you have reposed in me: And as I can truly affirm, That no Prince was ever more zealous to increase his own Authority, than I am to perpetuate the Liberty of my People, I hope you will think of all proper Methods to establish, and transmit to your Posterity, the Freedom of our happy Constitution; and, particularly, to secure that Part which is most liable to Abuse: I value myself upon being the first who U u hath

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is sitting.

House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every 1 Bay, before the Uoor is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is sitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning, to Four in the Afternoon, during this Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple Bar and Westminster-hall shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take care there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament: And that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster: And that he do see the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care, that no Footmen be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

The Earl of Hertford reported from the Committee, to Address on whom it was referred to draw up an Address, to be pre- the King's sented to his Majesty, upon the Resolution Yesterday, sPeech* That they had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

May it please your Majesty,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, do return our most unfeigned Thanks to your Majesty for your most gracious Speech from the Throne; and assure your Majesty, That our Hearts are filled with unspeakable Joy, upon your safe and happy Return to these your Kingdoms; and with the most just and grateful Sense of your unwearied Labours for our Welfare, and the Security of the Protestant Religion.

We heartily congratulate with your Majesty on the Success of your British Arms; and return the Thanks of this House, in the most dutiful Manner, for such Measures taken, by the Influence of British Counsels, as afford

The King’s Speech to be considered.

Wearing printed Calicoes, &c.

The King appoints to be attended.

the nearest Prospect of a general Peace abroad, and of enjoying, with Glory, the Benefits of Trade and Tran^ quillity:

And we crave Leave to assure your Majesty, That we will, on our Parts, by the Vigour of our Resolutions for the Support of your Government, and by the Dispatch which we will give to the necessary Supplies, convince the World, That, if our Enemies have conceived any Hopes from our Divisions at Home, this hath been the vainest of all their Projects: And we will enable your Majesty, in Concert with your Allies, effectually to support and perfect those just and equitable Measures which have been taken to establish a general Peace:

And we further assure your Majesty, That we will apply ourselves to find out the best Means for lessening the Debts of the Nation, and supporting the publick Credit; and will concur in all proper Methods to establish and preserve the Freedom of our happy Constitution, for which your Sacred Majesty has given so many tender Proofs of your Care and Affection.

The said Address was read a Second time.

A Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers, in the City of Worcester, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of Poor employed in the several Branches of the said Trade, and also in the behalf of many Hundred thousands of poor distressed Families belonging to the Woollen Manufactures of Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Cloathing Trade, joined with the rest of the Woollen Manufacturies of this Kingdom, has, for many Years last past, been the greatest Support of the Landed Interest, the Employing of the Poor, and Strength of the Nation: That the said Trade is in a very declining Condition, and many Thousands of poor Families ready to perish for Want of Labour; which is occasioned by the Exportation of Wool to foreign Markets, and by Wearing of Calicoes, and stained Linens, in Great Britain; which, if not timely prevented, may be of fatal Consequence, by forcing many Thousands of Workmen to foreign Parts; and ruining many Thousands of good Families, who have hitherto employed the Poor; and the Poor in general must perish: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the wdiole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Three Weeks, resolve itself into the said Committee.

A Petition of the Clothiers, and Manufacturers in Wearing Druggets, and other Inhabitants, in and about the Town of Printed Cal-Calne, in the County of Wilts, and Parts adjacent, was llcoes’ c% presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That die Petitioners are considerable Dealers in the Woollen Manufacture, and particularly in the Clothing and Drugget Trades; by which the Petitioners have always employed great Numbers of poor Families, who must otherwise become very chargeable to their respective Parishes:

That the Goods the Petitioners make are generally sold to the Turky and Italian Merchants, who export the same to Turky and Italy, from w hence they return great Quantities of raw Silk, which is again manufactured in other Parts of England, and employ great Numbers of poor People where those Manufactures are wrought: That, by the almost universal Wear and Using of printed and paint-ecf Callicoes and East India prohibited Goods, the Consumption of the said Returns of Raw Silk is so much lessened, and the Exportation of Woollen Cloth, and Druggets, so much interrupted, that the Petitioners are no longer able to carry on their Trade; whereby they are reduced towery miserable Circumstances, and the said Manufacture in great Danger of being lost: And praying to bevelieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Free^ men, and belonging* to the incorporate Company of Clothiers, in the City of Worcester, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of Poor employed in the several Branches of the said Trade, and also in the behalf of many Hundred thousands of poor distressed Families belonging to the Woollen Manufacturies of Great Britain, is referred.

Memorandum: By a Proviso in the Clause of Appropriation, in the Act 5® Georgii, Pag. 369. the Commissioners of the Treasury were enabled to issue and apply such Part of the Monies by that Act appropriated for the publick Uses, as should be necessary for or towards the Increase of Expence then arisen, or to arise, from such Augmentation, as his Majesty, in his great Wisdom, had made, or should think fit to make, of his Forces, by Sea or Land, to disappoint the Designs of his Enemies, both at Home and Abroad.

The House being moved, That a Proviso in the Act of the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for making more effectual the several Acts passed for repairing and amending the Highways of this Kingdom, might be read;

The same was read accordingly.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend the said Act: And that Sir Robert Dovers, Sir Samuel Lennard, Mr. Newland, and Mr. Hampden, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Ordered, That the Commissioners of the Customs do lay before this House, an Account of the Entries of all Goods for Spain, in the Years 1698, 1699, and 1700; and what Goods have been actually shipped, pursuant to such Entries.

Ordered, That the Commissioners of the Customs do lay before this House, an Account of the Entries of all Goods for Spain, from the Year 1713, to the present time; and what Goods have been actually shipped, pursuant to such Entries.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty;

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charge of the Guards, Garrisons, and other his Majesty’s Land Forces, in Great Britain, for the Year 1720; and also tho Estimate of the Charge of his Majesty’s Forces in the Plantations, Minorca, and Gibraltar, for the Year 1720; be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee.

Ordered, That the List of the reduced Officers that are to be on Half Pay for the Year 1720, with an Estimate of the Charge thereof, be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee.

The House according to Order, resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Farrer took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Farrer reported from the Committee, That they had made some Progress in the Matter to them referred; and had directed him to move. That they may have Leave to sit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider farther of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the.Clock.

Prayers.

A PETITION of the Bailiffs, Wardens, Assist- Weaving ants, and Commonalty, of the Trade, and Art, printed Ca-and Mystery, of the Weaveis, London, was presented ,icues’ &c-to the House, and read; setting forth, that for some Years after the Prohibition of East India wrought Silks, and painted Calicoes, <§v. took place; thet Woollen and Silk Manufactures in and about London very much increased; inso much that the Petitioners Trade wejre used to employ many Thousands of poor Families in the Weaving of Worsted Stuffs, and in the Winding, Weaving, Dressing, §c. of Silk, more than formerly; which latter is the Return of our Woollen Manufactures of all kinds, exported to Turky and Italy: That, by the clandestine Importation of foreign wrought Silks, and more

especially by the almost.....Wearing and Using of

Calicoes and Linens, the Petitioners Trade, of late Years, is so far decreased, that it is no longer able to subsist the Poor, and many Thousand Persons are reduced to the utmost Necessity and Want; and, unless some speedy Remedy be found, the Woollen and Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom will be in the utmost Danger of being lost; and praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others. Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of poor employed in the several Branches of the said Trade; and also in behalf of many Hundred thousands of poor distressed Families, belonging to the Woollen Manufactories of Great Britain; is referred.

A Petition of the Mayor, Sheriffs, Citizens, and Com- Ditt0(( monalty, of the City of Norwich, in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Worsted Weaving Trade of this ancient City has, for many Years past, been carried on, not only to the great Benefit of this City in particular, but also to the great Advantage of the Kingdom: That, of late Years, this most valuable Part of our Trade has been gradually decreasing, till it has been almost entirely lost, by the prevailing Use of printed Calicoes and Linens: That the Makers are no longer able to find the Poor sufficient Employment, large Quantities of manufactured Goods lying dead by them; so that they are now obliged to employ fewer Hands, many being obliged to leave off their Trade, and many of their Workmen are run away, occasioned by the general Use and Wear of our home, printed and painted Calicoes and Linens:

And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to w hom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of War vestin', in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of Poor employed in the several Branches of the said Trade; and also in the behalf of many Hundred thousands of poor distressed Families belonging to the Woollen Manufactories of Great Britain; is referred.

A Petition of the Company of Woolcombers, in the pjtt#k City of Coventry, on behalf of themselves, and many Hundreds employed by them, w as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Prevalence}' of the printed and stained Calicoes and Linens imported by the East India Company, and dispersed through these Kingdoms, are highly prejudicial to the Woollen Manufacture; and we, of this City, have a just Reason of Complaint: And praying, That the Use of printed and painted Calicoes and Linens may be suppressed.

A Petition of the Clothiers and Stuff Weavers in the Borough of Kidderminster, in the County of Worcester, on behalf of themselves, and Thousands of Poor employed by them, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that great Numbers of People have been employed in the said Borough, in manufacturing Woollen Cloths, and Worsted Stuffs; and Multitudes of poor People, in the circumjacent Towns and Villages, in spinning Wool and Jersey, to be the Materials of the said Cloths and Stuffs; but the Wearing and Use of Callicoes, and printed Linen, has been so universally obtained of late Years, that the said Manufacture is thereby much lessened; to the great Detriment of the Petitioners, and their Dependents: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of Poor employed in the several Branches of the said Trade; and also in the behalf of many Hundred thousands of poor distressed Families belonging to the Woollen Manufactories of Great Britain; is referred.

Ditto. A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Company of Silt Weavers in the City of Canterbury, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are the Descendants of the Protestants that fled from the Persecution of the Duke UAlva, in the Law Countries, in the Reign of Queen Elizabeth; who first brought the Manufacture of Silk, and Silk mixed with Wool, into this Kingdom, and first settled it in this City; That they employ above Two thousand poor People in and about this City, in the said Manufacture, beside as great or greater Number in Combing and Spinning f of Wool: That the Silk we use is of the Growth of

Turkey and Italy, and the Return of Cloth, and other Woollen Goods, exported to those Countries by our Merchants, whereby the Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom is advanced: That the almost universal Wear of printed, painted, and stained Callicoes, and other Linens, and French and Dutch Silks, that are run, has brought our Manufacture into such miserable Circumstances that they cannot find a Sale for their own Goods, without Lq$s; Vol. 19.

and, without Relief, must speedily end in the total Ruin of themselves, and Families: And praying Relief.

IdleNaviga- A PETITION of the Bailiffs, Burgesses, Free-tion. A holders, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of

East Retford\ in the County of Nottingham, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners conceive, the making of the River Idle, in the said County, navigable, from the said Borough to the River Trent, will very much advance the Trade and Commerce of all Markets, and other Places, near the same; and be highly advantageous not only to all his Majesty’s Subjects, trading in the Staple Commodity of Lead and Hops, Corn, Timber, Coals, and other Merchandizes, by a cheap and easy Conveyance, much lessening the Rates of Commodities within the said County, and Places thereto adjoining, which, by the great Charge of Land-carriage are much enhanced; but also to the Publick in general: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to make the said River navigable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. White, Lord Molestcorth, Sir John Norris, Lord Chetwynd, Mr. Bacon, Mr. Hampden, Mr. Pitt, Mr. Comptroller, Mr. Carter, Mr. Papillon, Mr. Farrer, Mr. Meyrick, Mr. Gybbon, Sir Tho. Crosse, Mr. A orris, Mr. Treby, Mr. Pigott, Mr. Butler, Mr. Chetwynd, Mr. Lewis, Sir John Curzon, Mr. Carterett, Mr. Brodrick, Mr. Bristow, Sir Samuel Lennard, Mr. Freeman, Mr. Earl; and all the Members that serve for the Counties of York, Nottingham, and Lincoln: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five a Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber: And have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Prayers.

A PETITION of the Bailiffs and Clothiers of Wearing Bromsgrove, in the County of Worcester, was pre- Primed Cal-sented to the House and read; setting forth, That the liCoes» Petitioners are Dealers and Makers of Woollen Cloth and Stuffs, and have employed great Numbers of Poor in and about this Place: but, by universal Wear of Callicoes and printed Linens, the Consumption of their said Cloths and Stuffs are much decayed, and lessened, that they arc not able to carry on their Trade any longer, and maintain the said Poor, who are thereby reduced to very great distress, and many Families ready to starve; and particularly the clandestine Running of Wool will be a Means to destroy them, and all the Makers of Cloth in the Kingdom, if not timely prevented: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, in behalf of themselves, and many thousands of Poor employed in the several Branches of the said Trade; and also in the behalf of many Hundred thousands of poor distressed Families belonging to the Woollen Manufacturies of Great Britain; is referred.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Ditto. Council, of the City of Worcester, in Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the City of Worcester is an ancient City, and the chief Manufacture is, and hath been, for several Ages, Making of Broad White Woollen Cloths for Exportation; whereby several Thousands of poor People have been employed, as well within the said City as the adjacent Parts; and that, for a considerable time past, they have had continual Complaints of the Poor, for Bread; and several Persons that assisted others, for want of Employment, do now apply themselves for Relief: The Master Clothiers complain, that all their Stock lies in Cloth; and that, if Trade doth not mend, they shall be obliged to discharge the Hands they now employ, and quit the City; being apprehensive that the Burthen of the Poor will be too heavy for them, or the several Parishes of the said City, to redress: The Clothiers inform us, that the Reason the Merchants

Waring A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Assistants, of printed Cal- the incorporate Company of Clothiers of the City of War-iiaw, cester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are Makers of Woollen Cloth, and have employed, in that Manufacture, great Numbers of Poor, in and about this City, who otherwise must have been a great Charge to their respective Parishes: That the Cloth the Petitioners make is usually sold to Merchants, who export the same to Turky and Italy; from whence Returns are made to them, most in raw Silk, which is again manufactured in England into wrought Silks, and great Numbers of Poor are thereby employed; but by the Wear and Use of the East India prohibited Goods, and the printed and painted Callicoes and Linens, the Consumption of the said raw Silk, in return for their said Woollen Cloth, is so much lessened, and thereby the Exportation of our said Woollen Cloths so much decreased, that their Stocks lie dead upon their Hands, and their Credit exposed to all that are able to assist them; so that the Poor are reduced to great Want, and the said Manufacture of Woollen Cloth in great Danger of being lost: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, iu behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of Poor employed in the several Branches of the said Trade; and also in the behalf of many Hundred thousands of poor distressed Families belonging to the Woollen Manufacturies of Great Britain; is referred.*

The first Eight Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The last Resolution being read a Second time, That a Sum, not exceeding Eighty-one thousand Seven hundred Twenty Pounds Two Shillings and a Halfpeny, be granted to his Majesty, for the Charge of the Office of Ordnance, for the Land Service, for the Year 1720;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereunto, by adding, at the End thereof, these Words, " and for " Exceedings in the said Office, for the Year 1719 And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That a Sum, not exceeding Eighty-one thousand Seven hundred Twenty Pounds Two Shillings and a Halfpeny, be granted to his Majesty, for the Charge of the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, for the Year 1720; and for Exceedings in the said Office, for the Year 1719.

A PETITION of great Numbers Of the Broad Woollen

Weavers and Narrow Weavers of Whollcn (’loth, Manufacture, in the Parishes of Stroud\ Minching Hampton, Bisley,

Painrwick, Rodburrdugh, Woodcheslcr, Horseley, Atemng,

Essington, Rahduick, Pilchcombe, and other Places in the County of Gloucester, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in the behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Woollen Cloth Weavers in the said Parishes andv County, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by a Statute made in the Second and Third Years of King Philip and Queen Mary, it is Enacted, That no Person usitig the Feat or Mystery of Clothworking, and dwelling out of a City, Borough, Market Town, or Corporate Town, should keep, retain, or have, in their Houses or Possession, any more, or above One Woollen Loom at one time; nor shall receive any manner of Profit by letting or setting any Loom, or any Houses wherein any Loom is, or shall be used; upon Pain of Forfeiture, as is therein mentioned: And it is further Enacted, That no Woollen Weaver using or exercising the Feat or Mystery of Weaving and dwelling out of City, Borough, Market Town, or Towns Corporate, shall have or keep, at one time, above the Number of Two Woollen Looms at one tiriie, upon Pain of Forfeiture: And that no Person ... shall use or occupy the Feat or Mystery of a Tucker, or Fuller, shall, during the time that he shall so use the said Feat or Mystery, keep or have any Loom in his House or Possession, or take any Profit by the same, upon Forfeiture: And that it shall not be lawful for any Person being a Weaver, or using the Mystery of Weaving, dwelling out of a City, Borough Town, Town Corporate, or Market Town, to have above the Number of Two Apprentices at one time, upon Pain of Forfeiture:

And that no Person or Persons shall set up the said Art r Mystery of Weaving, unless they have been Apprentices by the Space of Seven Years, upon Pain of Forfeiture: And, by an Act of the Fourth Year of King Edward the Fourth, it is Enacted, That the Clothiers shall pay to their Work-folks their Wages in ready Money, and not in Wares, on Pain to forfeit to such Work-folks Treble Damages: That, notwithstanding, for encourage-ing the Weaving Trade, there have been, for several Years last past, in the said Parishes, great Abuses done to the Broad and Narrow Weavers of Woollen Cloth; and by divers Persons working at the Trade, that have not served Seven Years Apprenticeship to the same; whereby x 3 A the

A Petition of the chief Inhabitants of the Town of Stowmarkett, in the County of Suffolk, and of several of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Tradesmen, and Freeholders, of the said County, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the River Oi'well, which runneth from the said Town of Stowmarkett, to the Town and Port of Ipswich, in the said County of Suffolk, being about Sixteen Miles by Water, which,

although anciently a navigable River, yet hath been so far neglected for many Years last past, that the same is now become wholly unnavigable; inso much that the Inhabitants are now obliged to have their Corn, Coals, Timber, and all other Goods and Merchandizes, carried by Land; which is very chargeable to the Country thereabouts: That the said Town of Stowmarkett is an ancient Market Town, situate in the Centre of the said County; and, by reason of the Decay of Trade, and the Neglect of the said River, the Charge of the Poor is, of late Years greatly increased, being Six Shillings in the Pound, and upwards; whereas, if the said River were made navigable, the Trade of the said Town w ould flourish; Timber for. his Majesty’s Navy, and other Merchandizes, would be carried at much easier Rates; and a Communication would be opened with several Places, to the great Benefit and Advantage of the Country thereabouts: And praying, That Leave, may be given to bring in a Bill for making the said River navigable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the Headmen, Wardens, and Assistants, of the incorporated Company of Worsted Weavers, in the City of Norwich, and County of Norfolk, on behalf of themselves, and Thousands depending upon them, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, for many Years past, the greatest Part of the Trade of this City and County consisted in a great Variety of Woollen, and Silk and Woollen, Stuffs; great Quantities of which were not only consumed at home, but also exported to, and consumed in, our Plantations; not only to the Advantage of these Places in particular, by employing and maintaining many Thousands of poor Families; but also to the Benefit of the Nation in general, by the working up the Wool of our own Growth: That, when this Trade w as very much obstructed by the frequent w earing and using East India wrought Silks, and Callicoes printed, painted, and dyed, there, an Act was obtained, in the Year 1700, which prohibited the wearing and using the m: That, in a few Years, the good Intent of that Act was eluded by the prevailing use of Callicoes and Linens; w hereby our Home Consumption of Woollen Manufactures is greatly hindered in their Exportation to our Plantations: That, unless this languishing Ma-nufactury be revived, it will be impossible to provide the Poor sufficient Employment $ many of our Manufacturers having been forced to leave Trading; and others have run away, and left their Families chargeable to the Parish; and scarce any will put their Children Apprentice thereto: And praying Relief.

_ Mr. Fairer, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolution they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Sum of Three Shillings in the Pound, and no more, be raised, in the Year 1720, upon Lands, Tenements, Hereditaments, Pensions, Offices, and personal Estates, in that Part of Great Britain called England, Wales, and the Town of Berwick upon Tweed: and that a proportionable Cess, according to, the Ninth Article of the Treaty for the Union, be laid upon that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

The said Resolution being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, upon the said Resolution: And that Mr. Farrer, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Chancellor of the Duchy, Mr. Solicitor General, Mr. Clayton, Mr. Lourdes, and Mr. Charles Stanhope, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A Petition of the Clothiers, Weavers, and others concerned in the Woollen Manufactury in the Town of Wilton, in the County of Wilts, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are considerable Dealers in the Woollen Manufactures, and especially in the Clothing Trade; whereby they have always employed great Numbers of Poor, who must otherwise become chargeable to the Parish: That the Cloth, and other Manufactures, are sold to the Turkey and Italian Merchants; who export the same, and return great Quantities of raw Silks; which again is manufactured in other Parts of England; and employ also great Numbers of poor People; but, by the almost universal Wear and Using of printed and painted Callicoes and Linens, the Consumption of the said Returns of raw Silks is so much lessened, and thereby the Exportation of the Woollen Cloth so much interrupted, that the Petitioners are no longer able to carry on their Trade, and maintain the said Poor, as they have done: And praying Relief,

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of John Farmer, John Wagstaff'e, Joseph Wagstaffe, John Hall, John Bacon, John Miles, and other Inhabitants of Nun Eaton, in the County of Warwick, on behalf of themselves, and many Thousands more, concerned in the Woollen Manufactury, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Wearing of Callicoes, printed and stained Linen, is very pernicious to the Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom; and that it hath so reduced the Worsted Trade thereof, that many Thousands of poor People employed therein are ready to starve for want of Employment: And praying to be relieved.

A Petition of the Masters, and Wardens, and Assistants, of the Company of Silk-throwers of London, in behalf of themselves, and the Commonalty of the said Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by the Manufacturing and Working of raw Silk imported, which is the Return of our Manufactures exported, the Petitioners have employed many Thousand poor Families: That they have found a sensible Loss of their Trade, in proportion as foreign Manufactures have been permitted, and obtained, within this Kingdom: That several Years ago, by the Wearing of India wrought Silks, stained and painted Callicoes imported, the Petitioners felt a proportionable Decay of their Trade; and the great Number of Poor employed by them were reduced to the utmost Necessity; whereupon an Act was made for prohibiting the Consumption of the several foreign Manufactures then complained of; after which Prohibition the Petitioners Trade revived, and the Poor were employed as formerly: That, of late Years, by the general Wearing of Callicoes and Linen printed in England, and of Indian wrought Silks, painted and stained Callicoes, clandestinely imported, several Parts of the Manufactures, which were made of Silk, and of Silk mixed with Worsted, and which were frequently worn in Great Britain, and also exported to foreign Parts, are now generally disused, and

not Half the Poor employed as were before: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to w hom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

; Mr. White reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Bailiffs, Burgesses, Freeholders, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of East Retford\ in the County of Nottingham, was referred, the Matter as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the Second of December instant, have considered of the Matter of the said Petition, and, by the Testimony of Mr. Thornhaugh, Mr. Clarkson, Mr. Gill) 1/, and Mr. Foi her gilly and other Gentlemen of the said County, it appeared to the Committee, that the River Idle is already navigable, within Seven Miles of the Town of East Retford:

That the River Trent, very often, in the Winter Season, overflows; and when it so happens, Goods cannot be carried by Land from East Retford to Gainsborough:

That the making the said River navigable, from East Retford to the River Trent, which is the Prayer of the Petition, will very much advance the Trade and Commerce of the Markets, and other Places near the same; and be advantageous not only to all the Traders in Lead, Hops, Corn, Timber, Coals, and other Merchandizes, but also to the Publick in general.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making the River Idle navigable* from the Borough of East Retford, in the County of Nottingham, to Bawtry Wharf, in the County of York: And that Mr. White, and the Lord Milton, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

That since the Act of Parliament, made for prohibiting the Wearing of India wrought Silks, and printed Callicoes, the Woollen Manufacture hath been very much increased, and Thousands of Families have been sufficiently maintained thereby; but, by the now almost universal Wearing of Callicoes, and printed Linens, and the Transportation of great Quantities of Wool, the Weaving of Stuffs is decreased; and several Masters, who have employed some Hundreds, are broke, and left off their Trades; and the Poor destitute of Business, and are ready to starve: And praying Relief.

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Merchants of England trading into the Levant Seas was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have, under a Royal Charter, carried on, for many Years, the Trade into the Dominions of the Grand Signior, notwithstanding the great Increase of the French Trade in those Parts: That the said Trade consists in the Exportation of the Woollen Manufactures, and other Products of this Kingdom, the Returns for which are raw Silk, and other manufactured Commodities: That,

by the Law to prohibit the Wearing and Use of wrought Silks, printed and painted Callicoes, and the Duties laid on the Importation of other foreign wrought Silks, the Silk Manufactures have been much increased, great Numbers of Poor employed, and the Trade to Turkey preserved; but, by the general Use and Wear of printed and stained Callicoes and Linens, the Trade to Turkey is severely affected thereby: That it carinot subsist under these insupportable Discouragements: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to w'hom the Petition of the Weavers; Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of Woollen Goods Wearing in and about the Town of Wakefcild, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Woollen Manufacture, in which are employed many Hundreds of Poor, lies under such Discouragements by the general Wear of East India Goods, printed Callicoes and Linens, as must necessarily sink and ruin it, together with the many Families now subsisted by it, unless some effectual Remedy be speedily applied:

And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, and Ditto* Town Clerk, of the Corporation and Borough of Wilton, in the County of Wilts, on behalf of several Hundreds of Spinners, Weavers, and others, Inhabitants of and within the Borough aforesaid, bred up in the Woollen Manufactory Business, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That they are now under very necessitous Calamities, and likely to perish for want of Employment; occasioned by the general Wear of painted and printed Linen in Great Britain; as also by great Numbers of Persons called Smugglers, making it their Business to transport great Quantities of Wool into foreign Countries, and importing great Quantities of East India Goods, and Callicoes, without paying Duty for the same: And praying to be relieved.

A Petition of the Merchants, Mercers, arid Drapers, - of Gainsborough, in the County of Lincoln, with others of the Inhabitants, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by an Act, passed in 1700, in favour of the Woollen Manufactory, they found the Benefit of it for Six or Seven Years after; but since hath very Sensibly declined, by the general Use or Wearing of printed and painted Callicoes and Linens: And praying, That the Wearing of Callicoes may be prohibited.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, W alkers, and others, Freemen,* and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the City of Bristol\ in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the ‘Petitioners being deeply affected with the general Decay of the Woollen and Stuff Manufacture in and about this City, occasioned by the general Use of printed and stained Callicoes and Linens; and the Worsted Stuff Manufacturers are, for want of Employment, become poor and burthensome, and prevented arriving to that Perfection with their Stuffs, which some Years since they were in a fair Prospect of: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Traders, Serge-makers, and other Inhabitants, of the Town of Wellington, in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the principal Business of the said Town is the Woollen Manufacture; whereby great Numbers of poor People found a comfortable Subsistence; but the said Trade is failed, and thereby the State of the Poor rendered calamitous and deplorable, occasioned by the general LTse of Callicoes, and printed Linens: And praying, That the Wearing of Callicoes, and printed Linens, may be prevented.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Eree-luen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of the Woolcombers, and Traders in Wool, within the County of Norfolk, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, for many Years past, have been employed in Manufacturing of Wool and Yarn; by which the Poor of this County, as well as of others, have been generally employed, and subsisted: That, by the general Using of printed Callicoes and Linens, their Trade is under the greatest Discouragement, and so very much declined, that the Wages of the Poor are not only reduced, but a great many of them are already out of Employment, and thereby forced to be chargeable to their respective Parishes: and, unless by some speedy Relief, many of the Petitioners will be obliged to desist from going on with their Business; andleaving great N umbers of poor Families wholly destitute of Subsistence: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A PETITION of the Inhabitants of the Town and Borough of MoretonMmstead, in the County of Devon; and also of the Weavers, Combers, Fullers, and others concerned in the Woollen Manufacture there; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That this Town, which formerly received its chief Subsistence from the Woollen Manufactures, hath, of late Years, been so sensibly disappointed, and felt so great a Decay in Trade, that several of its Dealers therein have been disabled to continue their Employments; occasioned by the almost universal Wearing and Use of Callicoes, and painted Linen, and the Exportation of Wool into foreign Countries; which will totally ruin the Trade of the Wool-Jen Manufacture, unless seasonably prevented; And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of the Mayor, Magistrates, Common Council, and other principal Inhabitants, of the Borough of Plimoulh, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Smuggling in this Kingdom is now so universal, as to become a national Grievance: That thereby great Sums of Money are constantly carried abroad, to purchase the Products and Manufactures of other Countries, which are spent here instead of our own: That French Wines and Brandy brought in that Way are sold so cheap, that they very much hinder the Consumption of our Malt, by brewing and distilling: That the Smugglers also carry off such great Quantities of Wool, that Thousands of Poor, bred up in the Woollen Manufactures, are, for want of Employment, forced to beg for Subsistence: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table,

Comptroller acquainted the House, That their Address of Yesterday, relating to the Ships employed in the Fishing oft' Newfoundland, had been presented to his Majesty: And that his Majesty had been pleased to give Order, That the Account desired by the said Address should be laid before this House.

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors in his Majesty’s Gaol for the County of Southampton was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have, by the inexorable Tempers of their Credit tors, been put into Gaol; most Part of them having been there for Five or Six Years, having no other Support than the Charity of the neighbouring Gentlemen: That the Petitioners have several times applied themselves to their Creditors, in order to obtain their Liberty; but nothing would mollify them, but the Payment of their Debts, which is more than they are able to do; and so must remain in a starving Condition in Gaol: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Makers of Druggets in the Town of Newbury, and Parts adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners are considerable Dealers in the Woollen Manufactures; thereby many of the Poor are employed, and their Families maintained, which must otherwise be burtheusome and chargeable to their respective Parishes: That the Druggets the Petitioners deal in are generally exported to Leghorn, or otiier Ports in Italy, from whence the chief Return is Silk: That, by the general Wear and Use of printed Callicoes and Linens, and prohibited East India Silks, the Consumption of Silk is much lessened; which Occasions so great a Discouragement to the Exportation of the Druggets, so that the said Manufactures are in Danger of being lost, and the Poor reduced to Beggary, for want of Employment: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers, in the City oi Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen,

- Clothiers, Serge-makers, Drugget-makers, Dyers, and other principal Inhabitants, of the Town and Parish of Collumpton, in the County of Devon, and Places adjacent, in behalf of themselves, and several Thousand poor Labourers, was presented to, the House, and read; setting forth, That the Making of Cloth, Serges, Druggets, and other Woollen Goods, hath been the principal Trade of this Town, and Places adjacent; and many Thousand Families usually employed therein, and the Poor thereby subsisted; but now, through the general Wear of East India Goods, printed and painted Callicoes and Linens, and the clandestine Exportation of Wool, the Trade, and Woollen Manufacture, in these Parts, is, in a great Measure, sunk and lost, many Traders ruined, and the Poor are now become extremely burthensome to their Neighbours: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred,

A Petition of the Bailiffs, and other the Magistrates, Inhabitants, and Spinsters, in and about the Borough of Clithero, in the County of Lancaster, in behalf of themselves, and others concerned in the Spinning of Worsted Yarn, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, for upwards of Twenty Years last past, a great many Thousands of Families in those Parts have been full employed, and full Wages paid them in the Spinning of Worsted Yarn, till within these Three or Four last Years, that there have been so great Quantities of painted Callicoes and stained Linen, worn in England, as also great Quantities of Wool transported, the said Trade of Spinning of Wool, and Worsted Yarn, is so exceedingly decayed, that the Master Combers cannot employ Half the Number of Spinners they used to do, and those employed are forced to abate One-third of their Wages; whereby they are reduced to great Poverty, and great Numbers of them are become chargeable to their Parishes: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of the Weavers, and other Tradesmen, on Wearing the behalf of themselves, and some Thousands in and about Pnntei1 the Town of Bernard- Castle in the County of Durham, ‘'oe:>, c* Makers of Camblets, Tammies, Shalloons, Serges, and of all Sorts of Light and Woollen Stuffs proper for Women, and Childrens Gowns and Cloathing, and for Curtains, and Hangings of Rooms, and for many other Uses, as well for our own People at home, as for those of our several Plantations abroad, as also of the Combers, and Dealers in combed Wool, and Spinning of Woollen and Worsted Yarn, and the Dyers, Dressers, and Prefers, there, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, some time alter the late Act made for preventing and prohibiting the Wearing of Callicoes, and India Stuffs, the Woollen Manufacture did very much improve and increase; and some Hundred of Families, kept and set on Work in the Combing and Spinning of Yam, got a handsome Livingfor themselves and Families;

That, by the now’ extraordinary Use of Callicoes, and the great Exportation of Wool, the said Trade is totally dropped and lost; and many Master Weavers, who employed some Hundreds, are now’ become incapable of pursuing their said Trades; and those employed under them are become chargeable to their respective Parishes l And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants, in Ditto, the Parish of Mid hell, in the County of Perth, for. themselves, and in Name and Behalf of Hundreds more concerned in making and trading in Linen, w as presented to the House, and read; setting forth* That they find; by several Petitions, craving, That an Act may be made for prohibiting tlte wearing or using Callicoes. or stamped or stained Linen Cloth, That the only Manufacture whereby they arc enabled to subsist, and maintain any Sliare in Trade, or to employ poor People, is that ot making Linen: That f lux is a very considerable Part of the Produce of that Country: That great Part of the Demand for Flax, and Linen Cloth, arises from the stamped and stained Linen: That they have already found the high Duty on stamped and stained Linen a very great Discouragement to their Linen Manufactures: However, if Callicoes which are of a foreign Manufacture, and foreign Materials, be discouraged; yet they had Reason to expect, from the Articles of the Union, all suitable Encouragement, to the Improvement of their Linen: That the Consumption of White Linen is much lessened by the Importation of Foreign Linen; and if the stumped or stained Linen shall be prohibited, the Country will be inevitably ruined, and many Thousands of the Poor starved: And praying, That the Linen Manufacture be encouraged.

The Committee have, according to the Order of the House, of the Nineteenth instant, taken the said Petition into Consideration; and, upon the Examination of William Parker, James Motteram, Francis Cockain, and Richard Goodwin, do find the Matter to be as follows; viz.

That the making the River Derwent, in the County of Derby, navigable, w ill very much conduce to the Advantage of the Markets, and other trading Places, near The same; and to all the Traders in Lead, Cheese, Butler, Malt, Marble, Millstones, Iron, Timber, and other Merchandizes, by lessening the great Charge of Land-carriage, and conveying the said Commodities at much cheaper Rates.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Clergy, and Freeholders, of the County of Sumy, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by an Act made in the Filth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, it is Enacted, That after the 29th Day of September 1719, no Waggon travelling for Hire shall be drawn with more than Six Horses, and no Cart with more than Three Horses, nor the Streak or Tire of the Wheels of the said Waggons or Carts to be under the Breadth of Two Inches and an Half when worn; under the Penalties and For- feitures in the said Act mentioned: That the Highways hi most Parts of the Petitioners County afe so very bad, especially in the Winter Season, that no Waggon or Cart carrying even moderate Burthens can travel the same, with the respective Number of Horses with any Expedition, or without apparent Danger of destroying the Horses by which such Waggons of Carts' are drawn; by means whereof, the Trader'and Commerce of the said County, between the several and respective Market Towns and the City of tendon, are in Danger of being very much lessened, and ill served, and the Price of Carriage very much enhancedto the great Detriment as well of the Inhabitants of the said City of London, and Parts adjacent, as to the Petitioners: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Bill to explain and amend an Act, passed the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for making more effectual the several Acts passed for repairing and amending the Highways of tills Kingdom, is committed.
