A Petition of the General Convention of the Royal Boroughs of North Britain, convened at Edinburgh the last Day of December 1719, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Linen Manufacture in Scotland is of very great Advantage to the Subjects, as the Woollen Manufacture is to England: That, should the Manufacturing of it receive any Discouragement, it must necessarily draw along with it intire Ruin to many Thousands in that Country, since it is the only Manufacture which maintains, and keeps at Work, their Poor; That the Trade of dying Scots Linen being quite lost, and the using it White being rendered impracticable by the Importation of foreign Linen, there is now no Way left for the Consumption or L^se of it, but by having it printed or stained: That it has been the established Maxim of the British Nation, to give all due Encouragement to their own Manufactures: so this of Linens painted and stained deserves that Encouragement in a particular manner, since it is intirely the Produce of the Country, and manufactured at home: That several Petitions have been presented, complaining of the Decay of Trade, by reason of Wearing of printed, painted, and stained Linen, though manufactured at home; but should any Prohibition of this kind be granted, it would at once intirely destroy the Manufacture of Linen in Scotland: And praying, That no Prohibition may be granted against the Wearing and Use-ing, of Scots Linen printed, stained, and painted.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others. Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of the Magistrates, Town Council, and Inhabitants, of the Burgh of Renfrew, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Linen Ma-nutactury of Scotland is of very great Advantage to the Subject; which, should it meet with any Discouragement, would be the intire Ruin of many Thousands of People, by which Manufactory they employ and keep their Poor at Work: That there is now no Consumption of the said Linen, but only by printing thereof: That several Petitions have been presented, praying the Prohibition of printed, stained, and painted Linen, which, if granted, will at once intirely destroy that Manufactory in Scotland: And praying, That no Prohibition may be granted against the Wearing and Using of Scots Linen, painted, printed, or stained.

A Petition, and Representation of the Provost* Bay-liffs, and Town Council, of the Burgh of Dumfreis, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, for themselves, and in Name of the said Burgh, and in behalf of many Thousands of the Subjects of North Britain, employed in the Scots Manufacture of Linen Cloth, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Subjects of Scotland have always had a particular Dexterity in improving the Linen Manufacture, and hath been hitherto encouraged; and have employed many Thousands of poor People in the Management of this Manufacture, which is their only Way of Subsistence; and, if discouraged, must inevitably become a Burthen to the Kingdom in general: That there is no other Manufacture in Scotland left, since the Union, whereby poor and i !Ie People can be employed, because the EngtishWoollen Manufacture is now imported and sold through all North Britain: That discouraging the Printing, Stamping, and Staining, of Scots Linen, w^ould, in effect, be a Prohibition of that Manufacture, because toe Using of it White and Brown is cut out by Importation of German and other Linen; and the Trade of dying Scots Linen is quite lost; so that the only Way to sell and consume it, is by Printing, &c. And praying* That the Petitions against Wearing and Using of Scots stamped Linen may be rejected.

A Petition of the Barons and Heritors within the County of Perth, for themselves, and in behalf of many Hundred thousands concerned in the Linen Manufacture within the Kingdom of Scotland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That whereas several Petitions have been presented by the Silk Weavers in and about the City of London, and others, in order to obtain an Act of Parliament for prohibiting the wearing or using printed, stamped, or stained, Linen Cloth; That, by granting the said Act, not only they will suffer thereby, in the most sensible manner, but many Hundred thousands of poor People, dispersed through every Village, Town, and County, in all Scotland, who are employed in the Manufacture of Linen Cloth; and, being made wholly of the Product of their native Country, ought to be equally preserved, and encouraged, with the Woollen Manufacture of England, there being no other Way for the Consumption of the greatest Part of their White Linen Cloth, but by printing, stamping, or staining: And praying, That Provision may be made for the preserving of their Linen Manufactures, by continuing the free Liberty for Stamping and Printing of British Linen Cloth.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the w hole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others. Freemen, and belonging to tire incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of the Burgh of Rutherglen, for themselves, and in Name and Behalf of many others employed in the Manufacture of Linen Cloth, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Manufacture of Linen Cloth is so common all over Scotland, that in several of the largest Counties there are as many Manufacturies of it as there are Families; the Poor subsist by their Labour and Industry, in manufacturing Flax into Linen Cloth: That, by the Treaty of Union, they hoped that all the Linen Cloth made in Scotland, and not consumed in it, might find Vent in England: That the Manufacturers of Linen have, by dear-bought Experience, felt how much the late Duty of Threepence per Ell on stamped Linen affects them; seeing the principal Use made of their Linen, when carried to England, has been to print and stamp it: That the prohibiting the Wearing of printed and stamped Linen will reduce the Poor to extreme Poverty: And praying to be relieved.

selves, and many Thousands concerned in the Woollen Manufacture was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have just Grounds to apprehend, that Wool and Yarn are frequently exported from Great Britain and Ireland to foreign Parts; for that, of late Years, but about one Half of the Woollen Cloth hath been made in those Parts as was in former times; and yet Wool continues as scarce and dear as in the most flourishing Times of Trade; and the Manufacturers are obliged to sell their Goods to Loss; whereby many Families are daily impoverished, and the Poor grow much more numerous and burthensome; and, if not timely relieved, will end in the utter Ruin of their Country and Families: And praying Relief.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 1 2th instant, have taken the said Petition into Consideration; and, upon examining Thomas Steers, John Sumner, and William Marsh, do find the Matter thereof to be as follows; viz.

That the River Douglas is capable of being macie navigable for Boats and Lighters, from the Borough of Wigan to the River Bible:

That there are many Dells and Pits of Stone, Slate, and Coals along and near the said River, the Carriage of which by Land is very chargeable and dangerous, by reason the Road goes cross Bible Sands Two Miles; which are overflowed every Tide; and in the "Passage w hereof, yearly, several Persons and Goods have been lost;

And that the Roads are*generally deep Clay, which, in Winter, and wet Seasons? are very troublesome and expensive to Travellers::

That; by making the said River navigable, it will not only remedy the aforesaid Difficulties; but be an Encouragement to several Manufactures, and thereby advance Trade, and be a N ursery for Seamen.

Mr. Norris reported from the Committee, to w hom the Drawback.* i Petition of the Merchants and Traders of Bristol was Exports w* referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which lre M j they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was 1

read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee have, in pursuance of the Order of the House, of the Fourteenth of December hot,

' taken the said Petition into Consideration; and, b

« having heard the Commissioners of the Customs, and examined John Beecher and Thomas Longman,

Merchants; and considerable Dealers in Tobacco,

Sugar, Hops, and other Goods, the Matter of Fact appears as, follows; viz.

That Tobacco, Sugar, Hops, and all other weighable Good's, are liable to many Accidents; and may, in being exported to Ireland, waste and decrease from One to Four Pounds in an Hundred, Weight:

And also that the Officers of the Customs at the Port of Bristol, by an Order of the Commissioners, of the Tenth of September last, deny to make out full Debentures for the aforesaid, Goods exported from thence to Ireland; though Certificates have been produced, that the Goods have been, Konafide, landed there and the Duty paid; for that no more Drawback can be allowed than for the Quantity particularly specified in the Certificate returned from Ireland; which, the Commissioners allege, they are justified in doing, by an Act, of the Fifth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, against clandestine Running of Goods; and that, as the Lawr now stands, they cannot make any Allowances for what is short-certified of such Goods:

And further appeared, That, since the Eighth Year of i

the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, there has been several Applications from the Merchants of Bristol and '

Liverpoole, concerning the Waste of Tobacco in Expor- j

tation from the aforesaid Places to Ireland;: .1. 1

And the Commissioners of the Customs did admit,

That, in particular Cases, there had been Allowances made for the Waste of Tobacco in Exportation; but that now they are so far restrained by the Letter of the Law, that they cannot give Directions to allow* for Waste in general.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Booth reported, from the Committee, to w hom the Weaver Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Free- Navigation, holders, and other Inhabitants, of the County Palatine of Chester, w as referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, in pursuance of the Order of the House, of the Thirteenth Instant, have taken the said Petition into Consideration; and, having examined William Squire, Thomas Steers, Samuel Clements, William Marsh, and Richard Vernon, do find the Matter thereof to be as follows; viz.

That there is now', and hath been anciently, a great Manufacture of Salt in the said County; and that many Parts of this Kingdom, as well as Ireland, and Parts beyond the Seas, have been supplied by the Salt made there; but, of late, the Parts beyond the Seas, by the great Expence of Land-carriage from the Salt-works to Frodsham Bridge, have been supplied from France and Spain; and that there formerly used to be a much greater Number of Ships come to lade Salt than now; they being discouraged from coming again, by the great Delay in their Lading, from the slow Dispatch by Land-carriage:

Thgt the Trade is so much reduced, that the Pits at Northwich, Namptwich, and Middlewich, and Parts adjacent, in which there are near One thousand Proprietors, or Shares, are many of them now become useless, to the Impoverishment of a great Number of People:

That if the River Weaver; which runs through the Centre of the said County, and near to which most of the Salt-works are erected, was made navigable from Wins-ford Bridge to Frodsham Bridge, the Salt would be delivered at Frodsham Bridge for about Three Shillings per Tun, which now costs Eight or Nine Shillings, and sometimes Ten Shillings, per Tun; and the Ships much sooner dispatched in their Loading; whereby the Salt Trade will not only be extended into foreign Parts, and in 'a great measure, retrieved, but such Navigation will likewise very much encourage and improve the Cheese Trade, which is the great Produce of that County, and most of it brought to London, by lessening the Land-carriage thereof to Irods-ham Bridge near Three Shillings per Tun, which is now Ten, Fifteen, and sometimes Eighteen Shillings, per Tun:

That also, by making the said River navigable, not only a much greater Quantity of Salt will be exported, by which the publick Revenue will be increased, there being a Subsidy of Five Pounds per Centum upon such Exportation, but will otherways increase Trade and Commerce, preserve the Highways, and be for the publick Good.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to make the River Weaver, in the County of Chester, navigable from Winsford Bridge to Frodsham Bridge, in the said County: And that Mr. Booth, Mr. Norris, and Mr.

Leigh, of Addington, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

That the Committee, ,to whom the Petition of Elizabeth Gomeldon, Widow, was referred, have, pursuant to the Order of this House, dated the fourteenth Day of January instant, examined the Facts; and find the same to be as followqth; vi,z.

That the Petitioner, being married to William Gomeldon J Esquire, did convey ail her Lands of Inheritance in the Counties of Kent, Middlesex, Nottingham, and London, of about the yearly Value of Seven hundred Pounds, to Thomas Gomeldon, Father of the said William, and his Heirs; and, in Consideration thereof, the said Thomas Gomeldon did, by Indenture of the Fifteenth of January 1700, grant to the Petitioner Three several Rent-charges, of Three hundred Pounds, Two'hundred Pounds, and One hundred Pounds, for her Jointure, to be payable out of several Lands in Kent; and, if he paid Two thousand Pounds, as therein is mentioned, and all Arrears of the said Annuity of Two hundred Pounds, then the said Annuity to cease;

That by Indenture, dated the 23d of May 1702, one George Peeke, in whom the Residue of a Term of 500 Years, of Lands of the said Thomas Gomeldon, was vested, assigned over the same, by the Direction of the said Thomas, to Meliora, one of the Daughters of the said Thomas, and Henry Sazvyer Esquire, in Trust for the better securing the Payment of the said Two Annuities of Two hundred Pounds, and One hundred Pounds, and for raising Fourteen hundred and Six hundred Pounds, to make good all Arrears thereof:

That, in 1702, the said Thomas Gomeldon died:

That, 011 the Sixth of February 1709, the said William Gomeldon died; and all the Estate of the said Thomas was limited to Richard, one other Son of the said Thomas, in Tail Male; with Remainder to Meliora, for her Life:

That, the better to protect the Petitioner's Jointure from Creditors, there was a Mortgage of Two hundred Pounds in 1677, assigned over in Trust for the Petitioner:

That Richard Gomeldon died in July 1718, without Issue; and Meliora having married with Thomas Stanley, late of Preston, the said Thomas became intitled, during the joint Lives of himself, and the said Meliora, to the Premises; and, by the Attainder of the said Thomas Stanley, who was attainted of High Treason, the said Premises are now vested in the Commissioners and Trustees for Sale of the forfeited Estates.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable Elizabeth Gomeldon, Widow, to put in her Claim before the Commissioners and Trustees for the forfeited Estates: And that Mr. Gybbon and Mr. Philip Yorke do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Quarter Sessions assembled at Hick's Hall the 13th of January 1719, w as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That several Persons of Quality, and others, have been lately, and in an unusual manner, attacked in their Coaches and Chairs, and some of them robbed, in the high Streets; and yet none of the Persons concerned in these Robberies have been taken; which is imputed to the Want of a proper and regular Watch: That there is no Law now in force for any Watch, except the Statute of Winchester, which has made no Provision between Michaelmas and Lady-day; and the Method now used is, for the Constables to appoint what Persons, and what Number of Watchmen, they think fit; and to raise and levy great Sums on the Inhabitants, under Pretence of paying them, without rendering any Account, there being no Law to compel them thereunto; and yet the Watch, so kept, is found not to be sufficient: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for regulating the Nightly Watch: And that the Lord JVII-liamPowlctt, Mr. Comptroller, Mr. Freman, Mr. At-, torney General, Mr. Solicitor General, Mr. Farrer, Mr. Lowndes, Sir Samuel Lcnnard, Mr. Broderick, Mr. Philip Yorke, and Sir Nathanael Mead, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Tradesmen, Freeholders, Farmers, and Inhabitants, of the Tow n of Loughborough, in the County of Leicester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, if the Bill for making the 'River Derwent navigable should pass into a Law, it will be very prejudicial to the Petitioners, by lessening the Rent of their Lands, and depriving them of the Advantage of uttering the Produce thereof to the Land Carriers who pass in great numbers through their Town from the County of Derby, and other adjacent Towns, to London; but, if the River be made navigable, they will send their Commodities by Water to London, and the Carriers forced to leave off their Employment: And praying to be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Bill for making the River Derwent, in the County of Derby, navigable, is committed.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Grand Jury, at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace held at Southzcell, in and for the Soke of Southwell, in the County of Nottingham, the Fourteenth Day of January 1719, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the making the River Dertcent, in the County of Derby, navigable, will be very prejudicial to their Country, by spoiling their Markets, and hindering them of the Supply of Salt, and other Commodities, which they are stored with by great Numbers of Carriers out of Derbyshire, Cheshire and Lancashire, who buy and take from them Malt, Corn, Hops, and other Things their Country yields, which they shall be deprived of, and a great many Persons, and their Families, impoverished, if the said Navigation take Effect: And praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred' to the Committee, to whom the Bill for making the River Denvent, in the County of Derby, navigable, is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, if they think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Bill for making the River Dem ent, in the County of Derby, navigable, is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard by their Counsel, before the said Committee, if they think fit.

Mr. Secretary Craggs presented to the House, pursuant Irish Linen to their Address to his Majesty, the Representation to his Manu*acture. Majesty from the Trustees of the Linen Manufacture in Ireland: -

And the Title thereof was read.

The said Representation is as follows; *ciz.

To the King’s most Excellent Majesty;

The humble Representation of the Trustees of the Linen Manufacture of Ireland, in behalf of the Protestants of that Kingdom concerned in the said Manufacture,

Sheweth,

THAT the People of Ireland always enjoyed the Liberty of exporting their Woollen Manufacture, until th§

Year 1699 5 when a Law was made in England toTestr&iii the Exportation thereof: '

But the Parliament of England was. so sensible of the great Loss and Damage the People of Ireland must there-byJsustain, that, before they made a Law against theif Woollen Manufacture- 'they thought it proper to invito and encourage them to apply their Industry to' that of the Linen:

Accordingly the Lords of England, on the Ninth of June 169 b, addressed his late Majesty King William in the following Words;

" We, the Loixis Spiritual* and Temporal, in Parliament assembled, do humbly represent unto your Ma-fC jesty, That the growing Manufacture of Cloth in Ireland, both by the Cheapness of all Sorts of Necessaries " for Life and Goodness of Materials for making all " manner of Cloth, doth invite your Subjects of England, with their Families and Servants, to leave their " Habitations to settle there, to the increase of the Woollen Manufacture in Ireland; which makes your loyal " Subjects in this Kingdom very apprehensive, that the " further Growth of it may greatly prejudice the said c< Manufacture here; by which the Trade of this Nation,

" and the Value of Lands, will very much decrease, and " the Numbers of the People be much lessened here:

" Wherefore we do most humbly beseech your most " Sacred Majesty, That your Majesty would be pleased,

" in the mostpublick and effectual Way that may be, to " declare to all your Subjects of Ireland, That the " Growthand Increase of the Woollen Manufacture there,

" hath long, and will ever be looked upon with great u Jealousy by all your Subjects of this Kingdom; and,

" if not timely remedied, may occasion very strict Laws " totally to prohibit and suppress the same; and, on the " other hand, if they turned their Industry and Skill to " the settling and improving the Linen Manufacture, for " which generally the Lands of that Kingdom are very " proper, they shall receive all Countenance, Favour,

" and Protection, from your Royal Influence, for the " Encoirragement and Promoting of the said Linen Manufacture, to all the Advantage and Profit that Kingdom can be capable of."

And the Commons of England, on the 30th of June 1698, likewise addressed his said Majesty in the Words following;

" We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects*

" the Commons, in Parliament assembled, being very " sensible, that the Wealth and Power of this Kingdom " do, in a great measure, depend on the preserving the " Woollen Manufacture, as much as possible, intire to " this Realm, think it becomes us, like our Ancestors,

" to be jealous of the Establishment and the Increase " thereof elsewhere, and to use our utmost Endeavours " to prevent it:

3 P " And

2 j8 26° — 27° Januarii. A. 1719-

u And therefore we cantaot without Trouble observe, ic That Ireland, which is dependent on, and protected " by, England, in the Enjoyment of all they have, and " which is so proper for die Linen Manufacture, the Establishment and Growth of which there, would be so en-u riching to themselves, and profitable to England, should " of late, apply itself to the Woollen Manufacture, to " the great Prejudice of the Trade of this Kingdom; u and so unwillingly promote the Linen Trade, which u would benefit both them and us:

" The Consequence whereof will necessitate your Par-u liament of England to interpose, to prevent the Mischief that threatens us; unless your Majesty, by your " Authority, and great Wisdom, shall find means to secure the Trade of England, by making your Subjects " of Ireland to pursue the joint Interest of both Kingdoms:

u And we do most humbly implore your Majesty’s 4t Protection and Favour in this Matter; and that you {t will make it your Royal Care, and use the utmost u Diligence, to hinder the Exportation of Wool from " Ireland, except to be imported hither; and for the dis-u couraging the Woollen Manufacture, and encouraging " the Linen Manufacture, in Ireland; to which we shall " always be ready to give our utmost Assistance."

And his said Majesty King William, by his Letter of the 29th of June 1698, to the then Lords Justices of Ireland, reciting the said Address of the House of Lords, directed and required them to take the most effectual Care that might be to countenance and encourage his Subjects of Ireland to turn their Industry and Skill to the Linen Manufacture; and to avoid all Occasions of giving Jealousy to his Majesty’s Subjects of England, by carrying on a Trade of the Woollen Manufacture prejudicial to them:

And, by a Second Letter of the Seventh of July following, reciting the said Address of the Commons, his Majesty did re-enforce his former Order.

Depending on these Assurances from the King, Lords, and Commons, of England, the People of Ireland betook themselves to the Linen Manufacture; and, though they laboured under many difficulties incident to new Undertakings, yet, the Parliaments of England and Great Britain having passed several Laws for their Encouragement, they at length brought the same to some Degree of Perfection; and, their Linens being, for the most part, proper for Staining, Stamping, and Printing, a great Part of them are employed that way.

That, several Petitions having been lately preferred to the House of Commons of Great Britain, complaining of the Use of printed or stained Linens, the said Trustees beg Leave most humbly to lay before Your most Sacred Majesty;

That, there being no Prospect of any other Market for those Linens which are now printed or stained, in case the Use of them should be prohibited in Great Britain, the Hands employed in them must necessarily stand idle; which would reduce many Thousand Protestant Families to a starving Condition, and oblige many others to leave the Kingdom:

This would greatly weaken the Protestant Interest of Ireland\ and be a Means to lessen your Majesty’s Revenues there.

May it therefore please your most Sacred Majesty to take into your Royal Consideration the Case of your Subjects of Ireland concerned in the Linen Manufacture; and recommend the same to the Parliament of Great Britain, in such manner as may most effectually secure to them the full Enjoyment of their ' Linen Trade; which they engaged in on the Encouragement and Assurances so solemnly given by the Crown and Parliament of England.

Ordered, That the said Representation be referred to the Gmnmittee of the whole 1 louse, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others, Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, is referred.

A PETITION of the Gentlemen, Tradesmen, Po£ Derwent makers, and Inhabitants, of the Tow n of Burslcm, Navigation, in the County of Stafford, in behalf of themselves, and many Hundreds of Families depending upon the said Trade of Pot-makitig in the said Town, and Places near adjoining, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the making Pots in and near the said Town is so considerable a Trade, that several Hundreds of Families gain their Livelihoods by the same: That the said Trade is very much improved; and the Makers, and Dealer^ therein, send very great Quantities of that Commodity by Water-carriage to several Markets; and to have great Quantities ofheavy Commodities, useful in the said Trade, to be brought up the the River Trent, to Witne Ferry;

That, for want of another convenient Wharf, divers Goods lie so long on the Wharf, before they can be carried down, or brought up to them, that the Owners cannot make such % Returns as otherwise they might; being forced to pay excessive Rates for Carriage, to the Ruin of divers Families, and the Danger of losing the said Trade: That the making the River Derwent navigable will be of very great Use to the said Trade, by affording a more speedy and cheap Conveyance of Goods: And praying, That the Bill for making the River Derwent navigable may pass.

Upon the Petition of the Justices, Gentlemen, Freeholders, Farmers, and other Inhabitants, of the Parish of Cammencell, in the County of Surry, referred also to the said Committee, the Committee have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find it to be as followeth; viz.

It appeared to the Committee, That two Acts of Parliament passed, in the Fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign; the one for amending the Roads from the City of London to the Town of East Grinstead, in the County of Sussex; and the other for repairing the Highways leading from the Stones End of Kent-street, in the Parish of Saint George's Sout/ruarke, in the County of Vol. 19.

Surry, to the Lime-kiln in East Greenwich, near Black-heath, and Lewisham Church, in the County of Kent, as in the Petition is set forth;

And the Petitioners0 produced several Witnesses, to prove the Allegations of their Petition; viz.

Aaron James, of Cammerwell, said, That the Inhabitants of Cammenvell, and others, cannot come to London, and return Home, w ithout paying to one or the other of Two Turnpikes erected on thg Road leading from Westminster Ferry, in the Parish of Lambeth, through the Towns of Newington, Cammeiwell, and Beckham, to New Cross, in the County of Kent:

That the said Road is above Four Miles in Length; and is very much used by the Quality, Gentry, and others* travelling to Tunbridge, Canterbury, Dover, and all the Parts of Kent, for avoiding going over the Bridge* and on the Stones, through London and Southwark; and all such Passengers pay to both the said Turnpikes, though they receive but little Benefit by the one, and none by the other, by reason those Road are not included in the said Acts to be amended thereby:

That he has known the said Road above Twenty Years; which was always repaired by the Overseers of the Highways; and that the Parishes of Newington and Cammer-well have always done their Statute-work, and last Year paid a Rate of Three Pence in the Pound over and above; yet the said Roads are so very bad, that it is dangerous to pass through the same in the Winter, by reason of the great Numbers of Cattle, Coaches, Carts, and other Carriages, using it; and, in particular, by the great Quantities of Gravel brought from Newington last Year, by the Trustees, for Amendment of the Surry Roads, beingabout 8,000 Loads.

Robert Symes and Robert Butcher affirmed, That what Aaron James had said was true: And the Petitioners had several other Witnesses to prove the same; but the Committee did not think it necessary to examine any more* being satisfied, that the Petitioners had made good the Allegations of their Petition.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term granted by an Act, passed in the Fourth Year of his Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highways leading from the Stones End in Kent-street, to the Lime-kilns in East Greenwich, near Blackheathy and to Lewisham Church, being the Tunbridge Road, in the County of Kent: And that Colonel Fane,

Sir Roger Bradshaigh, Mr. Serjeant Pengelly, and Mr.

Halsey, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen, who are to prepare and bring in, the said Bill, That they do provide for repairing and amending the Highways and Roads leading from Westminster Ferry, in the Parish of Lambeth, in the County of Surry, to New Cross, in the Parish of Deptford, in the County of Kent.

A Petition of Wriothesley D u ke of Bedford, Henry Earl of Lincoln, William Lord Bishop of Ely, and others, Noblemen and Gentlemen, Owners of Lands lying and being in the Counties of Cambridge, Huntingdon, Lincoln, Norfolk, Northampton, and Isle of Ely, whose Lands are drained by the Chanel and Out-fall belonging to the Port of Wisbich, in the said Isle of Ely, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That that Part of Great Britain, being a low and flat Country, is, on that Account, naturally subject to Inundations by Floods of Water; That, by reason thereof, great Sums of Money have been, and are annually, expended in raising, repairing, and strengthening, the Banks on each Side the River, from the City of Peterborough to the Town of Wisbich, and from thence through Wisbich River to Seaward, which is the chiefest Out-fall the Petitioners have: That the irnbank-ing the Salt Marshes has been the principal Cause of the Chanels being choaked up: That the imbanking any more will intirely destroy their Out-fall to Sea; by which means above One hundred thousand Acres of fruitful Land will continually lie underWater, and Thousands of Families be reduced to Poverty; and praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the Inning or Imbanking any more Marshes, which lie on either Side the said Chanel, from Wisbich Seaw ard.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Merchants, Sailors, and other Traders and Artificers, in the ancient Town and Port of Wisbich, within the Isle of Ely, and County of Cambridge, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors in the North Gate, in Chester, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands more confined in the several Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, through their Losses and Misfortunes, are brought into miserable Confinement, wherein they continually suffer, through the Severity of their Creditors; and many of them die for Want; being willing to deliver up their All to their Creditors: Ana praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the insolvent Debtors in the Prisons of Ludgate, Newgate, Wood-street, and the Poultry Compters, in the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are willing to deliver up their All to their Creditors, upon Oath, provided they may have their Liberty; yet Multitudes of them have perished through Hunger and Want, which the rest of them expect to do: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The Lord William Powlett reported, from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Dr. Thomas Green, Vicar,. Philip Davis and Giles Ilatris> Churchwardens, as also of the Vestry and Inhabitants* of the Parish of Saint Mar this in the Fields, in the County of Middlesex, 10

was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where it was read; and is as follows: viz.

That the Committee, in pursuance of the Order of the House, of the 25th Instant, have taken the said Petition into Consideration; and, upon examining James Hanly, Mason, Job Biggiter, Carpenter, Nathanael Lidgbird, Bricklayer, and other able and experienced Workmen, do find the Matter thereof to be as follows; viz.

That the said Church is very old and decayed; and, being built with Brick and Rubble, is incapable of being repaired; and thereby become so ruinous, that the same is apprehended to be in great Danger of falling:

That the Piers are split, and obliged to be cramped with Iron to support them; the Roof is very much decayed; and the Timber Piers, that support it, are sunk Six Inches lower than their first Basis; and the principal Rafters lean very much; and, by the Opinion of the aforesaid Workmen, the said Church cannot be supported by Repair:

And the Committee further find, That the Floor of the said Church is, in some Places, Four or Five Foot low’er than the Ground on the Outside of the same; by which means ’tis very damp and unwholesome.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for rebuilding the Parish Church of Saint Martins in the Fields, in the City of Westminster, at the Charge of the Inhabitants of the said Parish: And that the Lord William Powlett, Mr. Nicholas, Mr. Farm', and Mr. Comp* troller, do prepare, and bring in, the same

Colonel Midleton reported, from the Committee, to Montro* whom the Petition of the Magistrates, and remanent Town In* Members, of the Town Council of Montrose, in Scotland, Pryveffieut* was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where it was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and, upon the Examination of Mr.

Robert Read and Mr. John Meden, it appeared;

That the Borough of Montrose is well situate for Trade, and has a good and safe Harbour, to which Ships* of great Burthen can easily enter, when many other Ports are inaccessible:

That there are Two Hills which defend the said Harbour from the North-west and Easterly Winds; which Hills have suffered very much by late Storms; and, if the same be not speedily fortified, the Harbour will be soon ruined: '

That it also appeared to the Committee, That the Borough is in great Want of fresh Water; for the Water that is most used there is so bad, that it often brings Diseases on the Inhabitants, and discourages many from residing in the same, who would otherwise be induced to live there, the Town being very commodiously and pleasantly situated:

That the said Borough carries on a Trhde with Norway; to which they export the Product of Scotland; and, in Return thereof, import Money, Iron, and Timber; which Trade would be much improved and increased, if a convenient Dock wras made there:

That it likewise appeared to the said Committee, That the publick Stock of the Borough is very inconsiderable, and scarce sufficient to pay the Fees of the Servants thereof, and the necessary and unavoidable Contingences of the Borough; and therefore insufficient to do or maintain any of the aforesaid Works, w ithout some other Provision for that Purpose.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for laying a Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-sixth Part of a Peny Sterling, upon every Pint of Ale or Beer that shall be sold or vended within the Town of Montrose, and Privileges thereof, for preserving the Harbour thereof, and

Mr. FarrerT according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, who were to consider of that Part of his Majesty’s Speech, wdiicfi relates to the publick Debts, the Proposals of the Corporation of the Governor and Company of Merchants of Great Britain trading to the South Seas, and oth^r Parts of America; and for encouraging the Fishery; and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Proposals, and Resolution of the Committee, were read; and are as follow'; viz.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled:

The Corporation of the Governor and Company of Merchants of Great Britain trading to the South Seas, and other Parts of America; and for encouraging the Fishery; having under their Consideration how they may be most serviceable to his Majesty, and his Government; and to shew their Zeal and Readiness to concur in the great and honourable Design of reducing the National Debts, in such manner as may be consistent with, and for the Support of, Parliamentary Credit; do humbly apprehend, That, if the public Debts, and Annuities, mentioned in the annexed Estimate, were taken into, and made Part of, the capital Stock of the said Company, it would greatly contribute to that most desirable End: Which Debts, and Annuities, may he comprehended under the general Heads following; viz.

Therefore they do humbly propose, That the said Company may be permitted to enlarge their present Capital, by taking in the said Annuities, and Debts at any time or times until Lady-day 1721, on the Terms and Conditions following; viz.

1. That the said Annuities be taken into the said Company either by Purchase, or voluntary Subscription of the Proprietors thereof, and without any Compulsion on them, at such Price and Prices as shall be agreed between the Company, and the Proprietors of those Annuities.

2. That for the Annuities for 99 Years, or 96 Years, for every Five Pounds per Annum taken into the Company, there be £.5. per Annum added to the Company’s present Annuity, and £. 100. to their capital Stock, being after the Rate of 20 Years Purchase.

3. That the Residue of Lottery 1710 be estimated at 14 Years Purchase, for the 23 Years due on them from Michaelmas 1719; and that the Annuities of 9 per Cent. per Annum be also estimated at 14 Years Purchase, for the 22j Years clue on them from Christmas 1719; and that there be an Addition to the Stock and Annuity of the Company proportionably, viz. £. 70. Stock, and £. 3. 10s. per Annum Annuity, for every £.5. per Annum of those Annuities which shall be taken into the Company.

4. That the said redeemable Debts be likewise taken into the said Company, either by Purchase, Subscription, or paying them oft’ by the said Company.

5. That, for all the said redeemable Debts, there be added £. 100. to the capital Stock of the said Company, for every £. 100. so taken in by them; and the like Annuity added to the Company’s present Annuity as is now payable for the Interest of those Debts.

6. That the Company be allowed, for Charges of Management for their thus to be increased Capital, so much as it now costs the Government for the Charges of paying, assigning, and accounting for, the said Debts-; or such a Proportion thereof as the Sum which shall be taken in by the Company shall bear to the whole of those Debts.

7. That the present Annuities for the Company’s present Capital, and the Annuities for the thus to be increased Capital, be continued, at the Rates aforesaid, till Midsummer 1727; and that, from and after that Time, their then Annuity for their whole capital Stock shall be actually reduced to per Cent, per Annum, and likewise be thenceforth redeemable by Parliament.

8. That the Company’s present and to be increased Allowance, for Charged of Management, do continue till their Capital be redeemed, as their present Allowances for Charges of Management are.

9. That the Annuities to the Company, for their thus to be increased Capital, be paid them weekly, as their present Annuities are; and be charged on the Funds now appropriated to the said Debts and Annuities so taken into the Company.

10. That, for the Liberty of increasing their capital Stock, as aforesaid, the Company will give and pay into his Majesty’s Exchequer, for the Service of the Publick, and to be applied for paying off the publick Debts provided for by Parliament before Christmas 1716, the Sum of

That, though the Company’s Capital is proposed not to be redeemable till Midsummer 1727; yet they do submit, That so much as shall arise by the Sinking Fund before that time may, from and after paying off such Part of the publick Debts as may be redeemed within that time, and which shall not be taken into the said Company, be applied, at the End of every Year, towards paying off, in even Hundred thousand Pounds, that Part of the Company’s Capital which carries 5 per Cent, per Annum.

12. That the said Company do further submit, That, for such of the present Exchequer Bills as the Parliament shall continue, and for such new ones as they shall em*

By Order of the General Court.

The Corporation of the Governor and Company of Merchants of Great Britain trading to the South Seas, and other Parts of America; and for encouraging the Vol. 19.

John Fellaues, Sub Governor. Charles Deputy Governor.

This Corporation, further to manifest their Zeal, and earnest Desire, to contribute their utmost, to the reducing, and paying oft’ the publick Debts, crave Leave to offer the following Explanations and Amendments to their said Proposal; vie.

l st. As to the Sixth Article of their said former Proposal, wherein they have humbly desired to be allowed, for Charges of Management for their to be increased Capital, so much as it now costs the Government for the Charges of paying, assigning, and accounting for, the said Debts, or such Proportion thereof as the Sum which shall be taken* in by the Company shall bear to the Whole of those Debts;

They offer, by way of Explanation of that Article* That the Allowances therein mentioned are not to exceed a Proportion to the Allowances they now have, by Act of Parliament, on their present Capital, for that Purpose.

2dly, That whereas, w» the Seventh Article of their said Proposal, it is mentioned, That the Annuities for the Copqfeiny’s present and to be increased Capital be continued, at the Hates therein mentioned, till Midsummer 1727: and that,: from and after that time, their then Annuity on their whole Capital shall be actually reduced to Four Pounds per Cent, per Annw)lr and likewise be from tiienccforth redeemable by Parliament;

They do now humbly offer, That, if this House do think it more for the Interest of the Publick, that, in lieu of the said Seventh Article, all the Sums to be taken into the Company’s Capital, in pursuance of their Proposal, shall be redeemable by Parliament, from and after Midsummer 1724, in Sums not less than Half a Million at a time, they do consent thereto-, 3<Jly, And whereas, by the Tenth Article of their Proposal, they offered, for the Liberty of increasing their capital Stock, as is therein aforesaid. That they would give and pay into his Majesty’s Exchequer, for the Service of the Publick, the Sum of Three Millions and a Half;

They now humbly offer, that over and above the said Three Millions and a Half, they will further give and pay into his Majesty’s Exchequer, for the Use of the Publick, by Four equal Quarterly Payments, on the Days mentioned in their said former Proposal, Half a Million more, certain; and also upon all the said Annuities, for certain Terms of Years, which this Company shall take into their Capital Stock before the First Day of March One thousand Seven , hundred Twenty-one, after the Rate of Four Years and a Halfs Purchase, by Four Quarterly Payments; which, if all the said Annuities betaken into the said Company, will amount to the Sum of Three millions Five hundred sixty-seven thousand Five hundred and Three Pounds, or thereabouts; to which being added the said Three millions and a Half, artd the further Sum of Half a million, will amount, in the Whole, to the Sum of Seven millions Five hundred sixty-seven thousand Five hundred Pounds, or thereabouts.

4thly, That whereas, in the Eleventh Article of their former Proposal, they did submit, That so much as shall arise by the Sinking Fund before Midsummer 1727, may, from and after paying oft’such Part of the publick Debts as may be redeemed within that time, and Which shall not be taken into this Company, be applied, at the End of every Year, towards paying off, in even One hundred thousand Pounds, that Part of tire Company’s Capital, which carries Five Pounds per Gent, per, Annum;

They do humbly offer, in lieu thereof, That, if this* honourable House think tit to make their to be increased Capital redeemable at Midsummer 1724, that the said Sinking Fund may, till that time, be applied half-yearly to the paying off that Part of the Company's to he increased Capital, which is to carry Five Pounds per Cent. per Annum.

5thly, As to the Twelfth Article of this Company’s former Proposal, relating to the circulating of One million in Exchequer Bilk, they humbly offer this Explanation;

That their Intention is, That until their whole Capital be reduced to Four Pounds per Cent, per Annum, they will circulate One million in Exchequer Bills gvvtfw; and likewise pay the Interest for that Million, so as no other Exchequer Bills be issued than what shall be circulated by the Credit of the Exchequer, without the Aid of Subscription or Contract.

6thly, And lastly, That this honourable House maybfr folly satisfied of the sincere Intentions of this Company to use their best Endeavours to take in all the said Annuities for 99 and 96 Years, which amount to Six hundred sixty-seven thousand Seven hundred and Five Pounds Eight Shillings and One Penypej' Annum; this Company do further humbly offer to give and pay into his Majesty’s Exchequer, for the Service of the Publick, by Four equal Quarterly Payments, One Year’s Purchase upon all such of those Annuities as shall happen not to come into the Company’s Capital within the Time aforesaid.

And whereas this Company is very sensible, that the Prosperity of this Nation does greatly depend upon the discharging the publick Debts; a Motive which induced them to makfc the First Propositions of this publick and beneficial Nature; they do humbly submit these Explanations and Amendments to this honourable House; flattering themselves that the Readiness and Cheaduiness which engaged them, so much earlier than any other Society, to endeavour to reduce that great Debt under which this Nation is oppressed, will entitle them to the Favour and Preference of this House; since they are willing, and do hereby declare they are ready, to undertake this great Work upon w hatever Perms may be offered by any other Company.

By Order of the General Court,

1 February 1719. John Fellorwes, Sub Governor.

Charles Joye, Deputy Governor.

A Petition of Thomas Warburton Esquire, Ann his Wife, and George their Son, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner Thomas Warburton hath, at great Expence, made a Brine Pit, and a Rock-salt Pit, both which lie upon the River Weaver; and hath erected Buildings necessary for boiling, curing, and storing, his Salt, made of Brine; all which lie so contiguous to the River intended to be made navigable, that, if any Part of the Soil be cut between his Works and the River, or the Water brought to a Depth to carry Bbats or Barges, the said Works must of Necessity be ruined, being worth £20,000. and in the Jointure of the Petitioner Ann: And praying, That the Bill for making the River Weaver navigable may not pass; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against the same.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for making the River Weaver navigable from Winsford Bridge to Frodsham Bridge, in the County of Chester, be read a Second time.

A Petition of Charles Cholmondley, of Vale RoyalI, in the County of Chester, Esquire, was presented to the House and read; setting forth, That, should the Bill for making the River Weaver navigable pass, it would cause a great Quantity of the Petitioner’s Meadow-grounds, lying on both Sides the said River, to be wholly laid under Water: That the Petitioner cannot dispose of the Uplands of any of the Farms all along the said River, without his Meadow-grounds to use with the same; which will, by that means, be utterly spoiled and destroyed, as also a Salt-work which his late Uncle erected at Over: And praying to be heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for making the River Weaver navigable horn Winsford Bridge to Frodsham Bridge, in the County of Chester, be read a Second time.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for making the River JVeaver navigable from Winsford Bridge to Frodsham Bridge, in the County of Chester, be read a Second time.

Hertford "li >TR. Freman reported, from the Committee, to

Road*. IVl whom the Petition of the Justices of the Peace

of the County of Hertford, at the General Quarter Sessions, and of divers other Gentlemen and Freeholders of the said County, relating to the Highways in the said County, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the He--port in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee having taken into Consideration the said Petition; and examined several Witnesses, to prove the Allegations therein contained;

It appeared, That the Trustees in the late Act of Parliament, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for continuing the Acts formerly made for Repairing of the Highways in the County of Hertford, have borrowed £ 1,400. and expended the same, and divers other considerable Sums, in repairing the said Highways:

That the Money arising from the Toll has not been sufficient to discharge the said Debt of £. 1,400. borrowed upon the Credit of the said Act, but there remains 200. unpaid, which is now demanded; and must be paid out of the First Money arising out of the said Toll:

It also appeared, That the said Roads are in a vary

bad and ruinous Condition, notwithstanding the great Sums of Money expended in repairing the same, and although the Statute-work has been duly performed:

That the said Act is very near expiring; and, unless the same be continued, and some further Addition thereto, the said Highways will become un passable.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for

continuing the Acts formerly made for repairing the Highways in the County of Hert ford; and for making the said Acts more effectual: And that Mr. Freman, Mr. Northey, and Sir Thomas Sebright, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Wearing A Petition of the Bay-makers, and other Woollen

printed Calli- Manufacturers, in Bucking, Braintry, Coggcshalt, and coes, &c, Witham, in the County of Essex, on behalf of themselves,

and many Thousands of Poor employed under them, was presented to the House, and read: setting forth, That the Petitioners Trade is wholly in Woollen Manufactures exported to foreign Markets; in Return for which, great Quantities of Bullion, W ines, and other valuable Merchandizes, which pay great Customs to the Crown, are brought into this Kingdom: That, should the Wearing of Callicoes, and printed Linens, be prohibited, the Price of Wool will be thereupon raised, and the Petitioners Goods too dear for foreign Markets; which will induce them to wear Callicoes, instead of our Manufactures; and their Trade will be entirely ruined: And praying, That the Wearing of printed Callicoes and linens may not be prohibited.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and others,

Freemen, and belonging to the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcester, and other Petitions; are referred.

A Petition of the insolvent Debtors in Hertford County Insolvent Gaol, in behalf of themselves, and Thousands more in Deblor‘* the respective Gaols in this Kingdom, was presented to, the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, through numerous Misfortunes, are reduced, and brought i into Confinement; whereby they suffer unspeakable Calamities and Miseries, through which they are subject to daily Want and Necessities, and not in a Capacity to make satisfaction tQ their Creditors: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition dolie upon the Table.

Mr. Hampden reported from the Committee, to whom Importing the Petition of the Inhabitants of Ivmghoe, Slapton, and Straw lUts, Eddlesborough, Parishes and Places adjacent, in the *c‘ County of Bucks; and other Petitions, were referred; the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to, report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the ClerkV j

Table: W’here the same, and the Resolution thereupon, j

were read; and are as follow; viz. J

.That the Committee have taken the said Petitions into Consideration; and, upon examining Joseph Parrott,

Thomas Birch, John Robbins, and Samuel Turner, do find the Matter thereof to be as follow s;

That great Numbers of Poor have been, for many Years, employed in manufacturing Straw into Hats, and other useful Things; w*hereby they have supported themselves, and large Families:

That, of late Years, the said Trade has very much decreased; which has been occasioned by the Importation 1

of large Quantities of Hats, for Women, from Leghorn; and Chips, Shavings, and Plats, from several foreign*

Parts; whereby the said Manufacturers are reduced to Poverty and Want, and become chargeable to the seve- \

ral Parishes to which they belong. .<

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the great Importation of Shavings, Chips, and Plat,* ,

for Hats, from Holland, and of Hats from Leghornj is very prejudicial to the Manufacturers of Straw of this Kingdom; and has been, and is, the Occasion of a very great Decay in that Trade.

The said Resolution being read a Second time; j

An Amendment w'as proposed to be made therein, by leaving out " Holland, and Hats from Leghorn," anti, instead thereof, to insert " foreign Parts

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That the great Importation of Shavings, Chips, and Plat, for Ilats, from foreign Parts, is very prejudicial to the Manufacturers of Straw of this Kingdom; and has been, and is, the Occasion of a very great Decay in that Trade.

Mr. Farrer, according to Order, reported, from the Ways ani j Committee of the whole House, w ho were to consider *icans' j further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read: And the said Resolutions are as follow'; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, tow ards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, in this Session of Parliament, a Power be given for applying any Sums, not exceeding Two hundred thousand Seven hundred Thirty-seven Pounds Fourteen Shillings Nine Pence Farthing, out of the clear Produce of the Forfeitures for Treason, arisen, or to arise, into the Receipt of his Majesty’s Exchequer, over and above the Salaries, and other Charges, payable for the Recovery of the said Forfeitures.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty in this Session of Parliament, Duty be laid upon all Silver Plate to be made in Great Britain; and an addi-3 . tidnal

Geo. I.

6° — -8° Fe

tional Duty upon all Silver Plate to be imported into the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That the Duty upon Silver Plate in Great Britain be after the Rate of Six Pence for every Ounce Troy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty upon Silver Plate to be imported be after the Rate of Six Pence for every Ounce Troy, over and above the present Duties, payable on the Importation of the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duties upon Plate be granted to his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, redeemable by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a yearly Fund, not exceeding Thirteen thousand Pounds, be established, and charged upon the said Duties on Plate, to pay out of the same an Interest, not exceeding Four Pounds per Cent, per Annum, for a Sum, not exceeding Three hundred and Twelve thousand Pounds, to be raised by Sale of Annu ities, for his Majesty’s Supply, until the said yearly Fund shall be redeemed by Parliament

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Standard of White Plate, to be made for the future, be reduced to Eleven Ounces, and Two Peny-weight fine, and Eighteen Peny-weight Alloy, as formerly.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Draw back upon all British Hops exported to Ireland be taken off.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill, or Bills, be brought in, pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Farrer, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Chancellor of the Duchy, Mr. Solicitor General, Mr. Clayton, Mr. Lowndes, and Mr. Charles Stanhope, do prepare, and bring in, the said Bill or Bills.

Ouze Navi- 1 The Lord Hmchinbrooke reported, from the Committee, gation. to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and other Inhabitants, of the County of Huntingdon; and several other Petitions relating to the River Owe; were referred; the Mutter, as it appeared to them; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee have, in pursuance of the Orders of the House, taken the said Petitions into Consideration ;.

And, by the Testimony of Sir Edward Lawrence, Mr. Henry Ashley, Mr. William Man, Mr. Thomas Darwood, and Mr. Henry Allpress, the Matter appeared to be as follows;

That the River Ouze, which falls into the Sea at or pear king's Lynn, in the County of Norfolk} by reason of draining the Great J^yql of the Fens, and of the Decay of a certain Work, wl^ich was built on the said River, a little below St. Ives, commonly called St. Ives Stanch, is become so shallow at Overcoat St. Ives, and other Places, that Boats and Lighters, even in times of ordinary Waters, cannot pass up or down the said River without great Difficulty, Loss of Time, and long Voyages; ana, in times of low Waters, and dry Weather, cannot pass at all up or down the said River, but lie Three Months at a time for Want of Passage:

It also appeared to the Committee, That the said River becoming worse every Year, a great Number of Poor are unemployed; and the Price of Freight of Coals, Salt, and other Commodities, raised much higher than when the River was navigable, and the Passage without interruption:

And it further appeared to the Committee, That in dry Seasons, when there is no Passage on the said River for Boats, Gentlemen, and other Persons, in the Country near the said River, cannot be supplied, at any Rates, with the aforesaid Goods; to their great Loss and Detriment.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for preserving and improving the Navigation of the River Ouze, in the Counties of Huntingdon, Bedford, and Cambridge: And that the Lord Hinchinbrooke and Mr. Farrer do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Duach’sWill, A Petition of Elizabeth Dunch, Widow, and Relict of

Edmond Dunch Esquire, deceased, on behalf of her Threo Infant Daughters, Elizabeth, Harriot, and Arabella, Dunch, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That her Majesty Queen Elizabeth, in the Year 1586, granted to William Dunch, the Petitioner’s late Husband’s Ancestor, and to the Heirs Male of his Body, forever, certain Lands in Dorchester', in the County of Oxon, which are now improved to the Value of about^.500. a Year, paving a Fee-farm Rent of £. 33. 6 s. 4d. yearly; and descended to the Petitioner’s late Husband; who, by his last Will, the collateral Line being cut off by Fines, and otherwise, gave the same to his said Three Children, after Payment of his Debts and Legacies, to be equally divided between them: That there are FoOr Persons Issue Male of the first Grantee, living; and, until the Decease of every one of them without Issue Male, the Crown could have no Title to the said Estate; and yet, if the same was absolute, the Lands would sell for more Money for the said Infants Benefit: That in a Bill, now depending, for the supplying some Defects in, and better Performance of, the Will of the said Edmond Dunch, wherein is a general and usual Saving to his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, all Right and Title to the Petitioner’s said late Husband’s Estate; which will much lessen the Price of the Lands in Dorchester, granted as aforesaid: And praying, That the said Lands may be excepted out of the said general Saving; but still reserving to his Majesty the said Fee-farm Rent.

Mr. Secretary Craggs acquainted the House, That his Majesty had been applied to; and was pleased to give his Consent, that the same may be done.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for supplying the Defects in, and better Performance of, the Will of Edmond Dunch Esquire, deceased, is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do amend the Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition.

The Order of the Day bdng read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven- Supply night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning Nine of the Clock.

Norfolk, Northampton, and Isle of Ely; and had also heard Counsel upon the Petition of Mr. Woollaston; but that Mr. Bertie and Mr. Dayrell had wayed proceeding upon their Petitions; and also reported the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk s Table;

Where the same was read: And the Report, and Resolutions, arc as follow; viz.

That the Committee have taken into Consideration the said Petition:

And, upon the Examination of John Marshall\ Anthony Lumpkin, Samuel Norris, Jacob Norris, and Dr. Haley, the Matter thereof appeared as follows.

That the Town of Wisbich is an ancient Sea Port; and that in the Trade thereof there are constantly employed above Thirty Ships of Burthen, which import Wine,

Iron, Deals, Coals, Pot Ash, Pitch, Tar, and Hemp, and divers other foreign Commodities, as well as export those of our own Manufacture; whereby there arises to his Majesty a Revenue off. 4,000. per Annum; and that there has been shipped oft* yearly, from the Port of Wisbich to London, 1,000 Tun of Oil, and 40,000 Quarter of Oats;

That, besides the aforesaid Ships, there are near Thirty smaller Vessels, from 20 to ;jo Tons each, which serve to lighten the said larger Ships, and to carry Commodities to and from the neighbouring Ports; and, by such Traffic!* and Trade, great Numbers of Seafaring Men are :. employed, which increases the Breed and Number of Seamen; there having been, from Christmas 171S to Christmas 1719, cleared at the said Port 240 Ships, or more;

It further appeared to the Committee, That the Imbanking of the Salt Marshes, which lie upon the Chanel, from JVisbich, Seaward, has been very prejudicial to the

Port:

6 Geo. I.

Port; for the Imbanking of Walton Marsh, Which is about 400 Acres, in 20 Years, has so much spoilt the Navigation of the Chanel,* that Ships that came within Fqpr Miles of the Town of Wisbich, cannot now come within Seven:

.That what preserves the River, and keeps it navigable, are the Spring Tides, which overflow' the Salt Marshes, and fill the Creeks; the Reflux of which Water falling with a great Force, adds Strength to the Ebb, and by that means carries.out the Silt, clears and keeps open the Clianel, and preserves the Navigation: And that if Sutton. Marsh, which is above 2,000 Acres, was imbanked, the Reflux of Water will be very much lessened, and therefore the Navigation spoilt, and Ships trading the re be exposed to the greatest Danger of being lost; the large Creeks in Sutton Marsh, the ,only Places of Security against the Ice, being stopped up:

That Experience has shewn, by imbanking of Salt Marshes, navigable Chanels have been choaked up in other Places; and that, by an Act of the 43d of Elizabeth, Provision /was made to prevent the Inning or Imbanking of Marshes that might spoil or prejudice the Navigation of other neighbouring Ports.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have proved the Allegations, of the said Petition.

Resolved, That the House be moved for leave to bring in a Bill to prevent the Inning or Imbanking any more Salt Marshes, which may lie on either Side the Chanel, from Wisbich, Seaward.

Ordered, That Leave he given to bring in a Bill to prevent the Inning or Imbanking any more Salt Marshes, which do lie on either Side the Chanel, from Wisbich, Seaward: And that Mr. Clarke, the Lord William Powlett, and Mr. Whitchcot, do prepare, and bring in the same.

Sir- Charles Wager reported from the Committee) to whom the Petitions of the Master Shipwrights, and Master Mastmakers in the Port of London, and the Master Carpenters, and Master Joiners of London and Westminster, were referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read: And the said Report and Resolutions are as follow'; viz.

That the Committee have, in pursuance of the Order of this House, taken into Consideration the said Petitions:

And, upon examining of Mr. Brozvnsden, a Master Shipwright, Mr. Thomas Jones, Master Mastmaker, Mr. Thomas Coram, Mr. Buxton, Mr. Acworth, Surveyor of his Majesty’s Navy, and Mr.. Mditdand, do find the Matter to be as foUqweth;

That, for many Years last past, great Quantities of Fir Timber, Fir Planks, Masts, and Deal Boards, used in Great Britain, imve been imported from Sweden and Denmark, by their own Ships and Seamen, except in the late Wars; and that, by the great Consumption thereof, those* Goods are raised to a very high Price here:

That, by an Act of the 13th and 14th of King Charles the Second, no Deal Boards or Fir Timber can be imported from Germany:

That Hollandis greatly supplied with the said Commodities, from the River Elbe, at much cheaper Rates than from Sweden, or Norway:

That it would, lessen the Prices of the said Commodities, and be of great Advantage to the Navy and Kingdom in general, for his Majesty’s Subjects to have Liberty to import Fir Timber, Masts, Fir Planks, and Boards, from any Part of Germany, being of the Growth of Germany‘m British Bottoms, paying the same Duties as from Sweden and Norway: And the Committee came to the following Resplutions;

Resolved, That it is thq Opinion of this Committee,

. VOL. 19.

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations ia their said Petitions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill to repeal so much of the Act, intituled, An Act for preventing Frauds, and regulating Abuses, in his Majesty's Customs, passed in the 13th and 14th Years of King Charles the Second, as relates to the prohibiting the Importation of Deal Boards and Fir Timber from Germany.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Importation of the said Deal Boards and Fir*

Timber be restrained to British Ships only, duly navigated according to Law.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to repeal so much of the Act, intituled, An Act for preventing Frauds and regulating Abuses, in his Majesty’s Customs, passed in the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Years of King Charles the Second, as relates to the prohibiting the Importation of Deal Boards and Fir Timber from Germany; And that Sir Charles Wager, Mr. Comptroller, and Mr. Hampden, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen who are to prepare, and bring in, the said Bill, That they do provide therein, that the Importation of the said Deal Boards and Fir Timber be restrained to British Ships only, duly navigated according to Law.

Mr. Farrer reported from the Committee of the whole Supply, House, who were to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolution which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Rlace, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, in order to lessen the Debts of this Nation, a Power be given to the Commissioners of his Majesty’s Treasury, or the High Treasurer, for the Time being, at any time or times, within One Year, and from thence to the End of the next Session of Parliament, and by such Proportions at a time, as he or they shall find to be most for the Advantage of the Publick, to make forth, or cause to be made forth, at the Exchequer, any Number of new Exchequer Bills; so as all the Principal Sums, to be Contained therein, do not, in the Whole, exceed One million, over and above the Exchequer Bills mentioned in the Proposition of the South Sea Company, accepted by the House: And that the said new Exchequer Bills may bear an Interest, not exceeding the rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum:

And that as well the Money which was advanced by the South Sea Company, for their additional Stock, by means of the late Subscriptions, towards redeeming the Lottery Annuities of the Year 1710, and doth now remain in the Exchequer; as also the Surplus Monies arising quarterly upon the several Funds called the Aggregate Fund, and the Fund of the South Sea Company, and of the Revenues charged with the Fund called the General yearly Fund; as also the Overplus of the same General Fund, w'hen such Overplus shall happen, after the sum of £.520,000. according to an Act of the Fifth Year of his Majesty’s Reign, shall be applied for discharging and cancelling such Exchequer Bills as are therein mentioned; be made a Fund, or Security, for answering all Demands of Prin^ cipal and Interest upon the said new Exchequer Bills, which shall be authorized to be made forth, as aforesaid:

And that the said Commissioners of the Treasury, or High Treasurer, for the Time being, be also impowered to issue the said new Exchequer Bills, by way of Loan, or Advance, to such Person or Persons, Corporation or

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Merchants, and Importing Commanders of Ships, of the Town of Great Yarmouth, Silk in the County of Norfolk, w as presented to the House, rom evaMt# and read; setting forth, That the said Town is become one of the most considerable in his Majesty’s Dominions from the Trade of Herrings; and, from the said Cause, the N umber of Ships belonging to the said Town is at present exceeded by no other Place but the Metropolis of the Kingdom: That the said Trade is so far supported by the Consumption of Red Herrings in the Straits, that between 30 and 40 Sale of large defensible Ships, commumbus amis, £re sent, laden with that Commodity only, to the several Ports of Italy, Sicily, and the Port of Marseilles', the Returns of which are chiefly made in Goods, the Produce of the several Countries bordering on the Mediterranean Sea: That by the Bill now depending, for repealing so much of the Act of Navigation as allows the Importation of the Products or Manufactures ,of Asia from any Port within the Straits, or Levant Seas, will not only deprive the Petitioners of a great Part of their usual Returns m Commodities, for the Produce of their Herrings, but also a like Proportion of Returns of Freight, for the lading their Ships back; which, of course, will become a Charge on the outward Freight of their Fishj and, by that means, go a great way towards the Ruin of a Trade so beneficial to Navigation: And praying, That the said Bill may not pass.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for repealing so much of an Act of Parliament, of the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act for Encouraging and Increasing of Shipping and Navigation, as allows the Importation of the Product or Manufacture of Asiairom any Port within the Straits, or Levant Seas, is committed.

A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, and Aldermen, Captives in together with the Minister, and other principal Inhabi- Morocco, tants, of the Town of Falmouth, in the County of Cornwall, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That divers Persons belonging to that Place, and Ports adjacent, are in Captivity in the Country of the Emperor of Morocco, where they live in miserable Servitude, and are under great Temptations to Apostasy from the Christian Faith: That, through extreme hard Usage, and Despair of Deliverance, many have perished; and some, to obtain their Liberty, have embraced the Mahometan Religion: And praying, That some Means may be found out for their Deliverance.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Weaver The House being acquainted, that one of the Sheriffs Navigation. of London attended at the Door;

He was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House a Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then he withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; setting forth, That the City of London and Parts adjacent, are supplied with great Quantities of Cheese, Salt, and divers other Commodities, the chief Produce of the County of Chester;

the great Charge of Land-carriage whereof doth very much enhance the Price of the said Commodities: That the making the River Weaver, in the said County, navigable from Wimford Bridge to Frodsham Bridge, will very much lessen the Price of the said Commodities, by lowering the Charge of the Carriage thereof; and will greatly tend to the Relief of the Poor of the City, and Parts adjacent: And praying, That the Bill for making the River Weaver navigable, may pass.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the ancient Market Town of Middlenich, in the County of Chester, and Proprietors of Salt-works there, and parts adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That in that; Town there are, and have been, time immemorial, Brine-pits and Salt-works, worth, to the Owners, many Thousand Pounds per Annum: That great Numbers of Hands are employed therein; but, of late, through the Expence of Land-carriage, the Trade thereof is become unprofitable, and useless; to the Impoverishment of a great Niuijbej* of Families; That, if the River Weaver was made navigable, the Carriage of Salt from that Town would be reduced from Eight Shillings to Three Shillings per Ton; and thereby the Salt Trade, in a great measure, retrieved* and extended into foreign Parts: And praying, That the Bill for making the River Wearer navigable, may pass.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for making the River Weaver navigable from Win ford Bridge to Frodsham Bridge, in the County of Chester, be read a Second time.
