I) it to A Petition of divers Merchants, and Dealers in Salt, in the City of London, w as presented to the House, and rear); setting forth. That the Petitioners are concerned in divers Refineries, or Salt-works, for the Refining of

Rock Salt, and making Salt from thence, in several Parts of the Counties of Essex,' Suffolk, Devon, Somerset, and South Wales: That great Quantities of Rock Salt, w herewith the said Refineries are wholly supplied, are gotten in the County of Chester: That the Land-carriage of such Rock Salt to Frodsham Bridge, the usual Place of Delivery to be shipped off, is commonly more than double the prime Cost thereof; which is a great Discouragement to that Trade: That by making the River Weaver navigable, above 150 per Cent. will be saved in the Carriage of the said Rock Salt; And praying, That the Bill for making the River Weaver navigable, may pass.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for making the River Weaver navigable from Winsford Bridge to Frodsham Bridge, in the County of Chester, be read a Second time.

Mr. Abercrombie reported, from the Committee, to Bruntisland whom the Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council Town Re-of the Burgh of Bruntisland, was referred, the Matter, venue, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where it was read; and is as follows; viz.

That, the Committee having taken into consideration the said Petition; and having examined several Witnesses, to prove the Facts therein contained; it appeared;

That the Port and Harbour of Bruntisland, is the common Port of Safety to all British and foreign Ships which happen to be put up the Firth by Storm, or contrary Winds:

That the said Harbour is capable of receiving Ins Majesty’s Ships of War, for cleansing or careening; there being Twenty-six Feet Water at Spring Tides:

That the said Harbour, together with the Church, and the Town-house, or Prison-house, are so ruinous, that the common Revenues of the Town are so far from affording a sufficient Fund for defraying the Charge of the said Works, that the said Burgh is almost sunk in Debt, and upon the Brink of Ruin, unless timely relieved.

A Petition of some Creditors, on behalf of themselves, aiuf other Creditors of the Royal African Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, in 1716, did advance and lend to the said Company the Sum of ^.50,000. upon a Mortgage of all their Forts and Settlements, quick and dead Stock, to enable them to buy (Joods and Merchandize io carry on their Trade to Africa, which was at that time in great Danger of ..being lost: That the said Company did thereupon send out to their several Factories such Quantities of Goods as gave the Petitioners great Hopes would have been sufficient, by the Returns that might be reasonably expected, fully to have paid their Debt: fhdl the Petitioners have applied so long to the said Company, for discharging their said Debt, without receiving the least Satisfaction, that they are in Despair of ever recovering the same: That the Petitioners are credibly informed the said Company, by opening private Books of Subscriptions, do intend to transfer their Trade, Forts and Settlements, quick and dead Stock, to Persons unknow n to the Petitioners; by which they apprehend their Debts will be rendered precarious: And praying Relief.

Resolved, That the Petition be rejected.

A Petition, of several Importers of Shavings and Plats for Hats, and Makers of the said Hats, in behalf of themselves, and Thousands of poor Families employed, in this Kingdom, in manufacturing the same, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the making of the said Hats was at first a foreign Invention; and they were made abroad, and brought into this Nation; the making the same now being almost intirely in the Hands of the English Subjects, and employs many Thousands of poor Families; besides, the said Commodities are purchased abroad with the Woollen, and other the Manufactures of this Kingdom: That should any Restraint be laid upon the said Trade, it will not only be the Ruin of the many poor Families which arc employed therein, but will also be a very great Discouragement to our foreign Trade: And praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against any Law which may pass for preventing the Importation of Shavings, Chips, or Plats, into this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of dlvei's Merchants, Proprietors of Salt, Duty onSalt, and Fishermen concerned in curing Fish, w-as presehted to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by an Act, passed in the Fifth Year of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for recovering the Credit of the British Fishery in foreign Parts; and for better securing the Duties on Salt; whereby it was Enacted, That the

Curers of Fish should, from the 24th Day of June last, be allowed to import foreign Salt for curing Fish for Exportation for foreign Markets, without paying any Duty for the same, except the Customs payable upon the Importation thereof, under certain Restrictions and Directions in the same Act set forth; but, by the said Act, no Provision is* made, or Directions given to the Proprietors of foreign Salt imported before the said 24th Day of June last past, whereof the Duties were not paid, ndr secured to be paid: That the Petitioners, and others, are possessed of many Thousand Bushels of foreign Salt imported, and no Duty paid, or secured, for the same; but, before that Day, cellared, and secured under the Locks and Keys of the proper Officers, in the respective Places w here the same are lodged, and the Customs of the same paid, or well secured; yet the Petitioners cannot have the Benefit of the same, in regard the Duties thereof were not paid, nor secured, save by exporting the same again; whereby they will not only lose the Money paid by them for the Customs of the same Salt, but also the prime Cost thereof beyond Sea; which will tend to the great Impd-verishment of all the Petitioners, and Ruin of many:

And praying, That they may be put on the same Foot of other Proprietors, w ho had paid, or secured, the Duties on Salt; whose Duties were to be repaid, or Securities: ‘

vacated, by inserting some Clause to that Purpose in any publick Act.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Tabfo.

That the making the said Hats was at first a foreign Invention, and they were made abroad; That the making the same now being almost intirely in the Hands of the English Subjects, and employs many 1 housand of poor Families; besides, the said Commodity is purchased abroad with Woollen and other Manufactures of this Kingdom: That should any Restraint be laid upon the said Goods, it will not only be the Ruin of many poor Families who are employed therein, but will also be a very great Discouragement to our foreign Trade: And praying Relief.

Plttenweem Sir John Anstruther reported from the Committee, to Harbour. whom the Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of the Burgh of Pittemcccm was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; w’hich they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, in pursuance of the Order of the House, bearing Date the 25th of Feb ruary Vast, have considered of the said Petition; and, upon Examination of Robert Hamilton and James Christy, find the Matter thereof to be as follows;

That the Port and Harbour of Pittenxveem is very conveniently situated near the Mouth of the River Forth, where great Quantities of Herrings, and other Fish, are taken; but, by reason of several Rocks lying within the Harbour, and its present Narrowness, is not capable of receiving of Ships and Vessels, to the great Loss of the Inhabitants of the Town; and other Persons concerned in Trade there:

That the greatest Part of the said Town lies very low, and close upon the Harbour; by reason whereof the Inhabitants are at a continual Charge; being obliged to maintain a Pier, and other Works, to defend the Shipping, and for the Safety of the Inhabitants:

That although the Preservation and Improvement of the said Harbour, and Enlarging of the same, will encou-Vol. 19,

Martii. 589

rage Navigation, and increase the Trade of the said Town; yet the yearly Income, and publick Revenue, of the said Town, being but small, is not sufficient to raise a Fund for that Purpose, and for the carrying on and maintaining the other publick Works of the said Town.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for laying a Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-sixth Part of a Ptny Sterling, upon every Scots Pint of Beer and Ale that shall be vended or sold within the Town of Pitten-weem, and Liberties thereof, for repairing the Harbour there; and for maintaining the other publick Works of the said Town: And that Sir John Anstruther, and Mr.

Anstmther, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Hampden, according to Order, reported, from the Boston Eleo Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it tion. appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Boston, in the County of Lincoln, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; wLich they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report, and Resolutions, were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee have examined the Merits of this Election.

The Poll was,

For the Sitting Member, 81.

For the Petitioner, 60.

The Petitioner’s Counsel insisted, That the Right of Election is only in the Mayor, Aldermen, Common Council, and Freemen, of the Borough, resident in the Borough, and paying Scotland Lot: And produced a Resolution of the House, 20th March 1711, to that Purpose.

The sitting Member’s Counsel insisted, That none have Right to vote as Freemen, but such as claim Freedom by Birth or Servitude; and that it was necessary to have that Resolution explained, because of a late Practice in the Borough of admitting Freemen for less Fines than formerly, in order to govern the next Election:

To prove which, they called,

John Nettleton: Who said, that before this Election, the usual Fine for Freedom wasHrom Ten Pounds to Twenty Pounds, and none were admitted under; but that, since this Election, the Fine has been reduced to Five Pounds; for which Fine of Five Pounds, several have been admitted, with a View to carry the next Election.

The Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved', That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Right of Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Boston, in the County of Lincoln, is only in the Mayor, Aldermen, Common Council, and Freemen, of the said Borough, resident in the said Borough, and who pay Scotland Lot; such Freemen claiming their Freedom by Birth or Servitude.

The Petitioner’s Counsel objected Bribery:

To prove which; and to disqualify Ten Voters on that Head; viz. Samuel Mowbray, John Grant, John Harker, Richard Brown, John Ayscough, William Broughton, Edward Claxton, Henry Sesson, William Pepper, and Thomas Capps', they called,

Samuel Mowbray: Who said, He had Fifteen Pounds given him by John Garner and John Nettleton for his 4 E Vote,

Thomas Barker said, 'That, since the Election, John Grant told him, the Sitting Member gave him Two Guineas before the Election, and asked his Vote; and that, for some time before the Election, he was confined at Sir 1 Villi am Ellys't House, in order to his voting for the Sitting Member. ' i

Daniel Jennings said, That Edxmrd Claxton, Shoe-; maker, told him, He sold a Pair of Shoes for a Guinea-to the Sitting Member about a Week or Fortnight before the Election: And,

That Henry Scsson Said, He had sold One or Two Pair of Shoes for a Guinea to the Sitting Member: And the Witness said, Those Shoes might be worth about Six or Seven Shillings a Pair.

William Pepper and Thomas Capps severally said, That Mr. G a mar, the Sitting Members Steward, and who asked Votes for him, gave them Twenty Pounds apiece for their Votes.

The Counsel for the Sitting Member insisted he had a Majority, notwithstanding any Evidence given by the Petitioner; and objected Bribery to the Petitioner:

To prove which; and to invalidate the Evidence given against the Sitting Member; they called the following Witnesses; viz.

William Wright: Who said, That Thomas Duckering, who voted for the Petitioner, confessed, He had Forty Guineas for his Vote, and his Wife had a Present of Seven Guineas more: And that he told the Witness, He should have as much to vote for the Petitioner:

To invalidate which Evidence,

Thomas Duckering, being called, and confronting William Wright, said, That William fl right confessed to him, That he had Five Guineas from the Sitting Member for his Vote, and Six Guineas from his Friend:

Which Six Guineas J(Tight confessed to have received of Nettlelon; but said he returned them.

Thomas Burrell said, That Robert Darnell, who voted for the Petitioner, told him, He had Forty Pounds given him for his Vote by the Petitioners Friends.

Richard Broun said, That Samuel Abbott gave him Ten Guineas, before the Election, to vote for the Petitioner.

Christopher Wyles said, That Mr. Abbott asked Votes for the Petitioner; and gave the Witness, before the Election, Fifteen Guineas to vote for him.

Bartholomew Barlozv said, That Samuel Mowbray confessed to him, That he had received Twelve Guineas of the Petitioner for his Vote; which, lie said, he carried back after the Election: And that he heard some of the Petitioner’s Agents declare, They would give Thirty or Forty Guineas apiece for Votes, to carry the Election: That, if swearing or lying would carry it, they would not lose the Ca^isc; and that they never lost any Cause for want of either.

Robert Tunnard said, he was present when it was agreed by the Petitioner’s Agents, That, Charles Cheney % should have Twenty Pounds to vote for the Petitioner; and they gave him Five Guineas in Part; hut he died before the Flection.

Mr. Nathanael Ilill said, That the Sitting Member’s Voters were obstructed, and met with great Difficulties to get to the Poll, which the Petitioners Voters did not meet withal: And that the Sitting Member himself was insulted and misused by an Out down Mob in iaypurof the Petitioner; which Mob was composed of Priests, Papists, and Persons disaffected to the Government; and believed, that if the Situng Member had been as zealously affected to the Pretender as he is to his present Majesty King George, he would not have met with such Insults or Difficulties.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for regulating the Nightly Watch.

Mr. Speaker left the Chain

The Lord William Perwlett took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

The Lord William Poxvlett reported from the Committee, That they had made some Progress in the Bill; and had heard Counsel for the Dean and Chapter of Westminster, and for the Inhabitants of the City of Westminster, upon their several Petitions against the Bill; and had also heard Counsel for the Bill; and that the Committee had directed him to move the House, That the proper Officers for the several Parishes within the City and Liberty of Westminster may be ordered to lay before the House, an Account of all Collections, in their respective Parishes, for the Nightly Watch, for One Year last past; and how the same have been applied, and accounted for.

Ordered, That the proper Officers for the several Parishes within the City and Liberty of Westminster do lay before this House, an Account of all Collections, in their respective Parishes, for the Nightly Watch, for One Year last past; and how the same have been applied, and accounted for.

The Lord Wiliam Poxvlett also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move, That they may have Leave to sit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the said Bill.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

MR. Lade reported from the Committee, _to whom the Petition of the Rector, Churclnvardens, Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants, of the Parish of Lambeth, in the County of Surry, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerks Table: Where it was read; and is as follows: viz.

That, upon the Examination of several Gentlemen, the Committee find the Matter to be as followeth; viz. That by an Act, passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for amending the Roads from the City of London to the Tow n of East Grinstcad, in the County of Sussex; and to the Towns of Sutton and Kingston, in the County of Surry; it is, amongst other Things, Declared and Enacted, That the Road from Vauxhall Bridge, leading into the said Roads, One Mile, or thereabouts, shall be repaired and amended:

That, by a Clause in the said Act, for appropriating the Monies arising from the Duties or Tolls granted by the said Act, and applying a certain Proportion thereof on each respective Road to be amended thereby, no Mention is made of what Part or Proportion of the Monies arising by the said Act shall be applied on the said Road from Vauxhall Bridge aforesaid; no Repair or Amendment hath been made by the Trustees in the said Act mentioned:

That, by reason of the many Loads and Carriages of Timber, Stone, Coals, and other heavy Goods, the said Road still continues almost impassable, and very dangerous for Travellers to go through.

Ordered, That, Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Trustees named in an Act, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act to amend the Roads from the City of London unto

the Tow n of East Grinstead\ in the County of Sussex; and to the Towns of Sutton and Kingston, in the County of Surry; to pay so much Money, out of the Produce of the Tolls collected by the Authority of that Act, as shall amend the Road from Vauxhall Bridge, through South Lambeth and Stockzcell, into the Croydon Road: And that Mr. Lade and Mr. Banks do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Sir John Ward reported, from the Committee, to Allowances whom the Petition of the Merchants of London trading ou damaged j in Wines, in behalf of themselves, and others; as also the Wines’ Petition of the several Merchants of the City of Bristoll, in behalf of themselves, and other Importers of Wine; were referred; the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee have taken the said Petitions into Consideration: And, having examined Mr. Johnson,

Mr. Ludloc, Mr. Bernard, Mr. Eltonr and several other Merchants trading in Wine; and likewise having heard the Commissioners of the Customs, and Patent Officers; do find the Matter of Fact to be as follows;

That, by an Act of the Twelfth of King Charles, it is Enacted, Wines imported into London, of the Growth of France, Gcimany, and Portugal, pay £. 7. 10s.; those of Spain, and elsewhere, £. 8. 10s.; Vinegar, £.4. 10&; per Tun: By which it appears, that the Difference between Wine and Vinegar was then but £. 3. per Tun; and likewise, that no Wines should have any Allowance or Deduction out of the Customs, but such only as w ere so corrupt and unmerchantable, that they were fit for nothing but to distil, or make Vinegar:

That, by several Acts of Parliament, the Duties on Wines of the Growth of Portugal are augmented to £. 29. 4s.; Spain, £. 30.4s.; France, £. 58.4^; per Tun.

The Committee also find, That, upon the Importation of Wines, great Disputes have and do arise in relation to

Allowances; the Officers of the Customs alleging, That -«

the Words of the Law, as it now stands, are not sufficient to impower them to make Allowances on any Wines, except they are so corrupt and unmerchantable, that they are only fit to distil, or make Vinegar; though it frequently happens, that the said Wines are damaged and defective, and much lessened in their Value; and yet not so bad and corrupt as only fit for the aforesaid Uses; which is a very great Discouragement to the Importers of Wine; and, if no Allowances be made but under the aforesaid Restrictions, the Merchants cannot go on with that Trade, but to their Ruin:

That if the Time now limited by Law for Exportation of Wines to Twelve Months should be made Eighteen Months, and have Benefit of a Drawback, it would be an Encouragement to the said Trade.

That the Committee do likewise find, upon hearing the Commissioners of the Customs, and Patent Officers, That it will be expedient and necessary to make further Allowances, according to the Proportion of the Damage on Wines: And, in order to effect the same, and ascertain the said Allowances, the Commissioners of the Customs informed the Committee, That the Wine Merchants had made Proposals to them, what farther Allowances they.

A Petition of divers Merchants, Proprietors of Salt, and Fishermen concerned in curing Fish, within, the Borough of Saint Mazes, and Peaces.adjacent, in the County of Cornwall, was presented to the House, and..read;

setting forth, That, by an Act, passed in the Fifth Year of his Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for recovering the Credit of the British Fishery in foreign Parts; and foi better securing the Duties on Salt, it was enacted, That the Curers of Fish should, from the 24th Day of June last, be allowed to import foreign Salt, for curing Fisa for Exportation, without paying any Duty for the same, except the Customs payable upon the Importation thereof; but, by the said Act, no Provision is made, or Directions given to the Proprietors of foreign Salt imported, the Duties whereof were not paid, nor secured to be paid, before the said 24th Day of June: That the Petitioners, and others, are possessed of many Thousand Bushels of foreign Salt imported, as aforesaid, and no Duties paid, or secured, for the same; but, before that Day, cellared, and secured under Locks and Keys of the proper Officers, in the respective Places where the same arc lodged; and the Customs of the same paid, or well secured: yet they cannot have the Benefit of the same, in regard the Duties thereof were not paid, nor secured, save by exporting the same again; whereby they will not only lose the Money paid for the Customs, but also the prime Cost thereof beyond Sea; which will tend to the great Impoverishment of the Petitioners, and the Ruin of many; And praying. That they may be put on the same Foot of other Proprietors, who had paid, or secured, the Duties on Salt,

whose Duties were repaid, or Securities vacated, by inserting some Clause to that Purpose in utiy-publick Act.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Masters, and Governor, Assistants, Regulating Livery, and Freemen, of the Company of Barbers and Surgeons, of the City of London, was presented tothe dC’ House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act, made in the 32d Year of King Henry the Eighth, intituled,

An Act for Barbers and Surgeons, it is enacted, That all Persons of the said Company, then incorporate by the said Act, and their Successors, that should be lawfully admitted, and approved, and occupy Surgery, should be exempt from bearing of Armour, or be put in any Watch, or Inquests: That, by Charter granted to the said Company by King James the First, in the Second Year of his Reign, it is granted unto the Petitioners, That they, and their Successors, lawfully admitted to practise Surgery, should for ever thereafter be exempted from all and all manner of Watch, Inquest, and Juries, within the City of London, Suburbs, and Liberties thereof; and from all Contributions, Taxations, Assessments, and Sums of Money, to be imposed, taxed, or assessed, in respect thereof:

That they have quietly enjoyed the said Exemption to this present time: That they are apprehensive, that, by the Bill now depending, for the better regulation of the Nightly Watch, their said Exemption from watching, or contributing thereto, will be taken from them: And praying, That they may be heard; by their Counsel, concerning the same, before the said Bill"passes.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for regulating the Nightly Watch, is committed.

Mr. Carteret reported from the Committee, to whom Supplying the Petition of the Adventurers, whose Names are there- London, &c, unto subscribed, for supplying the Inhabitants of the Uities With Water* of London and Westminster with fresh Water, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerks Table: Where the said Report and Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

That, the Committee in pursuance of the Order of the House, of the 27th Day of February last, have taken the said Petition into Consideration; and the Peti* tioners, in order to prove the Allegations of the said Petition, called and examined, several Witnesses:

Who are as follow; viz.

Thomas Acherley: Who has been Twenty Years a Surveyor of Lands, Mines, Levels, and throwing out Waters, said, he had surveyed the Grounds between London and the Rivers mentioned in the Petition, from Station to Station, at every Fifty or Sixty Yards Distance, with proper levelling Instruments; and did find, by the Level, That those Rivers, and also the River Lea, IVhethamstead,

do lie about 100 Foot higher than the lowest Pond at Milford Farm, called Hampstead Ponds; which lowest Pond is about 20 Foot higher than the Top of Mountague House, in Great Russetl-street: And that the Waters of those Rivers may be brought to serve the Town higher than any Houses in London and Westminster:

And, as to the Quantity of Water that may be so brought, he, the said Thomas Acherley affirmed, That the M aters of any one of those Rivers were sufficient to answer the Ends proposed: But he alleged, That some small Parts drawn from each River, and united into One Trench, or Canal, will yield a Quantity of Water sufficient not only to serve such of the Inhabitants of London, Westminster, Southwark, and Villages and Places lying about the same, as shall be willing to take the same, but also to serve the Royal Palaces, and particularly the Royal Palace and Gardens* at Kensington, in every tiling that Water can make those Places delightful; and that too at reasonable Rates:

That the Damages that this Undertaking will occasion to the Meadows and Mills on the said Rivers would be inconsiderable, because the Waters drawn away maybe re-supplied, in his Opinion, by opening new, and cleansing the old, Springs, which abound on the Sides of those Rivers.

Doctor Edmond Halley said, That he had viewed the River Colne; and was of Opinion, that the Undertaking was practicable, and that there might be a sufficient Quantity of Water brought as is proposed by the Petitioners; for that there can be no Dispute of the Fall of this intended Course of Water, because the Source thereof is twice as high as that of the New River; and that, since the Fall will be Three Foot in every Mile at the least, he would undertake to effect the said Undertaking, if he were employed.

Whereupon the Committee came to the Resolutions following; vi£\

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners have made good the Allegations of their Petition, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; and that the Undertaking, in the said Petition mentioned, will be convenient and beneficial for the Inhabitants of the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee?

A PETITION of the Mayor, capital Burgesses* and other Inhabitants, of the Borough and Town of Weymouth, and Mclcomb Regis, in the County of Dorset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That divers Persons belonging to that Place, and Parts adjacent, are in Captivity in the Country of the Emperor ot Morocco; where they live in miserable Servitude, and are under great Temptations to Apostasy: That some, through hard Usage, and Despair of Deliverance, have perished; and others, to obtain Liberty, have embraced the Mahometan Religion: And praying, That some Ways and Means may be found out for their Deliverance.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir Thomas Hanmer reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Charles Earl of Arran was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same id his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee entered into the Examination of the Allegations of the said Petition; and the Petitioner, the Earl of Arran, in order to prove the same, laid before the Committee an attested Copy of a Deed of Settlement inrolled, dated the Sixth of June 1683, made and executed by James late Duke of Ormond, and Elizabeth Duchess of Ormond, the Petitioners Grandfather and Grandmother; whereby they did settle and limit all th^ir 6

Castles, Honours, Manors, Lands, and Hereditaments, in the Kingdom of Ireland, to several Uses; by virtue w hereof their Grandson James Butler late Duke of Qr-mond, the Petitioner’s elder Brother, became possessed of all foe said Estate, except what is by the said Settlement limited to the Petitioner foe Earl of Arran, for the Term of Ninety-nine Years, determinable upon his Death, without Impeachment of Waste; with Remainder to Trustees for his Life, to preserve contingent Remainders; with Remainder over to his First and other Sons in Tai} Male; with Remainder to the Petitioner, and his First and other4 Sons, for foe like Estates; with divers Remainders over, subject to several Terms and Incumbrances in the said Settlement mentioned; with Remainder to the right Heirs of the said James First Duke of Ormond.

That a Certificate was also produced to the Committee, from the Register to the Commissioners of the forfeited Estates; whereby it appears, That the Petitioner the Earl of Arran, and James Butler Esquire, by the Name of James Butler, of Kilveleacher, in the County of Tipperary, in the Kingdom of Ireland, have severally entered their Claims, before the said Commissioners of the forfeited Estates, for the several Estates, Interests, and Remainder, to them respectively limited by the Settlement before-mentioned; and that no other Person has claimed, before the said Commissioners, any Estate in Remainder, by virtue of, or under, the said Settlement;

That the said James Butler Esquire, who is the only Person claiming as aforesaid, besides the Petitioner the Earl of Arran, did appear before the Committee; and did declare himself ready to give his Consent to such a Bill as is desired by the Petition of the said Earl of Arran.

That the Committee have also inquired into the State of the Debts chargeable upon the Estates of the late Duke of Ormond; and they do find, that they did, at the time of his Attainder, amount to about the Sum of £. 84,703. of which about £. 8,300. hath been already paid, or provided for, by order of the Commissioners of Forfeitures; so that the Sum which does remain due upon the same, is about £. 76,403. besides which there are other Debts contracted by the late Duke of Ormond, which are supposed not to effect the Estate, amounting, in the Whole, to about the Sum of Fifteen thousand Pounds.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable Charles Earl of Arran, in the Kingdom of Ireland, in case he shall be admitted the best Purchaser by the Commissioners and Trustees of the forfeited Estates, by Mortgage or Sale of a sufficient Part of the Estate of the late Duke of Ormond, his Brother, to raise a Sum, which he shall contract with the Commissioners or Trustees to pay for the Purchase of his Brother’s Estate, subject to the legal Incumbrances thereon; and also such further Sutn as shall be sufficient to discharge the Debt9 of his said Brother, which are not legally charged on the said Estate, and are now without any Provision: And that Sir Thomas Hanmer, Mr. Freman, and Mr. Ward, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Which said Persons were accordingly summoned by the Order of this Committee: And the Committee did, pursuant to the Order of the House, take the Examinations; which are as followr; viz.

Mr. Robert Huntman said. That he was employed, as Attorney, by the Mines and Battery Company; but did not carry the first Order of Reference to the Attorney General, upon the Petition of the Company for an Incorporation for Insurance of Ships; but, in all other Matters of the Company, he was employed, so far as to prepare Breviates, and carry them to Counsel, and give them their Fees:

Being cross-examined, he said, There were Seven Attendances before the present Attorney General: That, at Six of those Attendances, they had Six Counsel on their Side; and sometimes there were Three, and sometimes Four, on the other Side: That he believed the First Attendance was upon the Nineteenth of November last; but he could not be positive of the Time: That there was an Attendance about a Week before, about the Twelfth of November; but that was only to put it off, because the Petitioners w'ere not prepared; and it was put off upon the Application of the Petitioners for the Charter: That he believed they were ready on the othec Side: That they attended again on the Nineteenth of November, when the Petitioners had Six Counsel, and the other Side Three 4 I Counsel;

and he believed tb&*e might be One hundred and Fifty People there; and upon the other Attendances there was a great Number of Persons on both Sides: The Point upon the Petition for a Charter was, Whether such an Incorporation for Insurance, as was desired for Ships and Merchandize, would be beneficial to the Nation: And the other Side insisted, that private Insurances would be most beneficial to the Merchants: And there was then also an Objection to the Company, as to their being a subsisting Corporation; and their Existence, as a Corporation, was disputed; their Charters were read; which were very long; and an Objection was made, in point of Law, to the Company's carrying on the Business of Insurance under such Charters, though existing; and all these Points were debated by Counsel on both Sides: That the Fees given to the Counsel^ upon their Attendance, were Ten Guineas apiece to each of the Six Counsel* upon the First Attendance; and after, Five Guineas apiece to Three of them; and Three Guineas apiece to the rest: That Ten Guineas apiece was always given to Tw o of the Counsel, and Five Guineas apiece always to Two of them: That there were Seven Attendances upon this Petition, with that of the Twelfth of November \ and that he believed, all the Counsel, except One, always attended; and that there was paid to the Counsel, for these Attendances, 142 Guineas, or within One or Two of it: That these many Attendances werte occasioned by want of Affidavits and Proofs, which the Attorney General required; there being only some Certificates, but no Affidavits to prove the Hands to those Certificates: That he believed there was not any Application at all made to the Attorney General, fur an Attendance during the Kings Absence; they found him ready as soon as they applied: That he issued his Summons for an Attendance, upon the Kings Return, without any Application:

Being asked, Whether from May to November, this Company did not go on to carry on their Project; he said, He could not tell, but believed they did; but that he also believed, there was not any Signification thereof of any kind, to the Attorney General; and said, That he distributed no Money, other than to the Counsel.

Mr. John Marsh, Agent or Solicitor for the Petition for Insurances by the Lord Chetwynd, Sir William Chap-man, and others, said, He left the Order of Reference on that Petition, wdth Mr. Attorney General’s Clerk, but no Fee with it: That he gave the Fees to the Counsel, upon that Reference, made the Eighth of January; and widely upon the Ninth, he left with Mr. Stephens, Mr. Attorney General’s Clerk: That he acquainted Sir William Chapman with it; and thereupon there was a Meeting, on the Monday or Tuesday following, of Sir Jacob Jacobson Mr. Hatley, and the major Part of those who were appointed Managers; and they resolved to wait upon Mr. Attorney with his Fee: That he believed Ten or Twelve of them attended him; and that Sir William Chapman gave him his Fee: That lie, the Witness, went with them to Mr. Attorney General’s Chamber; and, when he came there, lie acquainted Mr. Attorney General’s Clerk with several of their Names; and then he was introduced into an outer Room, and the Clerk went to Mr. Attorney General; and, having told him, as he believed, That the Witness was there, he was called to the Door; and then acquainted Mr. Attorney, That Sir William Chapman, and some others of the Petitioners for that Charter, were come to wait upon him with his Fee:. To which Mr. Attorney General said, What do they come to me for? Why do they not leave it with my Clerk ? The Witness, answered, That, considering it was Matter of Weight, and who were concerned in it, they desired to give him his Fee themselves: And, the Witness turning to them, they all came forward, and Sir William Chapman gave the Fee; and recommending the tiling to Mr. Attorney’s Favour* said, It would speak for itself; and hoped, if it should be found to be of Use to the Nation* that he would favour

it; and some Words of that kind; and then they withdrew: That, some time after ..this, a Caveat being entered by the Insurers, a Summons was taken out: Then there* came another Petition for a Charter; and thereupon Counsel w ere heard for the private Insurers, and Counsel for the Mines Royal, and Counsel on behalf of Sir William Chapman; and the Managers, Mr. Serjeant Comyns, Mr. York, and Mr Hale, were of Counsel; and the other Side had Three Counsel: That the Petitioners Counsel had Five Guineas apiece: They were all heard at that time; and Directions were given to bring the Subscriptions, and Subscription Books, and other Papers, relating to that Insurance; which Directions were given, as he thought, at the Desire of the Private Insurers: That, he believed, there weve several Attendances on Mr. Attorney General, upon this Petition of Sir William Chapman, besides Attendances to bring Papers:

That they attended only twice with Counsel; and the Witness desired the further Attendance: That the whole Fees to their Counsel amounted to no more than Fifteen Guineas at a Time, Five to each Counsel; That the First Attendance held from Seven to Ten or Eleven a Clock at Night: Upon the last Attendance there were Six.een or Eighteen Persons, at least, or their Side; and, he believed, as many more of the other Side:

That, upon this Petition, a Point arose, Whether, to prevent the Danger of a Monopoly from one such Corporation, a Second Incorporation of the same kind were not necessary: And another Objection arose, That some of those, who were Subscribers to this Petition for a Charter, were formerly Subscribers to a Petition against one; and they were requested to give their Reasons for altering their Opinion: There was also Charge of Fraud upon Ram, one of the Subscribers to this Petition*; which came upon the Petition of one He/bat; on which there was a distinct Attendance, and Examination; and touching which, Mr. Attorney General required an Answer upon Oath, as the First Charge w'as upqnOath: Whereupon several Affidavits were brought; but lie never heard they went any further to make good that Matter:'

That, upon drawing and framing the Report, he attended Mr. Attorney General, upon his Request, to see if he had collected all the Facts that had been laid be* fore him:

That there wfas never any other Fee to Mr. Attorney* than as aforesaid, that lie knew of; but the Witness ow ned he did tell Sir William Chapman, that he thought it was fit to wait upon Mr. Attorney General in Person; Whereupon Sir William asked, What he thought was a reasonable Fee: He answered, That he had given Ten Guineas in a Case of a private Act, and had known a larger Fee given; and believed, that Twenty or Thirty Guineas should be given: They debated the Matter; and the Witness understood they resolved to give Fifty Guineas for the Fee, and to trouble themselves no further; and believed no further Fee w>as ever given, or intended to be given: That lie never had any Discourse with Mr. Stephens, one of Mr. Attorney General’s Clerks, about Fees, only that he asked him, What was proper to give; but, he returned no Answer of any kind; and thereupon the Witness said, He would advise with his Clients, and do what was proper; and that he never hud any Discourse about Fees with Mr. Grub, Mr. Attorney’s other Clerk.

Mr. Thomas Dozvse said, That he was Solicitor, or Agent, upon that Petition, which was the Counter Petition to that for the Mine and Battery Charter; and gave Mr. Attorney General, in the Whole, Fifty Guineas at Four several Times; Three of which Fees, to his best Remembrance, lie gave Mr. Attorney himself, and One to his Clerk; and believed the Three, which he gave Mr* Attorney, were Ten Guineas each, and the other Twenty Guineas were left for him with Mr. Stephens, his Clerk:

Being examined, as to what Hints had been given him touching enlarging Fees to Mr. Attorney General, and Opon what. Occasions; he said. Several Hints had been

given him by his Clients, and by others he had conversed with, That the other Side had given very large Sums to Mr. Attorney General: Whereupon he applied to his Clients to amend their Fees, and desired Leave to enlarge them; but he could not prevail: They could raise Money but hardly; but, at last, they ordered Twenty Guineas should be given; and he gave it.

Being asked, Whether Stephens ever gave any Hint to enlarge the Fee; he answered, That, when he gave the Ten Guineas, and which was a Fee he had given to other Attorneys General, he had then only One Petition against the Charter; but he had entered Caveats against others; And then he asked the Clerk what Fees were to be given upon Caveats, that being a Piece of Practice which he was not so well apprised of: And the Clerk said, You must give something handsome: And believed the Clerk might say, in a cursory way, That they gave handsomely on the other Side; but believed he said it by no Direction; and, upon what was said by him, and others, he increased the Fee, and gave Twenty Guineas,

He gave an Account, That, on the Third of June, he carried the Order of Reference on the Petition to resume the former Charters of Mines Royal, and Battery Works, and Ten Guineas with it, to Mr. Attorney General; which, he apprehended, w as his usual Fee; and between that time, and about the Middle of September, when he went out of Town, and staid till the Middle of October, he frequently called on Mr. Attorney Generals Clerk, to know if any Application had been made for a Hearing by the other Side; and he received for Answer, There had not; Whereupon he told the Clerk, after some times calling, That, if the other Side would not proceed on their Part, he would proceed:

That lie staid out of Town above a Month; and the First Hearing the y had upon the Mine and Battery Business, was, upon the Eleventh of November, upon a Summons which he took out:

That he was Solicitor for the Merchants of London and Bristoll; who appeared, from the Beginning, to oppose such a Charter: There was Four or Five Sets against Charters, and he was concerned for them atl:

He was also Solicitor upon the Counter Petitions against the Mines Royal:

That there were Seven Hearings in opposing the Petitions for Charters; and he believed, Four or Five of them were particularly upon the Petition of the Mines Royal People:

That he gave no Fees since the last Caveat, nor any upon the Report:

That he left no other Fees than the Fifty Guineas: That the Discourse he had with Mr. Stephens, was at the Attorney General’s Chamber; and knew of no other Discourse upon that Subject: That he could not repeat the Clerk’s exact Words, only the Effect of them: That he and the Clerk talked only in a cursory manner, to know what other Attorneys gave: That he had no Directions for giving Fees, but to give the common and usual Fees; which he did, and gave or left no other than what he looked upon to be common and usual:

Being demanded to name the Person, his Client, who told him he must give good Fees; he declared, He could not say which Client, in particular, it was; and that it was only in common Conversation; as thus; Doivse, You must give good Fees; we hear they give very good Fees on the other Side:

That he would have given a better Fee than Twenty Guineas, and asked his Clients for that Purpose: but they refused to order that:

That the Hearings upon these Attendances generally began at Six; the last was at Five; and the Counsel generally got away about Ten: There was usually Six or Seven Counsel at a Hearing; and some of the Hearings were Three or Four Hours, and some longer: Once they had but Four Counsel: viz. Mr. Serjeant Cheshire, Serjeant Whittaker, Mr. Bootle, and Mr. Pittman: The Fees he gave, were to Serjeant Cheshire and Serjeant Whit-Vox. 19.

Mr. James Bradly, being examined touching the Affair of York Buildings, said, That he believed Mr. ' Billingsley carried the Order of Reference; but declared, That he did not know of any one Fee that was given upon Occasion of that Business: That he never spoke to Mr. Attorney in his Life, but upon a Case in relation to a Matter in Trade, which now lies before him; and never attended him upon any other Occasion:

Being cross-examined, he said, That he was one of those who solicited the Charter; and, upon that Occasion, attended the late Attorney and Solicitor General: That they advised with the Solicitor as their Counsel, and gave him Five Guineas; and that he put them in a Way of getting their Charter: He perused their Petition, and perused and corrected their Draught of a Charter; and told them, if they applied to the Clerk of the Council, he would get it referred to the Attorney or Solicitor, not Attorney and Solicitor, and to the Board of Trade:

That the Clerk of the Council having told him, That the Reference was made to the late Attorney and Solicitor General, and to the Board of Trade, the Witness staid till the late Attorney came out of the Council; when he took notice of those that were the Petitioners,

| then attending; and, upon speaking to him of it, he de-

clared, That he approved the Thing very much, and wondered how Insurances could be carried on so long without a Charter:

That he gave the late Attorney General Forty Guineas, and the Solicitor General Five-and-twenty, besides several Fees, which he before gave to the Solicitor, upon advising with him:

That he had long Discourses with the Solicitor upon Points and Objections raised against them by the Merchants: They raised all the Objections they could think of; and the Solicitor answered them; and, in the Conclusion, said thus upon the whole Matter; I can see no manner of Objection to a Charter unless we could hit 1 yponsomething that was never thought of by Man:

Sir Justus Becky being called, and examined as to any Pow'er given for Disposing of Money in the Affair of the Mines Royal; and as to any Money distributed; declared

He knew of no such Power to dispose; norvof any Money distributed, but what is entered in their Books.

And, being asked what Conversation he ever had with the present Attorney General; he said, He never had the Honour to speak*to him, or to the former Attorney General, or to the Solicitor General.

Mr. Zachariah Farall, being called, and exapuped touching the Letter sent Two Years ago by Billingsley to the late Mr. Attorney and Mr. Solicitor General, and the Time when it was discovered, said. That, between the Time of the Report of the late Attorney Geperal, nod that , of the Board of Trade, he was informed of a Letter sent by Billingsley to the late Attorney and Solicitor General, which he thought very scandalous: And therer upon he told Billingsley, That if he would not discover the Contents of the Letter, and by what Authority he sent it, to the end the Gentlemen concerned, and who knew nothing of it, might defend themselves, they would appear no farther in the Matter: And that, upon their asking him by what Authority he made the Oiler in that Letter, he said, He had a general Pow er to make what Offer he thought proper; but the Gentlemen of their Committee disowned giving him any such Pow er.

That there was a Hearing after the Sixth of March 1717, and no Notice was taken of any Letter received; but Mr. Solicitor took notice of Objections to the Charter, which he answered himself: And Mi\ Solicitor advised them to get a Petition for an Incorporation for the Thames Water Affair, and advised the Projectors to get the Reference to the Attorney or Solicitor General; and assured them, he would do them Justice; and said, That if it was referred to the present Attorney General, he might be against it, if he knew the Solicitor was interested in it: That this was about Four or Five Months ago: That upon this Application for a Charter, Mr. Solicitor struck his Name out of the Subscription; and said. It was because he did not know but that the Reference might come to him.

James Vernon Esquire, One of the Clerks of his Majesty's most honourable Privy Council, having Leave from his Majesty to be examined, said, That he attended in Council upon the Eighth of January, when the References were made to the present Attorney General alone:

And, being asked what was the Direction given in Council touching those References, he said, That the Direction was, That they should be referred to Mr. Attorney General.

And, being also asked, Whether the Orders of Reference are drawn up different from the Directions that were given in Council; he answered, That he was sure they were not:

And said farther, That, upon looking into the References in Council, ever since the Restoration, for One Reference to the Attorney General and Solicitor, or to the Attorney or Solicitor, there are Five to the Attorney alone.

Plantation Mr. Hampden reported from the Committee, to whom ,ron* the Petition of several Merchants, trading to Virginia, New England, and the rest of the Plantations in America, as well as of divers Ship-builders, liopemakers, and others concerned in Ship-building and Navigation, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee having taken into Consideration the said Petition; and examined several Merchants, to prove the Allegations therein contained;

Mr. Perry, Mr. Benja. Bradley, Mr. Jos. Gee, Mr. James Bradley: By whose Evidence it appeared, That the Manufacturers of Iron were under great Difficulties to carry on their Business, occasioned by the Dearness thereof; several Merchants declaring, that Iron was raised from Fourteen to Twenty-six Pounds per Ton:

That the Danes have raised their Deal Boards to double the Price they were at Four Years since:. And that Deal Boards, that used to be sold for Eight Dollard per Hundred in Nortcay, are now sold for Eighteen Dollars: And that Deals, that used to be sold for Five Pounds per Hundred in London, are now sold for Seven Pounds, and Seven Pounds Ten Shillings, per Hundred.

It also appeared to the Committee, That the Czar of Muscovy, having now got into his Possession Big a, Narva, Revetl, and divers other Places, from whence we receive our Supplies of Hemp and Flax, can prevent our importing sufficient Quantities to carry on our Navigation and Trade.

It likewise appeared to the Committee, That our Plantations in America; viz. Virginia, Maryland, Pensilvania, New York, New England and several other Places in the Plantations; do abound with Iron-stone, and all other Conveniences for making Pig-iron; and have all Sorts of Timber for Boards; and have Ground capable and proper for sowing Hemp and Flax.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for encouraging the Importation of Hemp, Flax, and Deal Boards, from the Plantations: and that Mr. Hampden, Mr. Barrington, Mr. Heysham, and Mr. Yonge, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of several Clothiers of the City and County of Gloucester, on behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the French drive a great Trade to the Dominions of the Grand Signior; and send large Quantities of Woollen Cloths of their own Fabrick, bringing the Return in Silk, and other Products of Asia: That, having the Privilege of sending such Silk, 8$c. to this Market, by Way of Leghorn, and the English being prohibited sending any Turky Goods to France, is a very great Discouragement to the Turky Trade, and Hindrance to the Exporters of the Woollen Cloths, and other Products, of this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for repealing so much of an Act of Parliament, of the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act for the Encouraging and Increasing of Shipping and Navigation, as allows the Importation of the Product or Manufacture of Asia from any Port within the Straits, or Levant Seas, is committed.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of the City South Sea of Bristoll was presented to the House, and read setting Company's forth, That the Petitioners have, with great Hazard, In- Trade‘ dustry, and Resolution, carried on, maintained, and very much increased, Trade and Navigation, where tolerated, and not confined to exclusive Monopoly; to the great Encouragement of the British Trade, and the Manufactures of this Kingdom: That, the Capital Stock of the South Sea Company being to be enlarged to a very great Sum, the Petitioners apprehend, that, if the said Company 12 should

should not be restrained from trading otherwise than they are allowed to do by the Act of Parliament which established them, they will be able to oppress all private Merchants in any Branch of Trade, whenever the Company shall think fit; so that the Petitioners, and all the Out Ports of Great Britain, must, in a few Years, be utterly ruined: And praying. Gentlemen, 25th March \ 720.

IN Obedience to the Commands of the House of Commons, I am to acquaint you, That the said House did this Day, come to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That Notice be given to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, That this House will, at the Feast of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which shall be in the Year of our Lord 1721, redeem the Annuity of Eighty-eight Thousand Seven hundred Fifty-one Pounds Seven Shillings and Ten Pence Halfpeny per Annum, payable to them for the principal Sum of One million Seven hundred seventy-five thousand Twenty-seven Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Ten-pence Halfpeny, pursuant to the Act, of the Third Year of his Majesty’s Reign, in that behalf.

A Petition of the Mealmen, Bakers, and others con- Supplying cerned in the Com Trade, in and about the Cities of London with London and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof, was pre- Water# sented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Bill now depending, for incorporating several Undertakers for the belter accommodating the Inhabitants of the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent, with Water, will be injurious to the said Inhabitants iu general, and ruinous to the Petitioners, and their Families; for that it will destroy a great Number of Mills, which alone can grind Bread Corn sufficient for the Food of the People in the said Cities and Suburbs: That though Part of the Bread Flour is now brought down the River of Thames, yet, when that is frozen, all the Bread Flour is brought from the aforesaid Mills by Land-carriage; and if, in such dase, these Mills should be destroyed, it would bring such a Dearth as might occasion the starving of many of the poor Inhabitants of the said Cities and Suburbs: And praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for incorporating several Undertakers for the belter accommodating the Inhabitants in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Parts adjacent, with Water, be read a Second time: And that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, if they think fit.

Baltonsbury The Lord William Pawlett reported from the Com-Inclosure. mittee, to whom the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for inclosing the Common commonly called Baltonsbury Common, in the Parishes of Baltonsbury and Bradly, in the County of Somersett, was committed, That the Committee had considered the Petition of the Persons who had Petitioned against the Eill; and thereupon had directed him to report the Matter, as it appeared to them, specially, to the House; and that they had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consents to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; and that the Committee had directed him to report the Bill to the House, without any Amendment; and he delivered the Bill in at the Clerks Table: Where the said special Report was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Petition of Robert Grinstead, Robei't Cuppy, and Edmund Austin, Tenants of the Manor of Baltonsbury , being read; and several Persons being examined; it appeared, by the Testimony of John Sever, That, about Ten Weeks ago, he was sent to all the Persons supposed to have Right of Common, to give them Notice of the intended Bill, to be brought into Parliament, for inclose-ing the said Common; and to ask their Consent, and particularly those who had now signed the Petition against it; who declared, They would not oppose the Bill; which was confessed at the Committee: And some of the Petitioners, although they had no Right of Common, owned they signed the same for no other Reason, than that they apprehended the Bill would be prejudicial to the Highways; they never having seen the Bill.

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the County Report from the Committee, to whom the Bill for conti- G*>U. nuingso much of an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Ann, intituled, An Act for reviving and continuing several Acts, therein mentioned, for the preventing Mischiefs which may happen by Fire; for building and repairing County Gaols; for exempting Apothecaries from serving Parish and Ward Offices, and serving upon Juries; and relating to the Returning of Jurors; as relates to the Building and Repairing of County Gaols; was committed;

And the Amendments, made by the Committee, to the said Bill, were once read throughout; and then a Se-' cond time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, some of them were disagreed with, and the Residue, with Amendments to some of them, agreed unto, by the House.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, for punishing such Persons, who shall be in actual Service and Pay in his Majesty’s Fleet, as shall, upon the Shore in foreign Parts, commit any of the Crimes mentioned in the Articles established by an Act 13* Car. lldi, for establishing Articles and Orders for the Regulating, and better Government, of his Majesty’s Ships of War, and Forces by Sea:

And the said Clause w^s twice read, with Blanks} which were filled up:

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon-agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, to impower Justices of Peace, within their respective Jurisdictions, to commit Vagrants, and other Criminals, for small Offences, either to the Common Gaol, or House of Correction, as they, in their Judgment, shall think proper;

And the said Clause was twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill,

That the Court of Lord Mayor and Aldermen of the City of London shall settle and limit the Fees of the Gaols and Prisons belonging to the City:

And the said Clause was twice read, with Blanks; which were filled up:

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, for repairing Gaols in Corporations and Franchises:

And the same was once read; and, by Leave of the House, withdrawn.

And other Amendments were made by the House to the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Col. Horsey, a Person concerned in the Management of the said Undertaking, being examined, gave the Committee the following Account of the Proceedings in taking in the said Subscription; viz.

44 That there was, some titne since, a Subscription*

4‘ taken in at the Marine Coffee-house in Birch in-lane,

44 for erecting and carrying on a Fishery, under the Title of the Grand Fishery of Great Britain', which being.

44 soon completed, several Gentlemen, w ho were desirous to be concerned in so useful and beneficial an Under- taking, were prevented coming into the same.

That there was a Petition signed by Sir Justus Beck, John London Esquire, Sir Alexander Cairnes, and several other Subscribers, presented to his Majesty; praying his Majesty’s Letters Patents, to incorporate them for insuring Ships and Merchandize at Sea; which wrfs deferred, by Order of Council, dated the 2d February 1717, to the late Attorney and Solicitor General: That there were also Two Petitions presented to his Majesty, against the said Petition, for an Insurance by a Corporation; one from the Merchants of London, and the other from the Merchants of Bristoll; which were likewise referred, by Order of Council, of the 2d of Febntary 1717, to the said Attorney and Solicitor General; who, having considered the said Petition of Sir Justus Beck, and others, as also the said Petition of the Merchants of London,

' made a Report thereupon to his Majesty, dated the 12th March 1717-18; in which they give the following Opinion; viz.

" On the whole Matter, it is agreed on all Sides, " That the Insuring of Ships is of absolute Necessity for " the Carrying on of foreign Trade; and that the same " has been always managed in the Method the same is " now in; and it has not been made out, that there is " any Corporation in Europe for insuring Ships: That the Want of a good Method of Insuring will be very " fatal to Trade; and we are humbly of Opinion, " That the making of an Experiment in a Thing of " this Nature, if it should prove amiss, would be of " the utmost Consequence to the Trade of this Nation; " and that it so highly concerns Trade $nd Commerce, " that it will be proper for the Consideration of the Par-<c liament: And therefore we cannot advise the erecting " a Corporation for the insuring Ships and Goods at

" Sea, against which these are so many and great Objecdbns; especially the Method now used being dpproved of both it home and abroad; and we are not " able to determine bf what Consequence the erecting of " another Corporation in London, with a Stock of a Miilion of Money, may be to the Publick."

The Committee do further find, That there is another Subscription for carrying on the said Undertaking "of* £. 1,152,000. dated the 27th of August 1718, under the Charters for the Mines Royal, the Mineral and Battery Works, on the following Conditions; viz. ’

Sir Joltn JV'dliams, One of the Governors of the said. Company, being examined, said, That he apprehended they were doing what w>as legal, and for the Advantage of Trade; for that, they had consulted, and had the Opinions of, several eminent Counsel, that they might insure Ships by virtue of the Charters for the Mines Royal, the Mineral and Battery Works: And that Two of the said Counsel are Sir Robert Raymond and Mr. Reeves:

That they have affixed the Seal of the said Corporation* to Policies, by virtue of the said Charter: That no Man, as a Member of that Company, is liable to pay any Losses in his private Capacity; but, as a Member of the Company, is obliged to pay in what Sums the Company shall think fit to call; and that the Corporation can sue, and be sued:

The Witness, being asked what the Charters for the Mines Royal, the Mineral and Battery Works, cost, said, That they did not buy the Charters; but that they had bought out the Shares of the old Proprietors, in Number about 124, at £.23. 8s. 6d. per Share; and that there is riot above Two or Three of the old Proprietors remaining:

That the Subscribers have paid in £. 10 per Cefit.; and that the Company have already insured Ships and Merchandize to the Value of £. 1,259,604. 10s.; and that no Man, that has dealt with them, can say, but that they have had Satisfaction: And that it was a preliminary Agreement, That there should be no Law-suits commenced against Persons assured, where the Difference could be decided by Reference:

That, when they first applied for a Charter, they had great Opposition, and they were then advised to make this Experiment; but that most of them that signed the First Petition against a Charter of Incorporation, now petition for it, and desire it to be established:

That the Reason of Merchants coming to them, is, because they think themselves more secure; for that there are Affidavits from abroad, That, before this Insurance, Business has been done at Amsterdam for English Merchants, which are now done here;

That there is a great deal of foreign Money brought into this Kingdom by Merchants insuring from Holland, and other foreign Parts.

Several Merchants desiring the y might be heard against this Undertaking; the Committee did accordingly examine,

Mr. Bemai'd, Merchant: Who said, That the Merchants of the City of London, being very much alarmed 7 - ' *t~

6 Geo. I. 27 Aprilis345

at an Attempt of a Body of People insuring as a Company, presented a Petition to his Majesty, signed by 370 of the most eminent Merchants in London: And that Petition, as also the Petition of the Merchants of Bristoll,t and the Petition for a Charter, were referred to the Board of Trade, and to his Majesty’s then Attorney and Solicitor General: That the Board of Trade have reported Matter of Fact; but gave no Opinion: And the Attorney and Solicitor General reported to his Majesty, That a Corporation for insuring would turn to a Monopoly, and be prejudicial:

That, notwithstanding the said Reports, all the old Subscribers signed a new Subscription, and began to insure Ships:

That then the said Merchants of London and Bristoll petitioned to have the Charters of the Mines Royal, the Mineral and Battery Works, set aside: That there were several Hearings thereupon before the present Attorney General; and he believes the Report is in favour of them:

That it was the Business of the Company to bring the Merchants in to insure with them, by insuring cheaper than the private Insurers; and by even paying when they had no Occasion, in order to beat the private Insurers out of their Business: And that there was a List, proved upon Oath, of 150 or 160 private Insurers, delivered in to Mr. Attorney General:

The Witness owned, That there were other Merchants and Gentlemen that had formed themselves into a Body, and had taken in & Subscription for £2,000,000.; for that Two Corporations would, in some measure, prevent a Monopoly, though it would effectually drive out the private Insurers:

That they had proved, before the Attorney General, That the private Insurers insure as cheap as possible; but the Company insure cheaper, to make themselves acceptable: And that, as to foreign Money, the greatest Part of it arose from the Ostend Traders, who were insured Two Guineas per Cent. cheaper by the Company than the private Insurers could:

That Foreigners used to give One per Cent. for insuring the Insurers; and that it was allowed to the English Merchants, for procuring good Insurers for the Foreigners:

That the private Insurers are sometimes under a Necessity of going to Law, when they meet with unjust Demands:

That what Gentlemen aimed at by incorporating themselves, is, to get a great Estate at once; for that the Company have blown their Stock up to a great Height: And that it was very few of those Merchants that signed the First Petition against a Charter, that now signed the Petition for one.

Sir William Chapman being examined, said, That they had petitioned his Majesty fora Charter of Incorporation to carry on the Said Undertaking, within a Day or Two after the Subscription was taken:

That he can’t tell whether any of the Stock issoldout, or whether it continues in the Name of the First Subscribers; but that no Transfer was made of any of the Stock; for it was the chiefest Care of the Persons concerned to think of Methods to prevent Stock-jobbing: That the most cheap and expeditious Way of insuring is the most beneficial Manner to the Merchants; and that £ 20,000. is as soon insured by a Corporation, as £500. by private Insurers: And that there has been a great Insufficiency in private Insurers; for that the Merchants have been Losers by private Insurers, within 20 or 25 Years, the Sum of £ 2,000,000.: And that it concerned the Interest of the Merchants, that the Premiums should be made easy:

That there has been several General Meetings of the Subscribers; and that there vras a great Appearance at the last; the Import of which was, to acquaint Gentlemen of the Progress they had made; and to consult, in order to bring this Undertaking to effect; which was set up to prevent Monopoly, and the too great Advantages that would accrue to One Company:

That they have received £ 20,000. and that £ 18,060. is deposited in South Sea Bonds: That there is near £1,000. in the Bank; and, in Mr. Baker's Hands, about £146.; and that of the whole Money there is about £ 150. expended: That if £ 1 o. per Cent, or any further Sum, were called in, they would come into a Security for the Advantage of the Assured.

The Committee do find, That the Petition afore-mentioned, signed by Lord Chetwynd, Sir William Chapman, and others; praying a Charter of Incorporation for insuring Ships and Merchandize; was presented to his Majesty; and referred, by his Majesty’s Order in Council, the 8th Day of January 1719, to Mr. Attorney General; who made a Report thereupon to his Majesty, dated the 7th March 1719; by which it appears, That he has been several times attended by Counsel, on behalf of this Petition; and has also, at the Desire of private Insurers* heard them, by their Counsel, against this Petition: And that his Opinion, upon the whole Matter, is, That it does appear, by the several Certificates and Memorials which have been made, upon the Examination of the present Petition, That the Sense of the greater Part of the Merchants of the City of London, who have concerned themselves on this Occasion, is in Favour and Approbation of such an Incorporation as is prayed: But, as no satisfactory Reason has been offered to me, for erecting such an Incorporation upon so large a Joint Stock as is prayed also in this Petition, the Ends of Trade will, I think, be sufficiently served by a far less Joint Stock than is therein proposed, in case his Majesty should think fit, that any such Charter should be granted; and by a Reduction of such Joint Stock to a competent Sum, sufficient only for the Purposes aforesaid, of Insurance, any Misapplication, which might otherw ise be made of such Joint Stock, to Purposes different from that of Insurance of Ships and Merchandizes, and which may be of great Inconvenience to the Publick, will be prevented: But if his Majesty shall be graciously pleased to erect such a Corporation un-3 der

ci As to the Proceedings upon the said Petition, l am " most humbly of Opinion, That the Corporation, created " by the Act of Parliament above-recited, was so instituted for the particular Purposes therein specified: And " though the Power therein given to purchase Lands is " not, by express WTords, restrained to any particular annual Value; yet, by a reasonable. Construction, the " Exercise of that Power ought to be governed and limited by the Purposes for which the Corporation was " erected; and cannot be understood to give Authority " to that Corporation, supposing it to exist, to purchase " Lands of w hat Value soever, and for Purposes wholly " foreign to the Ends of that Incorporation:

" And as to the Transaction between some of the Petitioners and the supposed Governor and Assistants of " the said Corporation, as the same is represented by the " Affidavit, and Articles, stated in the said Report, I " am of Opinion, That it is an unwarrantable Practice,

" and of a very dangerous Tendency, and highly in Derogation of your Royal Prerogative; there being no " Ground or Colour in Law for the said Corporation " to contract with others for taking in Subscriptions for " any Sum, but much less for so great a Sum as " £. 1,000,000. for the carrying on an Undertaking, in the Name of the said Corporation, so different from the ". U pon the several Matters before stated, the Committee have come to the Resolution following; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for some time last past, several large Subscriptions having been made by great Numbers of Persons in the City of London, to-carry on publick Undertakings; upon which the Subscribers have paid in small Proportions of their respective Subscriptions, though amounting in the Whole, to great Sums of Money: and that the Subscribers having acted as Corporate Bodies, without any legal Authority for their so doing, and thereby drawn in several unwary Persons into unwarrantable Undertakings; the said Practices manifestly tend to the Prejudice of the publick Trade and Commerce of the Kingdom.

The First of the said Resolutions being read a Second time, That the said Undertaking, proposed to be carried on by the Name of the British Fishery, wherein the Sea Ports and Royal Boroughs are concerned, may be successfully carried on, and prevent great Sums going annually out of the Nation; and secure a valuable Trade; and may, upon any Emergence, furnish Seamen to man the Royal Navy; and therefore highly deserves Encouragement;

jResolved, That the said Resolution be postponed*

The Second Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That, for some time last past, several large Subscriptions having been made by great Numbers of Persons in the City of London, to carry on publick Undertakings; upon which the Subscribers have paid in small Proportions of their respective Subscriptions, though amounting in the Whole to great Sums of Money; and that the Subscribershaving acted as Corporate Bodies, w ithout any legal Authority for their so doing, and thereby drawn in several unw ary Persons into unwarrantable Undertakings; the said Practices manifestly tend to the Prejudice of the publick Trade and Commerce of the Kingdom.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to restrain the extravagant and unwarrantable Practice of raising Money by voluntary Subscriptions, for carrying on Projects dangerous to the Trade and Subjects of this Kingdom: and that Mr. Secretary Craggs, Mr. Walpole, Mr. Comptroller, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Mr. Hungerjord, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Dorchester A Petition of William Speke and Joseph Earner Esquires,

Unction. Francis Kingstone, John Gollop junior, and Geo. Yeat, Gentlemen, in behalf of themselves, and several others who have a Right of voting for electing Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Dorchester, in the County of Dorset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the ancient and undoubted Right of voting for Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough is, and, beyond the Memory of Man, has been, in the Inhabitants paying to Church and Poor, in respect of their personal Estates; and in all Persons paying to Church and Poor, for or in respect of any real Estates they are seised or possessed of within the said Borough: That the Petitioners were, at the last Election, thus qualified to-vote; but Thomas Pitman, Mayor of the said Borough, at, and before, the said last Election, in an arbitrary and illegal manner, endeavoured to elude and destroy the Petitioners Rights; and to vest the Power of electing Members in himself, and the succeeding Mayors of the said Borough; by admitting and allowing Persons to poll who had no Right, nor were qualified: That, by the said illegal Practices, the said Thomas Pitman hath returned Robert Broxcne junior, Esquire, duly elected; when, in truth, Abraham Jansen Esquire, the other Candidate, had a Majority of Four Votes, by the Mayors own Poll; and a Majority of Six-and-twenty Votes, by a Poll fairly and indifferently taken: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House upon this Day Fortnight, the Sixteenth Day of May instant.

litto. A Petition of Abraham Janssen Esquire, was presented

to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, and Robert Browne Esquire, stood Candidates for a Member to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Dorchester, in the County of Dorsett: That the Petitioner had a Majority of above Twenty Votes of such Persons who had an undoubted Right of voting; and a Majority of Four Votes, at the least, by the Mayor's own Poll: That notwithstanding such Majority, the
