A Petition of Lieutenant Colonel Richard Mannings and Captain Benjamin Huffurn, on behalf of themselves, and the several Officers of Brigadier Hunt, Withers, and Colonel Charles de la Bouchetiers, late Regiments of Dragoons, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That after the 8th of September 1712, when the said Two Regiments were reduced, the Petitioners were directed, by Major General Pearce, Commander in Chief in Portugal/, to be in immediate Readiness, with the private Men belonging thereto, to march, upon the first Orders, to Gibraltar, and to observe and keep their Men in good Order and Discipline: That the Petitioners, with the Corps of the said Regiments, were left to continue in P.ortugall after the March of the other British Troops for Gibraltar, until an Opportunity could be had for their Passage to Great Britain, where they did not arrive till the 2 2d of April 1713: That, notwithstanding the aforesaid Orders to continue their Men in military Discipline, their being so long detained abroad at an extraordinary Expence, and being at last obliged to pay their own Passage to Great Britain, the Petitioners have received no more than Half Pay from the Day the said Regiments were reduced: That, on their arrival in Great Britain, they petitioned her late Majesty to be allowed full Pay to the 22d of April 1713, when they landed at Dover; which Petition was referred to the then Lord High Treasurer, and by him referred to the Comptrollers of the Army Accounts, who reported, That, allowing the Petitioners full Pay to the time of tl;eir landing in England, was agreeable to her Majesty’s Instructions for reducing the Forces, dated the 30th of July 1712: That the late Commissioners declined relieving the Petitioners, alleging the y had no Authority to take Cognizance of their Demand: And praying, That a Clause, or Clauses, may be inserted in the Bill, now depending, for appointing Commissioners to take, state, and determine, the Debts due to the Army, to impower the said Commissioners to examine and report the Fact to his Majesty; and, on his Majesty’s Warrant, to issue Certificates for completing full Pay to the time of their landing in Great Britain.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for appointing Commissioners to examine, state, and determine, the Debts clue to the Army; and to examine and state the Demands of several foreign Princes anil States for Subsidies, during the late War; is committed.

Earl of Arran entered his Claim before the said Commissioners, for the Remainder limited to him by the said Settlement of 1683; and the Petitioners not having a Part of the said Settlement, or any Copy thereof, in their Custody or Power, and being ad vised, by their Counsel, that the said Settlement being set forth in the said Earl of Arran's Claim, and the said Commissioners thereby acquainted with the several Remainders over to the Petitioners, and others, there was no Necessity for entering their Claims, inasmuch as the said Earl of Arran's Claim would effectually preserve their Rights under the said Settlement, which, as they were advised, could not be any ways affected by the Attainder of the said last Duke of Ormond, who was only Tenant of the said Estate, for a Term of Years determinable on his Death: That a Bill is now depending for enabling the said Charles Earl of Arran, io case he shall be allowed by the Commissioners the Purchaser of the said Estate, by Mortgage or Sale of tiny Part thereof, to raise Money for paying for such Purchase, and for paying all the said last Duke of Ormond's Debts; which Bill, should it pass without a Reservation of the Petitioners Right in Remainder, as aforesaid, the Remainders to the Petitioners will be intirely defeated, and they stripped of all Benefit thereof: That they are willing, and do consent, that a Bill should pass for enabling the said Earl of Arran to purchase the said Estate, in case the Remainders of the said Estate, after such Sale and Payment, may continue, and go to the same Uses as the same would have done before the said last Dukes Attainder: And praying, That a Clause may be added to the said Bill, for settling such Part of the said Estate as shall remain unsold, after the Payment of the said last Dukes Debts and Incumbrances, and the Purchase-money of the said last Duke’s Estate for Life, to the same Uses as the same would have gone, in case the said last Duke had not been attainted; or that a Clause may be added to enable the Petitioners to claim the Remainders to them limited by the said Settlement of 1683.

MR. Comptroller acquainted the House, that their Addresses of Yesterday, relating to the Account of the Two hundred and Fifty thousand Pounds granted to his Majesty in the Third Year of his Majesty’s Reign and also the Account relating to Pensions and Warrants for beneficial Grants granted to any Member of this House; had been presented to his Majesty; and that his Majesty had been pleased to give Directions to the proper Officers to lay those Accounts before this House.

Mr. Pelham reported from the Committee, who were appointed to prepare an Address pursuant to the Resolution of Yesterday, That the Committee had prepared an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was twice read; and is as follow's; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

WE your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our humble Thanks for communicating to this House the Applications made to your Majesty for obtaining Charters for insuring Ships and Merchandizes: Your Majesty being graciously pleased not to take any Steps in a Matter of such Importance to the Trade and Commerce of the Kingdom, w ithout the Advice and Concurrence of your Parliament, is an Instance of so much Condescension as deserves the highest Returns of Duty and Thankfulness.

We acknowledge your Majesty’s Ggodness in applying to the Use of the Civil Government the Advantages arising to your Majesty from such Proposals: It is a great Satisfaction to your Commons to sec the Honour and Dignity of the Crown supported under the Difficulties which the Necessity of your Majesty’s Affairs may have occasioned, without laying the Burthen of any new Aid or Supply upon your People:

And we beg leave to assure your Majesty, That this House is resolved to render effectual your Majesty’s gracious Intentions for the Ease, Security, and Welfare* of your trading Subjects.

Resolved, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to his Majesty.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council do humbly know Ins Majesty’s Pleasure, when he w ill be attended by this House.

A Petition of the Merchants of London, divers Owners of Ships, and others, concerned in the Trade and Navigation of the said City, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That whereas a Bill is now depending, for registering Seamen, and others fit for his Majesty's Navy; which Bill, should it pass, will be a compulsive Register; and will he so great a Discouragement to the Mariners and Seafaring-men of this Kingdom, as may induce them to abandon the Service of their Country; whereby the Woollen, and all other British Manufactures will be very nearly affected, for want of Exportation: That, should this Bill pass, the Seamen now employed in British Merchants Ships abroad, will desert the several Ships they belong to, and go into foreign Service, or join the great Body of Pirates; so that the petitioners Ships, now on foreign Voyages, will be in Danger x>f perishing abroad, for want of Seamen to bring them home: And praying. That the said Bill may not pass.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for registering and encouraging Mariners, Seamen, and Seafaring-men, of Great Britain and Ireland; and for the Ease of his Majesty’s Trading Subjects; is committed.

A Petition of Colonel Magnus Kempenfelt, Lieutenant Colonel George Iloicard, Major Richard Mullins, Captain Robert Byng, and Captain Alexander Wilson, in behalf of themselves, and of the other Officers of the late Regiments of Marines, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, during the late War, several Charges have fallen upon the said Officers, arising from Omissions of effective Men left out of their Muster Rolls; in that Service unavoidable, by their being disposed into small Detachments, into distant Parts of the World; from Levy-money disbursed, more than has been issued by the Government; and from double the Commissions, where Vacancies have been filled up by the Generals abroad, and other Commissions given out at home for the same Posts; in which Cases large Deductions have been made out of the personal Pay of the said Officers: And praying, That a Clause may be received for their Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for appointing Commissioners to examine, state, and determine the Debts due to the Army; and to examine and state the Demands of several foreign Princes and States, for Subsidies, during the late War; is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they have Power to receive a Clause for the Petitioners Relief.

A Petition of Major General John Pepper was pre-

sented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, when the Regiment which the Petitioner then belonged to was commanded from Portugall to Spain, he was left behind in Portugall, to command a Detachment of the Lord Ruby's and Major General Cuninghanis Regiments; and, being desirous to be with his ow n Regiment, which was then in Action, he obtained Leave to accompany the Fleet designed for the Relief of Barcelona: That, seeing the Fate of Spain depended on the Relief of Barcelona, Major General Stanhope offered Five thousand founds* to procure certain Intelligence: That the Petitioner, convinced of the Consequence, undertook to go alone through the Enemy’s Country; and learn from the Earl of Peter-bojvnv, then at the Camp near Barcelona, the true Posture! of Affairs; and, by that Means, was the Occasion of his Majesty’s not exposing his Royal Person, to the Hazard of cither being taken or destroyed, by'leaving the Town that Night, as intended by a Signal made just before; and, after having some few Hours Respite, having learned that the French Fleet were but 24 Sail, he returned back, in Two Days, to our own Fleet, and gave an Account of his whole Proceedings: That, upon this Information, our Fleet was encouraged to sail to Barcelona; the relieving of which, at that time, being the Means of saving b£th the King and Kingdom of Spain: That, besides the Fatigues and Hardships he underwent, he spent, on this account, a considerable Sum of his ow n Money, and has not as yet received any Satisfaction: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the w hole House, to whom, the Bill for appointing Commissioners to examine, state and determine the Debts due to the Army; and to examine and state the Demands of several foreign Princes and States, for Subsidies, during the late War; is committed., Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Pow er to receive a Clause for the Petitioner’s Relief.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for laying a Duty on wrought Plate, and for applying Money arising from the clear Produce by Sale of the forfeited Estates, towards answering his Majesty’s Supply; and for taking off the Drawbacks upon Hops exported for Ireland; and for Payment of Annuities, to be purchased after the Rate of Four Pounds per Centwn per Annum, at the Exchequer, redeemable by Parliament; and for appropriating Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament; and to prevent counterfeiting Receipts and Warrants of the Officers of the South Sea Company; and for explaining a late Act concerning foreign Salt cellared and locked up before the Four-and*twentieth Day of June One thousand Seven hundred and Nineteen; and to ^ive a further Time for paying Duties on certain Apprentices Indentures; and for Relief of Thomas Vernon Esquire, in-relation to a Parcel of Senna imported in the Year 1716; without any Amendment. And* also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to repeal so much of the Act, intituled, An Act for preventing Frauds, and regulating Abuses, in his Majesty’s Customs, passed in the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Years of King Charles the Second, as relates to the prohibiting the Importation of Deal Boards and Fir Timber from Germany, without any Amendment. And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for ascertaining the Breadths, and preventing Frauds and Abuses in manufacturing Serges, Pladings, and Fin-grums; and for regulating the Manufactures of Stockings; in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland; without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Charters for Mr. Farrer, according to Order, reported from the Assurances of Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill con-ips at Sea. cernj11g t}ie Assurances of Ships and Merchandizes at Sea; and lending Money on Bottomry; and for restraining several extravagant and unwarrantable Practices therein mentioned; was committed; the Amendments they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the said Amendments were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; as far as Clause B; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, several of them were disagreed with, and "the rest of them, with Amendments to some of them, were agreed unto, by the House.

Clause B being read a Second time, to prevent either gf the Corporations to be erected in pursuance of this Vol. 19.

Act from lending any Money on the Bottom of any Ship, or on Goods and Merchandizes on board, or to be put on board, any Ship belonging to, or employed by, the South Sea Company, without the special Licence of the Court of Directors of the said Company;

And the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Amendment;

It passed in the Negative.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That the South Sea Company might lend Money on the Bottom of any Ship, and on the Goods, and Merchandizes on board any Ship, of, or employed by, the said Company:

And the said Clause was twice read, and amended, so as to give the same Power to the East India Company to lend or advance Money for that Purpose:

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill,

That the Act should not hinder or deprive the African Company from having and enjoying such Powers, Privileges, and Advantages, as do or shall belong to them; except as to Insurance on Ships and Merchandizes at Sea, and going to Sea; and lending Money on Bot-tomry:

And the said Clause wras tw ice read; and amended:

And the Question being put, That the Clause be made Part of the Bill;

It passed in the Negative:

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill,

That the Act shall not 'prohibit the Carrying on of any Home or Foreign Trade in Partnership, in such manner as hath been hitherto usually, and may legally be done, according to the Laws of the Realm; excepting only as to the Insuring of Ships; and lending Money on Bottomry:

And the said Clause w as twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill,

That neither of the Corporations intended to be erected and established, in pursuance of this Act, shall, on Account of the said Corporations, or either of them, advance or lend to his Majesty, his Heirs or Successors, any Sums of Money, by w ay of Loan, or any Part of the Revenue belonging to the Crown, other than such Parts only on which a Credit of Loan is, or shall be, granted by Parliament:

And the said Clause was twice read, with Blanks; which were filled up:

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, for restraining Stock-jobbing:

And the Question being put, That the Clause be brought up;

It passed in the Negative.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday next, at Frauds in Twelve of the Clock, resolve itself into a Committee of Publick Re-the whole House, to consider further of the Bill for pre- venu*9, venting Frauds in the publick Revenues.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A Petition of Margaret Mac Donald, WTidow of the late Sir Donald Mac Donald, of Slate, Baronet, for and on behalf of herself, and Mary, Margaret, Isabel, and Janet Mac Donald, the Four infant Daughters of the said late Sir Donald Mac DonaUl\ Baronet, was presented tb the House, and read; setting forth, That the said late Sir Donald Mac Donald was, by an Act of the First of his present Majesty, attainted of High Treason, unless he should surrender himself before the last Day oijunc 1716; That he intended, even before that Act was passed, to Submit himself intirely to his Majesty’s Royal Clemency: He, in April 1716, by a Letter, surrendered himself to the Earl of Cadogan, not being able to make a personal Surrender, by reason of his indisposition, and Inability to travel; That the said Earl accepted of the said Surrender, and acquainted one of the then Secretaries ol State thereof; and his Lordship directed the said Sir Donald to go to Prison at Fort Willium, and gave Orders to the Governor commanding the re to receive him: That, before ;1 he could accomplish to surrender himself, he died: That

the Petitioner, however, apprehended, and was advised, that was a good Surrender in the Eye of the Law; and the said Sir Donalds^Estate not forfeited, though he did j not surrender himself personally: That the Petitioner is

intitled to a Jointure, and the Four infant Daughters to Fortunes, chargeable upon the said Estate; but they did not enter their Claims thereto before the Commissioners: That the said Surrender has been very lately adjudged not to be a Surrender within the said Act; and the said Estate is decreed to be forfeited: That the Petitioners, who have omitted to Claim, will be intirely cut off from their respective Rights; which is the only Support and Subsistence they have: And praying, That a Clause may be added to the Bill, now depending, intituled, a Bill for explaining the Nature of Conveyances to be made to the Purchasers of the forfeited Estates by the Commissioners \ and Trustees acting in Scotland; and for preventing Dif-

ficulties in determining Claims on the said Estates; to enable his Majesty to make the same Provisions for, and Settlements upon, the Petitioners, respectively, out of the Vol. 19.

said Estate, as they would have been intitled unto, bad the said late Sir Donald not been attainted, and his Estate forfeited.

Mr. Secretary Craggs acquainted the House, That the Petitioners Case had been humbly presented to his Majesty; and that his Majesty had been pleased to command him to signify to this House, That his Majesty has no Objection to the relieving the Petitioners, if the House shall think it reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House; to whom the Bill for the better explaining the Nature of Conveyances to be made to Purchasers of the forfeited Estates by the Commissioners and Trustees acting in Scotland; and for preventing Difficulties iu determining Claims on the said Estates; is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause for the Petitioners Relief.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Privilege. Mr. Hampden reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Complaint of a Breach of the Privilege of this House, by Thomas Barnett, in assaulting and insulting Lucas Kenn, a Clerk, who attended a Committee of this House, the last Session, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, That the said Lucas Kenn did, as Clerk, attend the Committee appointed, last Session of Parliament, to examine into the Allega-

tions of the Petition of the Creditors of Joseph Long, a Bankrupt; upon which Examination there were many Attendances and Hearings; and thereupon several Note* and Papers were exhibited before the Committee, and left in the Hands of the Clerk, in behalf of the said Creditors, by the said Thomas Barnett, one of the Creditors, who was examined as a Witness, for his own Interest, and for the Interest of the other Creditors; which Notes and Papers are detained by the Clerk of the Committee, until the Fees due from the said Creditors to him, and to the other Officers of the House, shall be paid:

And that the Assault made upon, and Abuse of, the said Lucas Kenn, by the said Barnett, was for not delivering the said Notes, w ithout Payment of the Fees due from the said Creditors to the Clerk of the Committee *ifc* and other Officers of the House.

Touching which Assault, and Abuse, the Evidence was as follows: viz.

Mr. Geo. Hastings said, That, on Tuesday the 24th of May last, Barnett, meeting Kenn in Cornhill, asked him, When he should have his Notes? Towhich Kenn answered, that he might have them whenever he pleased to pay the Fees due to the Officers of the House: And Barnett replied, That he would oblige him to part with them; and, about an Hour after, meeting him in Exchange-alley, Barnett took Kenn by the Collar, and told him, he was a Rogue, and worse than a Pick-pocket; and that he would have his Notes before he would part with him: Upon which there was a great Croud, and Kenn 3 Wig was torn, and his Hat beat off, and he wras mobbed out of the Alley; some crying out, That he was a Pick-pocket; and others, that he had sold Stock, but could not deliver it) though he publickly declared, he only kept the Notes till the Fees due to the Officers of the House were paid: That t^ie Mob followed them to the King's Arms Ta-> vern; where there happening to be some Gentlemen wha knew Kenn, no farther Mischief ensued to him; but the Mob pressed so much, that some were forced to be knocked dow n, to keep others out of the House; and that this Insult was made upon Kenn before he spoke one Word to Barnett.

Mr. John Cooper testified to the same Effect, as to Kenris being mobbed out of Exchange-alley: And said, That Barnett first seized Kenn there, and demanded his Papers, and declared, That he w'ould have satisfaction before he would part with him: To which Kenn answered, That he might have his Papers at any time, upon Payment of the Fees to the Officers of the House; and that they w ere detained upon no other Account: But this did not save him from the Mob.

On Mr. Barnett's behalf it was alleged, That Kenn had promised to deliver the Notes after Copies should be taken of them: And that he began the Affray in Exchange-alley.

Touching which, the following 'Witnesses were produced;

Mr. William Poyntz said, That Kenn had promised to deliver the Notes when the Chairman of the Committee should Older him, Copies being first taken; and lhat Barnett, who produced them, though he was a consider* able Creditor, did not sign the Petition; and was examined only as a Witness.

Mr. Abraham Cole said, He saw Barnett and Kenn holding and shoving one another in the Alky; but did not see them meet, nor could he say who began the Affray.

Mr. Gabriel Wallet's said, He knew nothing of the Affray; only that, when Barnett and Kenn came into the Tavern, they mutually complained of being assaulted by each other, and disputed who began the Assault

Mr. 77/o. Malay said, he saw Kenn strike another Gentleman in the Alley, on his Shoulder, with his Hand, without doing him any Hurt; but could not speak to the Bustle between Barnett and Kenn%

Mr. Richard Trotter said. He saw Barnett and Kenn come into the Tavern, but could not speak to what passed in the Alley:

Upon which the Committee came to the Resolution following; viz.

Resofoed> That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Thomas Barnett, having, on Tuesday the 24th of May last, assaulted, and otherwise insulted, and abused, Lucas Kenn, for what he did, as Clerk attending the Committee appointed, the last Session of Parliament, to examine the Allegations of the Petition of the Creditors of Joseph Long) a Bankrupt, is guilty of a! Breach of the Privilege of this House.

The said Resolution being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That the said Thomas Barnett be, for his said Breach of Privilege, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

Ordered, That the Clerk of this House do deliver back to the Clerk of his Majesty’s most honourable Pnvy Council, the several Petitions and other Papers, for and against granting Charters of Incorporation to insure Ships and Merchandizes at Sea; and for establishing Fisheries, or Annuities for Lives, and other Papers relating the reunto; which were presented to the House the First and Eleventh of March last, pursuant to their Addresses to his Majesty.

-The said Address was twice read; and is as follows;

viz.

Die Veneris, 3° Jnnii 1720.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

WE your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal in Parliament assembled, do most humbly return your Majesty our most hearty Thanks for the Continuance of your seasonable Interposition, in Conjunction with the other Protestant Powers, on the behalf of the poor persecuted Protestants abroad:

We also beg Leave humbly to express our Satisfaction in the Prospect there is, that, by your Majesty’s gracious Endeavours, they may obtain the Redress of their Grievances, and be restored to the‘Enjoyment of those Rights and Privileges, to which they have the justest Title, by the most solemn Treaties, and be secured in the future Enjoyment of them:

And we do assure your Majesty, That we will cheerfully concur with your Majesty in the Prosecution of such Measures as your Majesty, in your Wisdom, shall judge most conducive to so great and good an End.

The said Address being read a Second time, the Blank left therein, by the Lords, was filled up with the Words " and Commons."

Resolved, Nomine contradiccntc, That this House doth agree with the Lords in the said Address.

Ordered, That Colonel Berkley do go to the Lords, and acquaint them, That this House doth agree with their Lordships in thq, said Address.

Answer b TV Speaker reported to the House, That both Address. -LVJL Houses did, on Saturday last, attend his Majesty with their Address: To which iris Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I hope that my Endeavours, in Conjunction with the other Protestant Powers, to procure Ease and Security to our distressed Brethren abroad, will, by the Blessing of God, prove successful.

The unanimous and commendable Zeal which you express upon this Occasion cannot fail to add Weight to my Instances; and you may depend upon it, that nothing shall be wanting on my Part to comply with what you so justly desire.

A PROCLAMATION.

WHEREAS this present Parliament stands prorogued to the Twentieth Day of this instant tober: We, with the Advice of his Majesty's Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare, That the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, on the said Twentieth Day of October, to Friday the Twenty-fifth Day of November next: And that we have given Order, That a Commission be prepared for proroguing the same accordingly: And we do hereby further declare his Majesty’s Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Twenty-fifth Day of November next, be held, and sit, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs: And the fords Spiritual ‘ apd

the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners of Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons; are hereby required anil commanded to eive their Attendance accordingly, at IVon tl)e said Twenty-fifth Day of November.

Given at Whitehall, the Twelfth Day of in

the Seventh Year of his Majesty's Reign.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this Houv':' do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall see, or he informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is sitting: And that no Person, so taken into Custody, he discharged out of Custody without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker's Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House; and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to he locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speakers Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while Uie House is sitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex, and-Westminster, do take care, that from Ten of the Clock in the Morning to Tour in the Afternoon, during this Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between 'Temple-bur, and J Vest minster-hall shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament: And that there be ho Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otheru ise, therein, or thereabouts.

Mr. Pulteney reported from the Committee, to whom Address on it was referred to draw up an Address, to be presented to the King’* His Majesty, upon the Resolution Yesterday, That they Specch‘ had drawn. up an Address accordingly; which they bad directed him to report to the House; and lie read the same in his Place.; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same vyas read; and is as follows; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

WE your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our most dutiful and hearty Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We can never sufficiently express our Gratitude to your Majesty, for your constant Caj?e of the true Interest of of your Subjects; nor the Satisfaction of your faithful Com*

Dions,

380

mons., in seeing that the just Influence of your Majesty’s Counsels abroad has procured so near a Prospect of a general Peace throughout Europe; which is a fresh Instance to them, that your Majesty places your Greatness only in the Prosperity and Happiness of your People.

If any thing could more effectually endear your Majesty to us than the Mildness of your Government, it would be that tender and affectionate Concern you express for the present Misfortunes of your People, occasioned by the unhappy Turn of Affairs that hath so much affected the publick Credit of this Kingdom:

But your faithful Commons are met together with Minds fully disposed to take the most just and effectual Methods, and to do every thing that becomes an affectionate Parliament, at this critical Conjuncture, wherein your Majesty's Government, and the Interest of your People, are so highly concerned, to restore and fix the Credit of this Nation upon such solid and lasting Foundations as may effectually give Ease and Quiet to the Minds of your Majesty’s Subjects: And we flatter ourselves, that our Undertaking will be the more easy, since we are determined to proceed with all possible Care, Prudence, and Temper, to inquire into the Causes of our present Misfortunes; and, with the maturest Deliberation, apply the most proper Remedies for redressing the m.

The Improvement of our Trade is of so publick a Concern, and so necessary for the Support and Power of this Kingdom, that we will employ our utmost Endeavours to consider in what manner the Commerce of the Nation may be best secured, and extended.

And we beg Leave to assure your Majesty, That we w ill, with all Chearfulness and Unanimity, grant the Supplies which shall be necessary for the Service of the ensuing Year, and the Support of your Government, upon which the Happiness of the Nation, the Liberty of your Subjects, and the Security of our Religion, so intirely depend.

The said Address being read a Second time;

And the same were, upon the several Questions put thereupon, agreed unto by the Llouse.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made yi the said Paragraph, after " apply," to insert " ourselves to M find out:"

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made in the said Paragraph, by leaving out " Remedies," and inserting " Measures

And the same wras, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made in the said Paragraph, by adding, at the End of the said Paragraph, these Words, " and for punishing the Authors of "them-"

And the same w*as, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved\ Ntmine contradicente, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address, so amended, to be presented to his Majesty.

Mr. Booth reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Justices of Peace, Gentlemen, and Free-, holders, of the County Palatine of Chester, was referred, the Matter, fts it appeared to them^ xVhich he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same tvas^reaa; and is as follows; viz. '

That the Comriiittec havel, ih pursuance of aa Order of this House, taken the said Petition into Consideration; and, by the Testimony of Mr. 'William Squire, Mr. Samuel Clements, and Mr. Tho)na$ Faithfully the Matter appeared to be as followeth;

That the Brine Springs, and Rodks of Saft, in the County of Chester, are sufficient not only to supply this Kingdom, Ireland, and other foreign' Parts, with Salt; yet, by the great Expence of Land-carriage, which is; now at Seven Shillings and Six Pence per Ton, and the slow Dispatch of Shipping, the foreign Parts have of late been mostly supplied with foreign Salt; from whence the Proprietors of ancient Salt-works have almost lost their Trade, and the Crown the Duties which used to arise thereby: That if the River Weaver, which runs through the Centre of the said County, and near to which most of those Salt Springs, and Rocks of Salt, arise, was made Vol. 19.

1 Decembris. 381

navigable, from Frodshani* Bridge to W'tnsfofd Biidgei not only such Salt Trade would be extended into foreign Parts, but also the Cheese Trade, which is very great, there coming Eight or Ten thousand Ton a Year, for which they now Pay from Eight Shillings to Fifteen Shillings, would be much improved; the Duties to the Crown enlarged; and the Carriage of Salt reduced to Half a Crown pet Ton; and that; of Cheese to Three Shillings per Ton:

That several Gentlemen of the said County, who are desirous to have so great an Advantage accrue to the said County, and to the Publick in general, have subscribed the Sum of Ten thousand One hundred Pounds towards effecting the same.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to make the River Weaver, in the County of Chester, navigable from Frodsham Bridge to Wins ford Bridge; and that Wittoti Brook, from its falling into the said River Weaver to Wit ton Bridge, be comprised in the said Navigation: And that Mr. Booth, Sir George War burton, and Colonel Legh, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Supply. Air. Farrer, according to Order, reported from the

Committee of the whole House, who were to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

1 st, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Ten Thousand Alen be allowed for the Sea Service for the Year 1721, beginning from the First Day of January 1720.

2d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Alan per Month, be allowed for maintaining the said Ten thousand Men for Thirteen Months, including the Ordnance for Sea Service.

3d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred nineteen thousand Forty-nine Pounds Fourteen Shillings be granted to his Majesty, for the Ordinary of the Navy for the Year 1721, including Half Pay to Sea Officers.

4th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Fifty thousand Two hundred Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, for the Extra Repairs of the Navy for the Year 1721.

5th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Number of effective Men to be provided for Guards and Garisons in Great Britain, and for Jersey and Guernsey, for the Year 1721, be (including One thousand Eight hundred Fifty-nine Invalids) Fourteen

thousand Two hundred Ninety-four Men, Commission and Non-commission Officers included.

6th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, a Sum, not exceeding Five hundred sixty-seven thousand Seventy Pounds Three Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the said Fourteen thousand Two hundred Ninety-four effective Alcn for Guards, Garisons, and other his Majesty's Land Forces in Great Britain, Guernsey, and Jersey, for the Year 17 21.

7th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred fifty thousand Seven hundred Forty-three Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence Halfpeny, be granted to his Majesty, for maintaining his Majesty’s Forces and Gari-sons in the Plantations, Minorca, and Gibraltar, and for Provisions for the Garisons at Annapolis Royal, Placentia, and Gibraltar, for the Year 1721.

8th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Ninety-four thousand Five hundred Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, to reduced Officers of his Majesty’s Land Forces, and Marines.

The First Four of the said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, w>ere, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The Fifth Resolution being read a Second time;

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the said Resolution be re-committed;

It passed in the Negative.

Then the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

The rest of the said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a State of pok Committee of the whole House, to taJke into further Con- lick Credit’ sideration the present State of the publick Credit of this Kingdom.

A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Owners and Proprietors in sundry redeemable Debts, carrying Five Pounds per Centum, and Four Pounds per' Centum, Interest, payable at the Bank of England; and also in several Orders and Tickets in the Lotteries of 1710, 1713, 1714, and 1719; in behalf of themselves, and others; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, upon the Presumption of having the same Liberty of an Option and Choice as was some time before given the long Annuities by the South Sea Company, did, in the Month of July and August last, either by themselves, or their Attornies, subscribe their several and respective Shares in the above-mentioned redeemable Debts; thereby declaring their Willingness to accept of Stock, in the said Company, at such Rates as should be agreed on between the Proprietors and the Company: But the Governor and Company have not, as yet, come to any Agreement with the Petitioners, according to Law, what Stock they shall have for their several and respective Interests and Shares; neither have they accepted any Stock, in lien thereof: That, sometime alter, the said Company did propose to admit them into

Vol. 19.

their Stock, by allowing them for every Eight hundred Pounds in the redeemable Debts, taking them in at One hundred and Five Pounds per Cent, only One hundred Pound of their Stock; and that they would divide Thirty Pounds per Centum at Christmas following, and not less than Fifty Pounds per Cent, per Annum, for Twelve Years after: That, in a short time after, several of the Petitioners, complaining of, and disliking, the Proposal, the Company published another Scheme; thereby declaring, they would admit them into Stock at Four hundred Pounds per Centum, Midsummer Dividend included; but stilhvithout a Liberty to accept or refuse, as prescribed by the Law: That, by sundry Clauses in the South Sea Act, the said Company have undertaken to pay off all, and severally, the said Debts, at the Rate of One hundred Pounds per Cent. on or before the Twenty-first of March 1721; and that, if all or any of the Proprietors of the redeemable Debts should be willing or desirous to accept and take a Share in the Capital, or Joint Stock, it is to L>q at such Price or Prices as should be agreed on by or between the said Company, and the Proprietors of the said Debts, without Compulsion upon any of the said Proprietors: That, by an Advertisement in the Gazette of the 22d of October last, the said Company ordered their respective Interests and Shares in the several Annuities 7 transferable

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled:

THE Corporation of the Governor and Company of Merchants of Great Britain trading to the South Seas, and other Parts of America; and for encouraging the Fishery; being, in pursuance of an Act of the last Session of this present Parliament, in that behalf, become intitled to a Capital Stock, amounting, in the Whole, to about the Sum of £. 37,801,240. 10s.;

They do humbly propose;

That a Sum not exceeding Nine millions of the Capital of the South Sea Company, together with an Annuity 5-Per Cent, per Annum, issuing from the Exchequer, and payable weekly, be ingrafted into the Capital Stock of the Bank of England and be added to their present Capital Slock of £ .^559,99.5. 14s. 8*/.;

And that every Proprietor of the said Nine millions, so to be ingrafted, be intitled to a Share in the Capital of the Bank, at the Rate of £. 120. per Cent. viz. For every £. 1 jo. in the said Nine millions, to be ingrafted, each Proprietor to have £. 100. Stock in the Bank:

The remaining £. 20. per Cent. Part of the said Nine millions, making, in the Whole, One million and an Half, to be reserved for the common Benefit and Advantage of the Proprietors of the whole Capital, so increased:

And that a certain Sum he annually allowed to the Bank, towards their Charges of Management.

They also propose;

That a Sum, not exceeding Nine millions of the Capital of the South Sea Company, together with an Annuity of £.5. per Cent, per Annum, issuing from the Exchequer, payable weekly, be ingrafted into the Stock of the East India Company, be added to their present Capi-Stock of £. h 200,000.:

That every Proprietor of the said Nine millions, 90 to be ingrafted, be intitled to a Share in the Capital of the East India Stock, at the Rate of £.120. per Cent. viz. For every £. 120. in the Nine millions, so to be ingrafted, each Proprietor to have £ 100. Stock in the East India Company:

The remaining £. 20. per Cent. Part of the Nine millions, making, in the W hole, One million and an Half, to be disposed of, and distributed, pursuant to an Agreement betwixt the Courts of Directors of the East India Company and South Sea Companies:

And that a certain Sum be annually allowed to the East India Company, towards their Charges of Management.

And that a certain Sum be annually allowed to the Bank, towards their Charges of Management.

By Order of the General Court of 3d January 1720. the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, David Le Gros, Secretary.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled:

May it please your Honours,

THE United Company of the Merchants of England trading to the East Indies, having, on several pressing Occasions, given evident Proofs of their Readiness to serve the Publick, and being deeply sensible of the Nation’s present unhappy Circumstances, are very willing, at this Juncture, to contribute their utmost towards retrieving them, and repairing and supporting the National Credit even to their own particular Detriment: They are therefore willing to admit; viz.

That a Sum not exceeding Nine millions of the Capital of the South Sea Company, together with an Annuity of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum, issuing from the Exchequer, payable weekly, and free from all Incumbrances, be ingrafted into the Stock of the East India Company, and added to their present Capital Stock of Three millions Two hundred thousand Pounds:

That every Proprietor of the said Nine millions, so to be ingrafted, be intitled to a Share in the Capital of the East India Stock, at the Rate of One hundred and Twenty Pounds per Cent.; viz. For every One hundred ami Twenty Pounds in the Nine millions, so to be ingrafted, each Proprietor to have One hundred Pounds Stock in the East India Company; the remaining Twenty per Cent. Part of the Nine millions, making, in the Whole, One million and an Half, to be disposed of and distributed, pursuant to an Agreement betwixt the Courts of Directors of the East India and South Sea Companies: And that a certain Sum be annually allowed to the East India Company, towards their Charges of Management.

The said Company do humbly hope, That this honourable House will be favourably pleased to give them such Encouragements and Assistances as may enable them to carry on their Trade more beneficially, and for the greater Advantage of the Nation.

Signed, by Order of the Court of Directors,

Tho. Woolley, Secretary.

By Order of the General Court of

And that every Proprietor of the said Nine millions, so to be ingrafted, be intitled to a Share in the Capital of the Bank, at the Rate of One hundred and Twenty Pounds per Centum', viz. For every One hundred and Twenty Pounds in the said Nine millions, to be ingrafted, each Proprietor to have One hundred Pounds Stock in the Bank:

The remaining Twenty Pounds per Centum, Part of the said Nine millions, making, in the Whole, One million and an Half, to be reserved for the common Benefit and Advantage of the Proprietors of the whole Capital, so

increased:

The Account of the Inducements on which' the Directors of the South Sea Company took in the Third and Fourth Money Subscriptions at One thousand per Cent.; with the Inducements for declaring the Dividend of Thirty per Cent, at Christmas, and not less than Fifty per Gent. per Annum for Twelve Years; was read; and is as fol-low8-f viz.' ,.v,

: To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in :j ^Parliament assembled

IN Obedience to an Order of this honourable House, the 29th of December last, requiring the Directors of the South Sea Company to lay before this House, the Calculations, or Inducements, on which they took in the Third and Fourth Money Subscriptions at 1,000 per Cent, and also the Scheme, or Calculation, or other Inducements, upon which they grounded the Resolutions of making a Dividend of 30 per Cent. at Christmas, and of not less than 5Q per Cent, per Annum for Twelve Years after; the Court of Directors of the said Company do. hunfbly crave Leave to represent;

That, soon after the Act passed for increasing 41 pnL the Company’s Capital, they took a Subscription for the Sale of £. 2,250,000. at 300 perCent.; which was immediately full: After that, the Price of Stock, and of that Subscription, advancing, they had great Applications Jor another Money Subscription; and many of the Annuitants w^ere very desirous to take Stock, rather than. Money, for their long and short Annuities: And the Court of Directors being sensible, that their taking in those Annuities was what the Parliament had chiefly in View; and they being desirous effectually to accomplish the same;

I They agreed to open Books for taking in the

1 prU' long and short Annuities: The same Day they agreed also to take another Money Subscription at 400 per Cent:; which was immediately foil: And at the same time declared their Opinion, not to take any further Subscription in Money: And the Annuitants shewed such Forwardness, that in a few Days about Two-thirds of the Whole were brought in.

The Second Money Subscription being so soon filled, and so many of the Annuitants, which before were reckoned the most difficult Part of the Scheme, being come in, gave great Reputation to the Stock; and caused great Application to the Directors for a Third Money Subscription; to which the Court of Directors were then noways May the inclined: And therefore, on the 13th May 13th^ 1720, came again to a Resolution, That no further Subscriptions should be taken it at present for Money; whereby they hoped to have put a Stop to those Applications; but the Stock, and also the First and Second Money Subscriptions, rising greatly, they had Solicitations from Persons of all Ranks to open a Third Money Subscription:

And the Court of Directors considering the declared Sentiments of the Proprietors, and others, the Circumstances of Affairs, and the current Price of their Stock,

Which wras then near S06 per Cent.; and the Second Subscription, taken at 400, was at 500 per Cent. Advance; found themselves in such a situation, That by denying or delaying such voluntary Subscriptions, pressed with so much Eagerness, they would have been very much blamed by all the Proprietors, for disappointing the further Exc* cution of the Scheme, in refusing such an advantageous ‘ J*nc the Support: And therefore took in the 3d Money

Subscription at £. 1,000. per Cent.; at which Price, or higher, most Persons made Application to have it set

But there'wete such times of Payment allowed to the Proprietors, that the Discount thereof reduced it to under goo per Cent. ? andi with the 10 per Cent. Stock* for the Midsximmer Dividend, brought it to about 800 per Cent, t And the times’for' these Payments were adapted to the usual Times of making Dividends; so that their Divi* dends might be deducted out of their Paynents* to make them easier. ’ - "

As to the taking the 4th Money Subscription at 1,000 per Cent.; they humbly represent, That soon after the Third Money Subscription was taken, and the Price of Stock, and that Subscription, rose considerably; which occasioned fresh Applications for another Money Subscription; and the Directors were blamed very much for not having set the Third Subscription at a higher Price: But they resisted those Applications, and chose rather to proceed by taking in the Redeemables and Annuities which remained out; which they did on the 14th of July, and 4th August: And, the greatest Part of those Debts and Annuities being subscribed, this gave such Reputation to the Stock, as increased the Application for a Fourth Money Subscription from all Ranks of Persons, even with greater Importunity than had been for the Third Subscription: And, it being thought, that the Fourth Subscription would add considerably to the Security and Support of the Company, and to the Satisfaction of the Proprietors of the Redeemables and Annuities taken in on: the last Subscriptions, the Court of Directors did, on the 24th August, take in the same; and although a Fifth Part* being 200 per Cent, was paid down, there was 1,200,000 filled in a few HoursJ

The Court of Directors, to the best of their Judgement, endeavoured to make the Rate of each Subscription as easy and equal as they could for the Subscribers, with regard to the current Price of Stock, and of sonnet Subscriptions; and have, on this Subject, laid their Proceedings before a General Court, and received their Approbation. I

As to the Scheme, or Calculation, upon which their Resolutions were^grounded, for declaring the Dividend of 30 per Cent, at Christmas, and not less than 50 per Cent. p& Annum for Twelve Years after; the Court of Directors crave Leave to refer to the annexed Scheme, or Calculation:

Which Dividend they were, at the earnest Request of great Numbers of considerable Proprietors induced to propose to a General Court; who unanimously agreed to the same.

By Order of the Court of Directors,

The Lord William Powlett reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Undertakers for making the River Kennet navigable from Reading to Vol. 19.

Nezvbury, in the County of Berks, was referred, That they had examined the Matter thereof; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That it appeared, by the Act of Parliament produced to the Committee, That the Undertakers were obliged to finish the Navigation of the said River on or before the First of June 1721; on Failure whereof, all their Pow ers and Interests shall cease, and become void.

That it further appeared to the Committee, upon Examination of John Knight, Surveyor of the Works, and Workmen employed by the Undertakers, That the Undertakers have expended therein at least £.30,000; and, for the greatest Part of the Time from the Commencement of the Act, which was in June 1716, have employed near 400 Men, one Week with another:

That the new Cuts for making the said River navigable will, in Length, contain Thirteen Miles and an Half, whereof about Twelve Miles are already made:

That the Undertakers would have finished the said Navigation within the "l ime limited by the said Act, had not some of their Works been lately ruined by a very extraordinary Flood which happened a little before Christmas last, which will require above Two Months to repair, and make good.

Tho. Palsgrave, said, That he saw the Works and Cuts aforesaid a Week before Christmas last; and that 3 or 400 Men were then at work about the same: And that the hasty Floods had lately made great Breaches in the Works, which the Men were at that time repairing.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for enlarging the "Time granted for making the River Kennet navigable from Reading to Newbury, in the County of Berks: And that the Lord William PmHett, and the Earl of Hertford, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of the City of Bristol, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the visible Decay of the Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom in general, in and about that City, is such, that many Families are reduced to great Poverty, and the Poor in want of employ; which they attribute to the great Use and Wearing of India Chints, and painted and stained Callicoes; of which great Quantities are clandestinely run, and brought in from our neighbouring Nations: And praying Relief.

Petition of the Mayor, Sheriffs, Citizens, and Commonalty, of the City of Norwich, in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That tire Worsted Weaving Trade of that ancient City has, for many Years past, been carried on, not only to the great Benefit of that City, but also to the Advantage of the Kingdom in general; whereby their numerous Poor, and those of the adjacent Counties, have comfortably subsisted themselves and Families: That their said Trade is decreased by the use and Wear of printed, painted, and stained, Callicoes; and many Families are utterly ruined thereby: And praying Relief.

Woul.8 and Plantations, presented unto the House, pursuant to their Address to his Majesty, their Report to prevent the Running of Wool:

And the Title thereof was read.

The said Report is as follows; viz.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled.

In 01>edience to his Majesty's Commands, signified to us by the Right honourable Mr. Secretary Craggs, the 20th of May last, upon an Address from this honourable House, requiring us, during the Recess of Parliament, to consider of, and lay before his Majesty, and both Houses of Parliament at the beginning of the next Session of Parliament, what we shall find further necessary to be done, to prevent that pernicious Practice of running Wool from Great Britain and Ireland into foreign Parts; which is so destructive to the Woollen Manufactures of this Kingdom; we have considered the same: And that we might be the better informed, and enabled to propose such Methods as may most effectually prevent the Exportation of Wool for the future, we caused publick Notice to be given, for any Persons to bring us whatsoever they had to offer to that Purpose:

Accordingly, several Schemes and Proposals having leen delivered and transmitted to us; and having discoursed upon this Subject with many Persons, as well Manufacturers as others, who, by their Employments and Stations, have had frequent Opportunities of observing and discovering both the Practices of the Owlers, and the Defects of the Laws now in Force;

We humbly crave Leave to represent to tills honourable House,

That it is very apparent, by the Informations and Advices which we have received upon this Inquiry, That the Running of Wool is still continued from this Kingdom, but in a much greater Degree from Ireland to France, and other foreign Countries:

That notwithstanding it is difficult to detect, and hazardous to oppose, the Owlers, who usually carry on this pernicious Trade of transporting Wool by Gangs of Horsemen, in the Night, from the Places where it's housed, in Parcels, packed for that Purpose, to such Creeks or Places where it may be most conveniently shipped, either on Vessels which He ready to put to Sea as soon as they have received it, or on Boats in order to be carried oft' to Ships that hover on the Coast; and that the said Owlers are, in a great measure, secured against Discoveries, as well by their secret Management, as by involving their numerous Aiders and Dependents in the same Crime with themselves;

Nevertheless, since the Running of WTool is no new Grievance, and that some Attempts formerly made to prevent it have been attended with good Success, we hope these Practices, which are so very prejudicial to the Woollen Manufacture, and to the Poor of this Kingdom, may be prevented.

In the ist of Gnl. 8$ Mar. there was an Act passed, intituled, An Act for the better preventing the Exportation of Wool: and encouraging the Woollen Manufactures of this Kingdom; whereby several Persons were nominated and appointed Commissioners for putting in Execution the said Act, and all other Acts made against the Exportation of Wool: And it is still very well known, and remembered, that the said Commissioners, and their Agents, by their great Care and Diligence, soon pyt a Stop to the Exportation of Wool: But, no Fund being settled to defray their Expences, the Agents were ruined,

Vql. 19.

409

and forced to retire for want of Subsistence; and the Owlers returned to their Employment with greater Presumption than ever;

It must be likewise observed, That the Regulations Running of in the Act of the Ninth and Tenth Gnl. Illd. Ch. 40, Wool, relating to the Housing, Removal, and Sale of Wool, in the Counties of Kent and Sussex, have, in good measure, prevented the Running of Wool from those Coasts.

At the latter End of her late Majesty’s Reign, when the Exportation of Wool to France was carried on to a very great Height, it is manifest, that, after her said Majesty had issued out her gracious Proclamation, bearing date the 18th of October 1713, for putting in Execution the Laws and Statutes of this Realm for preventing the Exportation of Wool, isc. the extraordinary Reward of £.40. upon discovering, and bringing to Justice, any Persons who had exported Wool, during One Year, had a very good Effect.

From the good Consequences of the aforesaid Essays towards preventing the Running of Wool, we would humbly propose, That proper Persons may be specially appointed, either as Commissioners, according to the Statute of the 1st of Gul. <§' Mar. or in such other manner as may be thought more convenient, and vested with sufficient Authority to put in Execution all Laws relating to the Exportation of Wool:

That the said Commissioners may be impowered to . depute Agents in such Parts of this Kingdom, as may be necessary, to inquire into all Offences contrary to the said Statutes:

That the said Agents shall constantly make Returns to the Commissioners of all such Informations upon Oath, as they shall receive concerning the said Offences:

That the said Commissioners shall direct Prosecutions to be made, upon such of the said Informations as shall appear to them to be material, in his Majesty's Court of Exchequer, to be carried on at the Expence of the Publick.

And whereas the Running of Wool is an Offence of so clandestine a Nature, that it may be very difficult to get Witnesses sufficient to prove the same, unless the Party informing, though contrary to the Statute of the 12 th of Charles the Second, be allowed to give Evidence; it will be necessary that the Law should be altered in this Particular: And we would humbly submit to the Wisdom of his Majesty, and both Houses of Parliament, whether it might not be necessary, that the said Commissioners should have a Power to protect Informers from Arrests in all Suits not exceeding Ten Pounds, whilst Suits shall be depending on their respective Informations; because we have been informed, that it is a frequent Practice amongst the principal Owlers to lend their Accomplices small Sums of Money, who are thereby deterred from informing, lest they should be arrested for such Sums; whereby, in all Probability, many Discoveries have been prevented:

That notwithstanding it is hereby proposed, That all those Actions for the Running of Wool should be carried on at the Expence of the Publick, we are of Opinion, that the Informer should not only receive all the Rewards, Forfeitures, and Advantages, he is already intitled to by Law; but that, as a further Encouragement to the Discovery of so pernicious a Practice, the said Commissioners shall pay, or cause to be paid, to such as shall discover, and bring to Justice, any Person that shall export Wool, contrary to Law, or that shall be actually aiding or assisting in carrying Wool towards the Sea-coast, or to any Creek, River, Bay, Harbour, or any other Place, in order to be exported, the Sum of £.40. over and above all Rewards already given by Acts of Parliament, notwithstanding he or they who make such Discoveries, as aforesaid, be concerned in the same Fact:

And, as this will naturally occasion some Expence, we would humbly propose, That his Majesty would be graciously pleased to direct, That the Part of the Forfeitures which appertains to his Majesty should be applied to the Discharging of the extraordinary Rewards, and to the defraying the necessary Charge that will attend the aforesad 5 M Prosecutions

But as the Preventing of this evil Practice in Great JBf^vqnly, will he to little Purpose, unless the same can likewise be prevented in Ireland, from whence much greater Quantities of Wool are run to foreign Parts than from Great Britain; we would humbly propose, That such of the above particulars as, shall he approved of, may be likewise made applicable to Ireland, so far forth as they Are compatible with the legal Importation of Wool from Jrelmd tnprcQt Britain? And it is not to be doubted but foat i$ would bp very much for the Advantage of the Wpolfon Manufactures of Great Britain, that Encou-sagement should be given to the Importers of Wool from Ireland, and the Charge of bringing the same from thence rendered as easy as possible; that it may thereby become foe Interest of Ireland, as well as of Great Britain, to put the Laws against Running of Wool duly in Execution.

All which is most humbly submitted.

Prayers.

SIR John Norris reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, and Freemen, of the ancient Town and Port of Rye, in the County of Sussexv in behalf of themselves, and many hundreds of his Majesty’s faithful Subjects was referred, That they had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and by what means the Harbour of Rye became obstructed, and decayed; and what they conceive necessary to be done, to restore the said Harbour to its ancient Goodness; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, to whom the said Petition was referred, find, upon Examination of Mr. John Dixon, who said, He had known the Harbour of Rye, and used the Sea, above Fifty Years: That, in the Year 1666, a Ship called The Saint Andrew, a Second-rate Man of War, struck on the Rip Raps, and came into the said Harbour, and rid on Float for Six Months; and likewiseI'he Happy Return, a Fifty gun Ship, and some large Dutch Ships, taken in the First Dutch War, and other large Ships, rid afloat there; and, in the next Dutch War, many large Ships, and, in the War in the Reign of King William, the Ships called The Maidstone, Sea Horse, Greyhound, with other Ships and Frigates, rode afloat there:

That the said John Dixon said further, That, about 40 Years past, he sailed in a Hoy, of Sixty Tons, as far as Blaclewall; and that it was navigable to that Place, till about the Year 1684, when a Dam being made, and several others since, the Harbour has gradually decayed: That he remembers The Squirrel, and several Merchant Ships, taken in the late French War, for want of Water to come into the Harbour, the same being fallen to Decay; and that a Fly Boat, laden with Salt, was also lost at the Mouth of the Harbour, and most of the Men drowned:

That no Ships of Burthen can now come into the Harbour, to ride afloat at low Water; and that the Decay thereof is occasioned by the Inning of Lands, which prevents the Flux of the Tide:

That if the Tide had its Flux into the present drowned Level, it would restore the Harbour to its ancient Goodness.

Mr. Thomas Grebell said, He was born at Rye, and remembers upward of 40 Years: That the Harbour then w'as open, and One hundred Ships might ride afloat, having from 14 to 18 Foot Water, at low Water:

That, in the Beginning of the War in King Williams Reign, the Ships called The Sea Horse, The Maidstone, Swan, Sally, Rose, and several other Men of War, and several other Vessels, rid afloat at low Water:

That the Tide flowed, about 35 Years ago, up to Blackwall; and then the Harbour was good; but several Shuts, or Cross-walls, being made since, has prevented the Flux of the Tide, and been the Cause of the Decay of the Harbour:

That if the Tide was now to flow up to the Place called The Drowned Level, he believes, that the Weight of the Back-water would then restore the Harbour to its ancient Use:

That the WincheUea, Squirrel, and Ren Pink, Men of War, and other Vessels, were taken in the late War; which, iPthe Harbour had been in its ancient Condition, might have been saved:

That, in October 1717, about 50 Sail of Ships, sailing to the Westward, were put back by contrary Winds, and obliged to lie under Dunginess, because they could not come into the Harbour; and that most of them were lost, which otherwise might have been saved, if the Harbour had been as good as formerly.

15

Mr. Joseph Tucker, who had known Rye for 27 Years, being examined, said, That several Ships were lost, and a great many Vessels, of great Value, taken, off the said Harbour, which might have been saved, if the Harbour had been in the Condition it formerly was in.

Jacob Acworth Esquire, Surveyor of the Navy; IVm. Clevland Esquire, Commissioner of the Navy; Mr. Tippett, and Mr. Smith, elder Brothers of Trinity House; w ere severally examined; and said, That they, by Directions of the Navy Board, had lately taken a Survey of the said Harbour; and, in their Report to the Lords of the Admiralty, had set forth, what they thought was the Cause of its Decay, and the Method they apprehended most proper to restore it to its ancient Goodness, for the Benefit of Trade and Navigation: A Copy of which Report w as produced to the Committee, and read; As also, an Estimate of the Charge of performing the Work proposed for making the Harbour useful for Navigation; which amounts to £.17,852. 4$. 0d.: Which Report and Estimate, the Committee carefully examined.

That, upon the Examination of the Witnesses aforesaid, and by the Papers referred to the Committee by the House, it appeared. That the Inning of the ChaneJ, and waste Lands, of the Harbour of Rye, and preventing the Flux of the Tide, has been the Cause of the Decay of the said Harbour; and that the only way to preserve the Harbour from being totally lost, is, t<3 prevent the same for the future:

And that the most proper Method to restore the said Harbour to its ancient Goodness, for the Benefit of Trade and Navigation, would be, to let the Tide have its free Course from Scotch Flat and Craven Sluice into the present drowned Lands, between Blackwall and Maytham.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in# Bill for the better Preservation of the Harbour of Rye, in the County of Sussex: And that Sir John Norris and Mr. Gybbon do prepare, and bring in, the same.

From the House of Commons, the 31st Day of January 1720.

Sir,

The House of Commons having taken Notice of the Absence of several of their Members, I am commanded to acquaint you with it, that you may give immediate Summons to the Representatives of your County, and Boroughs within the same, That they do attend their Service in Parliament on Thw'sday the Ninth Day of February next, notwithstanding any Order of Leave to be absent; the House of Commons intending to proceed with all Severity against all such of their Members as shall then neglect to attend the Service of the House, and whose Excuses shall not be allowed: And you are to give an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereupon, to,

Sir,

Your humble Servauf,

A Petition of the Commissioners for putting in Execution an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for repairing, amending, and enlarging, the Highways, near the City of Bath, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, when the Petitioners Vol. 19.

first proceeded to put the said Act in Execution, the Highways thereby directed to be amended were in so bad and ruinous a Condition, that the Petitioners were under a Necessity of borrowing Three thousand Pounds; and engaged the Income of the several Tolls for the Repayment thereof, with Interest: That notwithstanding the said Money was laid out in repairing the said Highways, yet the same continued in so bad a Condition, that the Petitioners have been hitherto obliged constantly to apply the whole Profits arising by the said Tolls in amending the Said Roads; reserving only Aloney enough to pay the Interest of the said £. 3,000. and other necessary Disbursements: That a great Part of the Term granted is expired; and the Creditors of the said Tolls have obtained a Decree in Chancery, that the Profits of the Tolls shall be applied to repay themselves their Principal and Interest; so that the Petitioners are disabled to pay the same, and to perfect the said Repairs: And praying, That a Bill may be brought in for enlarging the Term granted by the said Act.

Mr. Bertie reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Tenth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for repairing the Road from Highgate Gatehouse, in the County of Middlesex, to Barnet Blockhouse, in the County of Hertford; and of the Inhabitants of the several Parishes of Bishops Hatfield, North Mims, and Northaw, in the said County of Hertford; and South Mims, in the said County of Middlesex; whose Names are also thereunto subscribed; in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parishes; w^as referred; the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Tattle: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find, That, by the said Act of the Tenth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty, the Duties and Tolls thereby granted were to continue for Thirteen Years, from the 24th Day of June 1712: And,

Jeremy Sambrook Esquire, Treasurer of the said Toll, produced the Books and Accounts of Receipts and Payments arising by virtue of the said Act, which had been examined and passed by the Trustees; and said. That the Money collected for the said Toll had been duly applied for amending the Roads, according to the Directions of the said Act; but, being obliged to send to Hampstead Heath, and Barnet Common, for Gravel, it hath greatly increased the Charge and Expences in amending the Roads; and the Trustees, for carrying on the said Repairs, have borrowed £. 720. at Interest, of several Persons; and there is also due to Workmen above £. 100. That, as to that Part of the Petition as relates to the Road leading from Hadley Windmill to the Sign of the Angel in Erf eld Chace;

Richard Hurlock said, He was above 80 Years of Age; and that he has for 70 Years past known that Highway, containing about a Mile and a Half in Length, and is Part of the great common Northern Road to London, which is now very much out of repair: And that he believes it never was repaired in the Memory of Man; it being Part of the said Chace, and not known to what Parish it belongs.

Edward Vass said, That he has known the said Highway for 30 Years last past; and never knew, or heard,

1

that the same was ever repaired, or to what Parish it belongs.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the Town of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, in Common Council assembled, was presented to the House and read; setting forth. That, in pursuance of an Act of Parliament made in the Twelfth Year of Queen Anne, for building a new’ Church or Chapel of Ease, in Great Yarmouth, by a Duty on all Coals, Culm, and Cinders, to be landed there, they have built a Chapel; but are not able, from the said Duties, to pay off the Monies borrowed, much less to finish the same: That the Inhabitants are desirous to have the Streets enlightened in the dark Nights, and also to finish and adorn the said Chapel: That they have consented to raise Money sufficient to pay oft’ what they have already, and shall hereafter borrow7 for that Intent, by a Duty on Coals, Culm, and Cinders, to be imported and consumed by themselves only; but the same Cannot be done but by an Act of Parliament: And praying, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

County of Lancaster, was referred, That they had examined the Matter thereof; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find,

That the said Towns do stand upon the Banks of each Side the River Invcll; which River, a few Miles below, joins the River Mercy; and so descends to the Port of . Lcccrpook, Twenty-four Miles from the said Towns.

That it appeared, by the Testimony of Mr John Mm, That the Trade is very great from Leverpoole to Man-Chester, the Towns adjacent; and that the Land-carriage betwixt Manchester and Leverpoole doth amount to about Fifteen hundred Pounds per Annum; and the Land-carriage doth so great Damage to the Highways, that the Charges of the Repairs thereof is very burthensome to the Inhabitants of the respective Towns, and other Places, chargeable therewith.

It also appeared to the Committee, That if the 9aid Rivers Mercy and Irwell, from Leverpoole, to Manchester, were made navigable, it would not only preserve the Roads about and between the Places aforesaid, but be a groat Advantage and Encouragement to the-Trade of those Pails:

That the River Mei'cy is already navigable from Lever-poolc to a Place called Bank Key, near I Farrington; which is Twelve Miles, and computed to be about Half-way betwixt the Two Towns of Leverpoole and Manchester:

That by effecting this Navigation, there will be a Communication opened hetvveen the West and East Seas of Great Britain; that is to say, from Manchester to Wike-field, being Twenty-eight Miles; and from Manchester to Leeds, in the County of York, being Thirty-two Miles by Land; which will shorten the present Land-carriage near One-half.
