The said Report is as follows; vizi

May it please your Lordships,

IN Obedience to your Commands, signified to us by Mr. Lowndes, in his Letter of the 25th Instant, inclosihgak Letter from Mr. Popple, Secretary to the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, relating to the prohibiting the Wear of printed Callicoes, and to the Difficulties the East India Company lie under in carrying on their Trade; your Lordships directing us to transmit our Report thereon, and, at the same time, to send a Copy thereof to the Board of Trade;

We humbly acquaint your Lordships, That some time since we received, from the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, Extract of a Memorial to them, from the Directors of the united East India Company, consisting of several Articles relating to their Trade; desiring our Opinion: But, observing that the said Memorial contained several Matters tending to the lessening the Revenue, we thought proper to acquaint the Board of Trade, that we did not think ourselves justified in giving our Opinion, as they have represented to your Lordships: And having now received your Commands therein, we herewith humbly lay before your Lordships the Copy of the said Extract, with our Observations on* each Article; viz.

In relation to the Company’s Trade at home;

They propose,

1st? To put a Rate on all unrated East India Goods; thereby to prevent the Computation of the Duties by a new-introduced Method of Algebra, contrary to all former Usage of Merchants, and very difficult to be understood by the Buyers, English or Foreigners; whereby their Sales are prejudiced.

2d. To take off the Retrospect charged on the Company, by that Method.

3d. To allow the Company the Five per Cent. prompt Payment on the Duties arising on the 15per Cent, additional Duty laid on all Goods made of Cotton, and not prohibited, payable on the gross Sale at the Candle; the Company allow 6 and £ per Cent. for prompt Payment on all their Goods the Directors apprehend, by the General Words of the Act, this Five perCent. is dub to the Com-Vol. 19* pany;

Commissioners Observations.

The Commissioners have no Objection to this Proposal, provided the Rates to be fixed upon unrated East India Goods be such as will not lessen the Produce of the present Funds; as they formerly represented to the Treasury: But the Commissioners observe, That these Duties are not computed by Algebra, as alleged by the Company, but by the Rule of Proportion, which is common Arithmetick.

The proper Officers have, for some time, been employed in drawing out an Account of such Retrospect, chargeable on the Company; but they have not yet been able* from the Nature of the Business, to perfect the same; so that we cannot now lay before your Lordships the Amount of that Charge: As to the taking off or discharging the Retrospect we humbly submit,

The not allowing the Company the Discount of Five per Cent, for prompt Payment on the Duties of 15perCent. bn Muslins and Callicoes, and other Manufactures of Cotton, not sold within 12 Months after their Importation, was according to the Opinion of Sir Edward Northey* late Attorney General, when that Matter was disputed; but, considering that the Company do, as they allege, 6E allow

4th. To allow the Company,' as all oth^r Merchants arev the Five per Cent. Discount on the Subsidies, and 6 and'J on the Imposts of Customs oihurtrfcfced Goods; because the Company cap sell but twice a Year; and-if thehr Griods will not go off* in one of the Two Sales, as sometimes is the Case, the Commissioners refuse to allow the said Discounts; whereas other Merchants can sell at any time.

5th. To grant a longer Time than a Year for Drawbacks on the Company’s Goods exported: By this means, the Goods, generally speaking, would sell the better, and thereby, the Revenue increased; the Merchants would not be under the Necessity of sending them so soon abroad as now, to wait for a Market; would save the Commission* and Warehouse-room, paid on that Account to Foreigners; and the Crown would have the Duties longer in their Hands before drawn back again.

..6th. To review and amend the Law, as it now stands, of giving Certificates for foreign Tea imported, as is now daily practised; which gives great Encouragement to the bringing it in from Ostende

7th, Jt would be a further Ease, and generally beneficial, to the Company, and encourage the home and foreign Buyers, if a Method could be settled, that the Customs on all the Company’s Goods should not be paid for till taking them away, as is already the Case in Coffee.

8th. It would be some Ease to the Company to pay no Duties on the prohibited exportable Goods till they are shipped out, as is directed in the Case of Tea.

9th. The Directors take Liberty humbly to represent, That the Deficiencies on their Fund are very great; and to pray they may be reimbursed, and the like Deficiencies prevented in future.

The Commissioners think the Cornpany’s Proposal for allowing them the Discount of 6 and \ per Cent, on the Imposts of unrated Goods, though sold after a Year, to be equitable, for the Reasons mentioned in the Proposal, and the Commissioners Answer to the foregoing Article; but as to their desiring the Allowance of Five per Cent. Discount on the Subsidies, there was no need of it; for the proper Officers have certified to us, that the said Allowance on those Daties, when paid, has always been -made to the Company on all Sorts of Goods, without any regard to the time of Importation, though more than fcr Year before the time of the Goods being sold.

The Commissioners have nothing to object to the granting the Company a longer time for the Drawback on their Goods exported, for the Reasons they offer, as is done in the Case of some other Goods.

Thb Commissioners agree to this; and are of Opinion, That no Certificate, or Licence, should be granted for Tea; they having observed, That, of late, Licences have been taken out for the bringing g eat Quantities thereof from Holland and Flanders, wherewith they acquainted some of the Directors of the East India Company.

As to what they propose in this Article; viz. That the Customs on all their Goods should not be paid for till they are taken away, as is already the Case on Coffee, the Commissioners cannot agree to this Proposal; forasmuch as the same will be a Detriment to the Revenue, by keeping the Crown out of the Money so long; besides, as the Officers have reported to us, should such a Liberty be granted, it would occasion much Trouble and Difficulty, with relation to the Number of Entries, and knowing the precise Times when their Goods w ere taken away; The Case of Coffee is extraordinary, and is but One Species; whereas the Species of other Goods, imported by the Company, are very numerous.

Unrated prohibited Goods pay only the Half Subsidy; but the paying thereof, in the manner proposed, will be a Prejudice to the Revenue, by keeping the Crown so long out of the Money.

This is not properly cognizable by the Commissioners.

3d. To lay Penalties on all Ships and Commanders that shall take in any Goods out of any East India Ship not being within the Limits of the Company’s Charter.

5th. To make the Goods, or the Value, afterwards liable to Forfeiture, if laden on board any Ship, to be afterwards, when at Sea, or in any Port, put on board an outward-bound East India Ship; and to make such Ship which puts them oh board forfeited.

6th. To extend to the Company, and their Officers, the same Benefits as the Laws provide for the Customhouse Officers more safe and easy seizing of Goods or Vessels; with like Penalties and Provisions, in case of Resistance, for so iar as relates to Goods to be carried to or from the East Indies.

7th. To give the Company a Share of the Forfeitures of East India Goods seized by the Custom-house Officers; which would prevent fraudulent Seizures.

Fast India Trade.

The Commissioners have no Objection to this Article!

The Commissioners cannot be of Opinion, That the Company should have Power to grant Deputations toseize Money or Goods shipped on board their Outward-bound Ships, without their Licence; which may encourage collusive Seizures, mentioned in the 15 Section of the Act of Frauds, 14 Car. II. and will be a Repeal of that Section which prohibits any Person making Seizure of any Ships, Goods, or Merchandize, for or by reason of unlawful Importation or Exportation, other than by Officers of the Customs: Brit the Commissioners may, on a Warrant from your Lordships, in that behalf, grant -their Deputation to One or more Persons, whom the Company shall recommend for the Service mentioned hi this Paragraph.

The Commissioners have no Objection to what is here proposed; arid think an Addition to it may be serviceable to the Company, viz. That if any Goods be unshipped at Sea, or at any other Place, out of a Ship from the East Indies, into any other Ship or Vessel; that then the same, or the Value thereof, shall be forfeited, with a Penalty on the Persons concerned either in unshipping or receiving the Goods.

If this shall be thought reasonable, it may be done by Authority to this Board from the Treasury, as mentioned in the Commissioners Answer to the 4th Article.

This must be a Prejudice to the Revenue, or the Officers; and the Commissioners do not see how it will hinder collusive Seizures.

The Commissioners having a Doubt, whether the Charter granted to the Company could warrant their Stores to be exported, free of Duty, they advised with Sir Edward Northey; then Attorney General, in March 1714; w ho was of Opinion, That if the Charter granted by King William was good, and warranted by the A*ct for settling the Trade to the East Indies, the Privileges to the Company could continue no longer than the then Continuance of the Customs; but, those expiring, the Grant could not discharge the Company of the like Duties, given de novo, in the 5th Year of her late Majesty, without there had been an Exception in favour of the Company: But we have no Objection to the Company’s Request, provided the Quantities and Species of Goods to be annually exported be ascertained.

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordships Consideration.

And then he withdrew.

A Motion being made, and the Question being put, That it appears to this House, That, during the time the Rill for enabling the South Sea Company to enlarge their Capital Stock, and Fund, was depending in Parliament, Fifty thousand Pounds Stock, being Part of the Five hundred seventy-four thousand Five hundred Pounds fictitious Stock, entered in the Cash book of the Company, as sold for One million Two hundred fifty-nine thousand Three hundred Twenty-five Pounds, was taken in, or held, by Robert Knight, late Cashier of the said Company, for Elias Turner, Jacob Sawbridge, and Sir George Caswall, a Member of this House, without any

valuable Consideration paid, or sufficient Security given for, the Acceptance of, or Payment for, such Stock;

The House divided.

The Yeas go forth.

Tellers for the No*^* } 92-

So it was resolved hi the Affirmative.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, by the Books Of the said Turner and Company, and the Examinations nowr before this House, That there was a clear Profit of Two hundred fifty thousand Pounds made of the said Fifty thousand Pounds Stock, so taken in, or held, as aforesaid.

Resolved, That the said Sir George Caswatt, by concurring with his Partners, the said Elias Turner and Jacob Sawbridge, in having the said Fifty thousand Pounds Stock taken in, or held, as aforesaid, has been guilty of a corrupt, infamous, and dangerous Practice, highly re^ fleeting on the Honour and Justice of Parliament, and destructive to the Interest of his Majesty’s Government.

Resolved, That the said Sir George Caswall be, for his said Offence, expelled this House.

Resolved, That the said Sir George Caswall be* committed Prisoner to his Majesty’s Tower of London: And that Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant accordingly.

Resolved, That the Estates, real and personal^ of the said Sir George Caswall, Jacob Sawbridge, and' Elias Turner, be subject and liable to answer, and make good,-to die South Sea Company, the aforesaid Sum of Twer hundred fifty thousand Pounds, which was the advanced Price, on the Eleventh Day of June 1720, of the said Fifty thousand Pounds Stock, over and above the Sum of One hundred twenty-five thousand Pounds parti to the said Company for the same.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought hr, pursuant to the said Resolution: And that Mr. Brodrick, the Lord Molesworth, Mr. Hutcheson, and Mr. Ward, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

The several Examinations of Mr. Jos. Stanbrough, Mr. Jacob Sawbridge senior, and Mr. Knight, taken before the Committee of Secrecy, this Day read, relating to the said Sir George Caswall; which had been delivered to the Clerk of this House by the Clerk who attended the said Committee of Secrecy; are bound up with the other Papers of this Session.

Ordered, That the Report from the Committee of Secrecy be taken into further Consideration upon Tuesday Morning next

A Petition of Richard Waring, Bryan Fairfax, and Thomas Ashurst, Esquires, was presented to the House, and read; settingforth, That, by Indenture, bearing Date the 8th Day of December, in the 43d Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, Sir Thomas Lee Knight, Thomas Spencer, Edward Rigby, and Thomas Ireland, Esquires, Trustees for William then Earl of Derby, did grant and convey to her said late Majesty, her Heirs and Successors, the Manor of Latham, and the Demesne and other Lands thereto belonging, in the County of Lancaster, Part of the ancient Instate belonging to the Ancestors of the said Earl, lo hold to her said late Majesty, her Heirs and Successors, Vo Lp 19*

to her and their own Use, for eves: That, by Letters Patent, her said late Majesty did give and grant to the said William then Earl of Derby the said Manor and Premisses, to hold to him, and the Heirs Male of his Bodyj Remainder to the Heirs Male of the Cody of Sir George Stanley, formerly Lord Strange; Remainder to her said late Majesty, her Heirs and Successors: That, by other Letters Patent, bearing Date the Third Day of July, in the 13th Year of his late Majesty King Charles the First, his said late Majesty did give and grant to James then Lord Strange, amongst other things, the Reversion of the said Manor of Lathom, and Premissses* to hold to the said James Lord Strange, his Heirs and Assigns, to the Use of him, his Heirs and Assigns, for ever: And his said late Majesty did, by such Letters Patent, will and declare, That the said James Lord Strange, or his Heirs, should, within One Year then next after, re-convey the said Reversion of the said Manor and Premises to his said Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, to remain as if that Grant had not been made; but the same was never so re-conveyed: That Fines and Recoveries were afterwards had and suffered of the same Premisses; and, upon a special Verdict in the Court of Exchequer, the said Manor and Premisses were adjudged to be the Right of the Daughters and Heirs of William George Richard last Earl of Derby; and, upon the Death of the Lady Elizabeth Stanley, did wholly vest in Hennetta Maria, late Lady Ashbumham, the surviving Daughter, as Heir general of the said Family: That, by Indentures of Lease and Release, bearing pate the 22d and 23d Days of July 1714, made previous to the Marriage of the said late Lady Henrietta Maria with the Right honourable John now Lord Ashbumham, she, the said late Lady Henrietta Maiia, did grant and convey to the Petitioners, and Richard Brook Esquire, since deceased, amongst other things, the said Manor and Premisses, to hold to the Petitioners, and the said Richard Brook, and their Heirs, upon Trust, to pay several Sums of Money therein mentioned; and, subject thereto, in Trust for the said Lady Ashbumham, her Heirs and Assigns:

That, by Indenture, dated the 30th August 1717, the said late Lady Ashbumham charged the said Manor with the Payment of several other Sums of Money: That the said late Lady Ashbumham is since dead, having left Issue only One Daughter, Henrietta Bridget Ashbumham, an Infant about Five Years old, who is intituled to the said Manor, subject to the several Charges thereon: That there are so many Heirs Male of the Family of the Earls of Derby now living, who must all be dead, without Issue Male, before the said Reversion of the said Manor, if the same should be re-conveyed to the Crown, pursuant to the Intention . of King Charles the First, can take place, that the same cannot be accounted valuable to the Crown:

That, by the Act of the First Year of Queen Anne, for limiting the Grants of the Crown, his Majesty is restrained from aliening any Right belonging to the Crown; so that the said Clause in the said Grant from King Charles the First cannot be discharged, nor the Benefit thereof wayed, without Consent of Parliament: And praying, that a Bill may be brought in for confirming the said Manor and Premisses in the Petitioners, and their Heirs, upon, and subject to, the several Trusts in the said respective Indentures of 1714 and 1717, discharged of the said Clause in the said Grant from King Charles the First, and all Benefit and Advantage to be taken thereof.

Mr. Comptroller acquainted the House, That the Contents of the said Petition had been laid before his Majesty; and that his Majesty had been pleased to command him to signify to this House, That his Majesty has no Objection to the bringing in a Bill in the manner desired by the Petition.

MR. Bertie reported from the Committee, to whom Bafoetto the Petition of the Inhabitants of the Parish of Hadley, in the County of Middlesex, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerks Table:

Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, to whom the Petition was referred, have met; and, upon the Examination of several Witnesses, do find the Matter to be as followeth:

That a lload, in Length about Half a Mile, from the Bear Inn to the Windmill, in the Parish of Hadley, Pars of the Saint Albans and Hatfield Road, being the great Road to the North Part of this Kingdom, is become so ruinous, that the same cannot, by the Course appointed by the Laws now in being, be kept in Repair:

That the Inhabitants are very small in Number, and have collected Two Six Peny Rates, and duly applied the same; yet the said Road is almost impassable.

Instructions for our trusty and well-beloved William Leathes Esquire, our Resident at Brussels. Given at our Court at St. James's, the 6th Day of February 1724. in the Seventh Year of our Reign.

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS Mr. Robei't Knight, late Cashier of the South Sea Company, did make his Escape out of this Country some time since, when he was under Examination of a Committee of the House of Commons, touching several fraudulent and corrupt Practices, of the Directors and other Officers, of the said Company:

And whereas also we have received humble Addresses Jrom both pur Houses of Parliament, That we would be graciously pleased to use our most powerful Instances , with all Princes and States in Alliance with us, that, in Case the said Robert Knight should betake himself to any Part of the Countries or Dominions belonging to them, they would cause him to be apprehended, and delivered up to us, in order to his being brought to Justice: Now, having received some Information, That the said Robert Knight may be, at this time, skulking either in the City of Brussells, or in some other Part of the Law Countries; and having strong Reasons to believe, that he knows tire Secret of many of the fraudulent and corrupt Practices abovesaid; which, perhaps, will never be brought to Light, unless he make Discovery of the same; and being also informed, That several extraordinary Reports, which highly reflect on ,the Credit and Reputation of the Administration of our Affairs, can best be cleared up, and set in a true Light, by the said Robert Knight; our Will and Pleasure is, That, without Loss of Time, you cross the Sea, and make the most diligent and strict Enquiry after the said Robert Knight, both in the said City of Brussells, and in all other Parts of the Law Countries; and that, if you shall learn, that he hath been stopped by any Prince or State whatsoever, you do immediately go and deliver to that Prince or State the Latin Letter which we have signed, and given to you, for that Purpose; and you will, at the same time, use the strongest and most effectual Instances, that the said Robert Knight be delivered up to you; which being done, you will use all necessary Precautions to bring him over, and deliver him up to Justice: And if you shall have Intelligence, that the said Robert Knight is either residing or travelling in any other Country or Part whatsoever, you are hereby required to follow him with the utmost Diligence; and make Application to that Prince or State in whose Dominion you shall then find him, in order that he may be delivered up to you for the Purposes above-said: You are carefully to send exact Accounts of all your Proceedings from time to time, in this most Important Affair: And you are to follow such further Orders and Instructions as you shall receive from us, or One of our Principal Secretaries of State.

G. R.

Sir, Whitehdll, 1 oth February 17^.

HIS Majesty having, upon my Lord Stanhope's Death; been pleased to command me to serve him again in the Office of Secretary of State, and committed to my Care the Department his Lordship had, in whose Province you were, Mr. Secretary Craggs, who is ill of the Small-pox, has sent me Copies of the Kings Latin Letter given you, and of your Instructions; by which I find you are fully apprised of his Majesty’s Pleasure with relation to the securing Mr. Robert Knight; so that all I have to send you at present, is, the Copies of the Addresses from each House of Parliament, the Prayer of which his Majesty has granted; and commanded you accordingly to make the proper Applications, and use the most effectual Instances, that the Person of the said Robert Knight, together with his Papers and Effects, may be secured, and delivered up to you: His Majesty would have you, in his N ame (which, most probably, you have already done), thank the Marquis de Frik for his Readiness in causing Mr. Knight to be seized; and acquaint him, That his Majesty hopes for a further Mark of his Affection, in delivering him, and his Papers and Effects, up to you, as before-mentioned: You will take a particular Account of them, being liable to Demands from the South Sea Company, as you will find by the inclosed Copy of their Representation, to whose Request his Majesty has been graciously pleased to condescend: I do not doubt but you will carefully inform me, from time to time, of what shall occur, in your Parts, that is proper to be laid before the King; which I shall not fail to do, and to send you his Majesty’s Commands, as often as they shall be requisite, for your Conduct in the Affairs under your Management; and, if in any thing I may be particularly serviceable, I shall be ready and desirous to shew you how much I am, fyc.

My Lord, Brussels, 24th February 172^.

YE S T E R D AY Morning, immediately, after my Arrival at this Place, I waited on the Marquis de Prie. When I had made him the Compliments he deserves, on his ready Compliance with the King’s Requisition to seize Mr. Knight, in case he should be discovered skulking in any Part of the Austrian Netherlands, I shewed him his Majesty’s Letter, which I received with my Instructions; the . Contents of which I need not repeat, because the Copy of it lies in Mr. Secretary Graggs' Off ice; and at foe same time 1 explained to him the Service it would be to the King, and foe Nation, to have Mr. Knight immediately delivered into my Care, and a sufficient Guard given me to conduct him to Ostend; from whence I would carry him, on board one of the King’s Packet-boats, directly to London, in case I did not meet with a Frigate there on my Arrival, as I had reason to expect; I told his Excellency how much the King had at heart, and in how strong Terms his Majesty had recommended to me, the Care of having him brought to England, in safe Custody, with all possible Dispatch: 1 enforced my Instances with the strongest Arguments I was Master of; and, I must own, I could not think of any so strong as those I had the ‘ Honour to receive from his Majesty’s own Mouth the Night before I left London, and those your Lordship was pleased to furnish me with.

The Marquis heard all I had to say on this Subject with great Attention; and made a very handsome return to the Compliment I made him in his Majesty's Name; which he concluded, by desiring me to assure the King, That lie had hitherto improved all Opportunities of shewing his Zeal and Attachment for his Majesty’s Service; and that he would always continue with Pleasure, and the greatest Sincerity, to do the same: He continued; What I have done on this Occasion will, I hope, he agreeable to big Majesty; and you may be assured, that my best Endeavours shall not be wanting to complete what I have already so luckily begun: But you are sensible, said he, that there ar6 Two weighty Considerations

which makes it impossible for the tb comply immediately with the Demand yoli have now made, in the Name of the King your Master: First, The Measures I am obliged to keep with the Court of Vieima; and, Secondly, with the States of this Province: Although I have seized Mr. Knight, at the King’s Requisition; yet I dare not presume to deliver ban to you, Or any othefr Person, before I have the Approbation of the Emperor, and h/s Imperial Majesty's piositive Orders for so doing; to whldi‘Purpose, I will write Tomorrow to Vienna, in such Terire, as I hope, will proctire me a satisfactory Answer: And I must tell you, that even then I shall be extremely embarrassed with the Privileges of this Province, which I have myself but lately sworn, in the Emperors Naifce, to maintain inviolably: You know,- by a long Experience, the turbulent Spirit df these People, and it Would be needless for me to enlarge on that Head; since I can’t sup1-pose, that you have forgot, that, notwithstanding all the Pains you were Obliged to take, how narrowly you escaped a Tumult in this Town, when the Lord North and Gray was arrested, on a groundless Report of your designing to carry him to the Castle of Ghent, where there was then, an English Garison; and at a time when the Administration of the Government of these Provinces was in the Hands of the King your Master, and of the States General: You have been ah Eye-witness of the late Troubles in these Parts; which, so far from being yet forgot, are scarce appeased; and you know from what small Beginnings they took their Rise: You will then, I flatter myself, make a just Representation to his Majesty of these Matters; and give me time to endeavour to procure the good Effect the King expects from your pressing Instances, in such' Manner as my Proceedings may be justifiable at the Imperial Court; and not give Grounds here to open anew the Sore, which, though skinned over, is full of Corruption at Bottom: 1 must not omit acquainting you, that some of the Counsel, and several of the Deputies, of the States of Brabant, have already cautioned me on this Head; and, should your Instances come to their Knowledge, they would apply to me in Form for the Preservation of their Privileges; and that would put it out of my Power to render the Service I propose to his Majesty, and the British Nation: Therefore, if you expect I should bring this Affair to a good Issue, it behoves you to leave the Management of it entirely to me; in which case, I promise you, I will use all my Skill and Dexterity to effect it; and, in the mean time, I will not only communicate to you the Advances I make, and the Obstacles I may meet with; but I will also concert with you the most likely Means to make it succeed.

I wish, my Lord, I could say, that the Marquis dePrib had represented the fore-mentioned Facts in a wrong Light: I have had but too much Occasion to know the Truth of them, and several others of that Kind; so that I cannot judge it for the King’s Service at present to declare the Purport of my Commission; nor to insist openly on the Demand I have made, before I shall have sounded the States of Brabant, or that I shall have received his Majesty’s particular Orders for so doing: Nevertheless,

1 hope your Lordship will not question my most assiduous Application, in concert with the Marquis,

for obtaining so just and so good an End as his Majesty proposes, by bringing Mr. Knight to Justice in England.

By the Accounts 1 have of the Manner of his being guarded, I think he is in safe Custody: There is an Officer constantly in his Chamber; Four Centinels by Day, and Nine by Night, at his Door and Windows, and the Lieutenant Governor of the Citadel has a watchful Ey© over him.

I am informed, that there were Three Trunks taken at Tirlemont, belonging to him, and carried to Antwerp, where they remain sealed; I think of going thither in a Day or Two hence, to have them opened; and an Inventory made of the Papers, and other Effects, in them; and

then to seal them up again in his own, and the Presence

of such other Persons as the Marquis de Prie shall appoint for that Purpose.

My Lord,

I WAS just going to send the inclosed Letter for my Lord Sunderland to the Post, when the Messenger, John Camara, brought me the Honour of your Lordship’s Dispatch of the 1 oth Instant, O. S. with Copies of the Addresses of both Houses of Parliament, and the Representation of the South Sea Company, to his Majesty, concerning Mr. Knight; on Receipt of which, I went immediately to the Marquis de Frit, and acquainted him with the Contents of them all: This gave me a fresh Opportunity of renewing my Instances, and of making the Marquis sensible, how agreeable it would be to his Majesty, and his Parliament, to have Mr. Knight put into my Hands to be transported to England\ with all possible Dispatch. I pressed his Excellency, in the strongest Terms, to comply with the King’s Request j and shewed him the Inconveniencies which might attend the least Delay in this important Affair: But all my Arguments were not sufficient to move him to a Compliance: The Marquis repeated what he had said in the Tw o Conferences I had had with him on the same Subject; and he renewed to me the Assurances of his utmost Endeavours to procure the Effects which his Majesty proposes from my repeated Instances; adding, That the Consideration the Emperor has for his Majesty, and the Interest his Imperial Majesty has in contributing all that in him lies towards Re-establishing of the Affairs of England, would bo strong Motives to induce him to comply with the Kings Request.

I shall ndt trouble your Lordship with a Repetition of tny Letter of the 24th Instant to my Lord Sunderland, since I anl persuaded it will have been put into your Lordship’s Hands before this can reach you: That Letter, and the inclosed, will, I hope, convince you, that I have not Emitted any thing that was ih my Power, or proper to be done in the Management of the Affair committed to my Charge, as they will likewise satisfy the Parliament of the just Measures his Majesty had taken for obtaining the Purport of their Addresses, even before they w ere presented: Arid I beg Leave to assure your Lordship, That I will continue to use the utmost Diligence in the Prosecution of my Instructions: Though I have the Mortification of meeting such Obstacles as cannot be immediately removed, yet I hope, in a little time, to get over them all* provided die Marquis de Prill acts with the Sincerity he expresses, and that Zeal for his Majesty’s Service, which he has effectually shewn on former Occasions. I must riot omit acquainting your Lordship, That the Privileges of this Province embarrasses him more than the Orders he waits for from Vienna; and, on thht Account, 1 am obliged to proceed with the greatest Caution and Privacy, to prevent the Alarm my Instructions would give here, in case they should come to be known by the States of Brabant: which Would infallibly put it out of the Marquis de Pries Power to render the Service to his Majesty, which he proposes, and which, I hope, his Inclination leads him to.

Your Lordship may remember the Inconveniencies we were like to have been brought into, by the Arrest of my Lord North and Gray: Had I not acted with great Pre-cauiion in diat Affair, it w ould surely have caused a Tumult in this Town; which, with all my Care and Management, I was barely able to prevent: However, if, after what I have said, your Lordship judges it absolutely necessary, I will persist in the Demand I have made in his Majesty’s Name; though, if I were to act wholly by Vol. ip.

- IN my last of the 24th Instant, by Stjuire the Messenger,

I did myself the Honour to give your Lordship a particular Account of the Conference I had, , on my Arrival at this Place, with the Marquis de Prii: I have since renewed my Instances, and, in the most pressing Terms, desired, That Mr. Knight might be given up to me, in order to have him carried to England. I repeated all the Arguments I had before made use of, and such others as then occurred to me; arid I enforced them, with the earnest Desire his Majesty expressed to have Knight brought over with all possible Dispatch i I assured his Excellency, as the King had directed me, That he could not, at this Juncture, do a greatef- Pleasure, nor tender a more agreeable Service, to his Majesty: To which the Marquis replied;

I hope the King will do me the Justice to believe, that had it been in my Power to comply with the Demand

Srou made in his Majesty’s Name, 1 would not have ba-anced One Moment, nor given you the Trouble of re^ newing your Instances. I thought I had already explained myself so fully, in our last Conference, as to convince you of the Necessity I am under to act in this Affair contrary to my Inclinations: And, that you may not doubt mv Sincerity, I will show you the Letter I have writ to Vienna, which, I hope, will procure me the Emperor’s Orders to commit Mr. Knight to your Care. In the mean time, I entreat you to have Patience; and to depend on my best Endeavours to procure you the Effects his Majesty expects from your Solicitations.

I read the Marquis’s Letter to the Prince of Savoy; in which he ha3 faithfully reported all that I had said to him in our First Conference: He told the Prince, howr much the King had this Affair at Heart, and in what pressing Terms I had applied to him; but the Marquis desired, 1 would excuse him from communicating to me, as yet, the Conclusion of that Letter, though it was not improbable he might do it at a more proper time. This, my Lord, is the Substance of what passed between us Yesterday:

And I have Reason to fear, that I shall have no other Answer from him, until he be fully informed of the Intentions of the Imperial Court on this Head.

Although I foresaw, before I left London, the Difficulties I should have to struggle with; yet, I must confess, the Delay gives me a very sensible Concern: But, as I have not omitted any thing that might contribute to the obtaining of the End for which I was sent over, I hope your Lordship will judge favourably of my Conduct, and Honour me with his Majesty’s Commands, in case it shall be thought necessary to renew my Instances before the Marquis has received an Answer to his Letter. I have the Honour to be, with the greatest Veneration and Respect,

My Lord, I§tr.

Whitehall, 20th Febnlary 172?-.

Sir,

I HAVE received your Letters of the 26th and 27th Instant, N. S. and have laid them before the King; who is well satisfied with the Endeavours and Arguments you have used to induce the Marquis de Prie to deliver up Mr. Knight; but at the same time his Majesty is not a little surprised at the Marquis declining to do it: This Case is so flagrant, and the Person demanded so notoriously guilty of those infamous Frauds and Artifices, that have brought the Nation into the utmost Disorder, that his Majesty dickhink the Marquis might have exerted himself) without particular Orders, in doing so exemplary a Piece

of Justice; mi givWg Satisfaction to the King, the Parliament, and even to many Thousands in foreign Countries, who have suffered irreparable Losses by those wicked Contrivances, in which this Robert Knight has had so great a Share: His Majesty cannot question, but that the Emperor will readily give his Consent to the surrendering such a Man; and that Colonel ChurchiWs Errand will produce that Effect, if the Marquis dePrii shall persist in judging it necessary to wait for such Orders: But as the King thinks the Marquis would run no Risque in complying immediately *uth his Desires in this Point; and would particularly oblige his Majesty, by making it, in such manner, his own Act; it is therefore his Majesty a Pleasure, That you should renew the most pressing Instances for the delivering up the said Mr. Knight, without expecting till the Orders come from Viennat And his Majesty hopes, that you will prevail nt last, and get into Your Hands one whom no Country, no Laws, or Privileges, should protect from being given up to Justice.

Brussells, the 6th March 1721.

My Lord,

PURSUANT to your Lordship’s Directions of the *Fenth February, O. S. I have been at Antwerp, where I opened, in the Presence of the Lieutenant Governor, and another Officer, the Three Trunks and a small Writing-box, which were seized withMr.iT»ig///; Although I searched and risked ail very exactly, I am to acquaint your Lordship, that, to my Surprize, I found neither Papers, Books, nor any Effects whatever, only his own, and his Son’s Wearing Apparel and Linen, and about 130 Guineas: I asked him several Questions concerning the Papers and Effects, which it was reported he had brought with him; lo which he answered, by a very solemn Delaration, That what I had seen in his Trunks, and a few Guineas he had spent on the Road, was all that he had brought off; That his Departure was so sudden he had not time to lay aside any Part of his Estate, which, on Inquiry, would be found considerable. Finding him so very positive in affirming what he had said, I took my Leave of him, and returned to this Place.

As I have not been honoured with any of your Lordship’s Letters, since that of the 10th ultimo, O. S. I have very little to add, more than a Repetition of what I mentioned in my last of the 27th February \ viz. That I do not expect any other Answer from the Marquis de Frit than what I have already acquainted your Lordship with, until he knows die Emperors Intentions on the Subject of KnightV being delivered up to me. However, as I have frequent-Opportunities of seeing him, 1 turn the Subject of our Conversation on this Affair; and, by the best Observations I can yet make, he appears very inclinable io do all that is in his Power to procure the Effects of my Instances: But I observe him daily more embarrassed how to deal with these turbulent People, who are very jealous of, and zealous in, the Preservation of the small Remains of their ancient Rights and Privileges. This Obstacle, I plainly foresee, as I did before I left England, will give me more than ordinary Trouble to surmount, after the Emperors Intentions are known; and till then the Marquis de Prit does not judge it proper to touch this nice Point to the States, of Brabant; for which Reason I must also be silent for some time longer. I have the Honour to be, with a most profound Respect,

My Lord, $c.

To the Right honourable the JVm. Leathes.

’E ,my last, of the’ loth Instant, by which, and my former Relations, your Lordship will perceive, that I had not discontinued my Instances, I have received the Honour of your Lordship’s Letter of the 20th Februaryf

O. S..; which gave me a fresh Occasion to press the Marquis de Prit, in the strongest Terms, to consent to Mr. Knight's being delivered up to me: I urged all the Arguments your Lordship was pleased to furnish me with; and I laid a great Stress on the Losses sustained by the People of these Provinces, by the Frauds and Artifices of the Person in question; which were so flagrant, that I could not doubt but his Conduct, in . delivering Mr. Knight up to Justice, would meet with the Approbation of the Emperor, since his Imperial Majesty’s Subjects would probably reap a considerable Benefit thereby $ and that I judged the Demand not only Just and reasonably but even the Interest of the Emperor, or of any other Prince, to contribute towards making an Example of so vile an Offender; by whose unwarrantable Practices a whole Nation had been brought into the utmost Disorder; And I assured his Excellency, That, had the Case happened in his Majesty’s Dominions, the King would not have made the least Difficulty in giving up a Person whose Crimes had rendered him obnoxious to his King and Country, and who had been One of the principal Instruments in the Ruin of an infinite Number of his Fellow Subjects, as well as Foreigners: That his Majesty, on these Considerations, and several others, too long to repeat here, hoped his Excellency would exert himself, without waiting for the Emperor’s Orders to do so exemplary a Piece of Justice; by which be would render a most agreeable Service to the King, the Parliament, and the whole Nation; especially at this Juncture, when the Parliament had the Conduct of Mr. Knight, and his Associates, under their Consideration: I also represented to him the ill Consequences which might attend the least Delay in this Affair.

When I had ended my Remonstrances* the Marquis, being a little ruffled, told me, with an Air of Discontent, That he was suprised to find me so warm in the Renewal of my Instances; and that he imagined the Reasons he had alleged in our former Conferences on this Subject, if truly represented, would have satisfied the King, and his Ministers, of the Reasonableness of his Proceedings: But since he found the contrary, by the Language 1 had held, he was obliged to repeat what he had formerly acquainted me with; viz. That however he might be inclined of himself to give his Majesty a Mark of his Zeal, on this Occasion he could not comply with the King’s Demand, without having first the Emperor’s Orders for his Justification: Besides, said he, since you press me so hard, I must tell you, That at the same time that I acquainted the Imperial Court with the Arrest, my Duty obliged me to inform the Emperor of the Difficulties I should probably meet with, by reason of the Privileges of this Pror vince, which I myself have but lately sworn to maintain inviolably: Therefore I hope his Majesty will not expect I should act directly contrary to the Oath I have taken in the Emperors Name, without so much as the Scrape of a Pen to justify my Conduct, either at Court, or to the States of Brabant; who are become more jealous than ever of the small Remains of their ancient Rights

tmd Privileges: And I hope his Majesty \viH consider from what a small Beginning the late Troubles, which, though appeased, are not yet forgot, took their Rise; and lest his Majesty, and his Ministers, Should have forgot it, I desire you will inform them, That our late Insurrections proceeded from no other Cause than his Imperial Majesty's insisting on the Doyens taking the Oaths, which they had never scrupled under the Duke of Anjou, nor during the Administration of the Two Maritime Powers. If the Animosities of the People rose then to such a Height as to take up Arms without any just Grounds, What may we not expect* should I, of my own Accord, comply with your Demand; which every Body is sensible would be a manifest Violation of the 17th Article of the Joyeuse Entree; of which I intreat you to transmit a Copy to my Lord Townshend? Besides, continued the Marquis, I will hot suppose the King your Master can expect his Imperial Majesty should violate the Privileges of his Subjects, when his Britt. Majesty is so religious an Observer of the Rights and Liberties of his Subjects, as by Law established, in all his Dominions: No; such a Supposition would be too injurious to that exemplary Justice and Clemency, for which his Majesty is so universally esteemed by all the World.

This, my Lord, is what passed in the Conference I had Yesterday with his Excellency; who gave me to understand, That he doubted of my having made a just RepcArt of what he had formerly said to me in this Subject; and concluded by telling me, That he had explained himself at large to Mr. Hoffman; and that he could not give any other Answer to my Demand, until he knew the Emperor’s Intentions thereupon.

I have the Honour to be, with the greatest Veneration and Respect, My Lord,

Your Excellency’s most faithful,

And most obedient humble Servant,

Right honourable Lord IVm. Leather.

My Lord, Brussells, the 19th March 1721, N. S.

I DID myself the Honour to give your Lordship, in my Letter of the 15th Instant, a full Account of the Conference I had with the Marquis de Brie the Night before, on the Subject of Mr. Knight: I have since discoursed him twice on the same Head; and particularly last Night; when he was pleased to acquaint me, That the News of Mr. Knight's being arrested had reached Vienna; and he could now tell me, That his Conduct had not been disapproved, although his Letter to the Prince of Savoy, which he sent from hence only Four Days after the Arrest, w as not then come to hand; and therefore his Highness waited for his Relation, with a particular Account of all the Circumstances of this Affair, in order to receive the Emperor’s Orders relating the reunto; so that he had reason to expect he should be able in a few Days to give me an Answer to the Demand I had made in his Majesty’s Name.

His Excellency at the same time acquainted me, That the Griffier of the States of Brabant had, about Eight Days since, presented a Petition to him, in the Name of the stud States; praying, That nothing might be done in this Matter to the Prejudice of their Privileges; and that some of the Deputies had spoke to him on the same Subject: To which he had answered in general Terms; That he would, on all Occasions, have a due Regard to their Privileges, and a particular Care of supporting the Emr peror’s Prerogative: That, having already informed the Court of this Matter, it was not in his Power to do more at present than to transmit their Petition to Vienna.; which, he told me, lie had done accordingly: This, said the Marquis, ought to satisfy you with how much Precaution I am obliged to act; and although this Petition is no

Vol. 19.

more than what I expected, yet, if the States should re- Apprehen-new their Application, it will require Time, and a great sjon of Mr-deal of Management, to induce them to wave their Pri- Kn,ght* vileges: W hereupon I told his Excellency, That had he, on my First Instances, given up Mr. Knight, all the Trouble he now' apprehends from the States, would have been prevented: And I desired Leave to observe to him,

That it would be a difficult Matter to reconcile his Conduct in securing Mr. Knight at the King's Request, with his delaying to give him up; since the latter seemed to lie a natural Consequence of the former; and the Emperor's approving the Arrest, was a Proof of his Imperial Majesty's Intentions to give him up to Justice: Wherefore I hoped his Excellency would do it of his own Accord, without waiting any longer for Orders from Court: But *11 my Argument could draw no other Answer from him than what he gave me before: Pie still insisted on the Measures he was obliged to keep with the Court, and the States of this Province; and repeated anew all that he had urged in our former Conferences on this Subject; which I shall not trouble your Lordship with, having already done it in my former Relations.

I have the Honour to be. witii a profound Respect,

My Lord,

Your Excellency’s most faithful,

And most obedient humble Servant,

P.S.

On the Arrival of the German Post, I waited on the Marquis de Prie, who opened his Letters from Vienna, of the 8th Instant, in my Presence; but there was not a Word in them concerning Mr. Knight; from whence he concludes, That his Relation had not got thither before the Departure of those letters. His Excellency acquainted me, That the States of Brabant, not satisfied with his Answer, had been again this Morning with him to remind him of their Privileges; and their Remonstrances were in such strong Terms, That he should be indispensably obliged to give a due Attention to them, and to represent their Reasons to his Imperial Majesty: That so far from taking upon him to deliver up Knight of his own Accord, without Orders, he doubted whether it ould be done without the Consent of the States; which Consent he could not ask until he had an Answer to the Letters he intended to write by next Post, on this Subject; and that the Matter in Question being of great Importance, both in relation to the Emperor’s Power, and to the Privileges insisted on, he w'as persuaded the Court would consider the Affair very attentively before they come to any Resolution thereon.

The said Resolutions are as follow; viz.

To the honourable the Commons df Great Britain in Parliament assembled.

IN Obedience to an Order of the 21st of February last, the Directors of the South Sea Company do lay before this honourable House the Resolutions of the General Court of the said Company, held the 9th, and continued, by Adjournment, to the 18th, Instant, relating to the Fdur Money Subscriptions; viz.

1st. Resolved, N. C. That no more Money than what Is actually paid on the Four Money Subscriptions, shall be demanded, or insisted on.

2d. Resolved, N. C. That Stock be given for the Money actually paid by the respective Proprietors in the First and Second Money Subscriptions; viz.

‘On the First, at 300 per Cent, with the Midsummer Dividend of 10 per Cent. in Stock:

On the Second at 400 per Cent. with the like Dividend:

And that the Receipts be called in, and Stock forthwith transferred to the Proprietors accordingly.

3d. Resolved, N. C. That Stock be forthwith given for "the Money paid on the 3d and 4th Money Subscriptions, at the Rate of 400 per Cent. with the Midsummer Dividend of 10 per Cent. in Stock.

By Order of the General Court of the South Sea Company,

South Sea House, D. Wescomb, Secretary.

A Petition of Archibald Douglass, of Cave?'s> Esquire, Jedburgh in behalf of the Borough of Jedburgh, in Teviotdale, was Town presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That nuc»^c-the said Borough has been engaged in considerable Debts; and their common Good, or Revenue, being since applied, partly for Payment of the Interest of those Debts, and partly for other Uses of the Corporation: That the said Debts are increased, by the Rebels seizing on the said Town: That the said Borough is in great Wantof Spring Water; which has obliged them to contract such new Debts, that they cannot, without some other Assistance, discharge: That the Bridges, Streets, and Buildings, of the said Town are very much decayed; so that the Inhabitants are unable to keep the same in Repair: That the Building of Work-houses for the manufacturing coarse Wool would be of great Use-and Advantage to the said Borough; as also to such Parts of the Country as lie near thereto: And praying, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for granting a Duty of Two Penies Scots, or the Sixth Part of a Peny, upon every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer brewed and sold within the said Town and Privileges thereof, to be added to the present Revenue of the said Town, for the Purposes aforesaid.

Mr. Comptroller acquainted the House, That his Ma- Apprehen-jesty, having Yesterday received a Letter from Colonel sion of Mr. Churchill, directed to the Lord Viscount Townshend, dated Vienna, the Fourth‘of March 1720-21, had commanded him, pursuant to the Address of this House, to lay a Copy thereof before this House: And he presented the same to the House:

And the Copy of the said Letter was read; and is as followeth: viz.

My Lord,

I HAVE the Honour to inform your Lordship, That I got here on Thursday, and went immediately to Mr.

St. Sapherin, who carried me directly to Count Sinzendorf; who received me with a great deal of Civility; and has promised me, on what I said to him* all the Assistance he can, as to the Delivery of Mr. Knight; and indeed shewed as great a Dislike to a Man of his Character as I could wish; so that, for my Part, I see no Difficulty in this Affair, unless the States of Brabant should mutiny; which I fancy they will not do, when they are rightly informed of the Virtues of the Man that is demanded.

I have no more at present to trouble your Lordship with, than to assure you, that my Solicitations shan't be wanting, both for the Delivering of Mr. Knight, and for 6 my

Punishing Mutiny and Desertion.

Mr. Farrcr, according to Order, reported from the Prohibits Committee of the whole House, to w hom it was referred «fCaik«w to consider further of the Representation from the Lords &c’ Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, relating to the Prohibition of Callicoes; and proposing what Methods may be most proper and effectual for securing to the East India Company their carrying on successfully a Trade so beneficial to the Kingdom; which was laid before this House upon the First Day of February, pursuant to the Address of this House to his Majesty; the Resolutions of the said Committee, which they had directed him. to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place $ and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk's Table: Where the said Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the carrying on of any Trade, by his Majesty’s Subjects, to the East Indies, under foreign Commissions, or in Conjunction with Foreigners, is of pernicious Consequence to the Commerce and Welfare of this Kingdom; and that an effectual Stop ought to be put thereto.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the clandestine putting of unlicenced Goods oft Board any outward-bound East India, Ships, and taking any such Goods out of the homeward-bound Ships, is a mischievous Practice; and highly detrimental and injurious to his Majesty's Customs.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That the allow'ing the Importation of Tea, by Certificates from Osternl, and other Foreign Places, not being the Place of its Growth, tends to promote the illegal Trade carried on by his Majesty’s Subjects to the East Indies, under foreign Commissions, and in Conjunction with Foreigners; and is very prejudicial to the Trade and Navigation of this Kingdom.

Rcsotved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it will be for the Benefit of the Trade of this Kingdom, That the time given for Drawbacks for all Goods and Merchandizes imported, and afterwards exported, be enlarged.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it will be for the Benefit of the Trade of this Kingdom, that the time given to the East India Company for their Discounts, and other Allowances, be enlarged.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the East India Company be allowed to ship out Stores, Provisions, and Necessaries, for maintaining their Garisons, and Settlements, free of all Duties. 1

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Fairer, Mr. Horatio Walpole, Mr. Herne, Mr. Hungerford, and Mr. Loicndes, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

and others are become ruinous and decayed, and therefore cannot be sold but at great Disadvantage; nor can any Building Leases be made thereof, but by Direction of the Court of Chancery: That the Petitioner William Pulteney, and his Ancestors, having held the said Premisses for several Generations, as Tenants to the Crown, the Petitioners are very desirous, that the same should be preserved in the Family, by a Settlement; according to the Uses directed by the Will; which, although there are above One hundred Years yet to come in the said Leases granted by the Crown, cannot be cftccted, unless the Inheritance thereof bo purchased of his Majesty, and for which the Petitioners are willing to pay the utmost Value*: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable his Majesty to grant the Inheritance of the said leased Premisses* which remain unsold, to Trustees, upon a full Consideration to be paid for the same, as shall be valued by the proper Officers of the Crown; to the end the same may be settled according to the said Will, and be preserved in the Family; and that the Petitioners may be enabled to make Leases of the Premisses for Sixty-one Years, in like manner as they have Power to do of the other Estates settled pursuant to the said Will.

Mr. Douglass reported from the Committee, to whom Jedburgh the Petition of Archibald Douglass, of Cavers, Esquire, Town Debts, in behalf of the Borough of Jedburgh, in Teviotdale, &c* was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same was read; and i$ as follows; viz.

That the Committee, to whom the said Petition was referred, have met, and examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find, upon Examination of Sir Gilbert Elliot, and William Elliot Esquire,

That the said Borough, before the Resolution, did en* gage in several considerable Debts; and the Revenues thereof have since been partly applied for Payment of the Interest thereof, and partly for other Uses of the said Corporation; which has put the said Borough under great Difficulties; and the Debts of the said Borough are much increased by the late unhappy Rebellion in 1715, when the Rebels seized the said Town, and put the Inhabitants to several great Charges:

That the said Borough has, of late, been in great Want of Spring-water, the River-water being often muddy, and unserviceable; which has obliged the Borough to contract new Debts:

# That the Building of Work-houses, and other Convc-niencies, for the Manufacturing of coarse Wool, the said Town being a very proper Place for it, would be of great Advantage to the same:

That the Bridges, Streets, and publick Buildings, belonging to the said Borough, are so much out of Repair, that the Inhabitants are unable to amend and keep the same in Repair, and to do the other Works before-mentioned, without some Provision be made for that Purpose:

That it also appeared to the said Committee, That the carrying on and completing the W orks before-mentioned will not only be very necessary for the Support of the said Borough, but also of great Benefit to such Part of the County as lie near to the same.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for laying a Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-sixth Part of a Peny Sterling, upon every Scots Pint of Ale or Beer that shall be vended or sold within the Town of Jedburgh, and Privileges thereof, for paying the publick Debts of the said Town; and for supplying the same with

1721, March 30th, N. S. Copy of Mr. Leather Letter to my Lord I owns hend.

Sir, my Brother,

I THAN K you with all my Heart for the obliging Manner in which the Marquis de Prie, upon the Instances my Minister had made by my Order, caused Robert Knight, Cashier of the South Sea Company, to be seized, who, having fled in 01'der to withdraw himself from the Justice of my Parliament, was so audacious as to take Refuge in your Imperial Majesty’s Dominions: I esteem this Proceeding as a Mark of your Friendship, of which I am very sensible; and I persuade myself, that your Imperial Majesty will be pleased to shew me the Continuance of it, by ordering, that he, with all his Papers and Effects, may be delivered up into the Hands of such Person as I shall employ to bring him Home, under a sure Guard, that he may undergo the Examination of both Houses of my Parliament; and that he may be prosecuted according to Justice’ and Equity I cannot doubt of obtaining so reasonable a Demand from your Imperial Majesty, whose known Justice will never permit, that, in whatever depends on you, any Means may be warning of obtaining an Inquiry into, and Punishment of, Crimes of so black a Dye as those of the Persons in whose Hands the Management of the Affairs of that Company’has been; whose plundering, having spread itself all over my Kingdom, has reduced so great a Number of Families of Distinction to the utmost Want, that my Parliament could not avoid taking particular Notice of it, and making the most lively Representations to me thereupon: I am persuaded the Calamity of so many Persons in Distress will mpve your Imperial Majesty’s Compassion; and I flatter myself, that you will grant me so just a Request; placing an intire Confidence in your Imperial Majesty's Friendship, and being persuaded you will oblige me in so sensible a Point, who am, with the most sincere Zeal and Attachment,

Your Imperial Majesty’s

most affectionate Brother,

St. James's, 1 oth February 172?.

To my Brother, GEORGE R.

the Emperor.

Sir, Whitehall, 10th February 1727.

THESE Lines will be delivered to you by Colonel Churchill, a near Relation of the Duke of Marlborough;

*7 Geo. L $7° Ma 497

rough; and who, I believe may be known to Prince Eugene, by the Means of his Service in the War in Flanders: Having a very particular Regard for him, I take the Liberty of recommending him earnestly to your Excellency, whose Goodness to him will most sensibly oblige me: He is charged with a Letter from the King my Master to his Imperial Majesty, containing an earnest Request, that he would cause to be delivered into such Hands as his Majesty shall intrust in that behalf, the Person, and all the Papers and Effects, of Robert Knight, late Cashier of the South Sea Company; who, being under the Examination of the Parliament, has thought fit to abscond, and to retire into Brabant, where the Marquis de Prie, upon the Instances of our Minister at Brussels, has been so good as to cause him to be arrested: The King reckons upon your good Offices in this Affair; both on Account of the good Inclination he is persuaded you have towards him, and because he cannot doubt the Compassion of a Person of your Generosity, and Love of Justice and Equity, towards so many Persons of Condition, distressed by the Rapine of those that had the Management of the Affairs of that Company; nor your Willingness to contribute towards bringing those Men to Justice, who not only have ruined a great Number of Families, but, having also violated the publick Faith, so necessary to Commerce, are become Criminals to all Princes and States with whose Subjects we carry on any Trade c And I am ordered to assure you, that you will, by this, do a most acceptable Service to his Majesty, apd most sensibly oblige him.

Your Excellency will permit me to take this Opportunity of assuring you, That I can never forget the Pleasure and Satisfaction I formerly enjoyed in the Honour of your Friendship and Conversation at the Hague; but should think myself most happy, could I give you Marks of the purest Zeal, and most perfect Regard, with which I shall ever be, fyc.

Instructions for our trusty and well-beloved Colonel Charles Churchill, whom we have Ordered to go to the Court of our good Brother the Emperor of Germany. Given at our Court at Saint James's, the nth Day of February 172^, in the Seventh Year of our Reign.

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS both the Houses of our Parliament have humbly addressed u$, That we would make the proper Applications, and use the most effectual Instances, that Robert Knight, late Cashier of the South Sea Company, who, as we are informed, is at present seized, and detained Prisoner, in the Citadel of Antwerp, may be delivered up to us, together with his Papers and Effects; we, being most earnestly desirous, that this just request of Our Parliament may be exactly complied with, have thought fit to make choice of you to go to Vienna on that account.

Therefore, upon the Receipt of these our Instructions, together with our Letter to our good Brother the Emperor, and likewise a Letter which our right trusty and well-beloved Cousin and Counsellor Charles Viscount Townshend, One of our principal Secretaries of State, has wrote, on this Occasion, to the Count de Sinzendorff, by our Command, you are forthwith to repair to the Imperial Court, with all the Diligence you can make; and upon your arrival there, you are to deliver the said Letters, as directed; and, as the Matter you are sent upon is of great Importance to us, you are to press to receive as favourable and as speedy an Answer as you can get upon the aforesaid Letters; and, having received the same, you are to return to us without Loss of Time.

You have, with these Instructions, Copies of the aforesaid Letters, which will fully shew you our Sentiments upon this your Errand; and accordingly you will conform yourself, in your Representations at Vienna, to the Contents of the Letters above-mentioned.

G. R.

MOST Serene King, my most dear Brother and Cousin, I have received your Majesty’s Letter, wherein, Vo l. 19.

after having

on the arresting the Person of Robert Knight, by Order of the Marquis de Prie, at the Request of your Majesty’s Minister, you acquaint me with your Desire, that he may be delivered to your Majesty, in order to his being examined by both Houses of Parliament, arid his receiving the Punishment due to his Offences; as having been the Occasion of the Ruin of so many of your Majesty’s faithful Subjects, who move my Compassion: Your Majesty will see, by the annexed Copy of the Order given to the Marquis de Prit, the earnest Inclination I have to comply with you, in executing what you desire should be done; as being unwilling to omit any. Opportunity of making your Majesty sensible of the Effects of that sincere Union and Friendship that is established between us; but the Difference there is between the Crimes of Rebellion, and those of Knight, will perhaps raise some Difficulties in the delivering him tip, on account of the known Privileges which the States of our Low Countries enjoy, and wlqch I will endeavour to overcome, if possible; and flattering myself that these my earnest Intentions will be acceptable to your Majesty, I remain, with an unalterable Friendship, and an affectionate Esteem,

Vienna, 18th March 1721.

To the most serene King of Great Britain, my most dear Brother and Cousin.

Your Majesty’s most affectionate Brother and Cousin,

CHARLES.

Copy of the Eetter writ by the Prince Eugene, of Savoy, to the Marquis de Prie, dated at Vienna, the 18th of March 1721.

THE Letter which your Excellency wrote to me the 26th of last Month, is come to my Hands: I found, by it, on one Side, the pressing Instances which Mr. Leathes, the King of Great Britain's Resident, made to you, That Rjobert Knight, Cashier of the South Sea Company, might be delivered to him, in order to be sent over into England; and, on the other Side, the Difficulties which you foresee in granting that Request, considering the Privileges of the States of Brabant, which have been sworn to by his Imperial and fcatholick Majesty, their Right of Asylum, or Sanctuary; and the continual Complaints which they made during the time of the Rebellion in Scotland, on account of the Treatment which the King of Great Britams Rebel Subjects, who had retired thither, then received; although their Case was very different, and more heinous than that of Knight.

Since that Letter from your Excellency, Colonel Churchill has brought one to his Imperial Majesty, from his Majesty the King of Great Britain; whereby he demands, with the strongest Instances, that the said Robert Knight may be put into his Hands.

His Imperial Majesty, being always disposed to give the King of Great Britain, and the Nation, all the most sincere Proofs of his true Friendship, desires nothing more than to have it in his Power to grant, and effectually to comply with, that Request, without any more to do: But, as it appears to you to be directly contrary to the Rights and Privileges of which all Nations are jealous, and particularly the People of Brabant, his Imperial Majesty has thought fit to refer this Matter to your Excellency; with precise and positive Order, That, being upon the Spot, and thoroughly informed of the abovesaid Privileges, and Obstacles, you should do all that you possibly can to remove them, and to satisfy the Desires of his Majesty the King of Great Britain with respect to the Surrendery which is demanded; and that without causing, as far as may be, any dangerous Troubles or Commotions.

My Lord, Viemia, 18th March 1721, N. S.

I HAVE received, by Colonel Churchill, your Excellency’s Letter, dated from Whitehall, the TV February: His personal Merit, his Name, and the Share he enjoys in your Friendship and Protection, are such prevailing Motives with me, that there is nothing upon Earth that I would not 6 t et

Apprelion- at any time, and upon any Occasion, do for his Service-: M^Krii ht *rn onty sorry that his short Stay here would not allow r* me to give him as many Marks of it as I wished: The Justice his Britarmick Majesty does me, in believing me to be* full of Zeal and Attachment for his Service, gives line, my Lord, a Satisfaction I cannot sufficiently express to you; arid will be a fresh Inducement to my giving, as long as I live, the most respectful Proofs of it: One can never admire too much that Monarch’s constant Application to the maintaining of Justice in his Realm, and to the relieving of the distressed; the Orders he has given against Robert Knight can bear no other Interpretation: And his Imperial and Catholick Majesty, who abhors all corrupt Practices, especially such as turn to publick Oppression, is entirely disposed to give his Britannick Majesty, upon this Occasion, all possible Tokens of his Affection and Friendship: Your Excellency has not forgot with what‘Readiness he gave his Orders in the Business relating to the Rebellion; and, if the Matter depended On his Will alone, those he now gives would be as precise, and as strong: But, you know, the Low Countries have their particular Laws and Privileges; and that his Majesty very lately caused a solemn Oath to be taken, in his Name, to the Observance of them: All that can be done, without a Violation of them, shall certainly be performed; and you will, in the mean time, see, by the inclosed Copy, what Orders his Majesty has thought fit to send beforehand to the Marquis de Prie upon that Subject: And now, my Lord, I desire you will be persuaded, no Man can be possessed with a greater Sense, than I have, of the Honour of your Remembrance, and of that valuable Friendship which you appear to have preserved for me: I hope Colonel Churchill will be pleased to testify the unbounded Esteem for you with which he found me filled: The Time that has lapsed since I was deprived of those pleasing Hours that passed in your Conversation, has not in the least altered it: Such Friends as your Excellency are never to be forgotten; nothing can make Amends for thdr Absence. I am, with the same Passion, and the same Respect,

My Lord,

Your Excellency’s Most humble and

most obedient Servant,

Count Philip of Sinzcnclorff.

My Lord, Brtissetts, the 30th March 1721.

I HAD the Honour to give your Lordship a particular Account, in my Letters of the 15th and 19th Instant, of what had passed between the Marquis de Prie and me on the Subject of Mr. Knight; since which, I have not been honoured with any new Commands from your Lord-Ship; and, though I had Reason to believe his Excellency was inclinable to keep Measures with the States of Brabant, I still persisted in my Instances for his being delivered up to me.

On Wednesday last, after the Departure of the Tost, I waited on the Marquis again, to try whether he would be more flexible than he appeared in our last Conferences; and to know whether the Information 1 had had that Morning was true; viz. That Mr. Knight's Son having preferred a Petition to the States df Brabant, they had made a Second Representation, in stronger Terms than the First: His Excellency told me, It was so; and that the States, in a Body, had presented it to him that Morning; and that they had pressed him very hard to declare in Favour of their Privileges, and urged the strongest Reasons to induce him to it; but, as he had not received any Orders from Court, on the Matter in question, lie avoided giving a direct Answer to their Demands;

- nevertheless, to satisfy them, he promised to do nothing precipitately, in Prejudice of their Request, until he had again represented the whole Matter to the Emperor; and that their Remonstrances had been duly weighed at Vienna, whither he would send them, with his Considerations thereon: The Marquis acquainted me likewise, That

Mr. Knight had, some Weeks since, petitioned him, and claimed le Droit d'Azile de cette Province.

The Marquis having then other Business to dispatch, he appointed the next Evening, to discourse this Matter more at Leisure: Accordingly, I attended him on the 27th instant; when he acquainted me, That he had just received a Letter from Prince Eugene, by a Courier, on the Subject of Mr. Knight; by which he observed, that th£

Emperor was inclinable to give his Majesty a Mark of his Friendship on this Occasion; but, as the Privileges of the Province of Brabant might be an Obstacle to it, he desired the Marquis to inform the Court very exactly how far those Privileges were binding; and, at the same time* directs his Excellency to use his Endeavours to remove those Obstacles; however, to be careful not to give new Grounds for any dangerous Troubles, or Agitations of the People.

This, my Lord, is the Substance of the Orders brought him by the Courier; at least, of all he thought fit to communicate to me: The Marquis told me again, That he had already given the Court his Sentiments; and that he would repeat them, with his further Considerations on the Matter; and that he would use his Endeavours to induce the States to wave their Privileges; but, by what he had observed in them, when they presented their last Representation, he had Reason to doubt of their Compliance; without which, he could not resolve to deliver up the Prisoner; being persuaded, that the Consequences would be such as the Prince had cautioned him to be careful in avoiding: He added, This is an Affair of the last Importance to his Imperial Majesty, the Management of which requires both Time and Dexterity: I have a jealous, obstinate, People to deal with; and you may remember* that, in Three Years Time, I was scarce able to compel them to take the Oath they had formerly made no Objection against: I must therefore acquaint you beforehand,

That, as the Success of this Affair depends chiefly on the Caprice of those I have to manage, I will not answer for it; nor can I promise more than my best Endeavours, which, you may assure his Majesty, shall be employed in bringing this Matter to a Satisfactory Conclusion.

Since the Marquis has promised me his good Offices,

I will endeavour to keep him in the favourable Disposition he now professes; and I will use all proper Arguments with the Deputies of the States, in particular (for I cannot apply to them in any other manner), to gain their Consent to Mr. Knight's being delivered up, and sent Prisoner into England.

J will not omit any thing that may contribute to the Success of this Affair; w'hich will, I am persuaded, give great Satisfaction to his* Majesty, and a general Content to the Nation, in case I can be so happy as to effect it. I have the Honour, fyc.

Wm. Lcathes.

Dundee A Petition of the Provost, Magistrates, and Council,

Town Debts. of the Town of Dundee, on behalf of themselves, and the Community of the said Town, was presented to the

House, and redd; setting forth, That, the Said Town being indebted, in the Year 1707, in a very considerable Sum of Money, an Act was passed in the Parliament of Scotland, laying a Duty of Two Penics Scots upon every Pint of Ale and Beer brewed or vended within the said Town for Twenty-four Years, to be applied to pay the said Debt; which it hath not hitherto done: That the Churches, Town-house, and Tolbooth, are become almost ruinous: That the Harbour, which is the principal Support of the Inhabitants, is lately so filled up with Sand, that Ships of Burthen, which formerly could enter at any time, cannot now come in, or go out, even at the highest Tides: That the Church is too small for the Inhabitants; and, if another Church were endued, it would be of great Advantage: And, praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the said Duty for a longer Term.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

From the House of Commons, 3d April, 1721.

Sir,

I am commanded by the House of Commons to acquaint you, That you are, immediately upon the Receipt of this, to summon the Representatives of your County, and Boroughs within the same, to attend their Service in Parliament on Friday the Fourteenth Day of this instant April, notwithstanding any Order of Leave to be absent; all such Orders being revoked by the House: And you are to give me an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereupon, upon Pain of incurring the Displeasure of the said House.

I am, Sir,

Your humble Servant,

Sp. Compton, Speaker.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Recorder, Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, and Principal Inhabitants, of the Borough of Saint Albans, in the County of Hereford, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they cannot but with the greatest Concern take notice of the many and great Calamities brought upon the whole Kingdom by the ill Management, treacherous Conduct, and sordid Practices, of the late South Sea Directors; who, by their false Cunning, have betrayed an unwary People into Poverty, Ruin, and Destruction, contrary to the Trust in them reposed: And praying, That the said late South Sea Directors, together with their Abettors and Confederates, may be brought to condign Punishment.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon Table.
