A Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, and Common Council, of the King s Town of Maidstone, in the County of Kent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, with the deepest Concern, represent their present miserable Condition, from the great Decay of their Trade, in common with the rest of this Kingdom, by the languishing State of publick Credit; occasioned by the infamous Practices of the late South Sea Directors* jointly with other Persons in higher Stations, to plunder the Nation, and enrich themselves by the Ruin of their Fellow Subjects; by which Means such a Stop hath been had to the Circulation of Money, that, at this time especially, when the Duty of Hops, the great Commodity of those Parts, is called for, the Payment of it will be attended with so much Difficulty and Hardship, that many Families thereby will be rendered destitute of almost a necessary Subsistence: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiff, and Burgesses, of the Borough of Leicester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That though, by indulgent Providence, the Petitioners are clear of South Sea Projects; and neither tainted with the Guilt of contriving, nor hurt by giving Credit to, the late cursed Impostureis; yet are they Sharers in the National Calamity, which involves all: No sooner had the South Sea Directors so imposed upon tire honest, credulous People, as to draw all their ready Money, and Treasure, into their own infamous Hands, but they saw Trade instantly struck dead; their Manufactures disregarded; their combed Wool, once the Staple and Glory of their industrious Corporation, lie neglected; in their Workhouses, their Poor increasing, for want of Employment; many, who cheerfully paid Taxes towards supporting our happy Government, reduced, by want of Trade, to a miserable Exemption from them: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table,

A Petition of the Chief Burgesses, and Assistants, G rand Jury, and many of the Inhabitants, of the City and Liberty of Westminster, on behulf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of that City and Liberty, w as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are deeply affected with the Calamity brought upon the Inhabitants of that City, and Upon the Nation in general, by the wicked Execution of the late South Sea Scheme; and the great Oppression which the subscribing Proprietors of the Publick, and especially of the redeemable Debts, now lie under; to the Ruin of very great Numbers of the trading Inhabitants of that City: And praying, That Justice may be done to an injured Nation* and Reparation made to the unhappy Sufferers.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Copy of Mr. Leather Letter to my Lord Viscount Townshend, dated Brusselks.

My Lord, Bnmcllcs, the 3d April 1721/

SINCE my last, of the 30th March, I have discoursed all the Deputies of the States of Brabant separately: I urged to each of them the Arguments I had formerly made use of to his Excellency: 1 shewed them the Advantages which would accrue to many of the Subjects of these Provinces, who are still concerned in our Funds: I endeavoured to satisfy them of the Justice of his Majesty’s Demand; and how much it is the Interest, not only of this Province, but of all the Princes and States of Europe, to contribute towards bringing so obnoxious a Person, and so notorious an Offender, as Mr. Knight, to Condign Punishment; I told them, that the Emperor was convinced of the Truth of what I said; and that H. I. Majesty was willing to comply with the King's Demand: That there was now nothing more wanting than their Consent, to bring this Matter to a happy Conclusion; and that their Compliance would not in any-wise prejudice their Privileges: To ail which, each of the Deputies gave very near the same Answer; viz. That le Droit cVAzyle, had always been looked on as one of the principal, and most valuable, Articles of their Privileges: That there was no Example of their having ever consented to any Person arrested in Brabant, of what Nature soever his Crime might be, being carried Prisoner out of this Province; and they hoped his Majesty would not expect they should on this Occasion give up a Privilege which they had hitherto preserved with the greatest Care and Exactness: I told them, that, in my Opinion, their Compliance with his Majesty’s Demand would not be looked upon as giving up a Point of their Privilege; since it was not reasonable to suppose, that the Design of the 17th Article of the Joy erne Entree, nor of the States in procuring it, could have been to exclude themselves from the Power of delivering a Criminal to Justice, when they judged the Case required it; that Article having been obtained chiefly to put it out of the Power of the Prince to carry any Inhabitant or Subject of this Province out of it, to be tried by a foreign Jurisdiction; which, indeed,

was a very prudent and necessary Precaution, in a Country so liable to Resolutions, and but too often exposed to the Misfortune of changing of Masters: That the present Case was of a different Nature; and that there was nothing more common than to wave a Privilege in favour of Justice; which, they must allow, had never been looked on, nor could it be interpreted, as giving up any Part of the Right they had acquired by the aforesaid Article: To which they replied, The Article is general, without any particular Case being excepted: That they could not break in upon it, even in case of Murder: And, each of them having taken their Oaths to maintain the Privileges of this Prov ince in their full Extent, they were resolved, on all Occasions, strictly to adhere to what they had solemnly sworn.

By what I could observe from their Discourse, and the Manner of delivering it, I have Reason to fear we shall meet with greater Opposition than could reasonably have been expected: However, my Lord, their Obstinacy shall ,not rebute me; but, on the contrary, it will engage me . to renew my Instances with more Force and Application,

both to the States, and to the Marquis: The latter, in-:deed, makes Profession of seconding my Endeavours; although I must own, that I have not yet found the Effect . which I had reason to expect from his Promises.

I have nothing more to add at present, than the Assure-ance of my utmost Endeavours to bring this Matter to a good and speedy Conclusion, and of my being, SfC. '

Sir, . Whitehall, 31st March 172,1.

I AM to acknowledge, at present, your Letter of the 3d of April, N. S. which has been laid before the King.

You will now see, by the inclosed Address from the Mouse of Commons, and the King s Answer to it, how much Vox- 19.

his Majesty, and the Parliament, have it at Heart to get so notorious an Offender as Robert Knight brought to Justice: You are therefore, upon the Receipt of this, to renew your Instances with the Marquis de Erie, in the strongest manner you are able: You have already exerted yourself with great Vigour; but you must now collect your whole Force, and make your very utmost Efforts, to have this Man delivered up; on whose Surrendry not only the King and Parliament, but, I may also say, the whole Nation, are intirely bent, with one Heart, and with one Voice: The King extremely approves of the Arguments you made use to each of the Deputies of the States of Brabant, on this Occasion; and was astonished to find, that after all those cogent Reasons you laid before them, they could still persist in the Resolution they seemed to have taken not to consent to the Delivery of Robert Knight: Indeed, if the Question had been. Whether he should be surrendered? without ever asking the Leave or Consent of the States of Brabant; then they might have had some Pretence to have urged the Preservation of their Privileges; and they might have looked upon that as an attempt to subvert their Rights and Liberties; and, consequently, have opposed it with all the Vigour they were able: But to assert, that, their Droit d’Azyle would be broken by their consenting, themselves, to deliver up a Criminal, who may be looked upon as a common Enemy, is establishing a Notion, which, I believe, was never yet allowed of in any Country where Liberty has flourished in the greatest Perfection; and where they might be the most nice and jealous, upon the least Breach in their Constitution: The Habeas Corpus Act here in England is very justly esteemed to be the most valuable Jewel of all our Liberties, and which is always the most carefully and scrupulously preserved: And yet the Parliament never thought themselves so tied up by this Act, as not to make use of their own Reason and Judgment in Cases of great Emergency; and either to dispense with it, or to suspend it, as the Circumstances In question should require: What a reproach, therefore, will it be, instead of an Ornament, to the Province of Brabant, when it shall be known, that they take themselves to be so much tied down in this Point, that they cannot give up a Man guilty of the most flagrant Crimes imaginable, without reckoning it a Loss of Privilege? Surely, a Liberty founded on such an indispensable Prerogative of harbouring the most infamous Villains, must make them be looked upon with Horror; as being, by their unalterable Constitution, the Protectors of the greatest Enemies to Mankind! And of what Consequence such a strange Maxim may prove to a Country where the Intercourse of Trade obliges them to have frequent Communication with the rest of their Neighbours, the King leaves them to judge.

You may likewise insinuate to these Deputies the vast Expence both of Blood and Treasure which England has been at in their Defence, and in securing to them the Liberties they now enjoy; and it is thought here very unsuitable, to say no worse, to have those very Liberties, now made use of against us in protecting so enormous a Criminal, w ho has ruined and undone more People in this Kingdom, and in other Countries, than ever any one did since the World began; for, as the Case now stands, all the late Directors throw the whole Blame upon him, as if all was contrived, managed, and transacted, by him, and with his Privity and Direction; so that, if we can be-, lieve them, we have nobody who can lead us through the various and intricate Mazes of this infamous and per* nicious Transaction, but this same Robert Knight: Can, therefore, the States of Brabant seriously think, that the -harbouring and screening a Man loaded with so excessive a Weight of Guilt can be either for the Credit, or Advantage, of their Country? Or can they imagine, that their denying the King a Demand of so much Consequence to the Welfare and Tranquillity of his;Kingdoms, is >a fit Return to what the Nation has done fol* them? I must therefore repeat , to you earnestly, that it is his Majesty s express Command, That you should employ your best and most vigorous Endeavours, by all those Arguments, G O and

Apprehension of Mr, Knight-

and what others soever your own Skill, and Knowledge of the People, will suggest to you, to obtain the delivering up of Knight; on which4 as you plainly see, so great a Stress is laid by all Orders and Degrees of People here.

I inclose to you Copies of his Majesty’s Letter to the Emperor on this Subject; and of the Emperor’s Answer; with the Orders Prince Eugene sent, by his Imperial Majesty’s Command, to the Marquis dc Erie: They may be for your information in this Matter; and it is fit you should want nothing you can possibly make use of, in bringing so important an Affair to the desired Conclusion.

Copy of the House of Commons Address to his Majesty:

House of Commons. 29th March 1721. RESOLVED, Nemine contradicente. That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, returning the Thanks of this House for the Instances he has been pleased to make, by a Letter under his Royal Hand to his Imperial Majesty, for obtaining the delivering up Mr. Knight, pursuant to the Address of this House; and for communicating to this House the Steps which have been taken, relating thereto; and to represent to his Majesty the Dissatisfaction which his Commons have at the Obstacles which, they find, have been raised, under the Pretence of the Privileges of the States of Brabant, against a Compliance with his gracious Endeavours; and also to represent, That this House is every Day more convinced of the high Importance it is to the Justice due to his People, that effectual Measures be speedily taken for bringing over Mr. Knight; and earnestly to beseech his Majesty to employ his most pressing Endeavours, in such manner as, in his great Wisdom, shall be thought proper, for attaining the just Desire of his Commons.

House of Commons. 31st Mar. 1721.

His Majesty’s Answer to the Resolution of this House, of 29th Mar. 1721.

I AM very well pleased, that the Instances which I have made for the obtaining the delivering up of Mr. Knight have given you Satisfaction: I shall continue to employ my utmost Endeavours for obtaining what you desire; and hope they will prove effectual.

Sir, brusselles, 1 oth Apr. 1721.

I WAS so ill Yesterday with a Lever, Head-ach, and a Rheum fallen on my Eyes, that I was not able to stir out of Red; which, I suppose, Mr. Gaudot told you:

: I find myself a little better this Morning, but not in a Condition to write to my Lord: Therefore I must desire you to acquaint his Lordship, That Marquis de Erie sent his Son Yesterday to acquaint me, That he had spoke to some of the Deputies of the States of Brabant, whom he found very much bent on maintaining their Privileges; however he would use his utmost Endeavours with the Greffier, and all the Deputies, to gain their Consent to Knight's being delivered up to me; and that I might be assured all Means should be used with them to effect it: Rut he gave me to understand, That the States had taken a private Resolution to send a Deputation to Vienna, on this Subject; which he would find means to prevent: Nevertheless, he foresaw’the complying with the King’s Demand, without the States Consent, would infallibly occasion new Tumults here.

I hope to be able to write to my Lord on Saturday;

before which time 1 will endeavour to discourse the Marquis de Erie, and the States of Brabant; and endeavour to know what we have to depend on, I am, 4

My Lord, $c.

Translation of Mr. Leathes Memorial to the Marquis de Prie, 21st April 1721.

To his Excellency.

THE underwritten Resident of his Majesty the King of Great Britain has tho Honour of representing to Voju Jft

whereby he is become unworthy the States of Brabant pretend to afford him; The King has seen with equal Concern and Surprize, by the Representation of the States of Brabant, the ill-grounded Opposition they make against his just Demand: It is well known how jealous diose Gentlemen, and their Predecessors, have always been of their Priviledges; and his Majesty allows, that, if it was expected the Captive should be delivered up without requiring their Consent, their Opposition might he looked upon as reasonable, and supported by some Appearance of Foundation; but, this Itequest haying been made, it was aot JJ2 thought

5il i^j6 Jprilis* 1721,

rrchen-oi Mr. ligbl*

thought one could have expected any Obstacle from them, in favour of a Man who, instead of deserving Refuge and Protection from the Prosecution begun against him, and from an exemplary Vengeance, is, by a pernicious Conduct, and such Crimes as were never heard of before, become a publick Offender, and, one may say, an Enemy to Mankind; so that he cannot pretend an; Right to the Benefit of the Privileges of any Nation in the World, how tender soever it may be of whatever may touch its Privileges, that can never have been granted with a View of protecting Villains, which would really be an Abuse, but of maintaining the Subject in the Enjoyment of his Liberty, and of the Advantages to which he may be intitled by the fundamental Laws of the Country: And it is not to be doubted but the Privilege intended by the 17th Article of the Joyful Entry of Brabant, was granted for that Purpose, and to prevent the Subjects and Inhabitants of that Province from being carried off against their Will, to be tried and punished by incompetent Judges elsewhere: And if one should interpret-this Privilege hi any other manner, or extend it as far as the said Knight would have it, an infinite Number of Absurdities would result from it, to the irreparable Prejudice of neighbouring Nations; since Brabant, by this Extension of a pretended Privilege, would become a Plate of Safety for all manner of Criminals; which would be inconsistent with the Friendship and good Understanding that should be cultivated and preserved, with great Care, between Great Britain and the Austrian Netkeiiands, and with the mutual Freedom of Access, that is so necessary for carrying on the Commerce, and for the fi-equefnt Intercourse, between the Two Countries: This is a Maxim ever allowed by all Nations, that no Privilege can be rnamiairred which is contrary to Reason, and would overthrow the Rules of Justice; and that it is never to be extended so far as to divest another of his Rights, or to make it degenerate into an Abuse and Corruption.

Whence it follows, That his Majesty’s Demand has nothing in it but what is consistent with the Privilege fh Debate, so far as it may be judged a reasonable one; since his Majesty, his Parliament, and the whole British Nation, have an unquestionable Right of obliging Knight, the Cashier, to give an Account of has Transactions, to pay the Balance he owes, and to punish him for his Misdemeanors: And it is equally certain, that the States of Brabant cannot deprive them of a Right they are so justly possessed of, without doing a manifest Injury to his Majesty, and to his Dominions; nor without completing the Utter Ruin of an infinite Number of Families.

The late Directors of the said Company allege, towards clearing themselves of the great Mischiefs done to the Nation, which have overw helmed it, and are but too notorious, that the said Knight is sole Aiithor thereof, by his ill Management, and by his Corruption, in !the Conduct of a Scheme of so great Importance, the Execution whereof had been entrusted to his Care Without any Restriction or Bounds; inso much that nobody but himself can lead the Parliament through the Windings of a Maze composed, and made up, of the tnost infamous Uoritrrvanees that were ever practised; which it is'impossibte to discover

Otherwise than by means of the Lights that itiety be given

by the said Cashier, and of the giving in of his Accounts, which ought to be made up in the ‘Place where he trans-

' acted, according to the Rules observed on the like Oeca-tions in all Countries of the reasonable Part of the World: an order to Which his Majesty therefore assures himself, that the States of Brabant will make no Difficulty of giving their Consent; and he has so much the mdre Reason so expect it, that it is not at all probable those Gentlemen should at this time insist on their Privileges, wrongfully interpreted, to the Prejudice of* the English Nation, which has spent so much Blood and Treasure to maintain them in the Possession thereof.

All these Arguments being weighed, the Under-written persuades himself, that the next General Assembly Of the States of B/wtof, being moved’withIndignation at tlidbase Practices of this infamous Fugitive,-and duly inclined*to

give, in so Important an Occasion, Marks of the Braban-cons Gratitude for the Friendship shewn them by the English, will not oppose his Majesty’s just Demand: And he does, with the greater Confidence, flatter himself it will be so, because it concerns the Interest of the Emperor, and of the States of all the Powers in Europe, that an Offender, loaded with so many Crimes, and accountable for immense Sums to his Majesty, to the South Sea Company, and in general to the whole N ation, should be brought to Justice: And, considering the Regard your Excellency has upon all Occasions, shewn for the King’s Service, and for the Good of the British Nation, the Under-written has the Honour to pray you most earnestly, that, irt pursuance of his Imperial Majesty’s Orders, you will interpose your Authority with the States of Brabant, that the said Knight may immediately be delivered up to him, and carried, tinder a secure Guard, to the Port of Ostende, in order to his being sent back from thence into England, to the end he may there give an Account, of his Transactions; and may be exemplarily punished according to the Enormity of his Crimes.

Done at Brusselles, the 21 April 1721.

Signed Win. Loathes*

Sir Thomas Crosse reported from the Committee, to South S«a whom it was referred to examine the several Duplicates Directors, of the Inventories or Particulars of the Estates of the late *utC5* Sub Governor, Deputy Governor, Directors, Deputy Cashier, and Accountant, of the South Sea Company, delivered in to this House; and to make Estimates of the Balances of the said several Duplicates’; That the Committee had considered the Matter to them referred; and had made an Estimate of the Balances of the said several Duplicates; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk's Table:

Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

In obedience to your Order of the 27th of March last, whereby the said several Duplicates of the Inventories and Particulars were referred to the -Consideration of a Committee;

Your Committee, for that Purpose appointed, in pursuance of the said Order, have employed some Part of their time in the inspecting and considering several of the said Inventories and Particulars: And, finding all or most Of them to contain different Methods in the Computations of the said Estates; and setting forth generally the ‘Particulars of their several Estates, as they were upon the First Day of June last; and then carrying on a Diary, or Journal Account, of their several Transactions, from that Day to the time they delivered in their Inventories to the Barohs of the Exchequer, pursuant to the.

Act of Parliament in that behalf;

Your 'Committee fount! it impossible, or at least exceedingly difficult, to represent to the House the just Balances of their respective Accounts, over and besides the Debts, and other Engagements, wherewith their Estates are said to be charged and affected:

Thereupon your Committee, the better to clear up this Difficulty in the raoAt irNpesditieus and certain Way, and to put this Matter in the fullest Light that could be, for the Information of the House, made several Orders, whereby the said Sub Governor, Deputy Governor, Directors,

Deputy Cashier, and Accountant, were ordered to lay before your Committee an Account of the present Estimate, or’Value, in Money, of their several real and personal Estates, contained in the said Inventories or Particulars, d. in

*7 Geo. L

in the most summary mafiher; and that, in such Estimate, or Valuation, they should estimate, or value, their Bank Stock, South Sea Stock, and East India Stock, at 1.50 per Cent. one with another; their Bank and Lottery Annuities, Lottery Tickets, Exchequer Orders, East India and South Sea Bonds, at ♦Par; their long Annuities at 20 Years Purchase; their short Annuities at 14 Years Purchase; and their other Stocks and Securities as they were currently sold for, or valued at, upon the 25th Day of March last:

That, in pursuance of the aforesaid Orders, the said Sub Governor, Deputy Governor, Directors and Deputy Cashier, attended your Committee, and left with them Abstracts, in Writing, of the estimated Values in Money of their several real and personal Estates, comprised and mentioned in their said respective Inventories and Particulars; and have balanced the same in such niauner as that the said several Balances may be taken as clear Money, over and besides what they Severally owe, or are indebted; except some Contracts for Lands, and other things, which are under Contest; and over and besides such Settlements and Provisions as they allege to have been made for their respective Families: And Mr. Grigsby not being able to attend the Committee, sent his Abstract, and Balance, in the same Form afc the other: All which Balances, amounting, together, to the Sum of £ 2,014,123, ibs. jld. your Committee have inserted in a Schedule, and annexed the same to this their Report, shewing what each Person’s particular Balance amounts to.

Your Committee craves Leave to inform the House, That Sir John Lambert having attended them, on the Third Day of April, with the Abstract of his Estate, and thereby stated his Balance to be £72,508. is. 5</. he afterwards, on the 6th of April, attended again, and alleged, That he was mistaken in his said Abstract; and desired your Committee to receive a supplemental Paper, by which he would have reduced his Balance, so delivered in as before, £ 22,610. 8*. 4d.; and thereby the said Balance of £ 72,508. 1 s. 5 d. would have been not more tlwm £49>#97» *3* *d: But, your Committee, foreseeing the inconveniencies that might probably arise to them from others, by their receiving such Paper, thought fit to reject the same, and to take only a Minute thereof to enable them to represent the Fact to the House.

As to the other Part of your Order, whereby your Committee are directed to make their Observations upon the said Inventories and Particulars; your Committee crave Leave to inform the House, That the said Inventories and Particulars are in themselves so voluminous, consist of such Variety of Transactions and Things* such great Numbers ol Persons must necessarily be examined, and so many Difficulties will naturally arise, that your Committee humbly conceive, that they cannot, in any reasonable time, make such proper Observations as will answer the Intention and Expectation of the House.

All which your Committee humbly certify, and submit to the Judgment of the House.

Mr. Haldane reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Provost, Magistrates, and Council, of the Town of Dundee, in behalf of themselves, and Community, was referred; That they had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to tlfe House: And he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as fellows; viz.

Vol. 19.

That the Committee, to whom the said Petition was referred, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 29th of March last, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find,

That an Act passed in the Parliament of Scotland, in the Year 1707, for granting an Imposition of Two Penies Scots, over and above the Duty of Excise, upon every Pint of Ale and Beer brewed, brought in, tapped, vended, and sold, within the said Town, and the Liberties and Suburbs thereof, for paying and discharging such publick Debts as were upon the said Town, incurred upon several Occasions; which Imposition, so granted, was to continue for the Term of Twenty-four Years, from the 25th Day of March 1707:

That an Account of the Receipts and Disbursements of the Money arising by the said Imposition was produced to the Committee; whereby it appeared, That the same has been duly applied, according to the Directions of the said Act; notwithstanding which, there is a considerable Debt on the said Town:

That the said Town is a considerable trading Towm:

And it appeared to the Committee, by the Testimony of Sir Patrick Strachan, Colonel Robert Read, and Mr.

William Kennedy, that, by reason of the Debt upon the said Town, the publick Works thereof have of late been neglected; and are much out of Repair:

And that the Harbour, which is d great Support to the Inhabitants, is now so filled up, that Ships of Burthen, which formerly entered at any time, cannot now come in, or sail out, at the highest Tides; nor can Ships lie there with Safety, by reason the Piers of the Harbour are gone very much to Ruin, and other Works so much decayed:

That, during the time of the late unnatural Rebellion, the said Tow n, and the whole Revenues thereof, were in Possession of the Rebels; and, since that, the Inhabitants of the said Town have been at considerable Charges, in quartering a great Number of his Majesty’s Forces, when they marched to and from the Northern Part of the Kingdom: And,

That it will greatly tend to the Cohveniency and Satisfaction of the Inhabitants, if another Church was built; by reason the present Churches will not contain the Inhabitants; their Number being, of late Years, very much increased. r

That it appeared to the Committee, Unless the Terni granted by the said Act, passed in the Year 1707, for raising the said Duty of Two Penies Scots, be enlarged, the said Town having no other Fund for paying their Debts, the publick Debts of the said Town cannot be discharged; nor can a new Church, although so much wanted, be built, and kept in Repair; rior can the Harbour be cleared, and the Piers repaired, any other of the publick Works of the said Town, carried on, and made useful.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-sixth Part of a Peny Sterling, laid upon every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer sold within the Town of Dundee, and Privileges thereof, for paying the publick Debts of the said Town; building a new Church; and for repairing the Piers and Harbour there: And that Mr Haldane and Mr, Treby, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

South Sea A PETITION of the High Sheriff', and Grand

Goiiipaoy. 1jL Jury, of the County Palatine of Chester, met

at the Assizes held for the said County of Chester, the Twelfth Day of April 1721, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have daily Experience of the calamitous and mischievous Effects of the Mismanagement, Avarice, and boundless Ambition, of the late Directors of the South Sea Company, their Aiders, Abettors, and Confederates, in the intended Destruction of their Country: That the Petitioners cannot enumerate the various Misfortunes which have attended this wicked Project; but find they have just Cause to lament the small Export and Consumption of the Manufactures and Product of this Kingdom, the great Decay of Trade, as. well as the Loss of publick Credit: That they submit whether such Grievances may not be the Overthrow of their happy Constitution, if not timely redressed: And praying, That such Aleasures may be taken as may make t rade flourish, Credit^be restored, arid Justice done to an injured People.

)undce Town Mr. Ilaldane reported from the Committee, to whom )ebts. the Petition of the Provost, Magistrates, and Council, of the Town of Dundee, in behalf of themselves, and Community, was referred; That they had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to tlfe House: And he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

VOL. 19.

That the Committee, to whom the said Petition was' referred, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 29th of March last, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find,

That an Act passed in the Parliament of Scotland\ in the Year 1707, tbfgranting.au Imposition of']Vo Penies Scots, over and above the Duty of Excise, upon every Pint of Ale and liecr brewed, brought in, tapped, vended, and sold, within the said 1 own, and the Liberties and Suburbs thereof, for paying and discharging such publick Debts as were upon the said 'l oan, incurred upon several Occasions; which Imposition, so granted, was to continue for the Term of Twenty-four Years, from the 2j(h Day of March 1707:

That an Account of the Receipts and Disbursements of the Money arising by the said Imposition was produced to the Committee; whereby it appeared, That the same has been duly applied, according to the Directions of the said Act; notwithstanding which, there is a considerable Debt on the said Town:

That the said Town is a considerable trading Town;

And it appeared to the Committee, by the Testimony of Sir Patrick St rack an, Colonel Robert Read’ and Mr. ITillium Kennedy, that, by reason of the Debt upon the said Town, the publick Works thereof have of Jate been neglected; and are much out of Repair:

And that the Harbour, which is a great Support to the Inhabitants, is now so filled up, that Ships of Bui then, which formerly entered at any time, cannot now come in, or sail out, at the highest Tides; nor can Ships lie there with Safety, by reason the Piers of the Harbour are gone very much to Ruin, and other Works so much decayed:

That, during the time of the late unnatural Rebellion, the said Town, and the whole Revenues thereof were in Possession of the Rebels; and, since that, the Inhabitants of the said Town have been at considerable Charges, in quartering a great Number of his Majesty’s Forces, w hen they marched to and from the Northern Part of the Kingdom: And,

That it will greatly tend to the Conveniency and Satisfaction of the Inhabitants, if another Church was built; by reason the present Churches will not contain the Inhabitants; their Number being, of late Years, very much increased.

That it appeared to the Committee, Unless the Tern! granted by the said Act, passed in the Year 1707, for raising the said Duty of Tw o Penies Scots, be enlarged, the said Town having no other Fund for paying their Debts, the publick Debts of the said Town cannot be discharged; nor can a new Church, although so much wanted, be built, and kept in Repair; nor can the Harbour be cleared, and the Piers repaired, or any other of the publick Works of the said Town, carried on, and made useful -

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-sixth Part of a Peny Sterling, laid upon every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer sold within the Town of Dundee, and Privileges thereof, for paying the publick Debts of the said Town; building a new Church; and for repairing the Piers and Harbour there: And that Mr. Haldane and Mr, Treby, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of Francis Eyles Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, having the Misfortune of being One of the late Directors of the South Sea Company, has been expelled his Seat in Parliament for Crimes charged on the late Directors of the said Company: That, by the Bill now depending, the Estates of the said Directors are to make Satisfaction for certain Losses therein mentioned: That he was no-ways concerned in promoting the Scheme upon which the Act passed, or in facilitating the same; nor was ever at any Meeting of the Directors, either before or after the passing the said Act, to consult or contrive the carrying on foe

Scheme; nor wAs ever of any Committee for executing the same; nor privy to the giving or taking in any Stock for any Minister of State, or Member of eitheF House of Parliament, or of foe Increase or Decrease of the Money Subscriptions: That he hath made a full Discovery of ail Matters that lay within his Knowledge, relating to the said Company, to the Committee of Secrecy: That he hath laid before the said Committee^ an Account of all his Transactions since December 1719: That he never made any Advantage by being a Director; but hath diminished his own Fortune, by subscribing in his Annuities: That he was absent in the Country whilst many of the said Matters were transacted: That he hath delivered to the Barons of the Exchequer a true Inventory of both his real and personal Estate: That he humbly hopes he shall not be equally involved in the future Punishments with those who contrived, and unjustly executed, the Scheme:

And praying Relief.

Ordered, That foe said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Richard Horsey, One of the late Directors Relief of of the South Sea Company, was presented to the House, S*jth and read; setting forth, That there being a Bill depending ufferert‘ for the Relief of the unhappy Sufferers in the South Sea Company; which Bill, if it pass, will divest the Petitioner of all his Estate: That from his first becoming a Director, in February 1714, be was appointed One of the Committee of Shipping, and continued therein all his Time: That he was not of those Committees, nor at all Consulted by them, who had the contriving the late Scheme: That, until the Inquiry by Parliament, he was not made sensible of the secret Evils that have run along with the whole Management of this Affair: That he hath given in a faithful Account of all his Transactions, and of his whole Estate: That his Estate was £.14,110.

10 s. 8 d. in December 1719, before the Scheme began; and is now but £. 15,222. 5s. 3d. the Deductions taken off that it is subject to: And praying, That a Provision may be granted him, and his Family.

A Petition of William Amtell, late One of the Directors Ditto,

of foe South Sea Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, on the 7th of January 1719* the Petitioner’s Wife and' several Children, with Part of his Substance, being destroyed by the dreadful Fire at his House in Austin Fn/ars, he was confined to his Lodging, or out of Town, for above Two Months afterwards: That he neither was of the Committee for the Scheme then on foot, or solicited the same: That he was an utter Stranger to the taking in, or holding, Stock for any Persons whatsoever, or ever heard of the same; which now appears to have been privately transacted by some particular Persons: That he never came into any Measures, but such as then appeared to be for the Benefit of the Company, and the Publick; and not to enrich himself, by any corrupt Means whatsoever: That, upon his Examination before the Secret Committee, he has fully discovered all the Transactions that he knew of the Company’s Affairs: That the Accounts he delivered in, shew how very little he dealt in Stocks; and that, instead of being enriched thereby, his Estate is much lessened:

And praying the Consideration and Compassion of the House, in tender Regard to his Family.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Sir Jabob Jacobson Knight, was presented

SoutI Sea to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner,

Sufferers. having been One of the late Directors of the South Sea

Company, hath the Misfortune to be under the Censure of the House; That, by the Bill brought in, pursuant to the Resolutions of the House, the Estates of the said Directors are to make Satisfactions, for certain Losses sustained by the unhappy Sufferers of the said Company: That he was appointed One of the Committee of Treasury: That, on the First of April 1719, he was removed; and was then appointedOne of the Committee for Buying of Goods and Merchandize: That, from the time of his Removal, he was never applied to for his Assistance, nor made acquainted with any of the Affairs transacted in the Committee of Treasury; nor was he ever admitted into any private Consultation with relation to the South Sea Company s Scheme, and the Execution thereof; those Transactions being industriously concealed from his Knowledge: That he never knew, nor so much as ever heard, either of the Taking in, or Selling, of Stock, by and for the Account of the Company, to or for the Benefit of any Member of either House of Parliament, or any Person in the Administration, until the Inquiry made this Session of Parliament; and never knew, or heard, of any Stock bought for the Company’s Account, till he was at the Btfth: That the Court of Directors impowered the Committee of Treasury to lend Money upon their Stock; but limited the Sum, at most, to Two million, and not to exceed Four thousand Pounds to any One Person upon One thousand Pounds Stock: That he had no Part in that Management, nor did know they had exceeded that Limitation: That he was not admitted into any private or separate Meetings, where the Method of setting the Company’s Stock to Sale by Subscriptions at high Prices, and the Calculating of their large Dividends, were concerted: That he hath given the Committee of Secrecy a full and true Account of all his Transactions in South Sea Stock from the First January 1719; whereby it appears he made no Advantage by being a Director; but, on the contrary, is a very great Loser, being reduced to a very small Part of what he was possessed of before the Act of the last Sessions passed for encreasing the said Company’s Capital: And praying Relief.

Ordered That the said Petition do. lie upon the Table.

£):tt0< A Petition of Ambrose Page, Brewer, One of the late . Directors of the South Sea Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, in the Year 1717, was elected One of the Directors of the said Company, and was appointed One of the Committee of Accounts, and House and Servants; but was never of any other Committee, nor had any Hand in forming or carrying on the late Scheme: That he conceives he is not guilty of the several Matters laid to the Charge of the late Directors, in the Bill now depending for Relief of the unhappy Sufferers in the South Sea Company: That he never took in, or held, or knew that the said Company took in, or held, any Stock for the Benefit of any Member of either House of Parliament, or any Person concerned in the Administration, or otherwise, till the late Examination in Parliament; nor did he ever know, till then, of any Stock pretended to be sold by the Company; nor Avas he privy; to, or concerned in, the Entry in the Cash Book for that Purpose: Admits he was present in a Court of Directors when Orders were given for lending Money, not exceeding £. 4,000. on each £. 1,000. Stock; but did not know, that the Company intended to lend any Money on Subscriptions, till after the same was actually lent; That, as to the Dividends, pressing Instances were made by the Members of the Com* pany to have One declared; and several of the Court of Directors were of Opinion, that the Company was in a Condition of making a Dividend of £.30. per Cent, at Christmas last, and a Dividend of £. ,50. per Cent. per Annum for Twelve Years afterwards: That he did acquiesce in the same; That he was wholly a Stranger to the Addition of 250,000 to the First Money Subscription, and the Addition of 500,000 to the Second Money Subscription; neither had he, directly or indirectly, any Part of those additional Subscriptions: That he did not know of any Deficiency in the Third and Fourth Money Subscriptions till some Months after they were taken in: That he is so far from being a Gainer since the Scheme took place, that he is a considerable Sufferer in his Estate: And praying, That he may be heard, by his Counsel, in relation to the said Bill, so far as it concerns himself.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Sir William Hammond Knight, was pre- Relief of sented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the South Sea Petitioner was One of the late unfortunate Directors Sufferers* of the South Sea Company; but not of any Committee that had the secret Management of the Company’s Affairs; nor ever bought of, or sold to, the Company, any Stock; nor privy to the giving any Stock, or taking in the same, for any Minister of State, or Member of either House of Parliament, or any other Person whatsoever: That he hath delivered to the Barons of the Exchequer a true Inventory both of his real and personal Estate; by which it will appear he hath been a great Loser since the late unhappy Scheme took place, by engaging himself in the Money Subscriptions, and in Buying of Stock at high Prices: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of John Grigsby, late Accountant to the Ditto, South Sea Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by the Bill now depending, he, as Accountant to the said Company, is made liable to sundry great and severe Penalties for the Actions and Conduct of others, That he was only a Servant, chose by the Court of Directors, and liable to be turned out at Pleasure; and, as he had no Share in their Debates or Resolutions, so he was no-ways accessary to the Misfortunes of the Company, either by taking in'Money Subscriptions, leading Money on the Company’s Stock, or Subscriptions, or by Buying or Selling of Stock, for the Company: That he hath always endeavoured to discharge the Duty of his Office with Integrity and Faithfulness:

And praying, That he hiay not be involved in Ruin for the Actions and Conduct of others.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Message from the Lords by Mr. Hiccocks and Mr. Fellows:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act Whitby for the better preserving and keeping in Repair the Piers Piers, &c. of the Town and Port of Whitby, in the County of York; and for explaining and making more effectual, the several Acts passed for lengthening and repairing the Piers of Bridlington, alias Burlingtonf in the said County; without any Amendment.

Mr. Brodf'ick, from the Committee of Secrecy, reported, according to Order, some further Matters, as they appeared to the said Committee; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee of Secrecy appointed to enquire into all the Proceedings relating to the Execution of an Act, passed the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for enabling the South Sea Company to increase their present Capital Stock, and Fund, by redeeming such publick Debts and Incumbrances as are therein mentioned; and for raising Money, to be applied for lessening several of the publick Debts and Incumbrances; and for calling in the present Exchequer Bills remaining uncancelled; and for making forth new Bills, in lieu thereof, to be circulated and exchanged, upon Demand, at or near the Exchequer; have proceeded further in the Examination of the Matters referred to them: And, observing, that, upon their former Reports, it was thought proper, that the Examinations referred to by your Committee should be laid before the House; and several other Matters appearing to your Committee fit for the Consideration of the House; your Committee report the same in the Words of the Examinations themselves, and according to the Papers laid before your Committee.

Your Committee, in a former Report, acquainted the House, That the Indisposition of Edmund Waller Esquire, had prevented their laying before the House, in that Report,.a more particular Account relating to the Sum of £794,451. 15 s. 9 received and paid, by Turner and Company, upon the Account of the said Mr. Waller, between the 28th of March 1719, and the 2ist of No*. verier following: And, having since, viz. on the 22d of March 1720, examined Mr. Waller, he saith, That he did, from time to time, settle Accoifhts with Mr. Aislabie, his Father-in-law, of his Transactions in Money Irnd Stock for him, and has not any Account thereof; That he did keep some Memorandums of his said Transactions in a Book, which Book he has since torn; but Bays, That he did keep a Copy of his Accounts with the Sword Blade Company: That he has, from time to time, destroyed all his Papers and Memorandums relating to his Transactions for Mr. Aislabie: Says, He cannot tell what Dealings he has had in Stock for Mr. Aislabie; but that far the greatest Part of his Transactions in Stock were upon his own Account: That Four-and-forty thousand Pounds, Part of the Balance of Seventy-seven thousand Pounds due from the Sword Blade Company, is the Examinant's own Money; and the remaining Thirty-three thousand Pounds belongs to Mr. Aislabie: Being asked, Whether, at the time of his beginning to deal in Stock, he was possessed of a considerable Sum of Money of his own; he refused to answer; alleging, It was his own private Concern.

Your Committee afterwards received a Letter from the said Mr. Waller, dated the 19th of April instant; wherein he desired to be again examined, to clear up any Mistakes, if there were any, in his former Examination, and to give the Committee the best Information he could: Whereupon your Committee did take his further Examination, which is as follows;

He says, That, in February or March 1719, when he began to deal in Stock, he had, of the Money of his Mother, his Brother his own and his Wife’s Fortune, about the Sum of Twenty thousand Pounds; of which, his Wife's Fortune was Five thousand Pounds, which he had in Bank Notes: That he employed the said Twenty thousand Pounds in buying Stock.

The House proceeded, according to Order, to take 1 into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of tive Adventurers, therein mentioned, for bringing Water to the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent, was referred:

And the said Report w as read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Cities of London and Westminster are, of late, greatly increased in their Buildings and Inhabitants; and that they are not, at present, sufficiently supplied with Water, for the necessary Occasions of the Inhabitants thereof.

And, upon the Examination of Dr. Desaguliers, Captain Robinson, and other Mathematicians, it appeared, That a great Quantity of Water may be brought from One or more Stream or Streams, that run by or near the Village of Drayton, in the County of Middlesex, to some Place near the said Cities.

Dr. Desaguliers said, That he had examined and tried the Quantity of Water, contained in the Cowley

A Petition of Sir John Blunt Baronet, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner is heartily sorry he ever had any Part in the Execution of the late Scheme for enlarging the capital Stock of the South Sea Company; which has been attended with such Consequences, as, when he engaged therein, he could not foresee, or in the least imagine: That, as to the selling any Stock, or Subscriptions mortgaged to the Company, and the Excess of the First Loan of £, 500,000. on Stock, at £. 250 per Cent, he was no-way privy to; nor did know what was issued on the other Loans: That he was not of the Committee of Treasury, under whose Care that Account lay; nor did he ever approve of the Dividends: That he had acquired a very plentiful Estate before Christmas 1719, and had a great Fortune with his present Wife: That the Petitioner hath, by a former Wife, Seven Children: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Palmer reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Traders, Farmers, and other Inhabitants, of the Town and Borough of Watchett, and Parts adjacent, in the County of Somer~ set, vras referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, to w hom the said Petition was

referred, have, pursuant to thfc Of del* of the House, examined the Matter thereof; and find,

That, by an Act of Parliament, made in the Sixth Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for repairing the Harbour and Quay of Wat diet I, in the County of Somei'sct, certain Rates and Duties were imposed and laid on all Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes, to be exported or imported at or within the said Harbour or Port, ill order for the raising a sufficient Stock and Supply for the rebuilding and repairing the said Harbour and Quay:

And that the said Rates and Duties, so imposed and laid, were, by the sa.id Act, to be collected for the Tern* of 21 Years, from Lady-day 1708; and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament:

That, after the Expiration of the said Term of 21 Years, the One-half Of thfc said Rates and Duties were to continue to be collected forever* in order for the raising a sufficient Stock and Supply for the keeping the said Harbour and Quay in good Repair.

That, upon the Examination of Mr. John Wakefield, and several other Persons, it appeared to the Committee*

That, when the said Quay was rebuilt and repaired, the same was built much too low, and not of sufficient Length to preserve the said Town, and the Ships and Vessel^ riding in the said Harbour, from the Rage and Violence! of the Sea.

It also appeared to the said Committee, That it will bfc absolutely necessary the said Quay should be raised at’ least Five or Six Foot higher than it. is at present; and that the Head of the same should be extended and lengthened Fifty Foot, or more, beyond the present Length thereof, for the better Preservation of the said Town, and Security of the Ships and Vessels riding in the said Harbour; which cannot be done, without some other Provision be made for that Purpose.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Duties granted by an Act, made« in the Sixth Year of her late Majesty's Ilcign, intituled,

An Act for repairing the Harbour and Quay of Watchett, in the County of Somerset: And that Mr.

Palmer, and Sir William Wyndham, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, that it appears to this House, That James Craggs Esquire, late Postmaster General, did, in Febmary One thousand Seven hundred and Nineteen, during the time that the Proposals of the South Sea Company w ere depending in Parliament, with a corrupt Intention, apply to, and solicit, Robert Knight, late Cashier of the said Company, for a large Quantity of South Sea Stock, to be held by the said Company, for his own Use and Benefit;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out these Words, " with a corrupt Intention

And the Question being put, That those Words stand Part of the Question;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question being put;

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That James Craggs Esquire, late Postmaster General, did, in February One thousand Seven hundred and Nineteen, during the time that the Proposals of the South Sea Company were depending in Parliament, with a corrupt Intention, apply to, and solicit, Robert Knight, late Cashier of the said Company, for a large Quantity of South Sea Stock, to be held by the said Company for his own Use and Benefit.

A Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears to this House, That, on or about the Tvrenty-seventh of February One thousand Seven hundred and Nineteen, a Sum of Thirty thousand Pounds Capital Stock of the South Sea Company, which had been taken in, and paid for, out of the Cash of the said Company, was, upon the Solicitation of the said James Craggs, held by the said Company, for the Use and Benefit of the said James Craggs without any Money paid, or Security given, for the same; which said Thirty thousand Pounds Stock was afterwards, on the Twenty-eighth of March One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty, transferred to the said James Craggs;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out these Words, without any Money paid, or Security given for the same

Mr. Comptroller acquainted the House, That his Majesty hath been pleased to command him to lay before this House, Copies of several Letters and Papers, relating to Mr. Knight, late Cashier of the South Sea Company: And he presented the same to the House, with a Schedule of them:

And the said Schedule, and Copies of the said several Letters and Papers, were read.

The said Letters and Papers arc as followxth; viz.

My Lord,

Brussels, 2 8th April 1721.

THE Deputies of the States of Brabant, finding that I w as no-ways satisfied with the Answer they gave me; but, on the contrary, that I renewed my Solicitations with greater Force and Application; at length thought fit to own, They were not sufficiently authorized to dispense with so essential a Point of their Privileges, as that of giving up Mr. K?ught, contrary, as they pretend, to the 17th Article of the Joyeuse Entre6; but, seeing I continued to press them so very hard on this Occasion, they were obliged to acquaint me, That in order to bring the Matter to a Conclusion, it ought to be proposed, by the Marquis dePrie, in a General Assembly of the States; which, they assured me, was the usual and indispensable Method of proceeding in Cases of the like Nature.

Upon this Declaration of the Deputies, I desired the Marquis de Prie to give the necessary Directions for convening the States of this Province; but that some other Pretext might be taken for calling them together; because I was not yet determined to put this important Affair on that Issue: He told me, That, as the Time for demanding the usual Subsidy drew near, he would order them to meet on that Affair; and that, in case I judged it proper, he would lay his Majesty’s Demand before them: And accordingly caused circular Letters to be written, directing the Spates to assemble the 23d Instant; and, at the same time, he promised to use his utmost Endeavours to try to induce them to comply v:i:L che King’s just Demand.

On the 21st Instant, I presented a Memorial to his Excellency; in which I urged the most pressing Arguments; and, I thought, such persuasive Reasons, as I had Groundi to hope would make an impression on them, and remove the Difficulties they had raised, under the Pretence of their Privileges: I imagined at least, that I had plainly shewn the Absurdity and Unreasonableness of all they had hitherto grounded their Opposition upon.

The 23d the Marquis de Prii sent for the Deputies, the Morning before the General Assembly met; delivered my Memorial; directed them to lay it before the States; and recommended, in pressing Terms, the Matter contained therein to their Consideration: His Excellency likewise acquainted them, That it was the Emperor's sincere Desire to gratify the King, in an Affair, which his Majesty had so much at Heart; and which was of the greatest Importance for the Welfare of all his Majesty’s Subjects, and highly necessary for restoring the Credit of the Nation; and that the Friendship, and strict Alliance, which subsisted betw een the King and his Imperial Majesty, made the latter look upon the King’s Demand, not only as just and reasonable, but as a Concern in which the Emperor’s Interest was very deeply engaged; and therefore he expected they would deliberate on the Business, and come to a favourable Resolution, without Loss of Time. In short, my Lord, he enforced his Arguments with strong Reasons; and seconded those I had made use of in my Memorial, with great Force: And that nothing might be wanting, which could any-ways tend to the Success of this important Affair, I employed my whole Time, from the 17th, iu soliciting the States, and desiring their Concurrence with Ins Majesty’s Demand.

That Day, the 23d, being appointed for the Subsidy, which was granted as usual, the Deputies did not lay my Memorial before the Assembly; but the 24th it was read, and met with great Opposition from the Clergy and Nobility; and especially from the former: The Marquis, being informed, That a great Majority of the States insisted violently on the Support of their Privileges; and that they were like to come to such a Resolution as would have been displeasing to both the King and the Emperor; found Means to get the Resolution deferred to thfc Day following, 25th Instant: In the mean time, he sent for such of the States as have a Dependence on the Government, and repeated to them anew the earnest Desire the Emperor had to give the King a Mark of his Friendship, and a Proof of his sincere Intentions to comply with his Majesty's Request, on this Occasion: His Excellency recommended to them with great Warmth, to use their utmost Efforts in the Resumption of their Deliberations the next Day; and in treated them to endeavour to bring the Matter to the desired Conclusion; viz. to give their Consent to Mr. Knight*s being delivered up, and carried into England\ in order to answer, before his competent Judges, to the Crimes and Misdemeanors laid to his Charge:

But notwithstanding the pressing Arguments which the Marquis de Prie urged to the Deputies, and my constant Solicitations; the Two first Members of the States, to wit, the Clergy, and Nobility, still insisted on their Privileges; and, without declaring themselves absolutely on the Matter in question, came to a Resolution to the following Purpose:

That a Remonstrance be made to his Imperial Majesty, in the most humble and respectful manner, representing the Prejudice that their Privileges would suffer, by a Compliance directly contrary to one of the most valuable Articles of their Liberties, of wrhich no Example could be produced, in any Case whatsoever; and the ill Consequences, wherewith it would unavoidably be attended, seeing all the neighbouring Powers would not fail to urge such a material Precedent, on all Occasions, which might, and do but too often, happen: and that their consenting to the Demand made by his Excellency, in the Name of the King of Great Britain, would be, in effect, the giving up of what the People of this Province have always esteemed Le Bijou de leurs LiberUs; and which they have hitherto preserved inviolably; and therefore humbly to

pray

6°

Maiu

7 Geo. I.

pray his Imperial Majesty would be graciously pleased to excuse them from consenting to the said Demand: However as the Tiers Etat, or Bourguemasters, and Pensionaries, of the Three Chef Villes; viz. Louvain, Antwerp, and Brussells, have no Vote in the General Assembly of the States, until the Two first Members, that is, the Clergy and Nobility have declared their Consent to the Matter proposed; they desired them, at their Return, to sound the Magistrates of their respective Towns; and to make a Report to the Deputies of the States; who assemble every Day, for the Dispatch of the current Business of the Province; that in case the Emperor should, at the King’s repeated Instances, persist in the Demand of having Knight delivered up, they might be apprised, at their next Meeting, of the Sentiments of the Chef Villes on this Head.

Yesterday the Deputies made their Report to the Marquis de Prii; and, their Greffier being sick, the Resolution could not be drawn up in Form; but I hope to be able to send it your Lordship by next Post, in case the Greffier’s Indisposition does not prevent me: His Excellency was extremely dissatisfied with this Resolution: Although the States, by their constant Opposition to the Demand, had, from the Beginning, given room to believe, that it would be with the greatest Difficulty they could be brought to comply; yet, considering it was grounded on the greatest Justice, and supported by solid and persuasive Arguments, and the most pressing Instances, we had still Reason to hope for a more satisfactory Resolution: Nevertheless, as the States are not yet come to a positive Conclusion, his Excellency assured me again last Night, That he would employ all his Credit with the Magistrates of the Chef Villes, to gain their Consent, and use his utmost Endeavours with the Nobility and Clergy, to try to remove the Objections they make; and, as soon as he discovered the Sentiments of the Tiers Etat, he will propose the Matter again to the General Assembly, and not depart from the Demand, until he has attempted all possible Means to procure the Satisfaction which his Majesty requires; since his own Inclinations do not only prompt him to exert himself, on this Occasion, but that he is likewise directed by the Emperor’s express Orders to procure the Effects which his Majesty expects from his repeated Instances, if they can possibly be attained without causing new and dangerous Troubles, and Agitations of the People.

I know’, my Lord, the Council of State, and the Sovereign Council of Brabant, are allowed to remonstrate Three times in Opposition to the Emperor’s express Orders, sent them directly in Writing, in Cases where they judge the Rights and Liberties of the Subject are concerned, or where such Orders tend to the Lessening of the Power of the said Councils: But if his Imperial Majesty persist in his First Orders, after the Third Remonstrance, they generally submit to his Will, with this Reserve; Sauf les Droits et Libertes du Sujet, et les Privileges ct Immu-nitbs du ConseiL I cannot affirm, that the Case is the same with the States of Brabant; the Council of State being in the Nature of a Council of Regency; and the Sovereign Council of Brabant, a Court of Justice; and the Judge established between the Prince and the People: Besides, it has not fallen in my way to be so conversant with the States as with the others; and, of course, I cannot be so well apprised of their manner of proceeding, in Affairs of this Consequence: But I will make it my Business to inform myself more particularly therein; and I will pursue the Business committed to my Care with the utmost Pains and Diligence, until I have brought it to a Conclusion; and, notwithstanding all the Difficulties I have to struggle with, I will not despair of Success; seeing the Marquis de Prie has espoused the Matter with great Vigour and Warmth; being resolved, as he declares, to give the King a convincing Proof of his Zeal and Attachment to his Majesty’s Service, and that of the British Nation, on this and all other Occasions that may offer.

My Lord, Brussells, 30th April 1721.

I RECEIVED the Honour of your Lordship’s Letter of the 10th Instant, O. S. to which mine, of the 28th, was a full Answer: Your Lordship will perceive by it, and by that of the 2 2d, in which I did myself the Honour to send you a Copy of the Memorial I presented to the Marquis de Prie, that I did not design to apply directly to the States of Brabant, but to his Excellency, as the Emperors Minister, appointed for the Administration of the Government of these Countries: I thought it, however, necessary to use my utmost Endeavours to prepare such of the States in particular, as I judged might be most useful to us on this Occasion, before the Marquis made the Demand in Form.

1 was in hopes to have been able to send the Resolution of the General Assembly to your Lordship by this Post; but the Greffier’s Indisposition prevents me: In the mean time, I have given your Lordship the Substance of it in my last, as near as I could remember, in the Terms the Marquis de Prie communicated it to me: Upon which, I shall wait your Lordship’s further Instructions: And I have the Honour to be, with the greatest Veneration and Respect,

My Lord, &;c.

JVm. Leathes.

Sir, Whitehall, 28th April 1721.

I AM now to acknowledge your Letters to me, of the 28th and 30th Instant, N. S. which have been both laid before the King.

His Majesty w*as, indeed, extremely well satisfied with your diligent and zealous Behaviour in the Conduct of the Affair you are pressing; but, at the same time, I'am ordered to tell yoq, That the King is no less surprised and displeased at the Proceedings of the States of Brabant; who must surely have very false and vitiated Notions of Liberty, since they look on the Power of protecting so enormous a Criminal as Robert Knight, against all Justice, Reason, and Sense, as the Bijou:v de leurs Libertez, as they term it; whereas it is rather a Duty incumbent on them to discourage such Villainies: It is consonant to the Law of Nations, and it is the very Foundation of Faith and good Amity among neighbouring States, not to suffer the Right of Sanctuary to be abused in so flagrant and crying an Instance as this is: But I sent you the King’s Sentiments on this Head so fully in my Letter of the 31 st of March; and the Remonstrance designed to be made by the Clergy and Nobility to the Emperor, seems to be founded on so slight and empty Reasonings; that I take it to be wholly needless to repeat any further Arguments to you, on this Subject: And although the perverse Obstinacy of the States of Brabant would be sufficient to discourage any other Prince less resolute, and less animated, than the King is, from pursuing this Point by any further Attempts; yet his Majesty looks upon the Case to be of such Importance, and his Heart is so much set on doing Justice both to himself, and to his People, that he is determined to omit no Endeavours to get this notorious Offender brought within the Reach of the Laws of his Kingdoms: His Majesty was therefore glad to observe, That the Matter was not yet absolutely and finally concluded: And as the Tiers Etat, as you tell us, has not yet concurred with the Clergy and Nobility in the Remonstrance they proposed to make; and the Marquis de Prib had promised you to employ all his Power and Cre-

Apprehen-sion of Mr. Knight.

54°

dit with those who compose that Tiers Etat, to bring them to consent to his Majesty’s Demand; the King would have you spare no Pains, nor lose any Opportunity, in pressing and persuading the Members of the Tiers Etat not to agree with the Clergy and Nobility in their intended Remonstrance; but rather to do Justice to his Majesty, and the British Nation, in so friendly and neighbourly a Point as the delivering up Knight, whom no civilized People ought to protect.

I should be very glad you would learn, and inform me, Whether the States of Brabant are obliged to submit to the Emperor’s express Orders, after the Third Remonstrance, if his Imperial Majesty still persists, as you say, the Council of State, and the Sovereign Council of Bra-bant, are used to do: because, if that should prove the Case, the Emperor has so far already declared his Willingness to gratify the King in this Matter, that we may, with good Hopes, renew our Solicitations at the Court of lri~ tnna, to induce his Imperial Majesty to insist positively on his being obeyed, in a Point where the Opposition of the States appears to be against all Reason and Justice.

In the mean time, as the King is fully determined not to give up this Matter, but to urge it by all Means, and in all Places, as far as possibly it will go: I am commanded to send Copies of your last Letters, and Memorial, to Mr Column, who is lately gone to Vienna, with his Majesty’s express Orders, That he should represent there what you have so vigorously urged at Bnmells, and enforce his Instances with all the Strength and Earnestness, towards the Imperial Ministers, that he can possibly use.

Last Night I had put into my Hands a Pamphlet, containing several Arguments relating to the State of the Case of the Surrender of Mr. Knight; in which I find a Precedent to the Point in Question, quoted concerning one Lievans of Amsterdam, who was surrendered, and put into the Hands of the Dutch Resident; with the Opinion of a Civilian, That those Privileges have been frequently abrogated, remitted, or suspended, as the Cases required; as you will more fully see by the Book itself, which I send you, that you may peruse the Whole, and make the best Use you can of what is asserted there, for obtaining the End his Majesty so earnestly desires.

I am, 8$c.

Translation.

Copy of the Resolution of the General Assembly of the States of Brabant, upon Mr. Leathes Memorial, presented to his Excellency the Marquis de Brie,

To his Excellency.

OUR Ordinary Deputies have given us an Account, That they have had the Honour to execute your Excellency’s Orders; having not only delivered to the General Assembly, which was held the 23d of April last, and continued the Two following Days, the Memorial which Mr. Leathes, the British Resident, presented to your Excellency relating to Mr. Knight, late Cashier of the South Sea Company, together with the Papers thereto annexed; but likewise made an exact Report of the lively Instances your Excellency charged them to make, in his Name, to our General Assembly, that we would concur, on our Part; to the end his Imperial and Catholick Majesty, our Royal Master, may have the Satisfaction, which he has so much at Heart, as we observed by his Answer to the King of Great Bi'itain, and the Orders he gave to your Excellency about sending back the said Cashier to

A. 1 1

Englandi of giving this new Proof of his constant Friendship for the King of Great Britain, and for the Interests of that Nation: We desire your Excellency will be fully persuaded with what Readiness we would lay hold of this Occasion, as we hope we have made it appear hitherto, on all other Occasions that offered, of seconding the Intentions of his Imperial and Catholick Majesty, and shewing our Respect and Obedience to such Orders as are signified to us in his Name: But we hope, at the same time, that his Majesty will take in good Part our representing to him the Observations we made in our last Assembly, touching the great Inconveniences, and irreparable Prejudice, that would arise from this Surrender; besides, that it would strike at the Privileges granted to the said States by the Royal Predecessors of his said Majesty, which your Excellency, by his Order, lately swore to in his Royal Name, and observed religiously hitherto: We confide also in the unalterable Equity of his Majesty, that he will vouchsafe to reflect upon the ill Consequences of such a Precedent, which would often expose us. to the like Demands from other Powers: who would the rather be offended at our Refusal, if we did not scruple to consent, that the said Knight should be surrendered, to be sent over to England; which Difficulty seems to us the more just and reasonable, in that the said Knight is not accused of any Crime of Rebellion, nor condemned for, or even convicted of, any Excess, imputed to him by the British Nation, or the publick Voice: It is true, it does not belong to us to enter into the Discussion of the said Excesses, though we are very sensible of the Misfortunes that attended them, for the strict Amity between his Majesty and the King of Great Britain, and the Friendship and Regard the Brabandons ever had for the British Nation, are so deeply rooted in our Minds, that nothing but our Duty, and the indispensable Obligation we are in of observing the fundamental Laws of this Land, can hinder us from yielding, with Pleasure, to whatever may be agreeable to his Majesty, and his Parliament.

Lastly, We hope that your Excellency will be pleased to give us Leave to lay our Representation directly at his Imperial and Catholick Majesty’s Feet: to the end we may the better justify our Conduct, and most humbly desire him not to disapprove the Difficulties we have made, as well for the good of his Royal Service, as for the Preservation of the Laws and Privileges; and to give us Leave to remain within the Bounds of the Oath we have made thereupon.

We have, however, forewarned the Burghermasters of the Three Chief Towns of Louvain, Brussells, and Antwerp, to sound, in so nice and important an Affair as this is, the Sentiments of the respective Magistrates, to be informed of the Dispositions that might be found to serve as a Direction to the Resolution to be taken, in case wc are so unhappy, which yet we do not fear from the Clemency and Equity of our Royal Master, as not to make him sensible of the Solidity of the Reasons which have been debated in our General Assembly; and which we shall have the Honour to represent to him with all the Submission becoming the Faithfulness of our Zeal.

Signed,

J. B. de Wilde, Loco Graphierii.

Then General Rosse said;

Mr. Speaker,

I C A N N O T have a greater Sense of any Honour done me, than I have of that which is done me by the Commands of this House, and expressed to me by a Person of so great Honour, and for whom I have the greatest Respect: 1 am sorry there was any Occasion for it; but thought it indispensably my Duty, in Execution of the Trust reposed in me by this House.
