.He was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, a Copy of a Warrant for a Commission to Robert Gordon of Houghs; and also a Copy of the said Commission; with a Schedule of them.

And then he withdrew.

And the Schedule was read. v The said Copy of the Warrant, and Copy of the Commission, are as follows:

OUR Sovereign Lord, considering that frequent Thefts, Robberies, and Depredations, are committed upon his loyal Subjects, in the Highlands, and Northern Parts, of Scotland, by lawless Persons congregated together in Arms; who, after committing such Villainies, conceal themselves in remote and mountainous Places, and so do evade the just Punishment of their enormous Crimes; and considering likewise, that, notwithstanding the many laudable Laws against trafficking Priests and Jesuits, Sayers of Mass, and frequenting Mass-houses, Erecting of Popish Semin ?rics, and Teaching or Instructing of Youth in the Principles of Popery; thereby seducing them from the true Reformed Religion, and from the Principles of Loyalty and A flection to his Majesty's Government; as also against unlawful Convocations, seditious Practices, Mobs, and Riots, Wearing and Using of Arms, within the Bounds and Counties where Wearing and Using of such Arms is prohibited; great Numbers, within the Bounds of the said Highlands, and Northern Part, of Scotland, daily take upon them to contravene the said Laws, in hopes of not being discovered, or brought to Justice; and, when prosecuted for such Crimes, either do abscond and sutler themselves to be denounced Fugitives, or, when convicted and se ntenced to Banishment, or to be transported to his Majesty's Plantations, do nevertheless, in Chntempt of the Law, and such Judgments given against them, openly reside and resort within the Bounds aforesaid, to the great Encouragement of the like Offenders, and contrary to all goo 1 Order and Government; and that, for preventing the like Mischiefs in time coming, necessary it is, that some particular Person be entrusted with proper Powers for seizing and apprehending such Offenders, and bringing them to Justice; and being well informed of the Ability of Robert Gordon of Houghes for discharging such a Trust, and of his Loyalty and Affection to his Majesty’s Person ftiifi Government; ordains a Commission to be expede, V o l. l y.

under the Seal appointed by the Treaty of Union to be used in Scotland, in Place of the Great Seal formerly used there; giving, granting, and committing, like as his Majesty hereby gives, grants, and commits, full Power, Warrant, and Authority, to the said Robert Gordon, and those having Warrant from him, under his Hand, to search for, seize, and apprehend, all Persons guilty of Thefts, Robberies, or Depredations, committed within the Bounds* and Counties after-mentioned; viz. the Shires of Dunbarton^ Stirling, Perth, Argyle, Angus, Kincardine, Aberdeen, Banff, Elgin, Nairn, Inverness, Cromartie, Ross, and Sutherland, and Caithness, within whatever County or Counties in Scotland such Person or Persons may be found; or who, being guilty of such Crimes, shall be found and apprehended within the sainen Bounds and Counties; and to commit them to Prison, in order to their Tryal; ami likewise to search for, seize, and recover, all Goods, Cat-tie great or small, that shall be stolen within the said Bounds, within whatever County or Counties in Scotland such Goods, great or small, so stolen, may be found or discovered; or that, being stolen in any other Place or County, shall \>e brought, kept, or reset, within the samen; and likew ise to search for, seize, and apprehend, all trafficking Priests or Jesuits, all Sayers and Hearers of Mass, all Popish Schoolmasters, or Teachers of Youth, and, generally, all Persons vvimtsomever guilty of Contempts, Breaches, and Contraventions of any Laws in Force, made, or to be made, for preventing the Grow th of Popery in Scotland; all Persons guilty of unlawful Using or Wearing of Arms, or of unlaw ful Convocations, Riots, or seditious Practices; and, generally, all Persons guilty of any capital or criminal Offence; all Persons convicted and sentenced, by any Judgment of the Court of Justiciary, or Circuit Courts, or w ho shall be outlawed, or denunced Fugitive, for not Compearance upon any criminal Indictment; and who contrary to, and in Contempt of, such Sentences, shall be found within the Bounds aforesaid; and, being so apprehended, to deliver such Offenders to a Justice of Peace, Sheriff, or Sheriff Depute, Stewart or Stewartrie, or Magistrate of some Burgh, with a subscribed Information of the Crime for which the Person so delivered is apprehended, to be by such Justice of Peace, Sheriff', or his Deputes, Stewart of Stew artrie, or Magistrate of a Burgh, committed to Prison, in order to Tryal, or until they be liberate by due Course of Law; willing and requiring, like as his Majesty hereby wills and requires, all Justices of Peace, Sheriffs of Shires, Stewarts of Stewartries, Magistrates of Burghs, and all other Officers of the Law whatsomever, to concur with and assist the said Robert Gordon in the lawful Execution of the Powers hereby given him; and to commit to Prison such Delinquents, as shall be by him delivered to them, in manner above directed; and likewise all Officers of the T'roops, to be assisting to him, conform to Directions to be given them by his Majesty, or the Commander in chief of the Forces in Scotland, for the Time being, for that Effect: Providing always, That the said Robert Gordon, so often as any Goods, Cattle great or small, shall be discovered and seized by him, as stolen, or suspected to be stolen, upon lawful Proof of the Property made before him to his Satisfaction, or, otherwise, before any Two Justices of the Peace within the County w'here the said Goods may be seized, be obliged to restore the same to the Proprietor, w ithout Fee or Reward, other than the true Expence of maintaining the Cattle, from the Time of their being seized, to the Time they shall be claimed, according as the same shall be taxed by any Justice of Peace; or, in Default of Justices of the Peace, by any Commissioner of Supply within the County where the Goods or Cattle shall be at the Time of claiming, and Proof made of the Property; unless the said Robert Gordon shall, before seizing such Goods or Cattle, have paid the Value thereof to the Proprietor or Person from whom the sumen was stolen; in which Case, the said Robert Gordon shall have Power to dispose thereof at Pleasure: Providing also, That the said Robert Gordon shall be obliged, so often ns he shall seize any Arms, within the bounds aforesaid, in the Custody

Mr. Denton reported, from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the High Sheriff, Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, and Freeholders, of the County of Bucks, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, to whom the Petition was referred, have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find, by the Testimony of Mr. Nicholas Merwiir, and also of some Carriers, viz. John Fla/'wocd and Thomas FI ebster; that the Road leading from JVendovtr to the Town of Buckingham are. and, of late Years, have been, very ruinous, and much out of Repair; and that several Parts tiiereof are so very bad in the Winter-season, that many Coaches, Waggons, and other Carriages, have frequently stuck therein; whereby Passengers have received great Prejudice, and their Goods and Cattle much damaged:

That the said*Road lies in several Parishes; and many Places thereof are now so much out of Repair, that Waggons laden cannot pass through the same.

That it appeared to the Committee, the said Road cannot be effectually amended, and kept in Repair, unless some other Provision be made for that Purpose.

Ordered, That Leave be given to brirfgin.a Bill for repairing the Road from Wtndover to the Town of Buck* tngham, in the County of Bucks: And that Mr. Denton, and the Lord Hillsborough, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiff, and Burgesses, of the Town and County of Southampton, was presented to the House; and read; setting forth, That, they are brought into a very low Condition by the great Decay of Trade; occasioned chiefly by the wicked Practices of some covetous Persons, who have diverted great Part of the Wealth of the Nation out of its proper Chanel, and taken it to themselves: And praying, That those who have been accessary to the general Calamity be brought to exemplary Punishment; and that some speedy Method may be provided for the Reviving of Trade.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, capital Burgesses, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of Stamford, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they declare their utmost Detestation of the Crimes of the late Directors of the South Sea Company, their Agents and Accomplices, who have been the Ruin of both publick and private Credit, discouraged Industry, and rendered them in such a Condition as otherwise would not have been know n to the trading People: And praying, That such Measures may be found as may be judged most proper to discourage, and, in due time, bring all the Criminals to just Punishment.

Edward Elliott Esquire, one of the Commissioners of the Excise, introduced himself into the Office of Portreeve of the said Borough; and did thereby, with a design to subvert the ancient Method of Election, refuse to admit the Votes of several of the Petitioners, and other legal Voters, who tendered their Votes to the said St. John Brodrick; and admitted several others, who had no Right, to vote for the said Philip Cavendish', and did return him contrary to Justice, and the Duty of his Office: And praying Relief in the Premises.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their opinion thereupon, to the House;

n Mr. London reported, from the Committee, to whom the

Petition of Colonel Francis Farquhar, in the Name and Behalf of the Officers of the Three Regiments of Wood, Douglas and Hamilton, who served the States General during the late War, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the said Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; where it was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find,

That, by an Act, of the last Session of Parliament, for appointing Commissioners to examine, state, and determine, the Debts due to the Army, amongst other Things, it is thereby provided, That the said Commissioners shall not proceed to issue Certificates to the States General for more than One Moiety of what shall appear due to them for Services in the late War, until the Accounts of the said Three Regiments, who were in the Service of the said States, be settled and allowed, by the said States, under the Hands of the proper Officer of the said States, and of the Agents or Factors of the said Three Regiments; and that, upon producing such stated Accounts, the Commissioners were to issue their Certificates for the remaining Moiety to the Agent, or Factor, of each particular Regiment, for so much as shall thereby appear due to them; and for the Remainder to the said States General: And that, in 'case no such settled and stated Account should be produced' to the said Commissioners on or before the Tenth of Febniary One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty, or to the Paymaster of lu§ Majesty's 6

fail. A>

Land Forces on or before the Tenth of March One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty, theh the remaining Moiety should be subject to the Disposition of Parliament.

That, by a Certificate from the said Commissioners of Accounts, it appeared to the Committee, That the whole Demands of the States General amounted to One hundred sixty-one Thousand Seven hundred Thirty-nine Pounds Five Shillings and Six Pence Seven-eighths; and that the Commissioners had issued their Certificate to the said States for One Moiety thereof, being Eighty thousand Eight hundred Sixty^nine Pounds Twelve Shillings and Nine Pence Seven-sixteenths, pursuant to the said Act, the like Moiety remaining due to them; and that no settled or stated Accounts of the said Three Regi-merits had been produced to the Commissioners.

It further appeared to the Committee, That, by virtue of Letters of Attorney from the Officers of the Regiments of Douglas and Hamilton, granted to Captain Mackloed, and George Anderson, Clerk, that they had full Powers to solicit the States General, for settling and adjusting all Accounts of Arrears due to the said Re4 giments:

That, in pursuance thereof, the said George Anderson, in August last, presented to the States General a Petition, praying, That, irt consideration of the long Services of the said Regiments, the said States would, with all convenient Expedition, appoint Commissaries for examining and settling the said Arrears; and to fix a certain Time for that Purpose: That some Person, deputed by the Officers of the said Regiments, might be present to act jointly with the Agents of those Regiments, in stating and settling the Accounts with the said Commissaries: And,

George Anderson said, That the said Petition was referred by the States General to the Council of State; and by them referred to the Heer Hop, Treasurer General, and the Heer Van Slingelant, Secretary to the said Council of State, for them to examine and report the same:

That the said Anderson, and the Agents or Solicitors for the said Regiments, often attended the Heer Hep, to put him in mind of the said Reference:* But he still delayed the Matter; saying, He would first speak with the Earl of Sunderland, upon his Return from Hanover: And, soon after his Lordship s Departure from the Hague, the said Agents, and Anderson, were ordered to attend the Council of State: And the Agents were separately called in, by the Council, and spoke with, touching their Accounts: but the said Anderson was not admitted:

That Captain Mackloed, and the said Anderson, by Order of the Heer Hop, attended one of his Clerks; and, finding it impossible to settle the Accounts verbally only, desired to have in Writing such Objections, as were, or might be, made against the sai(J Regiments Accounts; but could not obtain the same.

And it appeared to the Committee, That Mr. Dayrolle, his Majesty’s Resident at the Hague, had, in pursuance of his Majesty’s Orders to assist the Officers employed by the Three Regiments of Wood, Douglass, and Hamilton, in procuring a State of their Demands, presented Three several Memorials, all of them pressing the States General to cause to be delivered to the said Officers the Accounts, as made up by the Council of State, or their own Accounts approved, or the Objections the Council of State may have made against them, or a positive Answer, upon the Occasion of the Refusal, or Delay; and complaining in his last Memorial, of the 44th of March One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty, that, notwithstanding his Ins^nces, and the frequent Application of the Officers and Agents of the said Three Regiments, vet they had not been able to procure the same, nor any.* Answer thereunto.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, and the free Burgesses, and Inhabitants, of the Borough of Richmondin the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they being sensibly affected with the Calamities themselves and Fellow Subjects labour under, by the Decay of Trade, the Ruin of publick Credit, and the Weight of the National Debts; occasioned by the late South Sea Directors, their Aiders and Abettors, as the sole Authors of these Misfortunes: And praying, That publick Faith may be revived, Trade increased, and those Parricides brought to Punishments adequate to their Crimes.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Charles Earl of Arran, Second Son of Thomas Earl of Ossory, who was eldest Son of James First Duke of Ormond, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by Indenture made on the Marriage of James then Earl of Ossory, the Petitioners elder Brother, the said James First Duke of Ormond, and Eli-zafath his Duchess, did convey all their Lands and Hereditaments in the Kingdom of Ireland; whereby his said elder Brother became possessed thereof for a Term of Ninety-nine Years, determinable on his Death; with Remainder to his First and other Sons in Tail Male; with like Remainder to the Petitioner, and his Issue Male; with Remainder to several other Male descendants of their Family; which Estate is, by several Acts of Parliament, and otherwise, charged with many Incumbrances, as well of his Grandfather as Brother; besides which, there are many other Debts upon simple Contract, which are not charged upon the said Estate; and will be intirely

A* 17214

lost, unless otherwise provided for; the greatest Part of which Incumbrances remains yet unpaid; and;, in order to the satisfying the same, and of all other Debts due from his Brother, for which no Provision is made, is desirous to become the Purchaser of the forfeited Interest of the said Estate, that he may be enabled to raise Money, by Sale of Mortgage, for the satisfying the said lncum-brances, so as some Part of his Inheritance may be preserved to himself; and he did, the last Session of Parliament, apply for Leave to bring in a Bill to enable him to be a Purchaser of the said Estate; but, no certain Price being fixed thereon, and all Persons at Liberty to bid upon him, it w as not probable, that any Advantage could accrue to him: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to vest all the forfeited Estate of his said Brother in him, and his Trustees; to enable them to raise such Sums as shall be thought reasonable to require him to pay for the Purchase thereof, to the Use of the Publick; and that the Remainder may be preserved to him, subject to all the unsatisfied Debts and Incumbrances of his Grandfather and Brother.

Whereupon Mr. Comptroller acquainted the House,

That, the Contents of the said Petition having been laid before his Majesty, his Majesty had been graciously pleased to command him to acquaint this House, That his Majesty has no Objection to the bringing in such a Bill.

And the standing Orders of the House, of the Sixth of February, Sexto Anna Regina, relating to Bills brought from Ireland, being read;

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that General Lumley, Mr. Freeman, Mr. Hutcheson, Mr. Ward, and Mr. Iiungcrford, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

An ingrossed Bill for continuing the Duties granted by an Act, made in the Sixth Year of her late Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for repairing the Harbour and Quay of Watchet, in the County of Somerset, was read the Third time.

The Committee of Secrecy appointed to enquire into all the Proceeding relating to the Execution of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, Ati4 Act for enabling the South Sea Company to increase their present Capital Stock, and Fund, by redeeming such publick Debts and Incumbrances as are therein mentioned; and for raising Money, to be applied for lessening several of the publick Debts and Incumbrances; and for calling in the present Exchequer Bills remaining uncancelled; and for making forth new Bills, in lieu thereof, to be circulated and exchanged, upon Efemand, at or near the Exchequer; since their former Report, haying had Intimation given them, That several large Sums of Money had been lent to divers Persons mentioned in the Book of Loans, formerly laid before this House by the late Directors of the South Sea Company; for Security whereof no Stock hath been actually transferred; they did, by their Order bearing Date the Twenty-fourth Day of April/\&$A past* direct the present Sub Governor, Deputy Governor, and Directors of the South Sea Company, to lay before them Account of the Names of all Persons who are mentioned in the said Book of Loans to have borrowed Money on- Stock, and the Supis by them respectively borrowed,: for Security whereof no actual Transfer of Stock had: been tmadepursuant to which Order, upon the Nineteenth Day of May instant, the said Court of Directors did lay before your Committee a Book, by them intituled, An Account of the Names of such Persons to whom Loans have been made on South Sea Stock; who, at the time when such Loans were made, do not appear, by any Booka, to have trans* ferred Stock to the South Sea Company, for the Security thereof: And the Court of Directors have added to the said Title the Words following; " But as all or most of " the Money lent was by granting Permits to any Name " without Distinction, or any Regard had by whom the " Stock was transferred; it is doubted, that this Account " may be very defective; and it is probable, that many ‘ of the Names herein may be fictitious; and that many ‘ others may be able to shew bow, and by whom, the ‘ Stock for the . Money lent them, respectively, was f< really transferred, if they should be called upon so " to do:"

And your Committee observe, That the last mentioned Book contains the Names of several Persons mentioned in the aforesaid Book of Loans to have borrowed Money upon Stock, to the Amount of Two million One hundred eighty-one thousand Nine hundred Forty-four Pounds Eleven Shillings, upon the Security of Five hundred so venty-eight thousand Eight hundred Eighty-eight Pounds q Stock;

556 iof Mail.' A. 1721.

Sooth Sea Stock; which doth not appear to have been transferred Company. . q{ Company

And, in relation to this Matter, your Committee proceeded to examine, in the most solemn manner, the several Persons following: And do now lay before the House the Examinations by them taken, in the Words of the Examinations themselves:

Mr. Charles Lockyer, Accountant to the South Sea Company, saith, That he has carefully examined the Books of Loans, and the Books of Transfers, of the said Company, by order of the Committee of Secrecy; and, upon Inspection of the said Books, does find, that the Sum of Tw o million One hundred eighty-one thousand Nine hundred Forty-four Pounds Eleven Shillings has been lent by the said Company, at several times, to the particular Persons mentioned in an Account drawn Out by this Examinant upon the Sum of Five hundred seventy-eight* thousand Eight hundred Eighty-eight Pounds Stock, supposed to be transferred to the Use of the said Company, as a Security for such Money: But this Examinant, upon the strictest Examination of the Books and Accounts belonging to the South Sea Company, cannot find or discover, that any of the said Persons, or any other for them, at the respective Times of the Loans made to them, did make, or cause to be made, any Transfer of such Stock, upon which the said Loans are entered to be made, or of any Stock w hatso-ever, unto, or for the Use of, the Company, for securing the Repayment of the Money then borrowed, amounting, in the Whole, to the aforesaid Sum of Two millions One hundred eighty-one thousand Nine hundred Forty-four Pounds Eleven Shillings: And this Examinant does not know, that any Stock was transferred by or for the said Persons, for the Security of the said Money, or of any Part thereof.

Sir John Blunt, being examined, says, He takes it, there was a good deal of Money lent to Persons who had bought Stock; and, in such Cases, the real Borrowers were not the Transferrers; but the Persons of w'hom they had bought transferred the Stock to Mr. Knight, Surman or Powell, for securing the Money lent by the Company: Says, He really believes, That Mr, Knight generally made good the Stock which he has charged the Company to have lent Money upon; though he has heard, that some Persons are charged with borrowing Money, who never did borrow any: Says, That he believes, there is a considerable Quantity of Stock, on which Money is said to be lent, where no Stock is transferred: And the Examinant apprehends, that great Part of that Deficiency will be found among the Five hundred seventy-four thousand Five hundred Pounds fictitious Stock, said to be sold; which> he believes, has been transferred to the Loan Account.

Mr. Robert Surman, being examined, as to the Account of Loans, where no Transfers appear to be made, says, That he believes, that, Mr. Knight having Accounts of Stock with several Persons, he carried their Stock to the Account of Loans: Says, That, when the Loans were at first begun to be made, there were several Waste-books kept, wherein the Stuns lent out were first entered; and all the Papers and Memorandums, relating to the Loans, were given to Mr. Clayton, a Clerk in the South Sea House; who, from thence, made out the Account of Loans; Says, lie believes the Waste-books are at the South Sea House; but he does not remember whether he has seen those Books since the Inquiry began, or not: Says, That the Ledgers of the Loans, he believes, were made up about a Month before Mr. Knight went away: Says, He believes, that several of the Persons who had the fictitious Stock had Money lent upon it, on the Company’s Account; and, in such Cases, no Transfers could be made; and he believes, that Part of the Five hundred seventy-eight thousand Eight hundred Eighty-eight Pounds Stock, on which Money has been lent without Transfersappearing in the Account now produced to him, is Part of the Five hundred seventy-four thousand Five hundred Pounds fictitious Stock.

The said Christopher Clayton, being hereupon examined

by your Committee, says, He, and the Clerks under him, did, by Direction of the Committee of Loans, and of Air. Knight, make up the Account of Loans from Books, which, he now believes, are at the South Sea House, in the Custody of Mr. DeGols: That the Instructions given him were, to make the Account from the Copies of the Journals: That Mr. Knight perused this Account, when made up; and examined and corrected it by the Journals, and other Books of his own: That Mr. Knight had the Custody of the original Journals; and before the Copies, from which this Examinant took the Account, were made, the Examinant believes Mr.

Knight made some Additions to the original Journals, from his own Books: Says, That he never had any Instructions, or Order, from Mr. Knight, or any other Person, to make this Account in such a manner as not to exceed the Regulations of Four hundred Pounds per Cent.

Your Committee are proceeding in the farther Examination of the Matters referred to them; and will, in a short time, lay the same before the House.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the State of the publick Credit of this Kingdom.

Mr. Clayton acquainted the House, That the Com- south Sea mittee of Secrecy are preparing a Draught of a Report, Company, relating to several Members of both Houses, mentioned in the Account of Stock sold, laid before this House, and relating to all other Members of this House, mentioned in any Examinations taken by the said Committee; which the Committee have determined to report to the House:

And therefore desire the House to appoint a Day for receiving such Report.

Ordered, That the said Report be received upon this Day Fortnight.

I am, Sir,

A PETITION of the High Sheriff, Justices of the Peace, and Grand Jury, of the County of Derby, assembled at the Quarter Sessions of the Peace held at Derby, in and for the said County, the Eighteenth Day of April One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty-one; and of several other Gentlemen, Clergymen, and Freeholders, of the said County, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they beg Leave to express their Concern for the unspeakable Miseries this once flourishing Nation is reduced to, by the corrupt Management of the late South Sea Directors, their Agents and Abettors; who, notwithstanding the immense Sums they have cheated the Nation of, have yet the Confidence to conceal their Estates and Effects: And praying, That Trade may be revived, publick Credit restored, the grand Corruption detected, and no Obstacle to hinder the Plunderers of the Publick from being brought to speedy Justice.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the junior Bailiff’ the Aldermen, Common Burgesses, Clergymen, Gentlemen, and Freeholders, of, or near unto, the Borough of East Retford, in the County of Nottingham, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, being deeply affected with Concern for the calamitous Condition to which they see this Nation exposed, by the pernicious and wicked Execution of the South Sea Scheme, which has decayed their impaired Credit, and drained away the Money: And praying. That this Nation may be restored to a flourishing Condition, and become the Resort of Credit; and that the Offenders may be brought to condign Punishment.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Justices of the Peace, Aldermen, and capital Burgesses, of the Borough Vol. iy.

of Evesham, in the County of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they are deeply sensible of the deplorable Estate of this Kingdom, occasioned by the wicked and deliberate Contrivance of the South Sea Directors, in Concurrence with those w ho trusted and employed them: And praying, That Endeavours may be used to detect, and punish, such unparalleled Crimes, and the Authors thereof.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Aldehneri, and South Sea principal Inhabitants, of the Borough of Newark upon Company* Trent, in the County of Nottingham, in the behalf of themselves, Fellow Subjects, and Sufferers, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That never was the Cry more universal, or the Occasion more important, to see a whole Kingdom deluded, impoverished, and affronted, by the wicked Contrivances and Machinations of the late infamous Directors of the South Sea: And praying, That this House will persevere in the Course' they have begun, in detecting, and punishing all Offenders, of what Title or Quality soever.

Ordered, That the said Petition-do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Ditto, principal Inhabitants, of the ancient Borough of Neiebiiry, in the County of Berks, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they having a just Abhorrence of the late villainous Contrivance of the Betrayers of their Country, the deplorable State, and uncommon Miseries they labour under, by the fatal Decay of Trade, Manufacture, and publick Credit: And praying, That this House will proceed to punish the Betrayers of their Country.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Annuitants and Proprietors of the redeemable Debts, in behalf of themselves, whose Names arc underwritten, and many thousands concerned therein, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they have lent a great Part of their Estates, on the Credit of several Acts of Parliament, for the publick Service; and that they thought, they had sufficient Security; but find themselves betrayed, and given up, by the Managers appointed by their Trustees, contrary to the true Intent and Meaning of the Law, and contrary to the Faith of publick Credit: And begging the Justice of the House for Relief against the Fraud of the late South Sea Directors, as well as of the great and notorious Breach of Trust in the Managers; and that, in order to restore the publick Credit, the Petitioners may have a just and reasonable Satisfaction; and that their Case may be duly considered, and distinguished from that of the Money Subscribers, who have been excused Nine Parts in Ten in the Third Subscription, and Four Parts in Five in the Fourth: And humbly hoping, That such Relief may be granted them as may be equal and proportionable to their different Claims and Titles.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

An Account of the annual gross and net Produce, for Five Years ending at Christmas last, of the Duties and Impositions granted, since the Twenty-fifth of December One thousand Six hundred Eighty-eight, on Goods and Merchandizes imported from the East Indies, which were not payable before that Time, and are now payable:

The said Report and Accounts are as follows;

vis.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled.

IN Obedience to an Order of this honourable House, of the 5th Instant, That we should lay before you an Account of the annual gross and net Produce, for Five Years ending at Christmas last, of the Duties and Impositions granted, since the 25th December 1688, on Goods and Merchandizes imported from the East Indies, which were not payable before that Time, and are now payable;

We gave immediate Directions to the Patent Officers of this Port to prepare the said Account, without Loss of Time: And they having delivered to us the annexed Paper, containing an Account of the annual gross Produce, for Five Years, to Christmas last, of the Duties

.and

C.

140 Mail.

A. i*] s

and Impositions granted, since the 25th December 1688, on Goods and Merchandizes imported from the East Indies; which were not payable before that time, and are now payable; we herewith humbly lay the same before this honourable House, by the Hands of the proper Officers: And, as to the Accounts of the net Produce of the said Duties, we humbly acquaint this honourable House, That the said Officers have informed us, That " the rendering the said Account will be a Work which w ill necessarily take up much Time; for as East India Goods, " not directed by any Law to be kept separate from " other Goods, are daily entered outwards, intermixed ‘‘ with other Goods, in the same Certificates and Co* quets; so that every individual Certificate Entry for 4< the said Years must be examined; and what East India Goods are found therein, must be placed in ‘c Columns, under proper Heads, in order to compute the Drawbacks on the said Goods: And that they, the *6 Patent Officers, having consulted the Searchers in this Port, in whose Office, as well as from the d Searchers in the Out Ports, the Quantities and Species of all East India Goods exported can with Certainty c‘ be known, they find it will take up at least Three d Months to draw out the said Accounts:"

Whereupon we have repeated our Directions, That no Time be lost in preparing the Accounts of the Drawbacks, in order to come at the annual net Produce of the said Duties; which* when perfected, will be laid before this honourable House: In the mean time, we humbly report, That the Charge of Management, occasioned by the said Duties and Impositions granted since the 25th December 1688, and now payable, amounts to Seven hundred Seventy-four Pounds per Annum; which, with the Drawbacks of the Duties exported within the said Five Years, will give the net Produce required by the above-mentioned Order:

And, in Obedience to another Order of this honourable House, of the same Date, we herewith humbly lay before you, by the Hands of the Comptroller General, who is the proper Officer, an Account of the Totals of the gross and net Produce of the Revenue of Customs for Five Years annually, to Christmas last.

All which is humbly submitted.

Robert BayliSi

Custom-house, Walter Yonge.

London, J. Pulteney.

Mr. Clayton, from the Committee of Secrecy, reported s. Sea Com-to the House, That it appeared to the said Committee, pany — Sup-That Mr. Christopher Clayton, a Clerk in the Treasury Office of the South Sea Company, had endeavoured, by Threats and Menaces, to suppress the Evidence which Samuel Watts, another Clerk in the said Office, was able to give to the said Committee; which Report he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee of Secrecy appointed to enquire into all the Proceedings relating to the Execution of an Act, passed the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for enabling the South Sea Company to increase their present Capital Stock, and Fund, by redeeming such publick Debts and Incumbrances as are therein mentioned; and for raising Money, to be applied for lessening several of the publick Debts and incumbrances; and for calling in the present Exchequer Bills remaining uncancelled; and for making forth new Bills, in lieu thereof to be circulated and exchanged, upon Demand, at or near the Exchequer; having, on the Twenty-fifth of May instant, examined, in the most solemn maimer, Samuel Watts, a Clerk, in the Treasury Office of the South Sea Company; he says, That, some time in January last, about a Fortnight after the First Meeting of the Secret Committee at the South Sea House, Mr. Lockyer came up into the Treasury-room, from the Secret Committee, and said,

They wanted Mr. Christopher Clayton, then a Clerk to the South Sea Company: Who, not being the re, he asked for the Examinant; who said, " Here am 1And then Mr.

Lockyer enquired of the Examinant, Who the Clerks were that made out the Books of Loans: And the Examinant acquainted him, That himself, James Ottey, George Wol~ ley, and Stephen Crisp, were Clerks employed in making out those Books; and then Mr. Lockyer went down Stairs, and desired the Examinant not to be out of the Way:

That, soon after, the said Mr. Clayton came in; and the Examinant told him, The Committee wanted him below Stairs: Clayton then asked him, If the Examinant knew for what the Committee wanted him: The Examinant replied, He did not know; but that Mr. Lockyer had desired him to attend: Upon which Clayton said, He had heard the Examinant had given Mr. Lockyer the Names of the Clerks who assisted him in making out the Books of Loans: Upon this, Clayton said, with a Curse, " What " had you to do to tell their Names ? If you had a mind " to bring yourself into a Premunire, why should you " bring them P Am not I sufficient to give an Account " for them?" And, walking about the Room in a Passion, said, That the Examinant had nothing to do to discover any thing; especially to Mr. Lockyer, who was

Rogue, and a Villain, and had discovered all; and that he would therefore be despised, and pissed upon, by every body: And thdn said, That, if this Examinant was summoned before the Committee of Secrecy, he was to answer, That he knew nothing, but that the Examinant was subordinate to him; and that what the Examin-7 D ant

That Clayton then asked the Examinant, What he did know* To which the Examinant replied, He knew enough; and that, when he was examined before his Betters, he would tell the Truth: Clayton asked again, What the Examinant did know; to which the Examinant answered. He should know in time.

Your Committee are proceeding in the further Examination of the Matters referred to them; and will speedily lay tl)e same before the House.

Resolved, Neniine contradicente, That Mr. Christopher Clayton, a Clerk in the Treasury Office of the South Sea Company, by endeavouring to prevail with Mr. Samuel Watts, another Clerk in the said Office, by Threats and Menaces, to suppress the Evidence which he was able to give to the Committee of Secrecy, is guilty of a High Crime and Misdemeanor.

Ordered, That the said Mr. Christopher Clayton be, for his said Offence, committed Prisoner to his Majesty’s Prison of the Gatehouse: And that Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant accordingly.

A Complaint being made to the House, of a Paper Libellou* printed by N. Mist, in Great Carter-lane, London, in- Publication tituled, The Weekly Journal, or Saturday's Post; with freshest Advices, foreign and domestick; Saturday, May 27,1721;

The same was brought up to the Table: And several Paragraphs in the said printed Paper were read.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the Paper, intituled, The Weekly Journal, or Saturday's Post, with freshest Advices, foreign and domestick; Saturday, May 27, 1721; is a false, malicious, scandalous, infamous, and traiterous Libel; tending to alienate the Affections of his Majesty's Subjects, and to excite the People to Sedition and Rebellion; with an Intention to subvert the present happy Establishment, and to introduce Popery, and arbitrary Power.

Ordered, That N. Mist, the Printer and Publisher of the said Paper, be, for his said Offence, committed Prisoner to his Majesty’s Gaol of Newgate; And that Mr.

Speaker do issue his Warrants accordingly.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, expressing our utmost Abhorrence of the scandalous, infamous, and traiterous,

Libel, intituled, The Weekly Journal, or Saturday’s Post, with freshest Advices, foreign and domestick; May 27,

1721; and our Detestation of the Author of it; and to assure his Majesty, That this House will stand by and support his Majesty, and his Royal Family, against all traiterous and seditious Attempts that shall be made against his sacred Person, and Government; and humbly to beseech his Majesty, That he will give the most effectual Orders for prosecuting and punishing the Printer and Publishers, and also the Authors and Contrivers, when discovered, of the said traiterous Libel, and of all other seditious Libels, that tend to raise Discontent and Disaffection in the Minds of his Majesty's Subjects; and to assure his Majesty, That this House will proceed, with the greatest Care and Diligence, to find out, and discover, the Authors of such wicked, seditious, and traiterous,

Libels.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to enquire into the Authors, Contrivers, Printers, and Publishers, of the said seditious and traiterous Libel, and of all other seditious and traiterous Libels, which tend to raise Discontent and Disaffection in the Minds of his Majesty’s Subjects:

And it is referred to Mr. Chancellor of the Duchy,

A Petition of David Crawford Esquire, Marshal of the Prison of the Court of King s Bench, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Mr. Mist, Printer of the Weekly Journal, is in his Custody, in Execution upon a Judgment given against him by the said Court; and that he hath been also charged in his Custody with an Action of Debt for Five hundred Pounds: And that he, having Notice of the Order of this House for committing the said Mr. Mist to his Majesty’s Gaol of Nov gate, is ready to pay all the due Obedience to this House; but that Mr. Mist being a Prisoner in Execution, and for Debt, the Petitioner humbly prays, That he may be indemnified in such manner as to this House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said N. Mist, the Printer of the said seditious and traiterous Libel, do stand committed dose Prisoner to the said Prison of the Court of King’s Bench during the Pleasure of this House.

Ordered, That it be referred to the Committee appointed to inquire into the Authors, Contrivers, Printers, and Publishers, of all seditious and traiterous Libels, which tend to raise Discontent, and Disaffection in the Minds of his Majesty’s Subjects, to examine Precedents in what manner Persons who are Prisoners in Execution have been examined before this House, or any Committee thereof; and to report the same to the House with all convenient Speed.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Clergy, Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants of the Borough of Penryn, in the County of Cornwall, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they find the Kingdom brought to the very Brink of Ruin by the vile Practices of a Set of Men, tempted by their boundless Avarice, to betray their King and Country; the general Scarcity of Money, Decay of Trade and Manufactures, Clamours of Poor, and other Miseries, which they see daily increasing; occasioned by the fatal Mismanagements of the late Directors of the South Sea Company: And praying, That proper Measures may be found, conducive to the restoring the publick Credit, retrieving and encouraging Trade, redressing their Grievances, lessening the Nations Debts, and doing Justice to an injured Country.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Warrant from Mr. Speaker was ordered by the House, and issued, directed to Roger Wood Esquire, One of his Majesty’s Serjeants at Arms, and Serjeant of the Commons House of Parliament, requiring him to take the Bodies of Giles Simpson, the Plaintiff, and William Watkins, the Serjeant, then remaining Prisoners in the Fleet, into his Custody, and bring them into the saici House upon the Thirteenth Instant, at Eight a Clock in the Morning, to answer to such Matters as should bo objected against them: And then,

13 April, Sir Edward Hobby made Report of his Message to the Lord Chancellor; with my Lord Chancellor’s Answer, Why he sent Simpson to Prison:

Because, he said, the Arrest being upon the Day of his Majesty's Entrance, he thought none but hollow Hearts would so far contemn such a Day, as to disturb his Majesty's Servants in their Attendance, and the Solemnity of that Day: and therefore, in Discretion, as his Majesty’s Officer, did it.

Then Counsel were heard for Sir Thomas Shirley, and for the Warden of the Fleet: And,

It was ordered, upon this Arguraeut, That Simpson, at whose Suit, and Watkins, the Serjeant that made the Arrest, should be committed to the Prison of the Tower.

Your Committee examinirffr the said Mr. Gibbon as to the Account ot Stock entered in the Cash-book to be sold, he says, He never saw any Account of it, but what is in the Book, until a Paper, drawn up by Mr. Knight, wa9 shewn him, after the Order of the House of Commons; and he looked on it but cursorily: Says, That, about the latter End of February last, Mr. Knight said to him, it would be for the Company’s Advantage to sell some Stock, it being then at a good Price, between *i 70 and 180 per Cent.; and, if the Bill did not pass, it would be well sold; and, if it did pass, the rest would sell at a better Price: That he does not know', that the Company had then any Stock to dispose of.

That Mr. Knight said, He was to take upon himself the transacting that Stock; and the Persons to whom it was to be delivered, were to be accountable for the Price: But he was to transact this on tfip behalf of the Company; and the Persons who were to have it, might either have it transferred to them, or take the Difference:

Does not know of any Stock disposed of to any Member of either House of Parliament, except what is mentioned to be done by him, in the Account delivered in to the House; and does not remember any one else desired Stock:

Believes that Mr. Knight told him, That Mr. Ilohiitch and Mr. Hawes disposed of Stock to Members of the House of Commons, who are not named in the Account delivered in to the House.

As to the £. 20,000. charged in the Account to Lord Gower, he says, That Lord Gorrer sent to him, about the latter End of February last, to help him to buy£.20,000. Stock; which, this Examinant said, he would try to do, and believed he could do it: That, the same Day, or the next Day, this Examinant spoke to Mr. Knight, and asked him to undertake to deliver this Stock at Three Months time, at 180 per Cent.: Which he complied with; and this Examihant took Mr. Knight's Note for so tfroch Stock accordingly: and it was understood that the Stock was to be delivered Three Months after, if not paid 'for before, with Interest in the mean time: That he gave’ Lord Gower his own Note for the Delivery of this Stock in Three Months; and took his Lordship’s Note to accept it, and pay the Money in Three Months time with Interest in the mean time: That there w as £. 4,000. ttouth Sea Stock transferred to this Examinant by a Steward of the Duke of Rutlands: And Lord Gower told this Examinant, That the said £. 4,000. should be transferred to him as a further Security; and that the Duke of Rutland was concerned in the Bargain: Says, The Stock was accordingly transferred to him a few Days afterwards: And Lord Gower tole) him, Some Part of the £. 20,000. As to the Two Sums of £. 5,000. Stock each, charged, in the Account, to Lord Lansdtrwn, this Examinant had a Note from his Lordship, for Acceptance and Payment: And his Lordship agreed to give Security; but, the Price of Stock rising, this Examinant did not insist upon it: Vol. 19.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Barons, and South Su Freeholders, of the County of Caithness, in North Bri- Cun^i;. tain, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That the principal Trade of this County is the Exporting of Fish to the Ba/tick; a Trade most beneficial to the Nation in general, though of small Advantage to the private Merchant; But, by the boundless Ambition and Avarice of the late South Sea Directors, their Aiders, Abettors, and Confederates, has rendered all their Hopes abortive; and has so intirely drained their Country of Money, that their Merchants are forced to give up their Trade, and their Poor are reduced to the miserable State of Starving and Idleness: And praying, That this House will give Relief to an oppressed and impoverished People, that Trade may flourish, publick Credit be restored, and Justice done to an injured People.

e to A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are under-rian written, wholesale Traders and Dealers in English Bone-lerlauds. ]ace> in or about the Town of Wendover, in the County of Bucks, on behalf of themselves, and great Numbers of others, Traders and Dealers in Bone-lace, in and about the said Town, was presented to the House and read; setting forth, That the Manufacture of English Bone-lace has, of late Years, been very much improved, both for Fineness of Work, and Service, so as to equal any Lace imported from Abroad: The said Manufacture received great Encouragement by an Act, made in the Reign of his late Majesty King William, for prohibiting of Bone-lace from Flanders, great Numbers of Families then learning, and improving themselves in, the said Manufacture; but, since the Repealing of the said Act, have met with great Discouragements; and their Trade has very much fallen away, by the daily Increase of great Quantities of foreign Lace imported; the great Duty paid upon Thread imported, for manufacturing the English Bone-lace, is a great Discouragement to the English Manufacturers, and enables the Foreigners to undersell them at Market: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee appointed to consider of the State of the Trade between this Kingdom and the Austrian Netherlands.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to hear the Berealsto*. Matter of the Petition of several of the free Burgesses of Election, the Borough of Berealston, in the County of Devon, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough:

And the Counsel for the said Petitioners, and for the Sitting Member, were called in:

And the Petition was read:; '

And several Witnesses were examined, touching the Right of Election:

And several Returns of Burgesses to serve in former Parliaments for the said Borough were produced, and read.

And then the Counsel and Witnesses withdrew.

Resolved\ Netnine coniradicente, That the Right of Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Berealston, in the County of Devon, is in the Freehold Tenants of the said Borough, holding by Burgage Tenure, and paying Three Pence per Annum, . or more, ancient Burgage-rent, to the Lord of the said Borough; and in them only.

The Counsel were called in again; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them with the said Resolution.

Then a Copy of the Poll was delivered:

And the Petitioners Counsel proceeding to offer Evidence, in order to qualify some Persons, who offered to vote for St. John Brodrich Esquire; but were refused by the Portreeve;

The Counsel were directed to withdraw.

And the Sitting Member acquainted the House* That the Right of Election being adjudged to be in the Freehold Tenants only, he was satisfied lie could not maintain a Majority of Votes; aild therefore would not give the House any further Trouble.

And he being withdrawn;

And the Question being put, That Philip Cavendish Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Berealston, in the County of Devon;

It passed in the Negative.

Resolved, That St.John Brodrick Esquire is dyly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Berealston.

The House being acquainted, That an Indenture of Return, signed by the Freehold Tenants of the said Borough, had been tendered to the Portreeve of the said Borough, at the Time of the Election; but that he refused to accept the same; and that one of the Persons who had signed and tendered the said Indenture to the Portreeve, was at the Door;

Mr. Elfoi'd was called in: Who acquainted the House,

That, after the Election for the said Borough was over, the Electors signed and sealed a Return, by the Freehold Tenants of the said Borough; which he tendered to the Portreeve, to be returned to the Sheriff of the County; but the said Portreeve refused to execute the same; which Indenture he delivered in to the Clerk of the House; and the same w as read at the Table.

And the Clerk of the Crown attending the House in his Place, according to Order, with the Return for the said Borough;

A PETITION of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, and other the Inhabitants, of the Borough of Abingdon, in the County of Bucks, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Bill brought into this House, for supplying London with Water, which is intended to divert, and take away, the Water from several Rivers at or near Drayton, which used greatly to assist the Navigation of the said River Thames: The Barges lie on Ground several Weeks together, for want of Water to carry them over the Shallows: The Design of bringing Water into the River, will be advantageous; but the taking any out thereof, will be highly detrimental to the Navigation of the River Thames: Their said Borough is a considerable trading Town, and chiefly depends on Water-carriage; which if taken away, the Town will be impoverished: And praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better supplying the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent, with Water, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Warden, Bridgemen, Burgesses, and Supplying Commonalty, of the Town of Hoi ley upon Thames, in London with the County of Oxford\ was presented to the House, and W*er« read; setting forth, That the greatest Support of the said Corporation is maintained by Carriage of Meal,

Corn, and other Goods, to London, by the Navigation of the River Thames: That there are several Shallows in the said River, by which the Barges are frequently stopped, until supplied with more Water coming from the River Coin: And that if the Bill, now depending before this House, should pass into an Act, they would be greatly prejudiced, by the diverting the Water from falling into the River Thames, as usual: And praying to be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better supplying the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent, with Water, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Owners Ditto, of Lands bordering on the River Thames, in the County of Berks, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Bill, now depending before this House, for bringinganew Stream of Water to London, from the several Rivers near Drayton, will greatly prejudice the Navigation of the River Thames; their Estates, and the Produce thereof, chiefly depend on the said Navigation: And praying to be heard, by Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better supplying the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent, with Water, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Owners and Occupiers of the Paper Ditto, and Leather Mills at Foyle, in Middlesex, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they pay above Seven hundred Pounds a Year Excise to the Government, in respect of their Mills; which must stand still, to the Ruin of themselves, and Families, in case the Heatham Stream be turned out of its aucient Course, as is proposed by the Bill, now depending in this House, for the better sup> plying London with Water: And praying to be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better supplying the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent, with Water, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Occupiers of Lands lying near the River of Thames, in the County of Bucks, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Bill, now depending in this House, for conveying anew Cut or Stream of Water, to London, from the several Streams near Drayton, will greatly impede the Navigation of the River Thames, to the great Detriment of all the trading Towns thereon, and lessening the Value of all the Gentlemen’s Estates bordering on the same: And praying to be heard, by their Counsel, against the passing the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better supplying the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent, with Water, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Farmers, in and about the Parish of Staines, in the County of Middlesex, whose Names are thereto subscribed, in the behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Bill, now depending before this House, for the better accommodating the Inhabitants in and about London, with Water, will not only be prejudicial, but the utter Ruin of them: And praying to be heard, by their Counsel, against the passing the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better supplying the Cities of London and Westminster, and Parts adjacent, with Water, be read a Second time.

Fairer, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole 1 louse, to whom it was referred to consider of the State of the publick Credit of this Kingdom, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the said Resolutions were read; and arc as follow; viz.

1st, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Re-establishing of publick Credit, and quieting the Minds of his Majesty’s Subjects, the several Properties and Interests now depending, and concerned, with the South Sea Company, be ascertained and settled.

2d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in Order to put an End to all Disputes between the South Sea Company, and the Proprietors of the redeemable Funds subscribed in to the said Company; and for the further Relief of the said Proprietors, and the Proprietors of the Second, Third, and Fourth, Money Subscriptions, who have new Stock allowed them at the Rate of Four hundred perCent. with the last Midsummer Dividend of Ten per Cent. in Stock; an Addi-

Vo L. 19.

tion, after the Rate of Thirty-three Pounds Six Shillings and Eight Pence Stock upon every Hundred Pounds Stock already allowed, be given by the South Sea Company, to the Proprietors of the said redeemable Funds, and to the Proprietors of the Second, Third, and Fourth, Money Subscriptions.

3d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Four millions One hundred fifty-six thousand Three hundred Forty-one Pounds, with the Four Years and Half, and One Year’s Purchase, payable to the Publick by the South Sea Company, be remitted; so as, from the Twenty-fourth of June One thousand1 Seven hundred Twenty-two, Two millions of the Capital Stock of the said Company be reduced and annihilated; and a proportionable Part of their Annuity, or yearly Fund, in respect of the said Two" millions, from that time, cease.

4th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Second Subscription of the Irredeemables, as well the long Annuities as the Annuities of Nine per Cent. Prize Lottery Tickets, and . Blank Lottery Tickets, be made equal to the First Subscription of the like Annuities, and Tickets, by an Addition of Stock at One hundred and Fifty per Cent.

5th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all the Capital South Sea Stock belonging to the Company in their own Right, which, after the proposed Distributions made, shall remain undisposed of, be divided among all the Proprietors of the said Company, in proportion to their several and respective Interests therein; and that Credit be given them for the same in the Books of the said Company.

6th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Demands for Money borrowed of the South Sea Company, for which there is actually pledged Stock after the Rate of Four hundred Pounds, or under, for each One hundred Pounds Stock, with the last Midsummer Dividend, or on Subscription Receipts, after the Rate of Three hundred Pounds, or under, for each Subscription Receipt for One hundred Pounds, be discharged; and the Property of the said Stock, and Subscription Receipts, be absolutely vested in the said Company; and that the said Company do accept the Stock of the said Company, after the Rate of Three hundred Pounds per Cent, in Repayment of any Sum or Sums of Money borrowed of the said Company on Stock or Subscription Receipts, at any Price exceeding the Rates aforesaid, the same being tendered within a Time to be limited.

The First and Second of the said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House*

The Third Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out these Words, " so as, from the Twentyfourth of June One thousand Seven hundred Twentytwo, Two millions of the Capital Stock of the said " Company be reduced and annihilated; and a proportionable Part of their Annuity, or yearly Fund, in " respect of the said Two millions, from that time.

cease:

And the Question being put, That those Words stand Part of the said Resolution;

The House divided.

The Noes go forth.

Dagenham Sir Nathaniel Gold reported from the Committee, to

Brtacb. whom the Petition of Captain John Peny was referred,

the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had di-

Irected him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee were satisfied, that, after many unsuccessful Attempts had been made for Stopping of Dagenham Breach, on the River of Thames, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Fourteen, an Act of Parliament passed, to enable the Lord Mayor of London, and other Trustees, to contract with any Person for stopping the said Breach; in pursuance whereof, by the Journal of the Proceedings of the Trustees, it appears the Petitioner, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Fifteen, proposed to undertake the said Work, at the publick Hazard; but the Trustees declined hazarding the publick Money, and iusisted, that the Petitioner should find Security to refund all Money that should be advanced to him, in case he did not perform the Work; which Security, for the Performance of a Work so difficult and precarious, the Petitioner could not have obtained, but that several Russia Merchants, who had known his Works in Russia, were thereby induced to treat with him, and encouraged others; yet the Performance of the said Undertaking w as so very doubtful, that the Petitioner w as obliged to enter into Engagements to pay Premiums to the said Persons, to become Securities proportionable to the Hazard they run; and therefore he demanded Twenty-seven thousand Pounds, if to give Security; or Seventeen thousand Pounds, if the Trustees would stand the Hazard of the Work; which the Trustees would not agree to, but offered Twenty-five thousand Pounds on his giving Security: To which the Petitioner agreed, upon condition that the Trustees would recommend him to the Favour of the Parliament, if it should appear the Remainder of the Twenty-five thousand Pounds unexpended should not be a sufficient Gratuity for his Service in stopping the Breach: And thereupon he did, by Indenture, dated the Twenty-sixth of January One thousand Seven hundred and Fifteen, contract with the said Trustees, that for Twenty-five thousand Pounds he would stop the said Breach, being about Four hundred Foot wide, and repair the Walls, Banks, and other Works, in, and belonging to, the same; so that, for Three Years after stopping the same, there shall not be any Leakage through the Dam, to raise the Water on the Inside of the Creek above the Fourth Part of an Inch, upon a View, at any time to be appointed for that Purpose; and also to repair the Walls belonging to the Levels lpr Two hundred Yards on each Side of the Breach, in Vpp. 19,

such manner that, for the like time, the Thames shall not break into, and overflow, the Levels, by reason of any > Defect; and to make good any new Cuts; and fix sufficient Sluice, to the Satisfaction of the Trustees, for the Drain of the Land-waters; and repair all the Walls from Rainham Creek to Halfway-tree; and maintain the same for Fifteen Months, after the Breach is stopped; and also remove the Slielf, or Sand-bank, of about a Mile in Length, and almost Halfway cross the River, which had been cast up by reason of the said Breach; so that there should be full Six Foot Depth at Low-\yaterr mark, on a Neap-tide, in the Judgment, and to the Satisfaction, of Fifteen of the Trustees:

And the said Trustees thereby covenant to pay the Petitioner the said Twenty-five thousand Pounds at such Days and Times as are therein mentioned, upon his giving Security for the Performance of all and every the said Works, and maintaining the same, as aforesaid; or, in case of any Accident, to make good the Damage: And, lastly, the Trustees covenant to deliver up the Security-bonds, to be cancelled when the Conditions thereof are performed; as appeared by the original Agreement, and the Journal.of the Trustees, produced to the said Cqm-mittee:

That although the Petitioner hfith, in the Course of his Undertaking, met with many great Difficulties, ana unforeseen Accidents, which hath rendered his Works very tedious; as well as chargeable; yet he has overcome all Obstacles; as appeared to the Committee, by the several Surveys, and Reports entered in the Journal of the said Trustees; and hath now performed the several Parts of his Contract, to the Satisfaction of the Trustees, excepting what relates to the aforesaid Sand-bank, in the Petitioner’s Contract, said to be about a Mile in Length, and almost Half-way cross the River; which, upon a View of the said Trustees, on the Sixth of May One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty-one was reported to be not above Two hundred Yards long, and Fifty Yards cross the same River; and that upon the Sand-bank, at low Water, there was then from Seven Foot to Four Foot Water; and that he continues working upon the same; and in a little time they presumed he will make it so low, that the Water will be full Six Foot deep, at Low-water Mark, at a Neap-tide: And, for the completing and perfecting thereof, the said Trustees have reserved iq their Hands Five hundred Pounds, out of the Sum coi^ traded for with the Petitioner:

That, in order to procure Securities to repay the several Sums received of the Trustees, and to advance him Money to perform the said Work, the Petitioner was obliged to enter into several Articles of Agreement for the Payment of Premiums, at the Rate of Tvyenty, Thirty, and Fifty, per Cent.; which Premiums, in the Whole, amount to Eleven thousand Nine hundred Thirty-four Pounds Ten Shillings:

That by several Books of Accounts, and other Vouchers, produced before the Committee, it appeared, that the Petitioner had laid out, and expended, in Materials, Wages, and other Charges concerning the Breach, the Sum of Twenty-six thousand Five hundred Fifty-two Pounds: That he also stands indebted to several Persons for Materials, Wages, fyc. on Account of the said Work, One thousand Nine hundred Eighty-six Pounds Eight Shillings and Eight Pence Three Farthings:

So that his w hole Expence and Charge in stopping the said Breach, with the said Premiums, amount to Fifteen thousand Four hundred Seventy-two Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Eight Pence Three Farthings more than his Contract for Twenty-five thousand Pounds;

That several of the Persons with whom the Petitione contracted for the said Eleven thousand Nine hundred Thirty-four Pounds Ten Shillings Premiums attended the Committee in behalf of the Whole; and, in Consideration of the distressed Circumstances to which the Petitioner is reduced, did propose to the Committee, that they were willing to abate and remit One-half Part of the said Eleven thousand Nine hundred Thirty-four PoundsTen Shillings

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And it appeared to the Committee, upon the Examination of Samuel How, Erasmus Drape, William Rooke% and Daniel Roo/ce, That the said River Eden is capable of being made navigable for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, for many Miles, and from several Creeks within the Port of Carlisle, to Bank-end.

And it further appeared to the Committee, upon the Examination of the said several Persons, That the mak* ing the said River navigable will very much iirfprove large Tracts of Ground, lying upon, and adjacent to, the said River; which, for want of Coals, to burn Lime, are at present intirely waste and uncultivated; and, if the said River be made navigable, the Poor will be employed, and Seamen increased; and will be a general Good to that Part of the Country.

Mr. Brad rick, according to Order, made the furthet* Report from the Committee of Secrecy; and read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee of Secrecy appointed to inquire into all the Proceedings relating to the Execution of an Act, passed the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for enabling the South Sea Company to increase their present Capital Stock, and Fund, by redeeming such publick Debts and Incumbrances as are therein mentioned; and for raising Money for Payment of several of the publick Debts and Incumbrances; and for calling in the present Exchequer Bills remaining uncancelled; and for making Forth new Bills, in lieu thereof, to be circulated and exchanged, upon Demand, at or near the Exchequer; pursuant to the Instruction given them by the House on the Twenty-fifth of April last, That they should inquire what publick Money hath been employed by any Treasurer, Cashier, Collector, Receiver, or other Officer concerned in the Receipt or Payment of publick Money, or of any other Part of his Majesty’s Revenue, or by any in Trust for them, or by their Order, in buying Stock, or Subscriptions, in the South Sea, or any other Company, or Annuities, or other Parliamentary Securities; or otherwise making use of, or employing, the same to their private Advantage, since the First Day of December One thousand Seven hundred and Nineteen; have accordingly proceeded to inquire into that Matter; and have examined, in the most solemn Manner, the following Persons; and do lay before the House the Examinations by them taken, relating thereto, in the W ords of the Examinations themselves:

Your Committee directed Sir Harcourt Master, late Receiver General of the Land Tax for London and Middlesex, to lay before them, an Account of what publick Monies he had laid out in purchasing Stock, or Subscriptions; or otherwise applied to his own private Use: And thereupon he laid before your Committee a Paper, to the Effect following; viz.

That, about the beginning of November Jast, the said Five Ledgers, marked A, B, C, D, and E, were copied alphabetically into Four new Ledgers; which are now kept in the Office for publick Use; and, if any Dispute arise in searching into them, the Clerks have recourse to the said First Ledgers:

That Mr. Clayton did, a little before the Meeting of the Parliament, bring into the Treasury Office, a Book, which the Examinant believes was Mr. Knight's private Cash Book; the Examinant having often seen it; in which, at the Head of an Account, the Examinant saw the Name of Charles Stanhope: And this Examinant saith, That Clayton, with a white handle Penknife, erased the Letters, in the Name Stanhope, in order to make it Stan-gape; but whether Mr. Clayton altered the Letters with his own Hand, or the Examinant, by his Order, the Examinant does not now remember; but says, It was accordingly altered to Stangape: That this Book had a Green Cover, was about a Foot in Length, and about Two-thirds as broad, and an Inch and a Half thick.

The said Mr. Clayton, being hereupon examined by your Committee, says, He believes there w'ere Alterations made in the original Journals of the Loans: That all the Alterations which the Examinant, or any other Clerk, by his Order, made in those Journals, were made by the Direction of Mr. Knight: That Mr. Surman once, by Mr. Knight's Order, directed the Examinant to alter Four Names:

That the Examinant directed the altering large Sums into lesser Sums; and that he was informed by Mr. Knight, That such Alterations were made at the Request of the Persons to whom such large Sums were charged;

That he knows not, that the Name of any Member of Parliament was altered to any other Name; but Mr. Knight told the Examinant, That a large Sum being set down to the Lord Castlemain, his Lordship said, That Part of such Sum was on the Account of other Persons, a List of whose Names his Lordship gave to Mr. Knight; and the Sum, at first set down to Lord Castlemain, was accordingly split into lesser Sums, and set down to those Persons;

That, he saw the original Journals in Mr. Knight's Custody about Three Days before he w ent aw ay; but has not seen them since:

That he has seen Mr. Knight's Green Book; but he never made any Rasure or Alteration in it, either in any Name, or any Letter, or Part of a Name, in that Book; nor ever directed any to be made:

That he does not remember, that he ever saw the Name Stanhope, in Mr. Knight's Green Book; and denies that he ever rased any Letter, or any Part of a Letter, or made any Alteration in the Name Stanhope, in the said Green Book: That he cannot be positive whether the Name Stanhope was ever rased, or altered, in any other Book whatsoever; but he does not know', or remember, that he did direct any such Rasure or Alteration, or ever heard, that there w'as any such Rasure or Alteration, made in the said Name Stanhope:

That he remembers, he did once alter a Figure in an Account in the said Green Book, when Mr. Knight and a Gentleman w'ere settling an Account in that Book; but who the Gentleman was, the Examinant cannot tell:

That he does not know but the Name of Sir JVm. Thompson might be altered to Mr. William Thompson; and thinks it was altered: That he has heard Mr. Knight say, That Sir JVm. Thompson complained, that there was a Mistake in his Account of the Loan; and the Examinant remembers he saw Sir JVm, Thompson with Mr. Knight in his Closet:

That the First Ledgers of the Loans were begun to be made from the Journals in several Books; and in October 1720, those Ledgers not being ruled in a proper manner, there were new Ledgers provided; and the Examinant believes Sir JVm. Thompsons Name was altered in both the said original and new Ledgers:

That the original Journals were made up, partly by the Receipts taken at the Transfer-books, and partly by Direction of Mr. Knight, and Adjustments made with him:

Mr. Robert Surman being examined, says, That since the Inquiry began, the Examinant has seen the original Journals of the Loans at the South Sea House: That Mr. Clayton was the Clerk appointed to take Care of the Loans; and these Journals were therefore properly under his Care:

That he believes there were several Alterations made in these original Journals; but he believes all such Alterations were made by Mr. Knight's Directions, given to Mr. Clayton, as the first Clerk; who directed the other Clerks to make the Alterations, or else made them himself:

That these Journals were wrote by several Clerks: That all the Loans, as well as Adjustments, were, as the Examinant believes, entered in these Journals.

That the Examinant has not seen these Journals since Mr. Knight went away:

That the original Journals w ere not made alphabetically, but from Day to Day* as the Money was lent out: That the Examinant remembers, in Two or Three Cases, he had Orders from Mr. Knight to direct Mr. Clayton to make Alterations in the Journals; which the Examinant takes to be where there was a large Sum charged to particular Persons, exceeding the Regulations of the Loans:

That Mr. Knight had the Custody of the Subscription Receipts, on which Money was lent for the Months of June, July, and August, 1720; and until the Committee of Loans was appointed; and the Examinant believes the Numbers of those Receipts were entered in the Journals of the Loans:

That, some of the First and Second Subscribers not making their First Payment, Mr. Knight laid down the Money for them, and took their Receipts for his Security; which, as this Examinant has heard Mr. Knight say, brought his Cash under Difficulties; but nevertheless, such Subscribers had a Right to borrow', and often did borrow, of the Company, the £. 300. per Cent. on such Subscriptions:

That the Examinant has had Mr. Knight's Orders to direct Mr. Clayton to enter fictitious Names in the Journals of the Loans:

That the Loans on Stock, and those on Subscriptions, were kept irj distinct Journals: That there were Three Journals of the Loans on Stock; the First commencing at the Beginning of the Loan, and continued to May 1720; the Second carried on to Midsummer; and the Third to the End of the Loan: That there was but One original Journal for the whole Loan upon Subscriptions:

That the said original Journals were copied alphabetically some time after the Conclusion of each Journal;

That he remembers he has seen Mr. Knight and Mr. Clayton together, making Alterations in the said original Journals of the Loans; and he has heard Mr. Knight direct Clayton to make Alterations therein, and enter fictitious Names.
