X.

But if it should happen, that the Forces specified should not be sufficient, with respect to the Greatness of the Danger; that is, if the Aggressor should happen to be assisted by Succours from some Confederate or other of his, or should become superior, and too powerful, by his own Strength and Successes; then the other Confederate shall be obliged to help, as soon as possible, the Party injured and oppressed, with greater Forces, both by Sea and Land, and such as may be necessary; as also with Subsidies in Money; in such manner, however, that, when the Case shall exist, Deliberation shall be had, according to the Exigency of Affairs, concerning the Manner, Nature, and.Time, of giving such Assistance: And whereas it has happened, that the Kingdom of Sweden has, for a long time, been annoyed by divers neighbouring Powers, even while the Treaty concluded in the Year 1700 was in force; and as that War still continues; therefore his Sacred Royal Majesty of Great Britain acknowledges himself to be engaged, as well on account of the Treaty just now mentioned, as by virtue of this present Treaty, to furnish those further Succours which are hereunder stipulated.

XI.

And although all amicable Means are hitherto made use of for composing this present War in the North, according to the Desire of her Sacred Royal Majesty of Sweden; vet the Success does not answer those Desires; his Sacred lloyal Majesty of Great Britain doth therefore hereby declare, and oblige himself, in case these Attempts towards a friendly Reconciliation should prove ineffectual, that he w ill not let any more Time be lost to no Purpose; hut that lie will send, early next Spring, to the Assistance of the Kingdom of Sweden, a strong Squadron of Ships of War, that shall act under the Direction and Disposition of her Sacred Royal Majesty of Sweden, in Conjunction with her Ships of War, to repel the Czar of Muscovy s Invasions upon Sweden, and to obtain from him, as soon as possible, the Articles and Conditions of an equitable. Peace: But all the Operations which are to be performed by these joint Forces, must be d irected and ordered in a Council of War, which shall be previously held among the Commanders of the Naval Forces of each Crown; and for the future, before the Auxiliary Forces shall be sent, he that has suffered Violence and Injury, shall communicate with the other Confederates; and then each of the Confederates shall employ his Endeavours to bring the Invader or Disturber, by amicable Means, to abstain troui Violence and Injury, lest it should become necessary to have recourse to Arms: But in case the Aggressor should prove so obstinate, that he w ill, by no amicable Means, comply in doing what is equitable; and thereupon the Confederate w ho has been injured and offended, shall be forced to repel the Violence offered him, and to put a Stop to any further Trouble, by Force of Arms; then at length the aforesaid Forces shall be sent without further Delay; nor shall they leave off till entire Satisfaction be given to the Party aggrieved; and he that forces One by injuries to make a just Defence, shall be reputed an Aggressor.

XlL

It shall likewise be lawful for each of the Confederates, treaty wits* and for their Subjects, to bring their Ships of War, and Sweden, other armed Vessels, into the Ports of the other to winter and abide there, and to have and enjoy the Immunities and Privileges thereof; provided only, that those who are not common Enemies, be not annoyed in the >said Ports, or in their entering into the same; or that their Intercourse of Trade to the said Ports be not disturbed; much less; that it he wholly ruined: It has likewise beeii settled, by the mutual Consent of their Royal Confederate Majesties, That a particular Negotiation, concerning Navigation and Commerce, shall immediately, and without Delay, be set on Foot at Stockholm, for the mutual Benefit and Advantage of each Nation: In the mean while, and until those Transactions take effect, it is stipulated and agreed between each of the Confederates, That a mutual and entire Freedom of Navigation and Commerce shall be allowed on both Sides for all Sorts of Merchandize and Effects, through all and singular their Countries, Dominions, and Territories, situated in Europe; so that it shall be lawful for their Subjects mutually to come, freely and safely, by Sea or by Land, into the Kingdoms, Provinces, Islands, Towns, Cities, and Villages, of either Party; there to abide, and to carry on Trade in all Sorts of Goods and Merchandize, the Import and Export whereof are not particularly forbid and prohibited by the Laws and Statutes of either Kingdom: Provided however, That this Liberty of Trade be not extended to any other Places than to those Sea-ports which have been hitherto allowed for the Commerce of any foreign Nation; in which said Ports, Towns, Cities, and Places, it shall always be free and lawful for the Subjects of either of the Confederates, not only to abide, remain, and have Houses, there, as long as they please, without any Molestation, Grievance,

Constraint, or Limitation of Time; but also to remove themselves from thence, with their Goods, Merchandize, and Effects, whatsoever, and to go with their said Effects to /

another Place, whensoever and whithersoever they please, without any Inconvenience, Delay, or Hindrance whatsoever, under any Kind of Pretence, unless they shall be in Debt, and have contracted just and lawful Demands upon them; neither shall the said Subjects be obliged to pay any Taxes or Imposition of any kind, or under any Denomination whatsoever, while they remain mutually in the Dominions and Territories of either of the Confederates, which the Nation the most favoured is not obliged to pay: And to the end that the mercantile Affairs of the aforesaid Subjects may be settled and advanced in the best manner they can, and that Trade may be reciprocally promoted between each Kingdom, the said Confederates do mutually bind themselves, and engage on each Side, That the Goods and Manufactures of eacii Nation Shall, for the future, pay no more Duties, nor higher Customs, than those which are at present established; and they shall so long enjoy this immunity, till all these Matters appertaining to mutual Commerce shall be more clearly and effectually determined, by a particular Convention, or Treaty, to be forthwith made, and to be for ever after observed, for the Benefit and Advantage of each Nation; nor shall it he lawful for the respective Subjects of each of the Confederates to demand or exact higher Prices for weighing and measuring Goods and Merchandize, to he by them imported and exported, than such as are demanded from, and paid by, the Cities, Natives, and Citizens, of each Kingdom: It is further agreed and ordained, as a general Rule between the said Confederates,

That all and singular their Subjects, in the Countries'and Territories mutually under their Dominion, shall enjoy, at least, the same Favour in all Thing*, and on all Occasions, and shall have and enjoy the same Privileges,

Liberties, and Immunities, which the Subjects of any other Prince or State the most favoured have, use, and enjoy, or shall hereafter have, use, ari^ enjoy.

XIV.

But those Prerogatives which are specified, in the Beginning of the 12th Article, as granted by One of the Confederates, in his Ports, to the Ships of his Confederate, shall by no means be allowed to the Enemies of the other; so iuither shall the Subjects of either of the Confederates be allowed to use their Endeavours for the Enemies of the other, to the Disadvantage and Prejudice of the Confederate; and serve them in any manner, whether by Sea or Land, as Soldiers or Mariners; which, therefore, shall be very strictly forbid them.

XV.

The present Treaty, concluded between their most Serene Majesties of Great Britain and Sweden, shall in no wise derogate from either of the Allies in their Sovereignties, Rights, and Dominions, of the Seas; to wit, from his Sacred Majesty of Great Britain, in the Dominion of the Seas which are vulgarly called the British Seas; and from her Sacred Swedish Majesty, in the Dominion of the Baltick Sea; but both the Confederates shall, as now and heretofore, so hereafter, retain all the aforesaid Rights, with all their Dependencies, and shall fully and freely enjoy the same; which Enjoyment of every thing aforesaid is to be understood, on both Parts, with a Salvo to this present Treaty.

XVL

After the Prince requested shall, in the aforesaid manner, have sent his Succours, or satisfied his Obligation, according to the Laws of the Treaty, it is necessary, that due Provision should be made, on the other Side, for him, and his Security; And therefore it is agreed, on each Part, That the Confederate who sends Succours to the other Confederate, at his Request, may continue in the Quality of an Auxiliary, and not be involved in the War himself on account of the Succours so furnished: But, nevertheless, no Treaty of Peace, or a Truce, may be agreed upon, without including and securing him; nor even a Suspension of Arms which is of any long Continuance, and prejudical to the other Confederate: But, if he shall be engaged in open War with the Aggressor, or otherwise, on account of the Succours he shall have furnished; then neither of them may, without the Consent and Advice of the other, agree either to any preliminary or main Treaties with the Enemy or Enemies; but all 10

'furtiu -A: l72r«

things are to be managed arid negotiated by their mutual Assistance, Participation, and Advice, till*the most ample Provision be made for the sufficient Security, and due Sa^ tisfaction, of both the Confederates, with their common Consent; particularly, that Confederate, who was first engaged in War, may not conclude a Peace before the other Confederate, who, pursuant to the Treaty, sent Succours to his Confederate, shall, in every Point, be indemnified by the Enemy, and, at least, be fully restored to his former Condition which he enjoyed, or ought’ lo enjoy, before the War began, if his State and Condition shall have suffered any Diminution from the Enemy, and the War ensuing thereupon.

XVII.

To the Articles before-mentioned, concerning the Assistance to be given to each Confederate, at his Request, this Condition is expressly added; That if it shall happen; after the Request made* that One of the confederate Princes, so requested, should either be engaged in a War against the com 1 nop Enemy, or should be invaded in his own Kingdoms arid Provinces by any other neighbouring King. Prince, or State; so that the said requested Prince should take such Invasion for at real War, for the suppressing whereof the requesting Prince would otherwise, by virtue of this Treaty, be obliged to send Succours; then the confederate Prince, so invaded, incase any Auxiliary Forces shall have been sent at the Request of the other confederate Prince before the Invasion, shall be at Liberty, upon Three Months previous Notice, to recall the same, for the Defence of his own Kingdom and Kingdoms; and, during the said Invasion, shall riot be obliged to furnish the promised Succours; as it-fermorty happened in the long War between the Crown of Great Britain and the most Christian King: And though (I# aforesaid Treaty of the Year 1700, which shall be esteemed the Basis of this, was made upon this Condition; and that this present Treaty, now concluded, ought to be explained hereafter in the same manner; nevertheless, his Sacred Majesty of Great Britain, that he may give th6 clearest Testimonies of his Friendship to the Crown of Sweden, engages himself, pro hac vice, That the present War between the Crowns of Great Britain and Spain shall in no wise hinder her Sacred Majesty of Sweden from actually keeping back the Succours stipulated by this Treaty, nor from enjoying the benefit of the same, till the Peace shall be happily restored; that is to say, The Subsidies, and Squadron of Ships, promised in the Eighth and Eleventh Articles, till the Peace with the Czar of Muscovy; but the Subsidies, only so long as the War with the Crown of Denmark shall last; that is, if the said War should, contrary to all Expectation, continue after the Peace with the Czar: On the other hand, her Sacred Majesty of Sweden engages herself to admit of no Conditions which may be, either directly or indirectly, propo3cd or offered to her by the King of Spain, so far as those Conditions may occasion any Prejudice or Damage to the Cause which is, and has been, by a War of several Years, carried on against Spain: Her Sacred Swedish Majesty further engages for hrirself, her Ileirs and Successors, to maintain and guaranty the Succession in the Kingdom of Great Britain, as it is settled by the Laws of the Kingdom, in the Family of his present Britamnck Majesty; as likewise to defend all the Countries and Provinces possessed by his Majesty; and will not give or grant any Asylum or Refuge, in any Part of her Dominions, to the Person, or his Descendants, if he shall have any, who, in the Life-time of King James the Second, toot upon him the Title of Prince of Wales, and, since his Death, the Title of King of Great Britainj promising likewise for herself, her Heirs and Successors, not to give to the said Person, or his Descendants, directly or indirectly, by Sea or Land, any Aid, Counsel, or Assistance, whatsoever, either in Money, Arms, military Stores, Ships, Soldiers, Mariners, or any other Way whatsoever; and that she will observe the same with regard to those' who may be commanded or impowered by the said Person, or his Descendants, to disturb the Government of his Britawick Majesty, or the Tranquillity of his Kingdom,

XVIII.

And although the Confederates be obliged to send Succours to one another reciprocally in the manner aforesaid, yet that Obligation is not to be extended so far, as that all Friendship, and mutual Commerce, with the Enemies of the other Confederate, and their Subjects, should, on that Account, be wholly withdrawn and forbid; for if that case should happen, that one of the Confederates, even though he should have furnished the Succours requested of him, yet should not be engaged in the War himself, the Trade and Navigation of his Subjects, and Inhabitants, with the Enemies of that other Confederate who is in War, shall be free; and it shall be lawful to carry any sort of Merchandize to them, such only excepted as are expressly forbid, vulgarly called contraband, and are by the common Consent of all Nations, declared such.

XIX.

As both their aforesaid Majesties do hereby declare themselves bound by some certain Conventions and Treaties which they have before entered into with others; and that they are willing to observe the same duly, according to the Tenor'of the said Conventions; yet that they are, at present, obliged by no Conventions, or Clauses contained in them, which can or ought, in any-wise, or under any Pretence, to invalidate and obstruct this presen Treaty: so, in Order to make the mutual Faith of the Confederates, and their Perseverance in this Alliance, the more evident, and to confirm the Minds of their Subjects and Friends, both their aforesaid Majesties do reciprocally oblige themselves, and declare. That they will sincerely, and bonaJide, stand to all and singular the Articles of this Treaty; and that they will not, in the least, depart from the genuine and plain Sense of the aforesaid Articles, under any Pretence of Interest, Friendship, former Treaty, Convention, and Promise, or any other Colour whatsoever; but that they will, according as Occasion and Affairs shall require, either by themselves, or their Ministers and Subjects, speedily and fully, as is stipulated in express Words, and effectually, execute every thing which they have promised in this Treaty; and that without any Limitation, Exception, or Excuse; except those

VO L. 10.

Excuses which are expressed in the foregoing Articles of Treaty with this Treaty. Swedeti’

XX.

This Defensive Treaty shall continue for Eighteen Years; before the Expiration of which, the Confederate Princes may treat of a plenary Continuance thereof, if they shall both think fit so to do.

XXL

As these Articles are concluded by virtue of a Power received* and Commissions, on both bides; so the same are to be approved and ratified, in due form, by both their Sacred Majesties of Great Britain and Sweden; and the Instruments of Ratification to be exhibited and exchanged at Stockholm within the Space of Three. Months to be computed from the time of this Signature; or sooner, if it may be.

For the greater Certainty and Confirmation of all tilings before-mentioned, Two Copies of this Treaty are made; one whereof the said Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of his Sacred Majesty of Great Britain; and the other the said Senators, and Secretary of State, of her Sacred Majesty, and the Kingdom of Sweden; being all furnished with special Powers for that Purpose, have signed and sealed at Stockholm, and that on one and the same Day; to wit, the 21st of January 1744.

Carteret (L. S.)

Separate Articles.

I.

There shall be and remain for the future, a more strict and close Confederacy and Union than there has ever been heretofore between the above-mentioned Kings of Great Britain and Sivcden, for the preserving and protecting the Protestant Religion, both the Evangelical and the Reformed, as well in the Roman Empire, by virtue of the Peace of Westphalia, as in all other Countries, wheresoever those Religions have been either publickly allowed, or, at least, hitherto tolerated: Wherefore the above-named Princes, by these presents, do mutually bind themselves in the most close Alliance; and do promise,

That they will, through the Divine Providence and Assistance, defend, protect, and preserve, those Religions against any clandestine Contrivances, open Violence, or Persecutions whatsoever; and, for this End, they will faithfully join not only their Counsels, but also their Forces and Endeavours.

II.

Whereas, in like manner, it seems to be no less advantageous for preserving the Freedom of Navigation and Commerce in the Baltick Sea, than for the particular Interest and Security of the Kingdoms of Sweden and Denmark against the Power of certain Neighbours, which is increasing more and more every Day; besides that, by this means, the common Good of the Protestants would be particularly taken care of, if a firm and perfect Friendship could be restored between these Nations: For these Causes his Sacred Royal Majesty of Great Britain has not only offered his Mediation, which has likewise been lately accepted by her Sacred Royal Majesty of Sweden, and by his Royal Majesty of Denmark, for putting an End to the present fatal War, which has so long raged between the Kingdoms of Sweden and Denmark, and for restoring the former good Understanding; but also, by virtue of this present Treaty, does engage and promise, on the Word of a King, his Security and Guaranty of all the Treaties of Friendship and G uaranty heretofore made betw een the Crowns of Great Britain and Sweden, saving all those Things wffiich have been stipulated by the late Peace between the King of Great Britain, as Elector of Brunswick Lunenburgh, the Queen of Sweden, and the King of Prussia; as likewise those Things which shall further be stipulated, by his Mediation, in the Treaty of Peace between the Crowns of Sweden and Denmark: And that it may appear more evidently how much his Sacred Royal Majesty of Great Britain has the Tranquillity of the North, and the Affairs of the Protestant Religion, at Heart; he engages, for himself, and for his Successors, in that Kingdom particularly, to guaranty and maintain the 7 O Treaties

Treaties of Westphalia, not only in all the Articles and Clauses of the same which relate to the Liberty ^and Preservation of the Protestant Religion, but also all the Rights, Dominions, and Provinces, which were given and granted by the Germanick Roman Empire to the Kings and Crown of Sweden, by virtue of the said Peace; only the Particulars abovesaid being excepted, which have been alienated to the King of Great Britain, as Elector of Brunswick Lunenburg, and to the King of Prussia; as also such as shall be further stipulated, in the Treaty of Peace with the Crown of Denmark, with respect to the Dukedom of Slesreick; and, in the next Congress at Brunswick, with relation to the City of IVismar; so that his Sacred Royal Majesty of Great Britain will allow nothing at all further to be done or attempted against the Tenor of the Treaties of the Peace of Westphalia.

That the Committee have examined the Matter of the Breach of Privilege complained of; and do find,

That, on the Twenty-first Day of April last, Robert Colman and William Causey came to Mr. Smyth's House in Devonshire; and there arrested John Wills and Ilcmy Chernaw, Two of Mr. Smyth's menial Servants, knowing them to be such Servants, and knowing Mr. Smyth to be a Member of Parliament; which Arrest was in an Action of Trespass, at the Suit of Thomas Baymird Esquire, and Richard Needs Gentleman.

It appeared to the Committee, That Mr. Needs was the Person who caused the said Arrest; and that he made use of Mr. Baynard's Name in the said Action, without his Knowledge or Privity.

AP ETITION of the Mayor, Aldermen) and Com- Duties on mon Council, of the City of Exon; and also of the Soap and Merchants, Serge-makers, Fullers, and others, trading Candles, in the Woollen Manufacture within the said City; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Woollen Manufacture Trade hath been the chief Support of this City and Country for many Ages; and is so greatly decayed, that the poorer Sort are exceeding numerous, and the Traders and Dealers in the said Manufacture labour under great Difficulties, by reason of the high Duties on Soap and Candles; which is a considerable Clog, on account of the vast Quantities used and consumed in working, fulling, and doing, the said Manufacture; and are rendered incapable to dispose of their Goods in foreign Markets, being supplied by Foreigners on cheaper Terms: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the principal Inhabitants of the Town Ditto, of Ashburton, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Woollen Manufacture Trade, which is the chief Support of this Town, is gone to Decay; by reason of the high Duties on Soap and Candles, used in carrying on the said Trade; whereby the Dealers cannot afford their Goods to any Advantage; which hath so discouraged the Dealers, that the said Trade is likely to be lost: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Bay-makers, Ditto, of the Borough of Colchester, on behalf of themselves, and many Thousand poor Inhabitants within the said Town, who are Consumers of Soap and Candles, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the great Duties which are laid upon Soap and Candles are very burthensome to the said Manufacture, and highly oppressive to the Poor: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

London reported from the Committee, to whom Regiments in the Report upon the Petition of Colonel FrancisFarqvhar, Dutch Serin the Name and Behalf of the Officers of the Three Re- vice* giments of Wood, Douglas, and Hamilton; who served the States General during the late War, was recommitted; and who were to examine and state the Accounts uf the said Regiments; and to report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; the Af atter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the said Report and Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee did not find any Reason to alter the said former Report; but, in pursuance of the Orders of this House, have examined and stated the 7 Q Account*

6io 0 Junii. AriJ&i.

?egme"ts Accounts of the said Regiments; and considered

Service! the several Papers referred to them; and examined

several Witnesses thereupon; and find the same to be as follows; viz The said Colonel Farquhar, Major Patterson, and Mil-Ham Van Klhilcenbergli sworn Military Solicitor in the Hague, declared to the Committee, That the Officers of the said Three Regiments are obliged, by the Council of ' State, upon their being made Captains, to subsist them-

selves, and Companies, as long as they have Power, or Credit:

That the Officers, in Consequence of this Obligation, are necessitated to employ their own Money, or to borrow Money, for the Service^ of the States, at any Rate they can; which Money the Officers generally borrow from their Solicitors or Agents; who are sworn to do Justice to the States, and to the Officers.

It appealed also to the Committee, by a Resolution of the States of Holland and West Friezland, dated the 4th of March 1712, That South Holland allowed their Agents, or Solicitors, to take from the Captains whom they serve, Thirteen Stivers, as. monthly Interest* for 100 Guilders; which, at Nine long Months in the Year, is Five Guilders Seventeen Stivers per Annum:

And it further appears, by the ..said Resolution, That the States of North Holland allowed their Military Solicitors to take from the Captains whom they serve, Sixteen;: Stivers,;, as: monthly Interest, for 100 Guilders; which, at the aforesaid Rate, of Nine Months in the [Year, is Six Guilders Six Stivers per Annum.

And it further appeared to the said Committee, by the Testimony of the said IVm. Van Klhikenbergh, That the Agents, both in South and North Holland, charge the Officers, for Interest, by Monthly Accumulation;

buffi, upon any Dispute betwixt the Officers and Solicitors, is always allowed the Solicitors, by* the Bookkeeper, and First Clerk, of the Finances of the Province of Holland, to whom those Disputes are commonly referred; which further appeared, by Accounts so made up, and signed by the Agents, and produced to the Committee.

It also appeared to the Committee, by Contracts made betwixt the Officers and Solicitors of Hamilton s Regiment, confirmed by the States of the Province of Zeland, fJi!" , That the Solicitors take Six Guilders, as the yearly Interest of 100 G uilders, without Accumulation. s

' It appeared to the Committee, That the Officers of the Regiment of Wood; who Were upon the Repartition of , .: - Noi^ Holland, made an Agreement with their Solicitors

' i to pay Fourteen Stivers, as monthly Interest, for One hundred Guilders; which is Two Stivers less than the States allowed the Solicitors to take, as in the said Resolution of the 4th of March 1712.

It appeared to the-Committee, That the Officers of the Regiment of Douglas, who were upon the Repartition of South Holland, made an Agreement with their Solicitors to pay Eleven Stivers, as monthly Interest, for 100 Guilders; which is Two Stivers cheaper than the States

allowed the Solicitors to take, as in the said Resolution of the Fourth of March 1712.

It also appeared to the Committee, by the original Capitulation, signed at London, the 7th of March 1701, by Adrian Van Borsell, Heer of Galder Malsen, Minister of the States General, That the said Three Regiments were to be, as to Number of Companies, Men, and Pay, treated on the same Foot with other Three Scotch Regiments then actually in the Service of the States General: And the General Establishment, printed at the Hague by the States Printer, was produced to the Committee; and the Accounts of the Regiments of Douglas, Wwd, and Hamilton, are stated accordingly.

That upon the whole Matter of the Evidence aforesaid, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the States General ought to have paid the Regiments of Douglas, Wood, Q^ JIamiltm, &s^hoy~dk\ the other Scotch Regiments in their Service; and that the said Regiments of Douglas, Wood* and Hamilton,.ought now to be accounted with, according to the Capitulation signed at London, the 7th of March 1701, by Adrian Van Borsell, Heer of Gelder Malsen, Minister of the States General.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the same Interest be allowed the Officers of the several Regiments of Douglas, H ood, and Hamilton, who served the States General in the late War, as the said Officers are obliged to pay the Military Solicitors approved of by the said States, for Money advanced by the Solicitors to the said Officers, and their Companies, and for the Service of the States General; not exceeding Tfiirteeen Stivers monthly, for One hundred Guilders, for South Holland', Sixteen Stivers monthly, for 100 Guilders, for North Holland; and Six Guilders per Annum, for 100 G uilders, for the Province of Zeland.

After which the Committee proceeded to examine the several Accounts from the States General, referred to the said Committee; and the Accounts of the Officers and t Agents produced to the said Committee, Article by Article; whereby it appeared,

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out " the States General ought to have paid," and inserting, instead thereof, these Words; " the Regirnents of Wood, Douglas, and Hamilton, are intitled " to the like Pay with other Scotch ‘Regiments in the " Service of the States General And the Question being put, That the Words " the " States General ought to have paid" stand Part of the said Resolution;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Vol. 19.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That the States General ought to have paid the Regiments of Douglas, Wood\ and Hamilton, as they did the other Scotch Regiments in their Service; and that the said Regiments of Douglas, Wood' and Hamilton, ought now to be accounted with, according to the Capitulation signed at London the Seventh of March 1701, by Adrian Van Borscllen, Heer of Gelder Malsert, Minister of the States General.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Rogers and Mr. Hiccocks:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting Part of the Estate late of Anthony Lechmere Esquire, deceased, in Trustees, to be sold, for Payment of his Debts: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The Orders of the Day being read;

The House resumed the adjourned Consideration of the Report from the Committee of the whole- House, to whom the Bill-for Relief of the unhappy Sufferers in the South Sea Company; and for restraining John Aislabie Esquire from going* out of this Kingdom for the Space of One Year, and until the End of the next Session of Parliament; and for discovering his Estate and Effects; and for preventing the transporting or alienating the same; was committed:

And the Amendments, made by the Committee, to the Bill, as far as Fol. 19. L. 22. being severally read a Second time, were, with Amendments to some of them, agreed unto by the House: And One of the said Amendments was postponed; and another of the said Amendments was disagreed with.

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the said Report be adjourned till Tomorrow Morning.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Thursday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for examining, stating, and determining, the Debts due to the Army.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Mercurtiy 28° die Junii;'

Anno 70 Georgii Regis, 1721.

AN ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for vesting Part of the Estate late of Anthony Lechmere Esquire, deceased, in Trustees, to be sold, for Payment of his Debts, was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Sir David Dalrymple reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Arthur Balfour, Son of John Balfour, late of Ferric, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report io the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same w as read; and is as followeth;

That the Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

That it appeared, by the Appeal of the Commissioners and Trustees of the forfeited Estates, produced to the

Committee, that they do admit the Deed of Settlement made by Robert Lord Burley, deceased, to be of the very same Nature as is mentioned, and set forth in the said Petition of Arthur Balfour.

It appears further to this Committee, That the Petitioner went into Ireland in April 1715, and continued there, in his Majesty's Service, till June 1719; and that John Balfour, by virtue of a Letter of Attorney from ‘ the said Arthur his Brother, did present a Petition to the said Commissioners and Trustees, in Name of the said Arthur; wherein he set forth his Title, by virtue of the said D&ed of Settlement; but made no regular Claim, in the manner directed by the several Acts of Parliament for that’ Purpose.

5 ! And further it appeared to the Committee, That the

I Petitioner did not know of the Irregularity or Omission

‘ of his siid Brother,’ in hot entering a Claim in due Form,

'until atiout a~ Fortnight since.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table. (

Bushels of Salt were shipped at a Creek belonging to the said Earl, called The Methill; which Creek is Part of the Port of Kirkaldie: And that the said Salt was put on board Four"different Ships; and being exported to Parts bejond Sea, the said Earl’s Agents gave Bonds for the Duty thereof:

That the said Earl having, for many Years before the Union, a Privilege of exporting all Commodities of the Growth, Product, and Manufacture, of Scotland, from the said Creek of Methill, Duty-free; the said Earls Agents apprehended there was no Necessity for any formal Entry of any Salt exported from the said Creek beyond the Seas:

That, upon making Application to the Commissioners of the Salt-duty in Scotland, for Debentures for the Salt so exported, to answer the Bonds which were given for the Duty of the said Salt, the Commissioners refused to make out the Debentures so demanded, by reason the said Salt was not entered, and certified, in such time, and in such manner, as the Law directs.

That it appeared to the said Committee, That the said Six thousand Nine hundred and Sixty-two Bushels of Salt was, in Four Parcels, and at different times, actually, and bona jide, exported to Parts beyond the Seas; And although the same was so exported; yet the same being not certified in due Form, the said Earl cannot be relieved in the Premises, as the Law now stands, without some Provision be made for that Purpose.

Ordered, That the Report do lie upon the Table.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Rogers and Mr. Fellows:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for confirming the Manor of Latham, and divers Lands, in the County of Lancaster, to Richard Waring, Brian Fairfax, and Thomas Ashurst, Esquires, and their Heirs, subject to the Trusts to which the same are now'liable, discharged of a certain Clause, in Letters Patents of King Charles the First, for re-conveying the Reversion in Fee to the Crown, without any Amendment.

A Petition of Major Hubert Jenmngs, and Captain Matthew Coudell, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they being, in the Beginning of the late War, in the Enemy’s Service, did, upon the Proclamation published, by her late Majesty’s Order, quit the same, and came over to her Allies; and they should be entertained, in the same Quality, and with the same Pay, as they enjoyed under her Enemies: That on their Application/ her Majesty was pleased to express, That they should be cleared what Arrears were due to them, for the time of their Service; That, in 1718, Coudell applied himself to his Majesty for Relief; and his Memorial, and Papers, were referred to the Commissioners appointed to state and determine the Debts due to the Army; who reported, That it appeared to them ta be a just and national Affair: They thought the same was not under their Cognizance: That, upon Jennings’ Application to the said Commissioners, they cleared him for the time he served in Lord Gallways Regiment; but could not relieve him, as to what was due before he obtained his Commission, as being on the same Footing with Coudell: And praying, That a Clause may be inserted in the new Act for appointing Commissioners to examine and determine the Debts due to the Army, that they may be impowered to determine the Demands of the said Petitioners.

Resolved, That the said Petition be rejected.

A PETITION of Lieutenant John Crosse, Lieu-ms for l\. tenant John Jcjjrtyson, Ensign lhomas Prender-iyFay- gast, and Ensign Andrew Simson, was presented to the ilouse, and read; setting forth. That they were Lieutenants and Ensigns in General Hitt's, Colonel Kane s, and Colonel Disney's, Regiments, and served in Flanders; and afterwards went with the same, upon the Expedition to Canada: That there being Seven Detachments ordered from the Regiments that were upon the Service, for the Relief of the Garison of Annapolis Royal, they were commanded, with Detachments, as Lieutenants and Ensigns, upon that Service: Soon after, the Government thinking fit to form those Detachments in Four independent Companies, the same made way only for providing for the Four eldest Captains, Lieutenants, and Ensigns; and the Petitioners, who were, at that time, the youngest, were left out of the then new Establishment: They applied for Leave to come to England, in order to recover their Posts, to which they did belong; which being granted, they came as far as Boston, in New England, with General Nicholson; who, upon Account of her late Majesty’s Death, they were commanded back from thence to Annapolis Royal; where they continued doing Duty, till the Eleventh of June 1717, before they obtained Leave to come for England; they not only lost their Ranks and Posts, but have been great Sufferers, in want of their Pay: And praying, That a Clause may be inserted in the Bill, depending before this House, for appointing Commissioners to state and determine the Debts due to the Army, for their Relief.

Resolved, That the said Petition be rejected.

1st, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Coinj mittee, That all Contracts for the Sale or Purchase of Subscriptions, or Stock, of the South Sea Company, or any other Company or Corporation, or pretended Company or Corporation, which shall be unperformed, or not* compounded, on or before the Twenty-ninth Day of September next, be entered in Books, to be kept for that Purpose, by the respective Companies or Corporations, before the First Day of November next, or else to be void; and that such Entries shall express for whose LTse and Benefit such Contracts were made.

2d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,4 That no special Bail be required, in any Action brought, or to be brought, upon any Contract for the Sale or Purchase of any Subscription, or Stock, of the South Sea Company, or any other Company or Corporation, of pretended Company or Corporation.

3d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That no Execution be awarded upon any Judgment obtained, or to be obtained, in any Action brought, or to be brought, upon any Contract for the Sale or Purchase of any Subscription, or Stock, of the South Sea Company, or any other Company or Corporation, or pretended Company or Corporation, until the End of the Session of Parliament, which shall be next after the Twenty-ninth Day of September next

4th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Contracts for the Sale or Purchase of any Subscription, or Stock, of the South Sea Company, or any other Company or Corporation, which shall be unperformed, or not compounded, on or before the Twenty-ninth Day of September next, where the Seller, or the Person on whose behalf such Contract was made, was not, at 7 U the

The Third of the said Resolutions being read a Second time;

And the Question being put, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That no Execution be awarded upon any Judgment obtained, or to be obtained, in any Action brought, or to be brought, upon any Contract for the Sale or Purchase of any Subscription, or Stock, of the South Sea Company, or any other Company or Corporation, or pretended Company or Corporation, until the End of the Session of Parliament, which shall be next after the Twenty-ninth Day of September next.

That the Committee have taken the Report, which w as re-committed to them, into Consideration, and upon examining the several Surveyors of the Highways for the Hamlets of the Parish of Stepney, the Parishes of Whitechappel, Bow, and Bromley, the Committee find, That there is usually levied, in the said Hamlets and Parishes, about Four hundred Pounds per Annum; which has been laid out in repairing the Roads from the Stones End in Whitechappclto Bow Bridge; but that your Committee cannot be very particular, by reason the several Surveyors could not produce any Books by which they collected such Sums, or to shew how, or in what manner, they charged the Inhabitants; but say, That the Money is levied discretionally, what they can get of each Inhabitant, towards the said Repairs; and they have no certain Rule to govern themselves by, in collecting the Money for the said Repairs.

Nicholas Buckeridge Clerk, being examined, says, That there are Lands, amounting to near One thousand Pounds per Annum, late Parcel of the Possession of the Abbot of Stratford, in Essex, that are liable to the Re-pa'r of Bow Bridge, and Channelsea Bridge, and all the Road and Causeways between those Two Bridges; and that he is one of the Owners and Proprietors of these Lands; and produced Three Agreements between the Owners of the said Abbey Lands, and Persons by them employed as Undertakers to repair the said Bridges and Road; by which it appeared,

That, by the First Agreement, with one Shephard, Bow Bridge and Channelsea Bridge, and all the Road and Causeways between the said Bridges, were repaired, for Seven Years commencing from the 6th oi May 1695, for^.80. per Annum:

And, by another Agreement with the same Person, the Highways and Causeways only wrere repaired, for Five Years commencing from the 29th September 1702, for £86. 14s. 6d. per Annum:

And, by a Third Agreement with one Mayhem, that the Bridge, commonly called Channelsea Bridge, w as to be gravelled, and the Highways and Causeways, Posts, and Rails, between the said Bridge and Bow Bridge, were to he amended, and kept in Repair, for Eleven Years commencing at Michaelmas 1*708, for^. 94. 2S. j od. per Annum.

Mr. Preston, another of the Owners of the said Abbey Lands, being examined, says, That in the Year 1718, the Abl>ey Land-owners laid out £.126. 7s. 8d. in repairing Channelsea Bridge, and the Roads between that and Bow Bridge;

And, in the Year 1719, £. 129. 15s. 2d. in repairing the said Road and Bridges.

It further appeared to the Committee, That there are Three other Bridges on the same Road, between Bow and Stratford: That Two of the said Bridges, oWc'Pegs-holc Bridge, the other St. Michael's Bridge; and that they are repaired by the Mayor and Commonalty of the City of London, by reason of the Tenure of some Mills and Lands near adjoining to the same Road:

And Mr. Garbrand, Clerk to the Bridge-house, being thereto examined, says, That the Mayor and Commonalty of the City of London have, for several Years last past, repaired the said Two Bridges, and have Mills and Lands adjoining to the said Road; but in what manner the same are liable to the said Repairs, he knows not.

It also appeared to the Committee, That there is another Bridge on the same Road, called St. Thomas of Aeon's Bridge, which hath been constantly repaired af the sole Cost and Charges of the Owners of other Mills and Lands adjoining to the said Road, which now are in the Tenure of Thomas Chambers Esquire, who is Owner thereof; And, upon Examination of the' Steward and Vol. 1C).

Agent of the said Mr. Chambers, he owned. That the said Mr. Chambers was Owner of the said Mills and Land; and that both he, and his Father Sir Thomas Chambers, had used to repair that Bridge.

Mr. IVykes and Mr. Coker informed the Committee,

That they have made a Survey of the Road from the Stones End in Whitechappel to Bow Bridge, which is in Length about Two Mites, and Eighteen Rods; and say.

That, if. the Gravel is laid Three Foot deep, and Thirty Foot wide, it will cost, to put that Road in Repair, Three thousand Pounds; and about Six hundred Pounds per Annum to keep it in Repair, when it is so mended:

That, to amend the Road from Bpw - Bridge to Strafford will cost about a Thousand Pounds; and that the Charges to keep it in Repair afterwards will, irv their Judgment, amount to One hundred and Fifty Pounds per Annum.

Mr. Comptroller acquainted the House, That he had Cml List a Message signed by his Majesty; and he presented the Debta. same to the House: Which was read by Mr. Speaker; and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

HIS Majesty finds it necessary to acquaint his loyal House of Commons with the difficulties he labours under by reason of Debts contracted in his Civil Government; which, being computed at Lady-day last, do amount to more than Five hundred and fifty thousand Pounds.

If the Provision made by an Act, of the last Session of Parliament, for discharging this Debt had not hitherto proved, in a very great Degree, ineffectual, his Majesty had not been under a Necessity of applying again to Parliament upon this Occasion: But, being resolved to cause a Retrenchment to be made of his Civil List Expences for the future; and finding, that such a Retrenchment cannot well be effected without discharging the present Arrears; has ordered the Accounts thereof to be laid before the House; and hopes he may be impowered to raise ready Money, for that Purpose, on the Civil List Revenues; which, to avoid the laying any new Burthen on his People, his Majesty proposes shall be replaced to the Civil List; and reimbursed by a Deduction to be made out of the Salaries and Wages of all Offices, and the Pensions, and other Payments, from the Crown.

Resolved, That this House w’ill, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to take his Majesty's most gracious Message into Consideration,

We are also commanded to acquaint your Lordships, That the Commons having received Information, That Mr. Francis Ilawes, One of the late Directors of the South Sea Company, had negociated very large Sums for4 Mr. Aislabie; and had Dealings, for a considerable Time past, in South Sea Stock, with the said Mr. Aislabie; and that an Account thereof was kept in a Book, of which Mr. Aislabie had a Duplicate; which Accounts were continued in that Book till some time in November last; the Commons did, on the Seventh Day of March last, order that the said Book should be laid before them thp next Morning; at the making of which Order, Mr. Aislabie was present, in his Place; and did not object or offer any thing to the House, that the same could not be complied with; but the next Day, Mr. Aislabie\ attending in his Place* to make his Defence to the several Matters objected to him, an Obedience to that Order being required, Mr. Aislabie declared, That Mr. Hawes, if called in, would tell the House, That Mr. Hawes, with his own Hands, committed the said Book to the Fire: Upon which, Mr. Hawes, being called in, and examined, said, That the said Book was, in the Beginning of November last, upon Mr. Aislabie s pressing Instances, delivered up, by him, to Mr. Aislabie; and the same Book, and also the said Duplicate thereof, kept by Mr. Aislabie, were both then burnt together, Part by Mr. Aislabie, and Part by himself, at Mr. Aislabie s Instance; and that the Proposal for burning them came from Mr. Aislabie: And Hawes farther said. That he had not any Duplicate, or Entry, of what w as contained in the said Book.

vStati of Pub- Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer reported from the Trek Credit. Committee, to whom it was referred to draw up an Address, to be presented to his Majesty, representing to his Majesty the State of the publick Credit of this Kingdom; and to lay before his Majesty the several Resolutions of this House, relating thereto; That they had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the same in at the Clerks Table: Where the said Address was twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and is as follows; viz*

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, being sensibly affected with the Misery and Calamities that have befallen great Numbers of your Majesty’s faithful Subjects, occasioned by the heavy Losses they have sustained from the fatal Execution of the late South Sea Scheme; and taking into our serious Consideration the low State of publick and private Credit, which it seems impossible to us should ever revive, under the present uncertain and unsettled Posture of Affairs; have come to several Resolutions; which we humbly beg Leave to lay before your Majesty; and are as follow:

44 Resolved, That all Contracts for the Sale or Purchase of Subscriptions, or Stock, of the South Sea Company,

44 or any other Company or Corporation, or pretended Company or Corporation, w'hich shall be unperformed, 44 or not compounded, on or before the Twenty-ninth Day of September next, be entered in Books, to be kept for that Purpose, by the respective Companies or Corpora- tions, before the First Day of Novanber next, or else to be void; and that such Entries shall express for whose Use and Benefit such Contracts were made.

44 Resolved, That no Execution be awarded upon any 41 Judgment obtained, or to be obtained, in any Action brought or to be brought, upon any Contract for the Sale or Purchase of any Subscription, or Stock, of the South Sea Company, or any other Company or Corporation, or pretended Company or Corporation, until the End of the Session of Parliament which shall be next after the Twenty-ninth Day of September next.

44 Resolved, That all Contracts for the Sale or Purchase of any Subscription, or Stock, of the South Sea Company, or any other Company or Corporation, which shall be unperformed, or not compounded, on or before the Twenty-ninth Day of September next, where the Seller, or the Person on whose behalf such Contract was made, was not, at the time of such Contract, or within a time to be limited, actually possessed of, or intitled to, such Subscription, or Stock, shall be declared null and void."

When we first entered upon the Consideration of this extensive and perplexed Affair, we thought it most adviseable to leave every Man’s Property to be determined by due Course of Law; and were of Opinion, That no

Relief

7 Geo. I. 25* — 26b julii. 39

Relief or Abatement could properly be prescribed, or given, but from the South Sea Company: Hut the Discontents of the People daily increasing, and the uncertain and doubtful Events that threatened very great and valuable Properties, creating such infinite Anxieties and Dissatisfaction, as had a most fatal and general influence upon all publick and private Credit, the Interposition of Parliament became unavoidable; and we found ourselves under a Necessity of resuming the Consideration of this nice and intricate Matter; and to endeavour to remove, as far as possible, the chief and greatest Iticonveniencies.

The great Difficulty in remedying these Mischiefs seemed to arise from the several contending Interests engaged in the South Sea Company, which made it impossible to give relief to some but at the Expence of others: And, as all the new Proprietors, gs well those concerned in the publidk Funds, as the other Adventurers, were equally imposed upon by the Artifices of the late Directors, and equally drawn in by their own too great Credulity, and Desire of Gain; to have discharged any particular Set, had been not only an Injustice to the rest, but, by dissolving the whole System, had involved them in utter Ruin; which made a Distribution bf Losses, and some Abatement to all, absolutely necessary: It was indeed very much to be wished, that such Ease could have been given to the Proprietors of the publick Debts, as would have made their Property as valuable to them as they had enjoyed it for many Years: But, as they had voluntarily consented to take Stock, at some Rate or other, even at the time when they saw the Stock raised to the highest Pitch; the giving Stock at one and the same Price to them, and all others that were most immediately concerned, makes the Provision asjust and equitable as the Nature of the Thing will admit; it being impracticable so far to reconcile the different Interests in this general Concern, as to make the Conditions of those equal, that had engaged themselves at different Rates, and upon unequal Terms.

The great and principal Mischiefs arose from several concurring Circumstances; from the hard Terms of most of the Proprietors, occasioned by the high Prices at which they had purchased Stock; or the excessive Rates, at which as well the Proprietors of publick Debts, as the Money Subscribers, had obliged themselves to take Stock; from the Demand of above Seven millions payable to the Publick, which could only be raised out of the Properties of those that were already too great Sufferers, and which rendered the Company incapable of giving them any further Ease or Relief; from the Disputes and Contests at Law, which were preparing to be carried on, not only between the Company and the Subscribers of the redeemable Funds, but between infinite Numbers of private Persons engaged in Contracts for the Sale and Purchase of Stock, and Subscriptions; from the Impossibility of the Money Subscribers making any further Payments; from the great Loss the Company had sustained, by the late Directors having lent out above Eleven millions of the Company’s Money, w ithout any, or without sufficient, Security: and from the very little Prospect of recovering any considerable Part thereof, without which it was impossible for the Company to comply with the Demand of the Publick, but at the infinite Expence, and insupportable Loss, of all their Adventurers; which must have proved destructive to the Trade and Credit of the Kingdom.

These Considerations induced us to come to the foregoing Resolutions; being, as we conceive, the most proper Means to enable the Company to give Relief to such of their Proprietors as most wanted and deserved it; to put an End to all Disputes at Law; and to fix, settle, and ascertain, the several Properties and Interests of all Persons concerned with the South Sea Company; to deliver infinite Numbers of your Majesty’s good Subjects from the Apprehension of vexatious Law-suits and Prosecutions; and from the further Demand of such excessive Sums of Money as must sink and depress all publick and private Credit.

Vol. 19.

And, as the greatest Mischiefs, which wfe iioW So justly State of Ptfb* complain of, have arisen from the unwarrantable Methods lick Credit, used by the late Directors of the South Sea Company, in selling, and disposing of, such Part of their increased Capital Stock as belonged to the Company; to remove such a Foundation of Stock-jobbing, and to prevent the like fatal Consequences for the future, we thought it necessary to take care, that all the increased Capital Stock belonging to the Company, which, after the proposed Distribution is made, shall remain undisposed of, be divided among all the Proprietors of the said Company* in proportion to their several and respective Interests.

These Resolutions* if passed into a Law, and duly put in Execution, we humbly hope, will tend very much to the Re-establishing of publick Credit; to the Quieting of the Minds of your Majesty’s Subjects; and contribute to the Ease and Relief of great Numbers, though not sufficient to give Satisfaction to, or repair the losses oi] all that are unhappily involved in the present Calamity.

But, as the ancient Usa^e, and established Rules, of Parliament, make it impracticable for us to prepare Bills tot the Royal Assent, during the present Session of Parliament* for some of the Purposes contained in our Resoiu-

tions; we have humbly presumed to lay the same before your Majesty, for your Royal Consideration; not doubting but that your Majesty will, out of your great Wisdom, and accustomed Grace and Goodness to your Peo- 1 pie, as soon as the publick and private Bills, now depend- ing in Parliament, shall be dispatched, give us an early Opportunity of perfecting this great and necessary Work.

Resolved, That the said Address bfc presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of his Majesty's most honourable Privy Council do humbly nv his Majesty’s Pleasure, when he will be attended this House.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That in case it shall appear any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House w ill proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or directly, or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a High Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before the House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Membersto serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the 1 louse or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is sitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Mr. Farrer, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of his Majesty's Speech to both Houses of Parliament Yesterday, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the said Resolutions in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Re-establishing of publick Credit, Relief be given to the South Sea Company with Regard to the Payment of the Four millions One hundred and fifty-six thousand Three hundred and Six Pounds Four Shillings and Eleven Pence; and the Four and Half Years Purchase, and One Year’s Purchase, upon several Annuities, and other National Debts; the said Company giving such Consideration to the Publick, and such further Relief to the several Proprietors, and Persons concerned in Interest with the said Company, as this House shall think proper.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Re-establishing of publick Credit, and quieting the Minds of his Majesty’s Subjects, the several Properties and Interests now depending, and concerned with the South Sea Company, be ascertained and settled.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in order to put an End to all Disputes between the South Sea Company and the Proprietors of the redeemable Funds subscribed in to the said Company; and for the further Relief of the said Proprietors, and the Proprietors of the Second, Third, and Fourth, Money Subscriptions, who have now Stock allowed them at the Rate of Four hundred per Cent, with the last Midsummer's Dividend of Ten per Cent. in Stock; an Addition, after the Rate of Thirty-three Pounds Six Shillings and Eight Pence Stock, upon every Hundred Pounds Stock already allowed, be given, by the South Sea Company, to the Proprietors of the said redeemable Funds, and to the Proprietors of the Second, Third, and Fourth, Money Subscriptions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Four millions One hundred fifty-six thousand Three hundred Forty-one Pounds, with the Four Years and Half, and One Year’s, Purchase, payable to the Publick by the South Sea Company, be remitted; so as, from the Twenty-fourth of June 1722, Two millions of the Capital Stock of the said Company be reduced and annihilated; and a proportionable Part of their Annuity, or yearly Fund, in respect of the said Two millions, from that time, cease.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Second Subscription of the Irredeemables, as well the long Annuities as the Annuities of Ninester Cent. Prize Lottery Tickets, and Blank Lottery Tickets, made equal to the First Subscription of the like Annuities and Tickets, by an Addition of Stock at One hundred and Fifty per Cent.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all the Capital South Sea Stock belonging to the Company in their own Right, which, after the proposed Distribution made, shall remain undisposed of, be divided among all the Proprietors of the said Company, in Proportion to their several and respective Interests therein; and that Credit be given them for the same, in the Books of the said Company.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Persons as have borrowed Money from the South Sea Company, upon South Sea Stock actually transit

2° Angus ti. A. 1721.

ferred and pledged at the time of Borrowing, to or for Use of the said Company, shall, upon Payment of Ten per Cent, upon the respective Sums so borrowed, at a time or times to be limited, and not otherwise, be discharged from all further Demands of the said Company, in respect of the Monies so borrowed; and that all the Stock so transferred and pledged, together with all Dividends and Profits thereto belonging respectively, be absolutely vested in the said Company.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Persons as have borrowed Money from the South Sea Company, upon Subscription Receipts actually pledged to the said Company at the Time of Borrowing, shall, upon Payment of Ten per Cent, upon the respective Sums so borrowed, at a time or times to be limited, and not otherwise, be discharged from all further Demands in respect of the Monies so borrowed; and that all the Subscription Receipts so pledged, together with all Dividends and Profits thereunto belonging, be absolutely vested in the said Company.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Contracts for the Sale or Purchase of Subscriptions, or Stock, in the South Sea Company, or any other Company or Corporation, or pretended Company or Corporation, which shall be unperformed, or not compounded, on or before the Twenty-ninth Day of September next, be entered in Books to he kept for that Purpose by the res[>ective Companies or Corporations, before the First Day of November next, or else to be void; and that such Entries shall express for whose Use and Benefit such Contracts were made.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no special Bail be required in any Action brought, or to be brought, upon any Contract made since the First Day of December 1719, and before the First Day of December 1720, for the Sale *or Purchase of any Subscription, or Stock, of the South Sea Company, or any other Company or Corporation, or pretended Company or Corporation.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Execution be awarded upon any Judgment obtained, or to be obtained, in any Action brought, or to be brought, upon any Contract for the Sale or Purchase of any Subscription, or Stock, of the South Sea Company, or any other Company or Corporation, or pretended Company or Corporation, until the End of the Session of Parliament which shall be next after the Twenty-ninth Day of September next.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Contracts for the Sale or Purchase of any Subscription, or Stock, of the South Sea Company, or any other Company or Corporation, which shall be unperformed, or not compounded, on or before the Twenty-ninth Day of September next, where the Seller, or the Person on whose behalf such Contract was made, was not, at the time of such Contract, or within a time to be limited, actually possessed of, or in titled to, such Subscription, or Stock, shall be declared null and void.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Farrer, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Chancellor of the Duchy, Mr, Attorney General, Mr. Solicitor General, Mr. Walpole, and Mr. Loztmds, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

wth Sea A Petition and Representation of the Proprietors of the

idcreit. redeemable Funds, on the behalf of themselves, and all others pretended to be taken into the South Sea Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in pursuance of the Resolutions of this House, whereby their Rights are expressly referred to the Decision of the Law; and the Clause in the ingrafting Act, passed the last Sessions, whereby the same Rights are re-Vo l. ig.

served to them, in case the Law should determine in their Favour; the Petitioners have commenced several Suits against the South Sea Company, in order to try the Validity of their pretended Subscriptions, that it might appear whether the Petitioners Debts are, or are not,' legally taken in by that Company; but they did not make use of that Method, till they had first tried whether any Relief could be obtained from that Company; and, before the Commencement of any Suit, they presented a Memorial to the present Directors, w hereby they proposed to come to a final Agreement with the Company, upon any equal and reasonable Terms; but that Company never returned any Answer to their Memorial; though, at the same time, they took into Consideration the Cases of the other Contractors, and came to a Resolution to discharge the Money Subscribers from all their subsequent Payments, they not only refused to release foe Petitioners from any Part of their supposed Contract, but, at the same time, made their Case worse than it was before, by releasing the others: They are sensible of foe Miseries and Calamities brought upon this Nation by foe fatal Execution of foe South Sea Scheme; and the Difficulties this House has met with, in their Endeavours to revive the low State of publick and private Credit; and they cannot, without the greatest Grief and Concern, observe, that the late Resolutions of this House in relation to them, and the Bill brought in thereupon, will subject them to greater Loss than any other of their Fellow Sufferers; for, although the proposed Reduction of foe Petitioners Subscriptions to £ 300. per Cent, may seem to place them upon a Level with the other* Contractors, that their Subscriptions are equally binding with the others; yet that Reduction is vastly disproportionate, as is rather a Loss than any Relief; because that Reduction, being extended to all the Sufferers equally, will so far depreciate the Value of the South Sea Stock, that what Stock they are now to have, in pursuance of that Reduction, will not be of any greater real Value than what they were to have had before: But, in regard that the Petitioners have paid down the whole £ 400. for which it is pretended they contracted; whereas none of the Money Subscribers have paid down above One Haiti and some of them not One Quarter, of that Money; and as the Loss arises from foe Disproportion of the Money they have severally paid down for the Value of Stock; it will follow, that the Losses of the several Sufferers ought to be estimated in proportion to the Money they have paid down, for which they are obliged to take Stock: That, in order to reduce them, and their Money Subscribers, to a just Equality, it w'ould be necessary to give back foe Petitioners f fos, or One Half, of their Debts pretended to be subscribed; and oblige them to take Stock only, for the Remainder, at foe same Price with those Subscribers: Neither is their Case any better, if compared with that of the long Annuitants, even those who subscribed in some time after, and in the same manner with the Petitioners; those Creditors will have £ 1,153. 6* 8rf. in Stock for £ 100. per Annum, for which they paid the Government none above £. 1,600.: That they, for the like Annuity, paid the Government foil £2,000. will, on foe Foot of the present Reduction, have only £733. 6s. 8d. in Stock; which is £. 420. less Stock than those Annuitants are to have; and, according to the present Rate of Stock, amounts to the Loss of above £50. in every £ 100. lent by the Petitioners to foe Government: That the Loss upon the redeemable Debts supposed to be subscribed will amount to near Nine millions; and will be so much got clear by the South Sea Company from the Petitioners; and is more than sufficient to indemnify the Company from the IjOss they will sustain by their late Directors: And they observe, That, according to foe present Scheme, the Relief intended to be given to all the other Sufferers will, in a great measure, be made up at the sole Expence of them; and the giving Stock, at one and the same Price, to them, and all others, will not render foe intended Provision equal, to the Petitioners, with any the other Sufferers; unless either great Part of foe Petitioners Debts were

Given at our Court at Kensington, the Twenty-fourth Day of August, in the Eighth year of our Reign.

GOD save the King*

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have ordered my Lord Chancellor to deliver to you, in my Name and Words, the Causes of your meeting at this time in Parliament*

And that the Lord Chancellor thereupon acquairited both Houses, That he had received a Speech from his Majesty; which the Lord Chancellor read; and of which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent any Mistake, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is at followeth; viz*

My Lords and Gefitle'meri,

I accquainted you, when we parted last, with Our having renewed all our Treaties of Commerce with Spain; since which, Peace is happily restored in the North, by the Conclusion of the Treaty between the Czar and the King of Szveden; and, by that which I have made with the Moors, a great Number of my Subjects are delivered from Slavery; and all such of them as trade to those Parts 8 B of

6^.6 190 Octeb

of the World arc, for the future, secured from Falling under that dreadful Calamity.

In this Situation of Affairs we should-be extremely wanting to ourselves, if we neglected to improve the favourable Opportunity, which this general Tranquillity gives us, of extending our Commerce, upon which the It idles and Grandeur of this Nation chiefly depend; It is very obvious, that nothing would more conduce to the obtaining so publick a Good, than to make the Ex porta* tion of our own Manufactures, and the Importation of the Commodities used in the manufacturing of them, as. practicable and easy as may be: By this means the Balance of Trade may be preserved in our Favour, our Navigation increased, and greater Numbers of our Poor employed:

I must therefore recommend it to you, Gentlemen of the House of Commons, to consider how far the Duties upon these Branches may be taken off*, and replaced, without any Violation of publick Faith, or laying any new Burthen upon my People; and I promise myself, that, by a due Consideration of this Matter, the Produce of those Duties, compared with the infinite Advantages that will accrue to the Kingdom by their being taken off, will be found so inconsiderable as to leave little room for any Difficulties or Objections.

The supplying ourselves with Naval Stores upon Terms the most easy, and least precarious, seems highly to deserve the Careand Attention of Parliament: Our Plantations in America naturally abound with most of the proper Materials for this necessary and essential Part of our Trade, and maritime Strength; and if, by due Encouragement, we could be furnished from thence with those Naval Stores which we are now obliged to purchase and bring from foreign Countries, it would not only greatly contribute to the Riches, Influence, and Power, of this Nation; but, by employing our own Colonies in this useful and advantageous Service, divert them from setting up, and carrying on, Manufactures which directly interfere with those of Great Britain.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

It will be a great Pleasure to me, if, in raising the Supplies of this Year, it may be so ordered, that my People may reap some immediate Benefit from the present Cir* cmnstances of Affairs abroad: I have ordered Estimates to be prepared for the Service of the ensuing Year; and likewise an Account of the Debts of the Navy to be laid before you: You cannot but be sensible of the ill Consequences that arise from such a large Debt remaining unprovided for; and that, as long as the Navy and Victualing Bills are at a very high Discount, they do not only affect all other publick Credit, but greatly increase the Charge tind Expence of the current Service: It is therefore very much to be wished, that you could find a Method of discharging this Part of the National Debt, which, of all others, is the most heavy and burthensome; and, by that means, have it in your Power to ease your Country of some Part of the Taxes, which from an absolute Necessity they have been obliged to pay.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The unspeakable Misery and Desolation that has, of late, raged in some Parts of Europe, cannot but be a sufficient Warning to us to use all possible Precautions to prevent the Contagion from being brought in among us; or, if these Kingdoms should be visited with such a fatal Calamity, to be in a Condition, with the Blessing of God, to stop its further Progress: And, as all other Provisions jviU be altogether vain and fruitless, if the abominable Practice of Running of Goods be not, at once, totally suppressed, I most earnestly recommend to you to let no other Consideration stand in Competition with a due Care of preserving so many Thousand Lives.

The several Affairs which I have mentioned to you being of the ltjghest and most immediate Concern to the whole Kingdom, I doubt not but you w ill enter; into the Consideration of them with that Temper, Unanimity, iuid Dispatch, that the Necessity and Importance of them require. v

That we will cheerfully raise the Supplies necessary tof the Service of the ensuing Year; and endeavour to find out Means for discharging such Part of the National Debt as is most grievous and burthensome, in such a manner a* may enable us to comply with his Majesty's earnest Desires to sec tire Country eased of some Part of the Taxes, which, from an absolute Necessity, they have been obliged to pay.: And that we will not be wanting in our utmost Endeavours to prevent the Contagion from being brought into these Kingdoms; or, in case we should be visited with such a fatal Calamity, to do all that is possible ta stop its further Progress.

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our unfeigned Thanks ix ion
