for your Majesty's most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We congratulate your Majesty upon the Success that fins attended your unwearied Application for restoring Tranquillity to Europe \ for securing our Commerce by Treaties; and for releasing great Numbers of your Subjects from Slavery among the Moors, and for delivering the trading Part of the Nation from the Apprehensions of the like Calamity for the future t Which are so many Instances of your Majesty's Goodness, in which all your Subjects are so nearly concerned, that we are no less bound by Interest, than led by Inclination and Duty, most thankfully to acknowledge these happy Effects of your Majesty’s Care for your People.

: Your Majesty's recommending to us to improve the general Tranquillity abroad, towards extending and enlarging our Commerce, is an additional Proof how much your Majesty has the real Interest of Great Britain at Heart, in all your Counsels and Undertakings.

Your Commons are thoroughly sensible. That our Poor cannot be sufficiently employed, nor the Balance of Trade be long preserved in our Favour, while such Duties are continued as either clog the Exportation of our own Manufactures, or render the manufacturing of them at Home less easy and practicable: And they will most phearfully apply themselves to consider how far such Duties can be taken off and replaced, without laying any hew Burthen on your People, or violating the publick Faith; having great Reason to promise themselves, that the free Circulation of Trade, which must naturally succeed, upon the taking off this Pressure, will, in a short Space of Time, compensate any Diminution of the Customs, which this Alteration may occasion for the present.

And since the Trade, Navigation, and Safety, of this Nation, must remain, in some measure, precarious, as long as we are under the Necessity of purchasing and importing all our Naval Stores from foreign Countries; your Majesty’s most faithful Commons will do their utmost Endeavours, that this important and beneficial Branch of Trade may be supplied from your Majesty^ Plantations in America; and thereby divert our Colonies from setting up Manufactures, which directly interfere with those of their Mother Country.

Your Majesty's tender Concern to have the Supplies of this Session so ordered, that your Subjects may be among the earliest in reaping the happy Effects of the general Tranquillity abroad, cannot fail of exciting in your faithful Commons a Desire of making suitable Returns, by proceeding, with all Alacrity, to grant the necessary Supplies for the current Service of the Year, and for discharging the heavy Debt of the Navy: And we find ourselves engaged, by all the Ties of Duty and Interest, to second your Majesty's provident Intentions for suppressing the infamous and pernicious Practice of running Goods; which, besides that it defrauds the publick Revenues, and discourages the honest Trader, may, at this Juncture, endanger the Health and lives of many Thousands of your Majesty’s innocent Subjects.

- The several Points which your Majesty has been graciously pleased to recommend to us, carry in them such evident Marks of your Majesty’s paternal and most affectionate Concern for your People, apd are of such lasting Consequence to the Welfare and Safety of this Nation, that we should be inexcusable, if we did not by a ready Concurrence on our Parts, do all in our Power to render these your Majesty’s most gracious Purposes effectual; and proceed in the Consideration of them with such Temper, Unanimity, and Dispatch, as may fully answer your Majesty’s Expectations, and defeat the Designs of those who hope for any other Contentions amongst us, but of Zeal and Affection towards your Majesty’s Sacred Person, and Government.

The said Address being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nomine contradimite, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to his Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council do humbly know his Majesty's Pleasure, when he will be attended by this House.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Mohiing, Nine of the Clock.

A Petition of the Feoffees of the last Will and Testament of John Marshall, deceased, and of the Rector, and principal Inhabitants, of the Parish of Christ Church, in the County of Surrey, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by, an Act of Parliament, 6° et 70 Wil-liclmi III11, to enable the Inhabitants of the said Parish to make Rates for raising a Maintenance for a Minister; and to impower the Trustees of the Will of the said John Marshall to employ Money for finishing the said Church; it was Enacted, That all such Monies as the said Trustees had in their Hands should be laid out in completing the said Church, and other necessary Wrorks thereto belonging; and that, in lieu of the said Trustees purchasing £. 60. per Annum out of the Rents and Profits of Lands, for Endowment of the Church, which would not raise such a Fund in a very long time, the Minister and Churchwardens, and principal Inhabitants, should yearly rate and tax the Parish with £. 60. per Annum, and no more; but such Assessment not to exceed 3 d. in the Pound: That the Money in the Trustees Hands was all laid out, the £.60. per Annum raised and paid, till within Three Years past; but the Inhabitants are so poor, and the Rents so low, that the Rate aforesaid will not raise the £.60. per Annum: That the Feoffees have strictly performed all the Testator s Charities; save only that, by his Will, he directed, That the Rents and Profits of his Estate, not otherwise disposed of, should be for ever disposed in buying Impropriate Rectories to his Feoffees, and their Heirs, for continuing the sincere preaching God’s Word in this Land fof ever: That the Trustees have now in their Hands above £. 2,600. arisen by the undisposed Rents and Profits; which, they conceive, will be more than sufficient to rebuild the Church, and enlarge the Church-yard; the Church being very ruinous, and the Church-yard not sufficient to bury their Dead; and hope it will be thought as great a Benefaction in the pious Design of the Testator, the First Founder of the said Church, to have it rebuilt, and the Church-yard enlarged, out of the Trust-money, than otherwise to dispose of the same; the Parishioners being willing to make good the £. 60. per Annum to their Rector, provided their Rate do not exceed 6d. in the Pound for any one Year: And praying, That Leave be* given lo bring in a Bill for new -building the said Church, and enlarging the Churchward.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee; And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Lade, Mr. Cozcpcr, Sir John Philips, Mr. Ellis, Mr. Pelham, Mr. Bond, Lord Wm. P owlet t, Mr. Hey sham, Mr. Broderick, Mr. Gwyn, Mr. Clayton, Colonel Bladen, Sir John Bland, Mr. Palmer, Mr. Sandys, General Wade, Mr. Doddington, Sir Jacob Astlcy, Sir Tho. llanmer, Mr. Mason, Mr. Ash, Sir Tho. That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter <rf the said Petition; and find,

That, by an Act of Parliament, passed in the 6th And 7th Years of the lleign of his late Majesty King Wiliam the 11 Id, for the enabling the Inhabitants of the said Parish to make Rates for raising a Maintenance for a good and able Minister; and for the impowering the Trustees of the Will of the said Jofui Marshall, deceased, to employ Monies for the finishing tire said Parish Church; all such Money as had been raised out of the Lands vested ki the said Trustees, under the Will of the said John Marshall, and then remaining in their Hands, was, by the said Act* directed to be laid out in the completing the said Church, by building a Steeple, putting up a Clock and Bells for the same, and in other necessary Works; and that, in Lieu and Recompence of the said Feoffees purchasing an Estate of £. Go. per Annum for the Endowment of the said Church, which, by the Will of the said John Marshall, was to be purchased out of the Profits arising out of Lands not thereby otherwise disposed of, the Minister and the Churchwardens of the said Parish, for the Time being, together with Ten or more of the substantial Householders, were, by the said Act, impowered to rate and assess, by an equal Pound rate, nbtexceeding Three Pence in the Pound, the yearly Sum oi£. 6o. and no more, upon the Inhabitants, and Occupiers of Estates, within the said Parish, liable to the Poors Rates, for an additional Maintenance for the Minister; which was constantly raised, and paid accordingly, till within about Three Years last past; wherein there could not be raised, by the said Rate, more than £. 35. one Year with another.

That it appeared to the Committee, The said Parish Church, which has been built 50 Years and upwards, standing under-ground, and a slight lirick Building, is now in a very decaying Condition, both withinside and without; and that the Church-yard, which is but small, by reason of the greatTncrease of the Inhabitants since the said Church was built, and the frequent Burial of their Dead, is become uncapable to receive and cover their Dead; and that the Ground lies now almost as high as the Windows of the said Church; which being a marshy Ground, the Graves both within and without the said Church are filled with Water as soon as they are dug.

That the Will of the said John Marshall, dated the 21st of August 1627, was produced to the Committee; whereby he directed, in the last Place, thus; That the

Parish, who also attended the said Committee, ate desirous and willing to make good the £.60. per Annum to the present Rector, and his Successors, in such manner as is prescribed by the said Act of the 6th and 7th Years of his said late Majesty King William; provided such Rate do hot exceed the Rate of 6d. in the Pound for any One Year; and that the Inhabitants be not chargeable with such new Building of the Church, or Enlargement of, or purchasing, a new Church-yard.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for impowering the Feoffees under the Will of John Marshall, deceased, to dispose of the Money in their Hands for the Rebuilding of the Parish schiirch of Christ Church, in the County of Surrey; and to enable the Churchwardens and Inhabitants of the said Parish to make Rates for the Maintenance of a good and able Minister: And that Mr.

Lade and Mr. Halsey do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A PETITION of the Merchants, and others, concerned in the Making and Curing of Red Herrings, in the Town of Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth; That the Petitioners did, in the last Session of Parliament, petition this House; setting forth the Hardships and Inconveniences they lie under, as the Law now stands, in relation to Red-herrings consumed at home, by being obliged to cure them with Salt which has paid the Duty; and the House, being satisfied of the same, came to the following Resolution; viz. " That the taking off the Duties upon all Salt " used in Curing and Making of Red-herrings, and, instead thereof, laying a proportionable Duty upon all " Red-herrings consumed at home only, will be of Service " to the Makers of Red-herrings, and no Prejudice to " the Revenue but, the Session being at that time so far advanced* the Petitioners could not then obtain such Relief as they hoped for: And praying, That the House will take their Case into Consideration, and give them such Relief in the Premises as the i^ouse shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Ditto. A Petition of the Mayor, Common Council, princi-

pal Merchants and Traders, of the City of Exon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the chief Support of that Country is the Woollen Manufacture, principally carried on with Irish Wool; which, of Exportation for England, pays a high Duty of 15 d. for every Eighteen Pounds Weight; and 4id. more is required, and paid to the Lord Lieutenant, for Licence to export it; so that the French run Wrool from Ireland 20per Cent. cheaper than the British Manufacturer can have it; by which Means they have not only supplied their own Nation, but several other foreign Countries, with Wroollcn Goods, at a lower Price than the English possibly can, especially considering the great Duties on Soap and Candles, Oil, and Dye-stuffs; vast Quantities of which are necessarily used in the Manufacturing and Dressing of Wool, and Woollen Goods: And praying, That such Duties may be taken off as may tend to encourage the Woollen Manufacture, and benefit the numerous poor Labourers therein.

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Incorporation of Weavers, Fullers, and Sheermen, within the City of Exon, and others concerned in the Woollen Manufacture, w.as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Woollen Manufactury has been exceedingly decaying for many Years past; occasioned, as they conceive, by reason that the Traders therein have been incapable to dispose their Goods in foreign Markets to very little, if any, Advantage; they having been supplied by the French on cheaper Terms, as is very obvious; for, since the French have been visited with the Pestilence, their Commerce hath had a Stop, and our W’oollen Trade is greatly revived; so that the Decay of our Trade seems, to the Petitioners, to be intirely owing to the high Duties payable on the several Commodities used in manufacturing the same; and, particularly, the Duty on Wool imported from Ireland for England; which is near 20per Cent. dearer to his Majesty's Subjects than to Foreigners, who have it without paying any such Duty; and also the Duties on Soap, Candles, Oil, and Dye-stuff’ made use of in the Dressing and Manufacturing of Woollen Goods; so that, by reason of such Duties, Foreigners can sell their Goods much cheaper than the Petitioners; w hereby our Trade is in Danger of being mtirely lost: And praying the House to take effectual Methods to retrieve the same, and relieve the Petitioners in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Phil pot t reported from the Committee, to whom Kilburn the Petition of the Trustees appointed to put in Execution bridge, &c. an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, for repairing the Highway between Kilburn Bridge, in the County of Middlesex, and SparrorusAient, in the County of Hertford, was referred, That they had examined the Matter thereof; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That, by the said Act, passed in the 1 oth Year of her late Majesty’s Reign, several Tolls were laid on Coaches,

Carts, Carriages, and Cattle, for repairing the said Highways; which Tolls were to be collected for the Term of One-and-twenty Years.

That the Committee find, upon Examination of Witnesses, . William Buclcnall Esquire, and Mr. Francis Peters, That, the Roads being so very bad at the time of passing the said Act, the Trustees were necessitated to borrow Money for an immediate Supply, as by the said Act they were impowered to do, to put the same into such Repair, as that Passengers might travel in the Winter-season without Danger; and the Trustees have since borrowed a further Sum of Money on the Credit of the said Toll; so there is now owing the Sum of £.4,042. principal Money, besides the Sum of £.347. for the Interest of the said Suga so borrowed.

That it appeared to the Committee, That the yearly Income of the said Tolls amounts to about £.501. one Year with another, clear of all Charges; which, after Payment of the Interest of the said principal Sum so borrowed, and now owing, there w ill remain only £.299. per Annum towards discharging the said Debt:

That, there being but Eleven Years and a Half to come of the Term granted by the said Act, the Money arising by the said Toll during that time will scarce repay the Money borrowed; so the Trustees, during the Remainder of the said Term, will be prevented from Jaying out any thing in amending the said Roads; and the keeping them in such Repair as they now are will amount to about £.300. per Annum, one Year with another, while the present Act continues in Force.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highway between a certain Place called Kilburn Bridge, in the County of Middlesex, and SparrousAtern, in the County of Hertford; and for making the said Act more effectual: And that Mr. Plnlpott and Mr. Bertie do prepare, and bring in, the same.

An Account how the said Duties stand appropriated: Also,

An Account of the net Produce of the Duties on Candles from Midsummer 1719 to Midsummer 1721: And also,

A Petition of the Mayor, capital Burgesses, Freemen, out;egori and principal Inhabitants, of the Borough of Came/Jord, Soap, &c. in the County of Cornwall; and of the principal Merchants and Traders within the said Borough, and Places adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That their chief Support is the Woollen Manufacture, carried on by Irish Wool transported to Biddeford; but, of late, little or none has been transported thither; for want w hereof, a Third-part of their Spinners lie unemployed; which is occasioned by the Duty p&vabie on Exportation of Irish Wool for England; to save which Duty, it is evident the Irish have run vast Quantities of their Wool to France; whereby the French are enabled to undersell the Petitioners in foreign Markets; especially considering the great Duties now upon Oil, Soap, Can-, dies, and Dye-stuffs used in Woollen Goods: And praying, That the said Duties may be taken off; or such.

Means found out, as the House shall think most proper, for the Ease and Relief of the Petitioners.

THE House being informed, That Mr. Frecker, from the Treasury, attended at the Door;

He was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, a Copy of the Report from the Commissioners of the Customs to the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty’s Treasury, relating to Coals carried from Ellen foot to Bank-end on the River Eden, Duty-free.

And then he withdrew.

The Title of the said Report was read.

The said Report is as followeth; viz-

May it please your Lordships,

IN Obedience to your Commands, signified to usby One of your Lordships Secretaries, on the annexed Petition of Thomas Pattinson of Carlisle, in behalf of himself, John Hicks, and Henry Onne; praying, in regard it will be for the general good of the whole Country, and only for the Improvement of their Lands, That your Lordships will please to give them Leave to apply to Parliament for Liberty to carry Coals and Lime from Alien-foot to Bank-cnd, in the River Eden, without being Subject to the Payment of Duty for the same; your Lordships directing us to report a State of the Case, with our Opinion;

Wc humbly report, That, by Law', all Qoals shipped, or water-borne in order to be shipped, or laid on board rrr , Tr any Ship or Vessel, to be carried by

9 13 Sea; anc* w^ch shall ke carried by

9° cap! 6. Sea, in any Ship or Vessel, from any Port or Place within this Kingdom; and which shall be imported, brought, or landed, in any other Port or Place within the same Kingdom; being most usually sold by the Chalder; are liable to the Payment of 5 s. for every Chalder, Winchester Measure; and for such Coals as are usually sold by Weight, 3 s. 4 d. for every Ton, to consist of 20 C. Weight.

We further report, That we have, on this Occasion, consulted the proper Officers of the Customs; w ho have certified us, That Ellen foot, the Place where the Coals are proposed to be shipped, is about five Leagues out at Sea, Southw ard from the Mouth of the River Eden, in the County of Cumberland', by which the Coals are liable to the aforesaid Duties: The said Officers have also certified us, That there are great Tracts of Land adjoining to the said River Eden, which lie uncultivated for want of Coals and Lime:

That before the Laws which charge the Duty upon Coals water-borne, it was usual to carry Coals from several Places in the Bay or Firth of Eden, to several Places up that River; But there are some inland Collieries, from w hence Coals are now brought by Land, at less Expence than the Duty: Therefore no Coals have been carried up that River, as formerly, since the Duty was charged; nor is there any Expectation there ever will during the Continuance thereof:

For which Reasons we have no Objection to the Petitioners applying to Parliament to be excused from Payment of the said Duty, in this particular Case, for such Coals as are to be put on board any Vessel or Boat at Ellen foot, and landed at any Place in the said River Eden lying to the Northward of Ellenfoot; provided the Owner or Master of every Boat or Vessel carrying such Coals do 1

first enter into Bond, with sufficient Sureties, at least once a Year, with a general Condition, That all such Coals as he shall take on board his Vessel or Boat, by virtue of a Sufferance from the proper Officers, shall be landed in some Place in the River Eden, lying to the Northward of Ellen foot, and bring a Return, signed by the proper Officer, That such Coals were there duly landed; the Persons respectively concerned paying, for each Bond,

One Shilling, and no more, besides the Stamp-duties; and to the Officers granting the Sufferance and Return, for each Loading, the Sum of 4 d.: to be

distributed in such manner as the Commissioners of the Customs, now, and for the Time being, shall think proper.

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordships Consideration.

Robert Baylis,

Custom-house, London, Walter Yonge,

23d November, 1721. J. Stanley,

J. Pulteney,

T. Walker.

A true Copy: Examined by Mark Frecker.

28 th November 1721.

A Petition of the Soap-boilers, Retailers of Soap, Duties on Linen-drapers, Oil-makers, and Baltick Traders, in North SoaP* Britain, subscribing in Name and Behalf of themselves, and great Numbers of others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Duties upon Soap from the 24th of June 1714, to the 24th of June 1721, have produced but £.6,876. 3,?. 4%d.; yet the imposing it, has destroyed all the Soap-works, which were in a flourishing State before those Duties; and they have lessened the Trajie of the Retailers, and heightened the Price of Linen Cloth, to the Prejudice of the Dealers in it: That the Trade of making Fish-oil is thereby^much discouraged, and the Returns from the Baltick lessened, for want of the usual Consumption of Pot-ashes and Clapboards: Besides, these high Duties tempt evil Persons to run Soap; to which if is peculiarly adapted, as being put up in small portable Casks, and free from being damaged or embezzled; to which Liquors, and other Commodities, are liable; And this Duty, though but little in its Produce, is also a most heavy Tax upon all Persons and Families of inferior Rank: And praying, That the Prejudices arising to Trade, and this Nation, by the Duties on Soap, may be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A PETITION of the Portreeve, Freeholders; and Duties on Woollen Manufacturers of the Borough of Askbtir1 Soap.&c. ton, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House; and readsetting forth, That the Traders in the Woollen Manufactures have, in great Measure, quitted their,

Trades, by reason they are uncapable of disposing their Goods in foreign Markets, to any tolerable Advantage; the same having been supplied by the French on cheaper Terms; which, the Petitioners conceive, is intirely ow ing to the high Duties payable on the several Commodities used in manufacturing the same; and especially the Duty on Irish Wool, which is near 20 per Cent, dearer to his Majesty’s Subjects than the French; and also the Duties on Soap, Candles, Oil, and Dye-stuffs, used in Cleansing of Wool, and Woollen Goods; by means whereof, the said Trade is in great Danger of being lost: And praying the House to apply some proper Remedy for retrieving the said Trade.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Silk-weavers in and about London, in behalf of themselves, and Trade, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners were used to employ many Thousands of poor Families in the Winding, Weaving, and Dressing, of Silks, the Return of Woollen and other Manufactures exported to Turkey and Italy: That, by the clandestine Importation of foreign-wrought Silks, but more especially by the Running, and almost universal Wearing, of prohibited East India w rought Silks, the Petitioners Trade is so far decreased, that they arc no longer able to subsist the poor; by reason whereof, many Thousand of them, the Number daily increasing, will be reduced to extreme Want, and become an insupportable Burthen to their Parishes; and his Majesty’s Customs, and Excise, very much lessened; and the &lk Manufactures, by which an immense Treasure is saved to this Kingdom, is in the utmost Danger of being lost: And praying. That their deplorable Condition may be considered, and the Prohibition of the said East India Silks made more effectual.

A PETITION of the Mayor, Bdrgeases, and Com- Bristol monalty, of the City of Bristol, was presented to Exchange* the House, and read; setting forth, That the said City is very much increased of late Years in its Trade and Inhabitants; so that the Tolzey, or Exchange where Merchants meet, is become too narrow; and it being mostly an open Street, and very little Shelter from the Weather, the Health of those that resort thither, is often impaired:

That the Petitioners have found out a convenient Piece of Ground, near the said Tolzey, for building an Exchange, whereon are some old Houses; and have treated with the Owners thereof; some of whom are Infants, some Feoffees, in Trust for charitable Uses; and some Part entailed: That it is impracticable to carry on the said Design, without the Assistance of Parliament: And praying,

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Owners of the said Ground, and Houses, to contract with the Petitioners for the same, in order to build an Exchange thereupon.

Mr. Haldane reported from the Committee, to whom Salt erpwu the Petition of Robert Dalrymple Esquire, on behalf of the

Right honourable James Earl of Wemys, w as referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find,

That, in the Months of May, June, August, and Sep* tember, 1714, 6,962 Bushels of Salt were shipped at a Creek belonging to the said Earl, called The Methill, which Creek is Part of the Port of Kircaldie; and that the said Salt was put on board Four different Ships; and, being exported to Parts beyond Sea, the said Earl’s Agents gave Bonds for the Duty thereof:

That, the said Earl having, for many Years before the Union, a Privilege of exporting all Commodities of the Growth, Product, and Manufacture, of Scotland, from the said Creek of Methill, Duty-free; the said Earl’s Agents apprehended there was no Necessity for any formal Entry of any Salt exported from the said Creek beyond the Seas:

That upon making Application to the Commissioners of the Salt-duty in Scotland for Debentures for the Salt so exported, to answer the Bonds which were given for the Duty of the said Salt, the Commissioners refused to make out the Debentures so demanded, by reason the said Salt was not entered and certified in such time, and ih such manner, as the Law directs.

That it appeared to the said Committee, That the said 6,962 Bushels of Salt was, in Four Parcels, and at different times, actually, and bona Jidc, exported to Parts beyond the Seas; and although the same was so exported, yet, the same not being certified in due Form, the said Earl cannot be relieved in the Premises, as the Law now

stands*

stands, without some Provision be made for that Purpose.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upota the Table.

A PETITION of divers Gentlemen and Tradesmen Laws relat-inhabiting in the Borough and Liberty of St. Alban9s, ing to High-in the County of Hertford, and in the County of Bed- wa7s‘ ford, who have Goods carried to and from London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the great Road leading through St. Alban's, and some Part of Bedfordshire, hath been lately infested by Robert Cutk-bert, Tho, Edwards, and other Informers, who, under Pretence of putting the Law in Execution against Waggoners travelling with Wheels of less than Two Inches and an Half broad in their Streaks, or Tire, have unlawfully seized their Horses, and extorted divers Sums of Money from the Waggoners, although their Wheels, when worn, have been more than Two Inches and an Half broad, as has been proved before some Justices of the Peace; by which Seizures the Petitioners are very much incommoded, and Trade much hindered: And praying some speedy Remedy for preventing the said Mischiefs.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of Linen Mnnu-the City of Glasgow > was presented to the House, and factures. read; setting forth, That the vast Quantities of foreign 8 M Linen

686 7° Decem A. 1721.

linen imported into, and used in, Britain, have greatly lessened the Consumption of our own Linen at home; and is one of the Causes of their Decay, and the Want of employing their Poor therein: That the Drawback allowed upon Exportation of foreign Linen has encouraged the Exportation to the Plantations, lowered the Price of our own, and rendered it almost impracticable to export it thither; which, with the high Duty of 3d. per Yard upon all Linen printed, stained, or painted, in Great Britain, and the Duty upon Soap, has finished their Trade in the Linen Manufacture, which is the ancient Staple Manufacture of North Britain, as the Woollen Manufacture is of South Britain: That, since his Majesty, in 'his Speech, has recommended to the House the Encouragement of the British Manufactures, the Petitioners pray the Consideration of the House, so that the said Duties Qf 3d. per Yard, and upon Soap, may be taken off; and otherwise to redress the Grievances of the Linen Manufacture in Scotland, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Lineu Maau- A Petition of the Provost, Magistrates, and Common

factures. Council, of the Burgh of Kirkcaldie, in the County of Fifey North Britain, for themselves, and in Name of many Thousands in the said Town, and adjacent County, concerned in the making of, and trading in, Linen, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Linen Manufactures in Scotland is the main Support

of their common People; which is fallen under great

Decay of late, by reason of the heavy Duty of 3d. per Yard on their printed, stained, or painted, Linen, which is generally of so small a Value as from Six Pence to Ten Pence per Yard: That the evident Grievance of this Duty, and the Benefit that will accrue to the Nation, and the Revenue, by taking oft* this Duty, will more than sufficiently balance the inconsiderable produce thereof, by the Increase of Trade, and Employment of the Poor; and, hs the Woollen Manufactures, in England pay no Duty, it seems agreeable to an equal Encouragement of Trade in all Parts of the U nited Kingdom stipulated by the Treaty of Union, that the Linen Manufacture should be also free from Duty; And praying, That the State of their Linen Manufacture may be taken into Consideration, and the said Duty of 3d.. per Yard taken off.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ditto. A Petition of the Weavers and other Dealers in Linen

Manufactures, in and about the City of Glasgow, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the great Quantities of foreign Linen imported, and the Drawback allowed upon exporting the same, has very much lessened the Price and Consumption of the Scotch Linen Manufacture; but that which has principally affected them, is the high Duty of 3d. per Yard upon all stamped, stained, or printed* Linen, although the prime Cost is but from 6d. to 10d. pei' Yard, and is above £.30. per Cent, ad valorem; and also the Duty upon Soap, which is the chief Ingredient that brings their Linen to Perfection, more proper than any other to receive and retain the Impression, and Colours stamped upon it; so that, by the Decay of Trade therein, many Thousands of poor People are reduced to extreme Poverty, for want of Employment; and the Linen Manufacture, which was the Staple Commodity of Scotland, is likely to be utterly lost to them: And praying, That the Scotch Linen Manufactures may be free from Duty, as well as all other Staple Manufactures of Britain and the Petitioners put upon an equal Footing.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upoix the Table.

That the Committee, pursuant to the* Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Allegations contained in the said Petition:

Arid the Charter granted to the said Borough by Queen Elizabeth, in the Eighteenth Year of her Reign, was produced to the said Committee.

That it appeared to the Committee, The Port of the said Borough was heretofore a Place of great Trade and Commerce.

That John Thomas^ an Engineer, being examined, said. That the said Haven, having been neglected, is choaked up with Sands, and the Piers thereof much ruined; by % reason whefeof, there is not at this time, any Security for Ships; but the Haven is capable of being improved, and made very commodious for Shipping.

That Mr. Andreev Waif, being examined by the Committee, said, That several Ships had, by Stress of Weather, been Shipwrecked.

That it appeared to the said Committee, That, if the said Haven and Piers were restored and rebuilt, and a Sluice made to cleanse and scour the same, it would prevent Shipwrecks for the future; and be a Means to revive the ancient Trade of the said Borough, greatly augment his Majesty’s Customs, and much increase the yearly Value of Lands adjacent to the said Borough, and preserve the Lives of many of his Majesty's Subjects.

A PETITION of the Provost, Bailiffs, and Common Council, of the Burgh of Aberdeen, in North Britain, in behalf of themselves, and many thousands in the said Burgh and County, concerned about, making of, and trading in, Linen, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Linen Manufacture is the only Staple Commodity of Scotland, made out of their own Materials; and used to employ and maintain their Poor: But the same is fallen into great Decay, and lessened in the Consumption thereof; not only because they are obliged to bury in Linen; but, by the Duty of 3d. per Yard, laid on their printed, stained, or painted, Linen Cloth, from 6d. to 10 d. per Yard, which is chiefly used; and the Duty on Soap made use of in Whitening thereof; the Manufacture is, in a manner, lost: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises, so as the said Duties may be taken off, and the Petitioners thereby relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the People called Quakers, on behalf of Quakers’ such of their Friends who scruple the Form of solemn Affirmation. Affirmation, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That many of their Friends do conscientiously scruple the present Form of solemn Affirmation; whereby they have fallen under great Sufferings, by Imprisonment, or Loss of their Properties; they not being able to answer in Courts of Equity, take Probates of Wills, prove Debts on Commissions of Bankruptcy, verify their Entries on the Leather or Candle Acts, take up their Freedoms, be admitted to poll for their Freeholds, give Evidence for others, nor to declare their Fidelity to the present Government; all which they conceive to be Hardships: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for granting them such a Form of Affirmation as may remove the Difficulties they now lie under.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir John Ward, Mr. Hcyshani, the Lord JVm. Powlet, Mr.

Lawson, Mr. Walpole, and Mr. James Loidhcr, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Farrer, according to Order, reported, from the Ways and Committee of the w hole House, to whom it was referred Means, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the said Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

1. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the making the Exportation of our own Manufactures, and the Importation of the Commodities used in the Manufacturing of them, more easy and practicable, will greatly conduce to the Inlargement of the Commerce of Great Britain.

2. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an Allowance be paid upon the Exportation of all Stuffs, made in Great Britain, of Silk only, reckoning Sixteen Ounces to the Pound-weight.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Allowance upon the Exportation of the said Stuffs, made in Great Britain, of Silk only, be after the Rate of Three Shillings per Pound-weight.

4. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an Allowance be paid upon the Exportation of all Silks, and Ribbons, made in Great Britain, of Silk mixed with Gold or Silver.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Allowance upon the Exportation of the said Silks, and Ribbonsy made in Great Britain, of Silk mixed with Gold or Silver, be after the Rate of Four Shillings per Pound weight.

6. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an Allowance be paid upon the Exportation of Silk Stockings, Silk Gloves, Fringes, Laces, stitching and sewing Silk, made in Great Britain.

7. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Allowance upon the Exportation of Silk Stockings, Silk Gloves, Fringes, Laces, stitching and sewing Silk, made in Great Britain, be after the Rate of One Shilling and Three Pence per Pound-weight.

8. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an Allowance be made upon the Exportation of all Stuffs, made in Great Britain, of Silk and G rogram-yarn.

9. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Allowance upon the said Stuffs, made of Silk and Grogram-yarn, be after the Rate of Eight Pence per Pound-weight.

iq. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, i

That an Allowance be made upon the Exportation of all

11. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Allowance for Stuffs, made in Great Britain, of Silk mixed with Incle or Cotton, be after the Rate of One Shilling per Pound-w eight.

12. Resolved\ That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Allowance be made upon the Exportation of alL Stuffs, made in Great Britain, of Silk and Worsted.

13. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Allowance upon all Stuffs, made in Great Britain, of Silk and Worsted, be after the Rate of Six Pence per Pound-weight.

14. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That the said Allowances do continue for the Space of Three Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament.

15. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties payable upon the Exportation of the British Manufactures herein after-mentioned; that is to say, Apothecary and Confectionary Wares, Aqua-vitae; Ale, Beer, or Mum; Bags, Books, Maps, and Pictures, Brass and Copper wrought, Bridies, Buttons of all Sorts> Bricks, Coaches and Chariots, Cordage, Earthen-ware, Glass for Windows, Drinking-glasses, and Bottles of all Storts, Gloves, plain Leather, Gunpowder, Haberdashery-ware, Hair-cloth, Harness for Coaches, Holsters, Blowing-horns, small Lanthorn-leaves, Powder-horns, Horse-litters and Sedans, Ilorse-collars, Hoops for Barrels, Iron wrought, and Clock-work, Iron Ordnance, Lace of Gold and Silver, Leather wrought, Lime, Nails, Oker, Parchment, Paste-boards, Pewter, Rape-cakes, Saddles, great and small, Saddle-trees, Scabbards for Swords, Shovels, shod and unshod, Soap, hard Soap, Starch, Sugar refined, Silk wrought, Tobacco-pipes, Virginals, Watches; Wax, Bees and Sealing; white Woollen Cloths, Yarn, Grogfam, Upholders-ware, and Perriwigs; be taken off.

16. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties payable upon the Importation of the several Materials used in Dyeing, hereafter mentioned; that is to say, Agarisk, Alltim, Annotto, Antimonium crudum, Aqua-fortis, Argo), Arsenick, Bay-berries, Brazil Wood, Braziletto Wood, Cochineal, Copperas of ail Sorts, Crema Tartar, Fustick, Gauls, Gum Arabick, or Seneca, Indico of all Sorts, Issinglas, Litmuss, Logwood, Madder of all Sorts, Madder-roots, Nicaragua-wood, Orchal, Orchelia, Pomgranate-peels, Redwood, Sal Flower, Sal Armoniack, Sal Gem, Sal Petre, Sapan-wood, Saunders, Red Shumack, Sticklack, Tornsall, Va-ionia, and Verdigrease, be taken off.

17. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such of the said Materials used in Dyeing as shall hereafter be imported free of Duty, and shall afterwards be exported, be charged with a Duty equal to the Difference between the present Duty and the present Drawback.

18. Resolved\ That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Ten Pence, Part of the Duty payable for each Beaver-skin imported, be taken off

19. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That upon the Exportation of Beaver-skins a Draw back of Three Pence per Skin be allowed, and no more.

20. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties payable upon Pepper imported, and entered for Home-consumption, be reduced to Four Pence per Pound-weight, over and above the Half Subsidy.

21. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties payable upon the Importation of Hemp into Great Britain, from the British Plantations in America, be taken off.

22. Resolved, That Is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties payable upon the Importation of all Timber, Wood, and Lumber, excepting Masts, Oak, Ash, Beech, and Elm, imported into Great Britain, from the British Plantations in America, be taken off

A Petition of Richard Lord Viscount Dillon, in the Kingdom of Ireland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by Fine and Conveyance, in i 688, divers Manors and Lands ini the Counties of Mayo, Roscommon, and Westmeath, iii Ireland, were settled upon the Petitioner’s Father arid Mother for their Lives; Remainder to the Petitioner, arid his Heirsi Male; Remainder to Arthur Dillon, his Uncle arid his Heirs Male; Remainder to Luke Dillon, another Uncle, and his Heirs Male; and the Petitioners Father, Henry Lord Dillon, deceased, was thereby empowered to sell or mortgage ariy Part of the Premises, in Westmeath, to discharge Incumbrances that might affect the settled Premises; with Power for the Petitioner to mhke a Settlement upon his Wife, when he should be in Possession of the Estate: That, by Act of Parliament, passed 20 Anna, for Sale of Part of the Estate of the said Lord Dillon, for Payment of his Debts, the said settled Premises were vested in Trustees, discharged of all Estates for Life in Tail, and other Incumbrances in Trust, by Mortgage, Sale, or otherwise, to raise Money to pay all the Debts, to which the said Estate is liable; in which Act there is a- Saving Clause to the Queen, and all other Persons, except the said Henry Lord Dillon, and all others, to whom the Premises were, by particular Name, limited, by the sai4 Settlement-all such Right and Title as they then had to any the Premises: That the* said Arthur and LukeDillon were attainted for High Treason, on Account of the late Rebellion in Ireland; whereby their Remainders becanie forfeited, and vested in the Crown: And although the Lands intended to be sold were, by the said Act, vested in Trustees, in Fee-simple, discharged of all Remainders; yet, by reason of the said saving Clause to the Cfowri, all Persons have been discouraged to purchase under the said Act; and the Incumbrances still remain, and, by Interest, increase, to the Prejudice of all Parties concerned: That the Petitioner is desirous to make a Settlement upon his Wife, according to the Power given him by the said Settlement; but is advised he cannot legally do it, because the Freehold and Inheritance of the greatest Part of the Premises is in several Persons by Mortgages in Fee, made before the / Settlement; and the other Part is in his Mother, for Life; so that he is disabled to make any Provision for his Wife, and is in Danger of being foreclosed of his Equity of Redemption by the Mortgagees: That the said Remainders, now vested in the Crown, are so remote, as not likely ever to take Effect in Possession his Majesty is pleased that the said former Act may be made effectual: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend the said Act, by expressly discharging the said Lands vested in the Trustees, as aforesaid, of and from the said Remainders vested in the Crown; and to make such Provision for his Wife as the House shall think fit.

AP ET I T I O N of the Mayor and Commonalty of the City of 1 'ark, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, Time out of mind, there hath been within the said City a free Market for Butter; which, by V oj-. 1 9.

Mr. Thompson reported from the Committee, to whom ScarborooiH the Petition of the Bailiffs, the Gentlemen of the Coin- Harboan' mon Council, and other the principal Inhabitants, of the ancient Corporation of Scarborough, in the County of ‘

York, was referred, That they had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterw ards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same wa9 read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, to w hom the Consideration of the said Petition was referred, pursuant to the Order of this House, proceeded to examine the Matter thereof: And,

Air. John Lazinghy, being examined by the said Committee, said, That be has lived at Scarborough several Years; and that he believed the Harbour of Scarborough iscapa- (

ble of being made a very commodious one for all light 5

or Ioaden Ships using the Coast-trade; but, for want of I

an additional new Pier, the Ships lying in the present Harbour are often broke loose by the Violence and Surge of the Sea; and are very much damaged, and sometimes

lost:

8 Geo. I. i8° Decembrls. 697

lost; by whose Evidence it appeared, That the Harbour is not large enough for the Ships of the said Town that usually ride therein.

William Otbic, a Pilot, being examined, said, He was born at Scarborough; and confirmed what Mr. La-zingby had before said: And further informed the Committee, That there is a stock called Ramsdale Scar, which makes the Entrance into the said Harbour very dangerous to Strangers; and that many Ships have been lost thereby: But the Examinant said, If a new Pier was erected upon that Rock, as is intended, it will prevent all the Mischief that has happened.

Robert Allison, who had been a Master of a Ship for Fifteen Years, said, That he is very well acquainted with Scarborough Harbour; and that if the same was enlarged, as proposed, it would be a great Advantage to Navigation in general, and a Benefit to the Coal trade in particular; and be a safe Retreat for all Ships in time of War, or bad Weather.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Pier and Harbour of Scarborough, in the County of York: and that Mr. Hungerford and Mr. Thompson do prepare, and bring in, the same.

i^-rd Dillon's Mr. Carter reported from the Committee, to whom L&tates. the Petition ot Richard Lord Viscount Dillon of the Kingdom of Ireland wax referred, That they had exa-10

mined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and it appeared to the Committee,

That, by Fines, and other Conveyances, levied and executed in the Year 1688, divers Manors, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, in the several Counties of Mayo, Roscommon, and Westmeath, in the Kingdom of Ireland, were, upon the Marriage of the Petitioner’s Father and Mother, the late Lord Viscount and Viscountess Dillon, settled upon them for Life; Remainder to the Petitioner, now Lord Viscount Dillon, for Life, without Impeachment of Waste; with Remainder to his First and other Sons; Remainder to Arthur Dillon Esquire, the Petitioner's Uncle; with like Remainder, in Tail Male, to his First and other Son9 successively; Remainder to Luke Dillon, another Uncle of the said Petitioner’s, for Life; with the like Remainders, in Tail Male successively, to his First, and other Sons; with other Remainders over:

That the said late Lord Viscount Dillon, Father to the Petitioner the present Lord Viscount Dillon, had a Power, by the said Settlement, with the Consent of Frances Countess of Tyrconnel, to sell or mortgage all or any of the Lands in the County of Westmeath, towards discharging the Incumbrances affecting the Lunds comprised in the said Settlement; with Power to the Petitioner, the present Lord Dillon, when he should be Tenant of the Freehold in Possession, to limit any Part of the Premises, as he should be seised of, to any Woman as he should marry; so as the same did not exceed the Value of One-third Part of the said Estate:

That the Petitioner produced to the Committee an Act of Parliament, passed in the 2d Year of the Reign of the late Queen, for Sale of Part of the Estate of Henry late Lord Viscount Dillon, for Payment of his Debts; and for settling an Equivalent, in other Part of his Estate, on the Viscountess his Wife, for her Jointure; whereby' it appeared, That the^ several Lands in the said Act mentioned were vested in the Trustees therein named, in Fee-simple, discharged of all Estates for Life in Tail, and other Incumbrances whatsoever; upon Trust, that they, and the Survivor of them, with the Consent of Henry Lord Viscount Dillon, his Executors and Administrators, and not otherwise, should, by leasing, Mortgaging or absolute Sale, thereof, with the Rents and Profits in the mean time, discharge all the Debts which the Premises in the said Settlement mentioned were liable to, or so much thereof as the Lands thereby vested w;ould satisfy; with a Saving to the Queen, her Heirs and Successors, and all and every other Person and Persons, Bodies Politick and Corporate (except the said Henry Lord Dillon, and all others to whom the Premises were, by particular Name, limited for Life, in Tail Male, or in Fee, or for any other Estate, by the said Settlement), All such Right, Estate, Title, and Interest, as they, or any of them, then had in, to, or out of, the Premises.

That it also appeared to the Committee, That the said Arthur and Luke Dillon, the Petitioner’s Uncles, to whom the Remainders for Life were severally limited by the said Settlement, were attainted for High Treason, on account of the late Rebellion in Ireland; by means whereof their said Remainders became forfeited to, and vested in, the Crown; and though, by the said Act, the Lands intended to be sold were vested in the Trustees, in Fee-simple, discharged of all Remainders, yet, there being a Saving therein of the Crown's Right, as aforesaid, all Persons have been discouraged from becoming Purchasers under the said Act, by reason the Remainders are so vested in the Crown; and the said Trustees have not been able to discharge the said Incumbrances, which are thereby much increased; to the manifest Prejudice of those interested in the Premises:

That

8 Geo. I.

190 Decemb

699

That the present Lord Dillon is desirous to settle Part of the Premises on the Viscountess his Wife, for her Jointure, according to the Power reserved to him by the said Settlement: But it appearing, that, in Strictness, he cannot legally execute such a Power, the actual Freehold and Inheritance of the greatest Part of the Premises being in several Persons, by virtue of Mortgages in Fee, made before the said Settlement; and the actual Freehold of other Part thereof is in the present Lord Dillons Mother, by the said former Act; so that he is disabled to make any effectual Provision for the Viscountess his Wife, and is in Danger of being foreclosed of his Equity of the Premises.

That the Committee find the Remainder now vested in the Crown is very remote, and not likely ever to take Effect in Possession; and that it will be for the Benefit of all Parties concerned, that the said Debts should be paid off *, and the said former Act of Parliament rendered effectual, by expressly discharging the Lands, intended by the said Act to be sold, from the said Remainders now vested in the Crown.

7. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such of the said Materials used in Dyeing, as shall hereafter be imported free of Duty, and shall afterwards be exported, be charged with a Duty equal to the Difference between the present Duty and the present Drawback.

10. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties upon Nutmegs imported be reduced to One Shilling and Six Pence per Pound Weight.

A PETITION of the poor insolvent Debtors in the Castle of Chester, in behalf of themselves, and manyl111^ Thousands more in the several Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That as the late Act for Relief of poor Prisoners did provide against Extortions; yet, not looking so far back as to such who had given their Creditors Securities by Mortgages and Bonds, as soon as the Limitation of the Time and Sum appointed by the said Act was known, the Gaols were crouded (though the Creditors had the Prisoners All), and where they still remain; who, had they their Liberty, could provide for their Families, which are now kept by their respective Parishes: And praying, That the House will relieve them out of their miserable Circumstances, in such manner as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors in the North-gate, being the Gaol for the City of Chester, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands more in' the several Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by their Confinement, and the Miseries they suffer, many of them perish for Want; who ' are unable to satisfy their Creditors, though they are willing to deliver up their All; and this House having, in former Sessions, given Leave to bring in a bill for the Relief of insolvent Debtors, yet the same hath hitherto proved ineffectual: The Petitioners therefore pray the House to take their deplorable Case into Consideration, and relieve them as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors in the Castle Prison for the County of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are closely confined on the common Side of the said Prison, and have scarce Room to lie down; whereby, and for want of Subsistence, their Fatality increases: And praying,

That the House will grant them some Relief in their unhappy Circumstances.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Duties on A Petition of the Bailiff, approved Men, and Bur-

Soap, &c. gesses, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of Andover,

in the County of Southampton, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Trade of that populous Borough consists chiefly in the Woollen Manufacture; which though at present in a languishing Condition in those Parts, is, for the most part, the only Subsistence of their numerous Poor: That the Woollen Manufacture is deeply affected with the heavy Duties on Soap and Candles; the poor Workmen discouraged by that on Candles; the Masters by both; though chiefly by that on Soap, necessarily made use of in their Trade in great Quantities: That not only they of the Petitioners more immediately concerned in the Woollen Manufacture, and their Dependents, but the rest of the Petitioners, not so, are greatly sensible of the Weight of those Taxes: And praying, That the Duties on Soap and Candles, and the Burthen of them, may be lessened.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Gentlemen Adventurers, Copper Importation and Tin Miners, in the Counties of Cormcal and Devon, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of a themselves, and many Thousands employed therein, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Arts of making Copper from English Ores, and Brass of English Copper, and Lapis Calaminaris, have been, for several Years, carried on in this Kingdom, to the great Advantage thereof; especially by employing many Thousand Families in raising and digging Copper Ores; which, being frequently mixed in the same Mines with Tin, is a great Encouragement to the Miners to search for Tin Ores; and, were it not for such Copper Ores, several very considerable Tin Mines would not bear the Expence of working: That, by means of the Cheapness of Copper and Brass in foreign Parts, and the Importations thereof those Manufactures in Great Britain are in great Danger of being lost; to the irreparable Damage of the Tin-mines also: And praying,

That such Duties may be laid on foreign.imported Copper and Brass, as may preserve the making and manufacturing the same in this Nation.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of Ways and Means, for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Bill for giving further Encouragement for the Importation of Naval Stores.

and read; setting forth, That, by great Charge and Industry, many Copper-mines have been found out in Great Britain; the Working of which continues to be carried on, and converting it into Brass; whereby many Thousands are employed: That, to the Prejudice of our Manufactures, greater Quantities than formerly of black Kettles, and Brass Plates called Latten, continue to be imported at a lower Duty than Battery, when they are iequal in Value and Goodness to Battery; all which tends very much to the Decay of our own Trade, and lessening the Employment of our Poor: And praying, That a farther Duty be laid on Copper and Brass imported; and that black Kettles called Metal prepared, and Brass Plates called Latten, may pay the same Duty, on Importation, as Battery.

Mr. Pulteny reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of divers Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, in behalf of themselves, and others the Inhabitants of the said Places, and of the Publick; and also the Petition of divers Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the Counties of Kent, Sussex, Surrey, and Southampton, as well in behalf of themselves, and many others of the said Counties, as in behalf of the Publick; in relation to the building a Bridge over the River of Thames; were referred; and to whom the Petition of John Pond, Lessee of the Toll, or Wheelage, of London Bridge, was likewise referred; the Matter as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That upon Examination of the Matter of the said Petitions, the Committee received the following Evidence; viz.

Mr. Green said, That the Number of Inhabitants and Buildings in and about the City of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, are, of late Years, very much increased; and that such a Bridge as is desired, is become absolutely necessary; and will be not only a great Advantage to the said City, and adjacent Parts, but also to the neighbouring Counties.

Sir Jam. Thornhill said, That he has measured and bored the River where the Bridge desired is proposed to be built; viz. from a Place at Lambeth called The Prince's Wasty directly cross, to a Place just above Peterborough-house; and finds the same to be Seven hundred and Forty Feet; and that the Ground is very firm, and will make a good Foundation; and it is very practicable to make a good Bridge there, without causing any Overflowing, or diverting or altering the present Current, of the River, and without prejudicing or hindering the Navigation thereof; and that a Bridge where desired will be of great Advantage to the Publick.

Mr. Rowley, who measured and bored the River with Sir James Thornhill\ confirmed his Evidence.

Mr. Grey said, That a Wooden Bridge where proposed could in no sort prejudice the Navigation of the River* nor occasion any Overflowing: That Boats of all Sorts could go up and down as well then as they can now, either with or against Tide; and that the Fall of Water would not be an Inch at the lowest Ebb.

Colonel Armstrong said, That a Wooden Bridge will cause no Rise or Fall of the River, nor in the least prejudice the Navigation.

That Mr. Pond, whose Petition of the Toll or Wheel-age, of London Bridge, was referred to your Committee, produced a Lease which he had from the City of London, in which more than Twenty Years were yet to come, at the annual Rent of Four hundred and Fifty Pounds; and alleged, That, in case a Bridge was built at Lambeth, the same might prejudice him in his said Property near One-

third, and for which he paid a Fine of Eleven hundred Pounds.

It also appeared to the Committee, That divers Persons who have Possessions adjacent, which may be necessary for making convenient Ways and Passages to and from the said Bridge, are consenting to part with their Interests, having reasonable Satisfaction; and no Persons having any such adjacent Lands, appeared to oppose the same.

And the Committee do find, That a Bridge where proposed is very practicable, and absolutely necessary; and that convenient Ways and Passages may be made to and from the same, by which the City and Liberties of Westminster, and all Parts adjacent, and the several Counties before-named, may be better supplied and accommodated; and that such a Bridge as is proposed may be built and preserved by a reasonable Toll, and will be of great Advantage to the Publick.

Mr. Petlyzcard appeared for himself, and others concerned in the Ferry boats at Putney; and said, That he was a Proprietor of Two Parts in Four of the said Ferry; and has made, for One Share, One hundred Forty-six Pounds per Annum; but, take one Year with . another, it amounted to about One hundred Pounds per Annum:

And, being asked, Whether the Increase of the Buildings was not the Occasion of the Increase of the Profits of his Ferry, he did acknowlege, that it was; and that the Share that came to him from his Father was lettout at Lease for Twenty Pounds a Year; which Lease expired about Seven Years ago; That, about a Year ago, he would have bought in the Two other Shares, and was willing to have given Two thousand Five hundred Pounds for them.

And it appeared to the Committee, That there is one Bennett Hamond Uotobedy another Proprietor, whose Trustees have lett a Lease of his Fourth Part for Fifty Pounds a Year; and has nothing else to live upon.

Mr. MolineuXy Secretary to his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, acquainted the House, That he had, at the Instance of the Committee, desired his Royal Iligh-ness’s Leave, that one End of the Bridge intended to be erected might be set upon a Piece of Waste Ground which is Part of his Royal Highness s Possessions, as being Parcel of his Duchy of Cornwall; and that he had received his Royal Highness’s Commands to acquaint this House,

That his Royal Highness has no Objection to the erecting a Bridge in the Place where it is desired:

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put,

That the said Report be re-committed;

It passed in the Negative.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a Bridge cross the River Thames from a Place called The Prince's Wash, in the Parish of Lambeth, in the County of Surrey, to the opposite Shore, next Peterborough-house, in the Parish of Saint Margaret, Westminster, in the County of Middlesex: And that Mr. Pulteney and Mr. Molineux do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Prayers.

A PET IT I ON of the Merchants importing of Drugs, and Druggists, of the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Importation of Drugs is so much discouraged by high Duties, that many Species, and sufficient Quantities, are wanting; which occasions ill Practices in the Composition of Medicines; and will be fatal to us, if visited by the Plague, as is unhappily experienced in a neighbouring Nation: That if the high Duties are lessened, and Liberty of Importation granted, the Kingdom would soon be plentifully supplied with Drugs, the Revenue increased, and Smuggling discouraged: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders in Brass and Copper of the City of London, and Parts adjacent, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of others concerned, ufas presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners find sundry Petitions are presented; praying, That such Duties may be laid on Copper and Brass imported, as may preserve the making and manufacturing the same to this Nation: That, as the Duties stand at present on several Species of Brass, they are, in a manner, wholly discouraged from being imported; and, upon the other Sorts of Brass and Copper, the Duties are so high already, that it lays the Traders and Workmen of this Nation under very great Straits and Difficulties in carrying on their said Trades: And praying, That no farther Duty may be laid on Copper or Brass imported; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty: And that the Petitioners be heard before the said Committee, by their Counsel, if they think fit.

A Petition of the Woollen Stuff Weavers in the ancient Town of Amble side, in the County of Westmorland, on behalf of themselves, and many others, and many Hundreds of poor Families employed in Spinning of Woollen-yarn, in the Town, and Country adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have, for many Years, employed themselves in manufacturing Woollcn-stuffs, and maintained their Families comfortably; and have contributed to keep up a Market for Wool, to the Advantage of the Landholders in their Neighbourhood: That the said Employments are very much diminished, and the Price of Wool fallen, to the great Loss of the Farmers and Landholders; occasioned by the great Increase of the Use of painted Paper for Hangings: And praying, That the Use of painted Paper may be prohibited.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Assistants, of Silk Manu-the Corporation of Silk-weavers in the City of Canterbury, faclurcl* w as presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That the Petitioners have hitherto employed great Numbers of poor Families in w inding, dyeing, and weaving, great Quantities of Silk, the Return of our Woollen Goods from Turley and Italy; but, by the clandestine Running in, and general Use and Wear, of East India prohibited wrought Goods, the Petitioners have great Stocks of the said Manufactures unsold; and the Silk Manufactory of this Kingdom is in Danger of being lost:

And praying, That the Prohibition of East India Goods may be made more effectual.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to w hom the Bill for making more effectual an Act, made in the Eleventh and Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, An Act for the more effectual employing the Poor, byencourage-ing the Manufactures of tins Kingdom, wras committed, be received.

A Petition of the Virginia Merchants trading from the Tobacco Port of Lancaster was presented to the House, and read; Trade* setting forth, That the Frauds daily committed (and not possible to be prevented, whilst the Duties continue so high) have so much reduced the Price of Tob: cj(\ that it is now generally sold for less than the Duty; w?hich makes all fair Trade impracticable, and obliges the Merchants to burn their Tobaccoes, and take the Allowance from the Government, to the great Prejudice of his Majesty’s Revenues: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and others, Mer- Ditto, chants, Traders to Virginia, from the Port of Liverpool in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the high Custom on Tobacco for the Home-consumption hath, by many Years Experience, been found much more than it can well bear; but a far greater Discouragement is now fallen upon us, from a collusive Method used in Glasgow, ort weighing and passing their Tobacco there at Importation; so that they can afford to sell it for less than the Duty would amount to, if duly weighed and charged at the Importation; so that, if that beneficial Branch of our Trade be not preserved, it will be in Danger of being lost: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of the City Ditto, of Bristol, concerned in the _ Importation of Tobacco from Virginia, was* presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, for some Years past, great Quantities of Tobacco have been brought from North Britain, and> sold at a lower Price than is consistent with the Payment of his Majesty’s Duties, and other necessary Charges of Importation; to the great Loss and Detriment of the fai$

Traders: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A PETITION of the Magistrates and Inhabitants LinenManu of the City of Dimkeldm the County of Perth, for factuve. themselves, and in the Names of several Hundreds of People living in and about the said City, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Manufacturing of Linen Cloth, of their own Product, is the only staple Commodity in Scotland; their Woollen Manufac-turies being intirely 3unk, by the Importation and Wearing of E?igtish Woollen Manufactories since the Union:

That the Manufacturing of Linen Cloth is so universal, that there is scarce any Part of North Britain that does not, in some measure, depend upon this Trade; and it is the main Work wherein the common People are employed, and enabled to maintain themselves: That the said Manufacture is under great Decay; occasioned by the great Duty £hat is laid thereon; and that the Dyeing of Scots Linen is generally disused; whereby many Thousands of poor People must inevitably starve, or beg, should they be deprived of the Means of their subsistence by this Manufacture: And praying, T‘hat the great Duties on Linen may be taken off, and the said Manufacture encouraged.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the British Merchants trading to Portugal, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That it hath been usual for the said Merchants to pay, for Relief of shipwrecked Mariners, and others, British Subjects, in Distress, in the said Kingdom of Portugal; and for maintaining of a Minister there; and for other pious and charitable Uses; certain small Sums upon the Valuation of their Goods in the Custom-house at Lisbon; and on Sale of all Goods that pay no Duty; or on such Goods as pay Duties in Specie; which Sums have been collected, and distributed, from time to time, to the Uses aforesaid, according to the Directions of the Consul General, and the Majority of the British Merchants, residing in Portugal: That several Persons have, of late Years, evaded the said Payments by consigning their Goods and Merchandizes to Foreigners; to the great Discouragement of the British Merchants: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for better collecting the Sums usually paid by the Merchants trading to Portugal, for Relief of Shipwrecked Mariners, and distressed Persons, his Majesty’s Subjects there.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine" the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

O IR James Campbell reported from the Committee, to Hackle whom the Petition of Alexander Hamilton, Agent for don^d’s for-and on behalf of Alexander, John, Alargaret, Isabel, and feitc 'sUte# Janet, Machdonalds, all Infants, under the Age of Fifteen Years, the Children of James Alackdonald, deceased,

Brother of the late Sir Donald Mackdonald, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they bad directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the said Infants are the Children of the said James Mackdonald, deceased, who was the Brother of the said late Sir Donald Mackdoiudd; and that the late Sir 8 U Donald

Price's

Estate.

718 190 Januarii. 1721.

Donald Mackdomld was, by Act of Parliament, declared to be attainted of High Treason, in case he should not render himself to One of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace on or before the last Day of June 1716:

That the said late Sir Donald, being extremely ill in his Health, was thereby disabled from personally surrendering himself, according to the Words of the said Act of Parliament; but that he did all in his Power to Shew his Intention of making such Surrender of himself; and that he died while he was on his Road to the Place appointed for his Surrender.

The Committee do further find, That the said late Sir Donald Mackdonald has since been adjudged to be attainted of High Treason:

That the Followers of the said late Sir Donald, by his Orders, delivered up their Arms to the said Colonel Clayton; and took the Oaths to his Majesty:

That the said James Mackdonald, the Father of the said Infants, in the Year 1718, when some Spaniards landed in Scotland, and joined with several of his Majesty’s Subjects, then in Rebellion against his Majesty, not only refused to join in the said Rebellion, though threatened with Fire and Sword by Campbell of Glen derule, and Rob Roy, who were the Messengers sent by the late Earl of Sea-forth, and others, who then commanded the Rebels; but also, the said James, by his Persuasions, and other Methods, prevented his Relations, and the Inhabitants of that Country where the Estate of the late Sir Donald lies, from joining in the said Rebellion; and that the said James likewise took effectual Care to secure the Ferryboats employed between that Country and the Continent; so as the People of that Country were prevented from joining the said Rebels.

The Committee do further find, That Arms and Ammunition were offered to the said James, and the Tenants, and others, of the said Country, where the said late Sir Donald's Estate lies; but the said James absolutely refused to accept thereof, notwithstanding such Threatenings as aforesaid.

That the said Infants are educated in the Protestant Religion; and are now in very low , and miserable Circumstances.

And, lastly, It appears to this Committee, That the said James Mackdonald, deceased, the Father of the said Infants, would have succeeded, as Heir Male to the Estate of the said late Sir Donald Mackdonald, in case he had not been attainted; there being no issue Male living, of the Body of the said late Sir DonaUl Mackdonald.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable his Majesty to make such Provisions as his Majesty shall think fit for the Children of James Mackdonald, deceased, out of the Estate of the late Sir Donald Mackdonald, their Uncle, which was forfeited to his Majesty for High Treason: And that Sir James Campbell, and Colonel Douglass, do prepare, and bring in, the same.
