Distressed Sir John Ward reported from the Committee to whom Mariners in the Petition of the British Merchants trading to Portu-

lWtog.1. ga

was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee* pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find the same to be as followeth; viz. William Poyntz Esquire, Merchant, said, That he resided in Portugal many Years, and was Consul General there from 'March 1715 to June 1719; during . which time, and many Years before, several usual Collections were made, and paid, by the British Merchants residing at Lisbon, and other Ports and Places in the Dominions of the King of Portugal, for Payment of a Minister for Divine Service; a Judge Conservator, Lawyers, and Solicitors, for the Maintenance of their National Privileges; and especially for the Relief of shipwrecked Mariners, and others, taken Prisoners in time of war; which have amounted to from 100 to upwards of 400 Men per Annum for many Years past; besides for many other charitable Distributions for the Relief of many distressed. British Subjects residing in Portugal: That many Irish Roman Catholick Merchants, and others, have evaded Payment of these necessary Collections, for want of a due Power to oblige them to it; though, at the same time, they insist on enjoying all the National Privileges as British Merchants; whereby the chief Burthen lies on some few of the Merchants, who are well disposed to pay the said Collections; to their very great Prejudice:

That the Method hitherto used for raising the said Collections, has been at the Rate of Four Reas per Mil, on the Valuation of their Goods in the Custom-houses of Portugal; and Four Reas per Mil, on the Sale of such Goods as pay no Duty to the King of Portugal, or such as pay Duties in Specie; by which means a Thousand or £. 1,200. per Annum bas been usually collected for the Purposes aforesaid; but has been very much lessened of late Years by the Refusal of several Persons to pay the same, as aforesaid; and, by the Scheme following, now proposed, the former Collection will be reduced upwards of One-fourth part; and all the Merchants trading to Portugal will bear an equal Proportion:

And further said, That the Dutch, and other Nations do oblige the British Subjects residing in Portugal to pay Contribution for all Merchandize which they import from Holland, and other Countries, respectively, by inserting it in their Bills of Lading.

Mr. James Holland\ Charles Savage junior, and Henry Samuel Eyre, all Merchants, who lived at Lisbon many Years, confirmed what Mr. Poyntz said to be true.

The Lord Molesworth reported from the Committee, Supplying to whom the Petition of the Adventurers and Undertakers, whose Namesare thereunto subscribed, relating to supply- NU 1 ing the City of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, with Water, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; and which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee have examined the Matter of the said Petition; and find the same to be as followed!:

viz.

Mr. Watts said, That the Land from the River Thames to Olivers Mount, which they propose to make use of, was Sir Richard Grosvenors, except crossing the Road; and that he had agreed with Sir Richard Grosvenor for it.

Air. James Scanlan, Mathematician, said, That he had surveyed and levelled the Ground; and that, with Engines working by the Reflux of the Tide, they can raise any

Quantity of Water to the Height proposed, without any Prejudice at all to the Navigation of the River:

That they proposed to make one large Reservoir, of about Ten Acres, to hold from Five to Ten Foot Depth of Water, according to the different Changes of the Tide; and that they can inlarge the same to 30 or 40 Acres, if necessary:

That the Back-water makes no Banks in the River; because the Water falls into it in the same Plane with the Chanel at Low-water, and in the same Place where there is, at present, a Drain of the Marshes into the said River.

That, upon the whole Matter, the Committee do find,

That there is, at present, a great Scarcity of Water in that Part of Westminster; arid are of Opinion, That the proposed Undertaking is practicable, and will do no manner of Prejudice to the Navigation of the River; and may, if perfected, be of great Use and Benefit to the Publick.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better supplying the City and Liberties oi Westminster, and Parts adjacent, with fresh Water: And that the Lord Molesworth, and Mr. John Chetwynd, do prepare, and bring in, the same-

paying Customs, Subsidies, or Duties, on the importing hither any Goods, Wares, or Merchandizes, of the Growth, Produce, and Manufacture, of the said Islands: That, in consequence of those Privileges, no Officers of Customs are established in the said Islands; and, although the Commissioners of Customs obtained Two several Orders of Council in 1708, yet, upon the said Inhabitants representing their Privileges, her late Majesty was pleased to repeal the said Two Orders, and all former Orders, in relation to Officers of the Customs in the said Islands: That her said Majesty did, by that last Order, give some Powers and Authorities to an Officer of the Customs there, relating to Prize Goods, during the Continuance of that War, and no longer: That, as there are not Custom-house Officers established in the said Islands, the Parliament have thought fit, from time to time, to entrust the granting Licences, making Certificates, and other ordinary Matters, with the respective Governors, Lieutenant or Deputy Governors, in the said Islands: That, by a Bill, depending, for the Encouragement of the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom, several Allowances arc directed to be paid to the Exporter of the British Silk Stuffs, upon Security being given, that such Goods shall not be relanded in Great Britain; which Securities are to be discharged for such of the said Goods as shall be entered for the Island of Jersey, by a Certificate signed by the proper Officer or Officers of Customs there: That that Part of the said Bill, which requires the Certificates to be signed by an Officer of the Customs, will, if it passes into a Law, greatly affect and prejudice the Inhabitants of the said Islands, by laying them under the Misfortune either of not having the said Allowances on Exportation, or else of having Officers of the Customs established amongst them, in Breach of their Privileges; whereas, if that Part of the said Bill were amended, and the Certificates to discharge the said Securities directed to be signed by the respective Governors, <S[C. it will be a great Ease and Benefit to the Inhabitants there: And praying to be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

A Motion being made, and the Question being put. That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee of the whole House;

It passed in the Negative.

Mr. Farrer, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, who were to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Table: Where the said Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

1st, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the better encouraging and supporting the Copper and Brass Manufactures of this Kingdom, a further Duty be laid upon Metal prepared, and Black Latten, and raw Copper, imported, except raw Copper from East India.

2d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said further Duty upon Importation of Metal prepared be such as shall ipake the present Duty thereon equal to the Duty on foreign Battery imported.

3d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That t' e said further Duty upon Importation of Black Latten be Ten Shillings and Seven Pence per Hundred Weight.

4th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said further Duty upon raw Copper imported, except from East India, be Seven Shillings per Hundred Weight.

5th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said farther Duties upon Metal prepared, Black Latten, and raw Copper, imported, except raw Copper from East India, be granted to his Majesty for the Term of Three Years, to commence from the Twenty-fifth Day of March 1722.

6th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Fifty-six thousand Eight hundred Seventy-two Pounds Thirteen Shillings Three Pence and One Fifth Part of a Peny, granted for the Service of the Year 1721, exceeding the Services voted or enacted for the Service of that Year, be applied towards making good the Supply granted to his Majesty in this Session of Parliament.

7th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for raising the Sum, not exceeding One hundred forty-one thousand Ninety-three Pounds Fifteen Shillings and One Peny Farthing, Part of the Supply granted to his Majesty, for discharging the Principal and Interest on the Debentures which were granted to the Sufferers at Nevis and Saint Christopher's, an Annuity, after the Rate of Four Pounds per Cent, per Annum, be charged on the Fund commonly called the General Fund, redeemable by Parliament.

8th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, instead of the Duty ad valorem, now payable for Pictures imported, such Pictures be charged with certain Duties, according to the following Dimensions; that is to say, For every Picture of Four Feet square, or upwards, the Sum of Three Pounds; for every Picture of Two Feet square, and under Four Feet square, the Sum

A. 1721.

of Forty Shillings; and, for every Picture under Two Feet square, Twenty Shillings.

9th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, a farther Duty be laid upon all Apples imported into Great Britain.

10th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said further Duty upon Apples imported be after the Rate of Two Shillings per Bushel.

nth. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Further Duty upon Apples imported be granted to his Majesty for the Term of Three Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament.

Copper from East India;

Sir John Eyles presented to the House, a Report of the Trustees, in whom the Estates of the late South Sea Directors, and of John Aislabie Esquire, and of James Craggs senior, Esquire, are vested.

The Title of the said Report w as read.

The said Report is as follow’s; viz.

To the honourable the House of Commons.

THE Trustees appointed by an Act of Parliament, made in the Seventh Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act, for raising Money upon the Estates of the late Sub Governor, Deputy Governor, Directors, Cashier, Deputy Cashier, and Accountant, of the South Sea Company; and of John Aislabie Esquire; and likewise of James Craggs senior, Esquire, deceased; towards making good the great Loss and Damage sustained by the said Company; and for disabling such of the said Persons as are living to hold any Office, or Place of Trust, under the Crown, or to sit or vote in Parliament, for the future; and for other Purposes in the said Act expressed; humbly crave Leave to lay before this honourable House the following Account of the Effects of their Doings and Proceedings hitherto, in the Execution of the Trusts reposed in them.

The said Trustees, as soon after the passing the afore-mentioned Act as they conveniently could, by reason of the Absence of the Barons of his Majesty’s Court of Exchequer* who were upon their respective Circuits; viz. on the Twenty-third Day of August 1721; met together; and, before Mr. Baron Mountague, took the Oath prescribed for their respective Qualifications; alter which, having agreed to fix their publick Office at the South Sea House, in Broad-street, London, as being the most convenient Place for the Dispatch of Business; of which they Vol. 19,

gave publick Notice in the Gazette; they met at the said Office the same Day, and proceeded immediately upon Business; and sat from Day to Day, that the several Persons, whose Estates are, by the afore-mentioned Act, vested in the Trustees, might have all Opportunities of delivering up their Deeds, Books, Accounts, Papers, and Writings, within the Time limited by the said Act; which was ac- / cordingly done by all of them, Mr. Robert Knight only excepted; and they were severally sworn to the Truth of such Delivery, as the said Act directs.

They beg Leave further to take Notice, That the Daughters and Administratrixes of the late James Craggs senior, Esquire, did, on the Twenty-third Day of December last, deliver to them, upon Oath, Two Inventories, or Accounts, of the said James Craggs’ Estate; the one of them being an Account of the said Estate, as it stood on the First Day of December 1719; and the other being an Account of the said Estate, as it stood at the time of the Decease of the same James Craggs:

That John Aislabie, Esquire, did likewise, on the Twenty-fifth Day of December last, deliver to them, upon Oath, Two Inventories, or Accounts of his Estate; the one of them being an Account of his Estate, as it stood on the First Day of October 1718; and the other being an Account of his Estate, as it stood on the First of June 1720:

That they have also secured, and got into their Possession, some Writings concerning Mr. Robert Knight's real Estate, which were in his late Dwelling-house in London.

The said Trustees also crave Leave to acquaint this honourable House, That all the Persons required by the Act, except Sir John Blunt, John Turner Esquire, Robert Knight Esquire, and John Grigsby, have, respectively, exhibited to them, upon Oath, Accounts of such Parts of their personal Estates as have been by them, or by their Order, disposed of since the First Day of June 1720, to the Day of their exhibiting such Accounts; and also of the Debts by them paid; and of the perishable Goods disposed of since the first Day of June, to the time of their giving such Account.

They beg Leave to take Notice, That, immediately upon the Receipt of the above-mentioned Deeds, Books,' Accounts, Papers, Writings, and Inventories, such Bonds, Bills, and Cash, and other Notes, as were contained among them, were put into the Hands of the Cashier of the South Sea Company, in order to his getting in the Monies then due; or which should, from time to time, grow due upon them; and that the Residue of such Deeds, Books, Accounts, Papers, Writings, and Inventories, were referred to the proper Officers, by them to be carefully perused and examined, in order to a speedy, and strict Inquiry into the respective Estates in them vested.

The Time limited by the Act for the entering of Claims on the said Estates, by or for Persons residing in Great Britain, being expired, the said Trustees beg Leave to inform this honourable House, That there have been entered, before them, One thousand and Thirty-one Clairra on the said Estates, which are of different Natures:

That by the Inspection hitherto ftiade,f many of these are, on Account of Agreements, set forth as entered into since the First Day of June 1720, by the Persons whose Estates are vested in the said Trustees, for the Purchase of Lands at exorbitant Prices; many others on Account of Monies paid to the said Persons for South.Sea and other Stocks and Subscriptions, purchased; others for Leases and Grants made by them, out of their Estates; some for Monies by them already paid, but paid since the Fifth Day of January; others for Annuities, Pcent-charges, Tythes, fyc. wherewith their Estates are chargeable; some for Monies due on Mortgages on the Estates so purchased, or agreed for, as aforesaid; others for Goods sold and delivered, and Work done; others on Account of Partnerships, in which the late Directors, or some of them, were concerned; many others on their Marriage Settlements; and several for Estates and Interests 9 B wherein

738 6° — 7 0 PA. 1721.

Estates of Th« South Sea Directors.

wherein they wore only Tiustees for the Claimants:

And here the said Trustees, foreseeing great Difficulties likely to ensue, in relation to the many Claims entered on Account of Purchases of Lands at exorbitant Prices, on some of which great Sums of Money have already been, and on some others, no Money yet, paid; and also on Account of Claims of Estates iu Partnership with the late Directors: which, as they have many small Debts standing out, and open Accounts depending, both here and beyond the Seas, it may be thought more expedient to compound; as likewise iu relation to Claims of mere Trusts; which the said Trustees humbly conceive, upon Hearing, and Allowing, might properly be re-vested in the late Directors, <$'c.; the Trustees most humbly beg Leave to represent these several Matters to this honourable House; submitting the same to your Honours Consideration.

As there were great Numbers of Contracts for the Sale of South Sea Stock, and Subscriptions, made by the late Directors, and others, whose Estates are vested in the Trustees, which were not executed, either in the Whole, or in Part; the said Trustees thought it their Duty to cause a diligent Inspection to be made of the printed Copies of the Inventories delivered by the said Persons, the Originals not being in their Possession, and of the Accounts by them delivered to the Trustees and to register, pursuant to the Act of Parliament, all such Contracts as they could get any Information of.

As to the securing, and taking into their Possession, the Estates in them vested by the Act; the said Trustees humbly beg Leave to say, That they have taken all convenient Care to put such Goods and Chattels, and Parts of the Personal Estates of the above-mentioned Persons, as have come to their Knowledge, into the Possession and Custody of proper Agents, till such Parts as they are entrusted with can be sold:

They have also caused the said Goods, (§‘C. to be carefully inventoried, and appraised, in order to dispose thereof, pursuant to the Act, with all convenient Speed.

As to the real Estates, they have, pursuant to the Act, appointed Stewards and Receivers of and for such Parts thereof as have come to their Knowledge; with Powers and Instructions, as far as they were enabled by the Act of Parliament, to the said Stewards and Receivers, to take Possession of the said Estates, receive the Profits thereof, and Account for the same; and to do all things for the good Management of the said Estates; and also inquire into their respective Natures and Values, in order to have the same sold in the best manner, pursuant to the said Act of Parliament:

But, inasmuch as the said Trustees have not yet been able to get the said Estates surveyed, and the Time limited for foreign Claims is not yet expired; nor the Claims which are now entered, yet heard and determined; the said Trustees cannot, at present, make any certain Computation of what the said Real Estates may be worth, or what the clear Produce thereof may be.

They crave Leave further to represent to this honourable House, That they have found the Powers they are by the Act entrusted with, in some respects deficient: And they must, in all humility, acknowledge his Majesty’s great Goodness, in giving Directions for the securing, in Holland, the Effects and Monies belonging to the late Directors, and others, whose Estates are, by the Act vested in the said Trustees; in pursuance whereof, several Effects have accordingly been secured by his Majesty’s Agent there; who has since given them Information thereof: Whereupon proper Orders have been dispatched for the getting in the same.

John Eylcs,

South Sea House, John Rudge,

Broad-street, February the 6th, 1721. Mat. Lant,

Roger Hudson, John Ladty Richard Hopkins, Tho. Crosse,

G. Robei'ts.

cssjno A Petition of divers Merchants, and others, trading to at}. ° several Parts of the West Indies, and our Northern Colonies, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, for several Years past, many of his Majesty’s Subjects, turning Pirates, have committed continual Robberies on the British Trade in the West and East Indies; so as the said British Trade hath already sustained greater Losses by the said Pirates than were suffered during the late French Wars: That, notwithstanding his Majesty’s ijiost gracious Pardon to such of the said Pirates as would accept thereof; yet the said Pirates do increase, and gather Strength, daily; and they commit Murders and Villainies to such as fall into their Hands: That, unless some more effectual Remedies be taken, or more sufficient Force be employed, in reducing, the said Pirates, than hath hitherto been, the Western Navigation must be unavoidably ruined: And praying Relief.

A Petition of the Merchants, and others, Traders of the City of Bristol, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, notwithstanding the Endeavours that have been used to suppress the Pirates, they increase daily, and commit unheard of Cruelties; and study how to toiture; force his Majesty’s Subjects with them; burn, plunder, and destroy, almost all Ships they meet with: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in for the more effectual Suppressing of Piracy, upon the Debate of the House.

Sir Thomas Crosse, according to Order, reported, from i the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to enable the South Sea Company to dispose of the Effects in their Hands, by way of Lottery, or Subscription, in order to pay the Debts of the said Company, was committed; the Amendments which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same iu his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, and Amendments, in at the Clerks Table: Where the said Amendments, were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, That Purchasers of the Souih Sea Company’s Annuities, payable at the Exchequer, shall enjoy the same; and, if purchased by any Body Politick or Corporate, that they may unite such Capital, so created, to the then Capital Stock of the Company so purchasing the same; and that the Purchasers of the said Annuities may raise Money, by taking in Subscriptions for Sale of the Capital Stock; and that the Capital Stock, Annuities, and Shares, shall be deemed personal Estates, and free from Taxes; and be transferable, and disposed of by Will; but that the Persons employed for making an Agreement for Sale of the said Annuities, shall not be disabled, for that Cause, to serve as Members of Parliament; nor the Persons intitled to Stock, pursuant to such Agreement, be liable to Bankruptcy; or the Stock to any foreign Attachment, by the Custom of London, or otherwise; but, upon Repayment, by Parliament, of the Capital Stock, the Annuities to cease; and that, after Redemption of the Annuities, the several Duties applicable by the Act shall be understood to be redeemed by Parliament; and shall not be applied to any Use without Authority of Parliament:

The said Clause was once read with Blanks:

And a Debate arising in the House upon the Clause;

Ordered, That the Debate be adjourned till Wednesday Morning next.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A Message from his Majesty, by Sir TllUiam Sanderson, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up

753

to attend his Majesty in the House of Peers: 'Where his Majesty was pleased to give the Royal Assent to several publick and private Bills:

And his Majesty w as afterwards pleased to say;

And thereupon the Lord Chancellor acquainted both Houses, That he had received from his Majesty’s Hands, from the Throne, his Majesty’s Speech to both Houses of Parliament: Which he read:

And then the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty’s Command, said;

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty’s Royal Pleasure, That this Parlia- Parliament* ment be prorogued to Thursday the Fifteenth Day of prorogued, this instant March: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the Fifteenth Day of this instant March.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I HAVE ordered my Lord Chancellor do declare to The King’s you, in my Name and Words, the Reasons of my com- sPeech* ing this Day to Parliament.

By the KING.

A PROCLAMATION,

For dissolving this present Parliament, and declaring the speedy calling another.

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS we ha^ thought fit, by and with the Advice of our Privy Council, to dissolve this present Parliament, which now stands prorogued to Thursday the Fifteenth Day of this instant March: We do, for that End, publish this our Royal Proclamation; and do hereby dissolve, the said Parliament accordingly:

And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal; and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are discharged from their Meeting on Thursday the said Fifteenth Day of this instant March: And we, being resolved to meet our People, and have their Advice in Parliament, do. hereby make known to all our loving Subjects, that we will speedily call a new Parliament.

Given at our Court at St. James's, the Tenth Day of this instant March, in the Eighth Year of our Reign.

GOD save the King.
